AUCUBA

Pages 288-292

One <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; viz. japonica. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. 1328. LITTORELLA. One species; viz. * lacustris. 1275. CICCA. One species; viz. disticha. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. 1052. BETULA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Birch-tree. Eight species; viz. * <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, * alnus, * nana, dalecarlica, nigra, lenta, pumila, incana. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, N. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. 1053. BUXUS, or Box-tree. One species; viz. sempervirens.—The wood is very hard and smooth, and not apt to warp, and therefore well adapted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the turner. Combs, mathematical instruments, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> handles, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> are made of it. An empyreumatic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, distilled from the shavings, is often used as a topical application for the piles, and seldom fails to procure ease. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> frequently relieve the toothache, and has been given internally in epilepsies. The leaves, powdered, destroy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. In the south of Europe it is cultivated in gardens, and kept in flower-pots, with as much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> as we bestow upon myrtle. 1054. URTICA, or Nettle. 28 species; viz. * dioica, * pilulifer, * urens, balearica, dodartii, pumila, grandiflora, cannabina, alienata, cylindrica, parietaria, ciliaris, spicata, macrophylla, rhombea, vestans, capitata, divaricata, canadensis, interrupta, nivea, baccifera, arborea, capensis, frutescens, stimulans, japonica, villosa. Europe, N. Amer. E. and W. Indies. * U. leaves opposite, heart-shaped; bunches in pairs. This species is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> nettle. Its stings are very curious microscopic objects: They consist of an exceedingly fine-pointed tapering hollow substance, with a perforation at the point, and a bag at the base; or they are sharp tubes seated upon a bag. When the sharp point of the tube, that is to say the sting, is pressed upon, it readily punctures the skin, and the same pressure forces up an acrimonious fluid from the bag, which is squirted into the wound, and produces an effect which most persons have experienced. The plant was formerly used as an astringent, but is now disregarded. A stalk of it, when the leaves are in their prime, put into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, coagulates it, and may serve to prepare it for being made into cheese. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, put upon the tongue, and then pressed against the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the mouth, is pretty efficacious in stopping a bleeding at the nose. Paralytic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> have been recovered by stinging them with nettles. The young shoots are gathered early in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> to boil in broth or gruel. Cows eat the leaves when they are a little withered. The leaves are cut to pieces to mix with the food of young turkeys and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. Cows, horses, sheep, goats, and swine, refuse them. Asses are fond of it, and cows eat it in hay. The stalks may be dressed like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> for making cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a> they make use of no other material in the manufacture of cordage or sailcloth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; and consider these fabrics, when produced from nettles, as superior in every respect to those made from hemp and flax. As the nettle seems of all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> the most congenial to our <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, growing in all situations both fertile and barren, in spite of every attempt to extirpate it; and as there exists no doubt, that as a material of manufacture, it is not inferior to either flax or hemp, it is a singular circumstance that it has never come into general use. This, perhaps, is chiefly to be accounted for from the difficulty of collecting its seeds and handling it: difficulties, however, which a little attention and industry would probably soon enable us to overcome. 1055. MORUS, or Mulberry-tree. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> species; viz. alba, nigra, papayrifera, rubra, indica, tartarica, tinctoria. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, Japan, America.—The mulberry is chiefly remarkable on account of the value of its leaves, as the food of that valuable insect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-worm. The morus alba or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> mulberry, with leaves obliquely heart-shaped and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, grows in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as far northward as the frith of Forth, and silk-worms may be fed with it. The fruit of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mulberry has the common qualities of other sweet <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, abating <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, quenching thirst, and promoting the grosser secretions; a syrup, made from the juice, is kept by the apothecaries. The bark of the roots has been in considerable esteem as a cure for worms; its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is bitter and somewhat astringent. ORDER V. PENTANDRIA. 1277. NEPHELIUM. One species; viz. lappaceum. India. 1056. XANTHIUM, or Lesser Burdock. Five species; viz. * strumarium, orientale, echinatum, spinosum, fruticosum. S. Eur. Ceylon, China, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. X. stem thornless; leaves heart-shaped, three-fibred. The leaves are bitter and astringent. A decoction of the whole plant affords a showy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but it is better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> only the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are used. Horses and goats eat it. Cows, sheep, and swine refuse it. 1057. AMBROSA. Four species; viz. trifida, elatior, artemisiifolia, maritima. 1058. PARTHENIUM, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">Bass</a> Feverfew. Two species; viz. hysterophorus, integrifolium. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, Jamaica. 1059. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVA">IVA</a>, or False Jesuits-bark Tree. Two species; viz. annua, frutescens. Virginia, Carolina, Jamaica. 1329. CLIBADIUM. One species; viz. surinamense. Surinam. 1060. AMARANTHUS, or Flower-gentle. 24 species; viz. albus, griseicans, melancholicus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRICOLOR">tricolor</a>, polygamus, gangeticus, mongostanus, tristis, lividus, oleraceus, blitum, viridis, deflexus, polygonoides, scandens, hybridus, paniculatus, sanguineus, retroflexus, flavus, hypochondricus, cruentus, caudatus, spinosus. Europe, E. and W. Indies, America. 1276. LEEA. Two species; viz. sequata, crispa. Jamaica. ORDER VI. HEXANDRIA. 1062. ZIZANIA, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-oats, Tare-grass. Three species; viz. aquatica, palustris, terrestris. Malabar, N. America, Jamaica. 1063. PHARUS. One species; viz. latifolius. Jamaica, S. Amer. ORDER VII. HEPTANDRIA. 1064. GUETTARDA. One species; viz. speciosa. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, W. Indies. ORDER VIII. POLYANDRIA. 1065. CERATOPHYLLUM, or Hornwort. Two species; viz. demersum, submersum. 1066. MYRIOPHYLLUM, or Water Milfoil. Two species; viz. spicatum, verticillatum. 1067. SACITTARIA, or Arrowhead. Five species; viz. sagittifolia, obtusifolia, lancifolia, acutifolia, trifolia. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, America. S. leaves <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>-shaped, acute.—It grows in ditches and on the banks of slow-running <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. There is always a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> at the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the root, growing in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> beneath the mud. This bulb constitutes a considerable part of the food of the Chinese, and upon that account they cultivate it. Horses, goats, and swine eat it. Cows are not fond of it. 1156. BEGONIA. Three species; viz. ferruginea, capensis, urtica. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, E. and W. Indies. 1068. THELIGONUM, or Dog's-cabbage. One species; viz. cynocranbe. S. of Europe. 1069. POTERIUM, or Garden Burnet. Three species; viz. sanguisorba, hybridum, spinosum. P. without thorns; stems somewhat angular.—The sanguisorba leaves and seeds of this plant are mildly astringent, and sorba have been used in dysenteries and hemorrhages. The seeds, when bruised, smell like cucumbers. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tracts of the finest parts of what are called the South <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a> in England, upon which this plant forms half the indigenous pastureage. It seems to grow naturally (without being sown) only on chalky soils; but it will flourish, when sown, on any soil; on sand, clay, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>, &c. It is chiefly valuable for sheep pastures that are to be kept fully stocked. It forms a fine herbage when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> bitten; but when suffered to run to a height it is rather coarse. 1070. QUERCUS, or Oak-tree. 20 species; viz. phellos, molucca, glabra, acuta, glauca, cuspidata, serrata, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ILEX">ilex</a>, suber, coccifera, prunus, dentata, nigra, rubra, alba, esculus, robur, egilis, cerris, femina. Q. leaves on leaf-stalks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, broadest towards the end; indentations rather acute, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> blunt; fruit nearly sitting. Q. leaves oblong, on short leaf-stalks, blunt, wing-femina, cleft, with indentations; fruit mostly solitary, on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fruitstalks. Withering, vol. iii. p. 387. The oak is a native of the temperate climates. It loves hilly better than boggy ground, and thrives best, while young, in large plantations. Its roots descend deep into the earth, and therefore will not bear to be transplanted. Much lopping destroys it. Grass will hardly grow beneath it. The wood is hard, tough, tolerably <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, not easily splintering; and therefore is preferred before all other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It is well adapted to almost every purpose of the carpenter; but an attempt to enumerate the uses of this well-known wood, would be equally superfluous and difficult. Oak <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> indigenous vegetable used in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> fustian. All the varieties of drabs and different shades of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> are made with oak saw-dust, differently managed and compounded. The balls or oak apples are likewise used in dyeing, as a substitute for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>. The black, got from them by the addition of copperas, is more beautiful than that from galls, but not so durable. The bark is universally used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; and it is said, that the saw-dust has been used for the same purpose with equal success. The bark is used to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>. Its astringent properties might be rendered useful in medicine. An infusion of it, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of copperas, is used by the common people to dye woollen of a purplish blue: the colour, though not very bright, is durable. The balls or galls upon the leaves, are occasioned by a small insect with four wings, called cynips quercifoli, which deposits an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> in the substance of the leaf by making a small perforation in the under surface. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> presently begins to grow, and the egg in the centre of it changes to a worm; this worm again changes to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, and the nymph to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insect, with four wings. Horses, cows, sheep, and goats, eat the leaves. Swine and deer fatten on the acorns. The oak grows in a good soil sometimes to a most immense size. At Little Shelsley in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, shire, an oak measured close to the ground nearly 48 feet, and about two yards from the ground 22 feet four inches. Lightfoot mentions one growing near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a> in 1764, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of which measured 68 feet in girth, and 23 in length; so that allowing 90 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> feet for the larger branches, it contained 1,555 feet of timber. An oak near Welbeck measured in girth, at 11 feet from the ground, 38 feet; and one growing at Cowthorpe near Wetherby, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, measured 48 feet in circumference at three feet from the ground, and 78 feet close to the ground. 1071. Juglans, or Walnut-tree. Five species; viz. regia, alba, nigra, cinerea, baccata. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, N. America.—This tree, when planted in Scotland, seldom ripens its fruit. 1072. Fagus, or Beech, Sweet Chestnut. Three species; viz. * castanea, pumila, * sylvatica. Europe, N. America. castanea. * F. leaves spear-shaped, with tapering serratures, naked underneath.—In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of this species, called the chestnut, nothing will thrive. The wood is applicable to the same uses that oak is. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">Pipes</a> made of it to convey water under ground, are said to last longer than those made of oak. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> for espaliers, &c., made of it without removing the bark, also last very long. Some of the oldest buildings in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> are said to be constructed of the wood of the chestnut tree. At Tottsworth in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, is said to be a tree 52 feet round, which is proved to have stood since the year 1150, and was then very old. It is supposed to be 1100 years old. In 1759, its girth, at six feet from the ground, was 46 feet six inches. The nuts are used to whiten linen cloth, and to make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>. They constitute a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> proportion of the food of the common people in the south of Europe; and hogs, feeding on them as they run wild in the forests, are reckoned particularly excellent. sylvatica. * F. leaves egg-shaped; indistinctly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>. Common beech.—This tree is large and beautiful, but no verdure is found under its shade. It retains its old leaves during the winter, and may be trained to form very lofty hedges. The wood is brittle, soon decays in the air, but endures under water. It is formed into tool handles, planes, mallets, chairs, and bedsteads. Split into thin layers, it is used to make scabbards for swords. It is excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and its ashes afford much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>. The leaves, gathered in autumn before they are much injured by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, make much better mattresses than straw or chaff, and last seven or eight years. The nuts or mast, when eaten, occasion giddiness and headache; but when well dried and powdered, make wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. They are sometimes roasted and substituted for coffee. They fatten swine, and are devoured greedily by mice, squirrels, and birds. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> use the expressed oil instead of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. Sheep and goats eat the leaves. 1073. Carpinus, Hornbeam-tree. Two species; viz. * betulus, ostrya. Europe, N. America. betulus. * C. scales of the cones flat.—This, which is the common hornbeam, loves a poor stiff soil on the sides of hills, is easily transplanted, and bears lopping. Cattle eat the leaves, but no pasture grows under its shade. The wood burns like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>: it is very white, very tough, harder than hawthorn, and capable of supporting a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. It is useful in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>, and for many implements of husbandry. Cogges for millwheels made of it are superior to those of yew. The inner bark is used in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a> to dye yellow. 1074. Corylus, Hazel, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">Nut</a>-tree. Two species; viz. * avellana, colurna. Europe, N. America. * C.—This wood is profitably planted in many places in hedges and coppices, for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> portions in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>, to be converted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> for forges. The wood is used for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>-rods, walking-sticks, hoops, &c. The roots are preferred where beautiful wood is wanted for inlaying or staining. It is a practice in Italy, to put chips of hazel into turbid wine to clear it, which it does in 24 hours. In countries where yeast is scarce, they twist together hazel twigs, so as to leave a multitude of chinks; these they steep in their ale while it is fermenting; then hang them up to dry, and when they brew again they put them into the wort instead of yeast. Charcoal of hazel, when used in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, leaves stains which are easily rubbed out. The nuts, which are agreeable to most people, afford, by pressure, an oil for the use of painters. 1075. Platanus, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">Plane</a>-Tree. Two species; viz. orientalis, occidentalis. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, N. America. 1076. Liquidambar, or Sweet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">Gum</a>. Two species; viz. styraciflua, peregrina. Levant, N. America.—The resinous juice of the former of these species, brought from America, was once used as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>, but is now neglected. ORDER IX. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">MONADELPHIA</a>. 1077. Pinus, or Pine-tree. 12 species; viz. * sylvestris, pinca, teda, cembra, strobus, cedrus, larix, picea, balsamica, canadensis,abies, orientalis. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Asia, America. * P. leaves in long pairs, rigid; cones egg-conical, mostly in pairs, as long as the leaves; scales oblong, blunt. Scotch fir.—This species, which is a native of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, flourishes best on a poor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> soil. In a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> the trunk is tall and naked; in open places branched. It does not bear the least clipping, as the terminating buds send forth the branches. The roots spread near the surface of the earth, except the central root, which pushes perpendicularly downwards. If it is either broken off or interrupted in its passage, the stem ceases to shoot upwards, and the tree remains a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a>. Hence is apt to suffer by transplanting. The bark will tan leather. In the north of Europe bread is thus made from it by the inhabitants: They choose a straight tree, as these have least resin, and strip off the bark in the spring, when it separates most readily. This they first dry gently in the shade; then in a greater heat, and reduce it to powder. With this powder they mix a small quantity of corn <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and with water they knead it into bread. This they eat, not only in times of scarcity, but at other times, from an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, that long disuse might render it disagreeable. agreeable to them. Their children are very fond of the fresh bark in the spring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, either shaved with a knife or grated with a rasp. The young shoots, distilled, afford a fragrant essential oil. Sheep and goats are not fond of it. Horses refuse it. Burnt with a close smothering fire, the wood of this species yields tar. The species called larix has risen into considerable reputation in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, rapid growth, and the value of the timber. It is extremely hardy, growing in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> almost to the coasts of the Icy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; but this very hardiness, or capacity of vegetating with a very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat, renders it in this country delicate when young. The first warmth of the spring is sufficient to bring forth its buds, which are thus, by the unsteadiness of our climate, exposed to frequent pernicious frosts. In this way nurserymen often suffer great losses by the larix, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an early spring and a premature vegetation, which is afterwards nipt by frosty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. From the trees of the genus pinus the different turpentine are extracted by bleeding the trees, by wounds in the bark or branches. 1079. CUPRESSUS, or Cypress-tree. Six species; viz. sempervirens, disticha, thyoides, juniperoides, pendula, japonica. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, Cape, Japan, N. America. 1080. PLUKENETIA. One species; viz. volubilis. E. and W. Indies. 1081. DALECHAMPIA. Two species; viz. colorata, scandens. W. Indies, New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>. 1082. AGALYPHA. Five species; viz. virginica, virgata, indica, villosa, australis. N. America, E. and W. Indies. 1083. CROTON, or Base Ricinus, Tallow-tree. 23 species; viz. variegatum, cascarilla, castanefolium, palustre, glabellum, tinctorium, glandulosum, argenteum, seiferum, japonicum, acutum, tiglium, lacidum, lacciferum, balsaminferum, aromaticum, humile, ricinocarpus, moluccanum, flavens, capense, lotum, spinosum. China, Japan, W. Indies, N. America. 279. COPANIA. One species; viz. americana. West Indies, Coromandel. 1084. JATROPHA, or Cassada, Manihot. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> species; viz. gossypifolia, moluccana, curcas, multifida, manihot, janipha, urens, herbacea, elastica. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, S. America. 1085. RICINUS. Four species; viz. inermis, communis, tanarius, mappa. Vera Cruz.—The species called R. communis produces nuts about the size of small beans, which like bitter almonds are deleterious. An oil is obtained from them by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a> oil, which is used as a safe and mild laxative; half an ounce or an ounce for an adult, and a dram for an infant. 1086. STERCULIA. Three species; viz. balanghas, fretida, platanifolium. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, E. and W. Indies, China. 1087. HURA, or Sandbox-tree. One species; viz. crepitans. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, W. Indies. 1088. HIPPOPHANE. Three species; viz. mancinella, biglandulosa, spinosa. 1278. GNETUM. One species; viz. gnemon. India. 1279. STILLINGIA. One species; viz. sylvatica. Carolina. ORDER X. SYNGENESIA. 1089. TRICHOSANTHES, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">Serpent</a>-cucumber. Four species; viz. anguina, nervifolia, cucumerina, amara. E. Indies, China. 1090. MOMORDICA, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">Male</a> Balsam-apple. Eight species; viz. balsamina, charantia, operculata, luffa, cylindrica, triflora, pedata, elaterium. S. Europe, India, America. 1091. CUCURBITA, or Gourd. Seven species; viz. lagenaria, hispida, ovifera, pepo, verrucosa, melopepo, citrullus. E. and W. Indies, America. 1092. CUCUMIS, or Cucumber. 13 species; viz. colocynthis, prophetarum, angurias, africanus, acutangulus, melo, dudaim, chate, sativus, anguinas, flexuosus, conomon, maderaspatanus. Levant, India, Africa, Jamaica.—The species called sativus, is the ordinary garden cucumber. It is less apt to grow rancid by keeping than others of the class. The C. colocynthis, called colocynthida or bitter apple, is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. The fruit is about the size of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>. Its medulary part, freed from the rind and seeds, is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, white, and spongy, composed of membranous leaves, of an extremely bitter, nauseous, acrimonious taste. Colocynth is one of the most powerful and violent cathartics; but is accounted dangerous by the best physicians. The best <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of abating its virulence, consists of triturating it with gummy farinaceous substances, or oily seeds. Without this precaution, a few grains of it will often disorder the body, and even occasion a discharge of blood. The C. melo is used in hot countries as a cooling and agreeable food. 1093. BRYONIA, or Bryony. 11 species; viz. alba, dioica, palmata, grandis, cordifolia, laciniosa, africana, cretica, scabra, scalbella, japonica. Crete, Africa, E. Indies. * B. leaves <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-shaped, rough on both sides, with dioecious callous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; male-and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers on different plants.—The root is purgative and acrid. A dram of it in substance, or half an ounce of it infused in wine, is a full dose. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> infusion of the root in water is used externally in sciatic pains. A cataplasm of it is a most powerful diuretic. A decoction, made with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the fresh root, is the best purge for horned cattle. The plant is rough, growing on dry banks under hedges, and climbing upon the bushes. The roots are large, sometimes as thick as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s thigh. Their juice, when fresh, soon excoriates the skin, but in drying they lose much of their acrimony. 1094. 1694. Sicyos, or Single-seeded Cucumber. Three species; viz. angulata, laciniata, garcini. America. ORDER XI. GYNANDRIA. 1695. Andrachne, or Base Orpine. Two species; viz. telephioides, fruticosa. Italy, Levant, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. In the class Monoccia are 78 Genera, including 392 Species, of which 83 are found in Britain.

BADDENSDALE

Pages 861-861
or BETTISDALE, a town of Suffolk in England, seated in a dale or valley, and its street takes in a good part of Ricking, all which together make up the town; for of itself it is but a hamlet, having a small chapel, and an endowed grammar-school, to which belong certain scholarships, assigned to Bennet or Corpus Christi college in Cambridge, being the gift of Sir Nicholas Bacon, lord keeper of the great seal. E. Long. 1. 8. N. Lat. 52. 25.

BOOM

Pages 38-40

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> with. with which the clew of the studding-sail is spread out; and sometimes the boom is used to spread <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boom out the clew of the main-sail. Boom, denotes also a cable stretched athwart the mouth of a river or harbour; with yards, top-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, battling or spars of wood lashed to it, to prevent an enemy's coming in. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOMING">Booming</a>, among sailors, denotes the application of a boom to the sails. A ship is said to come booming forwards, when she comes with all the sail she can make. Boonen, Arnold, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> in 1669, and at first was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Arnold Verduis, a painter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portrait. Afterwards he placed himself with Godfrey Schalcken, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> for six years. The sweetness of his colouring, and the neatness of his touch, with a striking likeness in his portraits, procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of admirers. He painted in the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, particularly subjects by candlelight, which were very delicate, and very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and much more of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was requested by the lovers of the art than it was possible for him to undertake. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to paint the portraits of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy; of Frederick I. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; of the victorious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, as well as many of the princes of Germany; and most of the noblemen who attended the czar. His style of colouring was extremely good, and he had an elegant manner of disposing the attitudes of his figures: his handling was neat, and the whole had so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> that he was justly ranked among the ablest artists of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The small pictures of Boonen are in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of his master Schalcken; but his excessive application, to answer the multitude of his engagements, impaired his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and destroyed while it enriched him. He died in 1729. Booptalmus, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circles in it, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to an ox's eye, from whence it has got this name. Boops, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of baleen. See Baleena, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOSHATTER">Booshatter</a>, formerly the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, famous for the retreat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cato, lies about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles inland from Porto Farina in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. Nothing remains of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> except <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a large aqueduct, some cisterns, and other magnificent ruins, which cover a large <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, and show it to have been a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The sea, it is known, came up anciently to this city, though now seven miles distant. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOT">Boot</a>, a leathern cover or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> for the leg, used on horseback, both to keep the body more firm, and defend the part from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Boots seem to have taken their name from the resemblance they bear to a sort of jacks or leathern bottles formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and called botte, in the old French boots. Borel derives the name from the old French word bot, a stump, by reason the boot gives the leg this appearance. The Chinese have a kind of boots made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or fine stuff, lined with cotton, a full inch thick, which they always wear at home. This people are always booted; and when a visit is made them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they happen to be without their boots, their guest must wait till they put them on. They never stir out of doors without their boots on; and their scrupulousness in this respect is the more remarkable, as they are always carried in their chairs. The boot was much used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by the foot as well as by the horsemen. It was called by the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> ocrea; in middle-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, greva, gamberia, bainbergia, bembarga or benbergia. The boot is said to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Carians. It was at first made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> both against cuts and thrusts. It was from this that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> called the Greeks brazen-booted. The boot only covered half the leg; some say the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> leg, which was more advanced than the left, it being advanced forwards in an attack with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but in reality it appears to have been used on either leg, and sometimes on both. Those who fought with darts or other missile weapons, advanced the left leg foremost, so that this only was booted. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>-boots, are a thick strong sort used in dragging ponds and the like. Hunting-boots, a thinner kind used by sportsmen. Jack-boots, a kind of very strong boots used by the troopers. Boot, is likewise a kind of torture for criminals; to extort a confession, by means of a boot, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>, or buskin of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; which being put on the leg moist, and brought near the fire, in shrinking squeezes the leg violently, and occasions intolerable pain. There is also another kind of boot; consisting of four thick strong boards bound round with cords: two of these are put between the criminal's legs, and the two others placed one on the outside of one leg and the other on the other; then squeezing the legs against the boards by the cords, the criminal's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> are severely pinched, or even broken, &c. The boot is now disused in England and Scotland; but it subsists still in some other countries. Boot-tree, or Boot-last, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by shoemakers to widen the leg of a boot. It is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> slit into two parts, between which, when it is put into the boot, they drive by main force a wedge or quoin. Bootes, a constellation of the northern hemisphere, consisting of 23 stars according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, of 18 in Tycho's, of 34 in Bayer's, of 52 in Hevelius's, and of 54 in Mr Flamstead's catalogue. Booth, Barton, a famous English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> in 1681, and educated in Westminster school under the celebrated Dr Bushby, where his success in the Latin plays customarily performed by the scholars gave him an inclination for the stage. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but running away from school to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, he there commenced acting. His first appearance was in the part of Oroonoko, in which he came off with every testimonial of approbation from the audience. From this time he continued daily improving; and after two successful campaigns in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, conceived thoughts of returning to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and making a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of his abilities on the English stage. To this end, he first, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, reconciled himself to his friends; and then, as a farther step towards insuring his success, obtained a recommendation from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Fitzhardinge (one of the lords of the bedchamber to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>) to Mr Betterton, who with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> candour and good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> took him under his care, and gave him all the assistance in his power. The first part Mr Booth appeared in at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was that of Maximus in Lord <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, his reception in which exceeded even his most sanguine expectations; and very soon after his performance of Artaban, in Rowe's Ambitious Stepmother, which was a new tragedy, established his reputation as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at least to his great instructor. Pyrrhus, in the Distressed Mother, was another part in which he shone without a rival. But he was indebted to a happy coincidence of merit and chance, for that height of fame which he at length attained in the character of Cato, as drawn by Mr Addison, in 1712. For this play being considered as a party one, the Whigs, in favour of those principles it was apparently written, thought it their duty strongly to support it, while at the same time the Tories, who had too much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to appear to consider it as a reflection on their administration, were still more vehement in their approbation of it, which they carried to such a height, as even to make a collection of 50 guineas in the boxes during the performance, and present them to Mr Booth, with this compliment, "That it was a slight acknowledgment for his honest opposition to a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, and his dying so bravely in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." Besides this, he had a present of an equal sum from the managers, in consideration of the great success of the play, which they attributed in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to his extraordinary merit in the performance; and certain it is, that no one since that time has ever equalled, or even nearly approached, his excellence in that character.—But these were not the only advantages which were to accrue to Mr Booth from his success in this part; for Lord Bolingbroke, then one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state, in a little time after, procured a special license from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, recalling all the former ones, and nominating Mr Booth as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> manager with Wilkes, Cibber, and Doggett; none of whom were pleased at it; but the last especially took such disgust as to withdraw himself from any further share in the management. In 1704, Mr Booth had married a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Barkham, Bart. who died in 1710, without issue. Being now established in the management, he once more turned his thoughts towards matrimony; and in the year 1719 united himself to the celebrated Miss Hester Santlow, a woman of a most amiable disposition, whose great merit as an actress, added to the utmost <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> and prudential economy, had enabled her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> up a considerable fortune. During the 20 years in which Mr Booth continued a manager, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was in the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and his illness and death, which happened on the 12th of May 1733, contributed not a little to its decline. Mr Booth wrote a dramatic entertainment called Dido and Æneas; but his masterpiece was a Latin inscription to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Mr William Smith, a celebrated actor, who died while he was young. As an actor, his excellency lay wholly in tragedy, not being able to endure such parts as had not strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to inspire him. And even in this walk, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, rather than complacency, rage rather than tenderness, seemed to be his taste. For a particular idea of his abilities, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> Mr Cibber has given of him in his Apology; and the admirable character drawn of him by that excellent judge of dramatic perfection, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill, Esq. in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published by him called the Prompter, which may be seen at length in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>'s Lives of the Poets, and Chetwood's History of the Stage. His character as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was adorned with many amiable qualities, among which, a goodness of heart, the basis of every virtue, was remarkably conspicuous; and so particularly was he distinguished and caressed, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> sought by the great, that, as Chetwood relates of him, not one nobleman in the kingdom had so many sets of horses at command as he had.

BOOTY

Pages 40-40

whatever is taken from an enemy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Among the Greeks, the booty was divided in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the general only claiming a larger share. By the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, spoils taken from the enemy belonged to the republic, particular persons having no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to them. The generals who piqued themselves on their probity carried it wholly to the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. Sometimes indeed they divided it among the soldiery, to animate them, and serve in lieu of a reward. But this distribution depended on the generals, who were to conduct themselves herein with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and moderation; otherwise it became a crime of peculate to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the pillage, as regularly belonging only to the state. The consuls <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Vaturnus were condemned for having sold the booty taken from the Equi. Among the Jews, the booty was divided equally between the army and the people, though under the kings a different kind of distribution obtained. Among the Mahometans, two thirds of the spoils are allowed to the army; the other third to God, to Mahomet and his relations, and to the orphans, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the pilgrims.—Among us, formerly, the booty was divided among the soldiery. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the general be in the field, every body takes what he can lay hold on; if the general be absent, the booty is distributed among the soldiery, two parts being allowed to the cavalry and one to the infantry. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> is allowed ten shares, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> six, and a cornet four.

BOPPART

Pages 40-40

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and subject to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; it is seated at the foot of a mountain near the Rhine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 35' N. Lat. 50° 19'.

BOPSINGEN

Pages 40-40

a town of Swabia in Germany, seated on the river Egar, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 55' N. Lat. 48° 51'.

BOQUINNIANS

Pages 40-40

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, so called from Boquinus their founder, who taught that Christ did not die for all mankind, but only for the faithful, and consequently was only a particular Saviour.

BORACK

Pages 40-40

among Mahometans, a fabulous animal, supposed to be of the middle kind between an ass and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, whereon their prophet was carried in his nocturnal flight from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> into the heavens. This animal the Arabians call Al Borak, q. d. shining. The night when the journey was performed is called Lailat al Mevraga, i.e. the night of ascension; and the flight itself Al Mesra; concerning which there is a multitude of traditions.

BORAX

Pages 40-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in appearance somewhat similar to crystals of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, brought originally from from the East Indies in an impure state, and afterwards freed from its impurities by certain processes in the European countries. It was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of uncertainty whether this salt be a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fictitious substance in those countries from whence it is brought; but it is now beyond a doubt, that it is naturally produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Thibet, from whence other parts of the eastern continent are supplied. According to an account in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxxvii., by Mr Blanc, it is produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Jumlate, about 30 days journey <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Betowle, a small principality about 200 miles northeast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is found is said to be a small valley surrounded with snowy mountains, in which is a lake about six miles in circumference; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of which is constantly so hot that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> cannot bear it for any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Around this lake the ground is perfectly barren, not producing even a blade of grass; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is so full of a saline matter, that after falls of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or snow it concretes in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flakes on the surface like the natron of Hindostan. On the banks of this lake, in the winter season, when the falls of snow begin, the earth is formed into small reservoirs six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: when these are filled with snow, the hot water from the lake is thrown upon it; which, together with the water from the melted snow, remains in the reservoir, to be partly absorbed by the earth and partly evaporated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; after which there remains at the bottom a cake of sometimes half an inch thick of crude borax, which is taken up and reserved for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It can only be made in the winter season, because the falls of snow are indispensably requisite, and also because the saline appearances upon the earth are strongest at that time. When once it has been made on any spot, it cannot be made again on the same spot till the snow has fallen and dissolved three or four times, when the saline efflorescence appears as before. See Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBEOMAGUS

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Vangiones on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, in Germany. BORBONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBORITES

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Gnostics, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who, besides embracing the errors of these heretics, denied the last judgment. Their name comes from the Greek Borboros, "filth;" on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they had of daubing their faces and bodies with dirt and filth.

BORCH

Pages 41-41

a town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 14' N. Lat. 52° 25'.

BORCHLOEN

Pages 41-41

a town of the Prussian states in Germany, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 28' N. Lat. 50° 30'.

BORCOVIVM

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Ottadini in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now Berwick on Tweed.

BORDAT

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a small narrow stuff, which is manufactured in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and Damietta.

BORDE

Pages 41-42

ANDREW, a physician, was born at Pevensey in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, early in the 16th century, and supposed to have been educated at Westminster school. In his Introduction to Knowledge, he says, that he was a student of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but of what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> he does not mention. He left the university without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and entered himself a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of a Carthusian convent in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but not liking the severe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of that order, he returned to Oxford, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he embarked for the continent; and, as himself expresses it, "travelled through and round about Christendom, and out of Christendom into some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>." In the years 1541 and 1542, he resided at Montpelier in France, where he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and after his return to England was incorporated into the same degree at Oxford. From the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his introduction above mentioned, it appears that he had been in Scotland, which probably was soon after his return from France. Having now satisfied his inclination for travelling, he settled first at Pevensey where he was born, afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and finally in London, where he is said to have become a fellow of the college of physicians, and first physician to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. But notwithstanding his eminence in his profession, he had the misfortune to spend the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the Fleet prison, where he died in the year 1549. As to his character, Wood says that "he was esteemed a noted poet, a witty and ingenious person, and an excellent physician." Pits calls him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of sufficient learning, but too volatile and inconstant. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> and some others, on the contrary, abuse him grossly. His writings are, 1. A book of the introduction of knowledge, the which doth teach man to speak part of all manner of languages, &c. Lond. 1542, 4to; dedicated, from Montpelier, to the Lady <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Henry VIII. It is written partly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and partly in prose, containing 39 chapters, before each of which is a wooden print of a man. 2. The breviary of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, wherein are remedies for all manner of sicknesses and diseases, &c. Lond. 1547, &c. 4to. 3. Dietary of health, Lond. 1576, 8vo. 4. The merry tales of the madmen of Gotham. Printed, says Wood, in the time of Henry VIII, in whose reign, and after, it was accounted a book full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and mirth by scholars and gentlemen. Afterwards being often printed, it is now only sold on the stalls of ballad-singers. 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> pleasant and merry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the mylner of Abington, with his wife and his fair daughter, and of two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> scholars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. Lond. printed by Richard Jones, 4to. 6. A book of every region, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; which shows the miles and leagues distant from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> to city, and from town to town, with the noted things in the said cities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Wood says that the author <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> the manuscript of this book. BORDEL book to his friend Thomas Cromwell, who lost it, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grief of the author, who would otherwise have published it. In this instance, however, the an- tiquary was misinformed; for it has since been published by Hearne at the end of Benedictus abbas Peterb. de vita Henrici II. Oxf. 1735, 8vo. 7. The principles of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the which diligently persecuted is in a manner a prognostication to the world. Lond. printed by Robert Copland, 12mo. The author says that he wrote this little book in four days, with one old <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> without mending.

BORDE-HALFPENNY

a small toll by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the town for setting up boards, tables, booths, &c., in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>.

BORDE-LANDS

Pages 41-41

the demesnes which lords keep in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for the maintenance of their board <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>.

BORDE-LODE

Pages 41-41

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> required of tenants to carry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> out of the woods of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is also used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of provision which the bordmen paid for their bord-lands.

BORDE-SERVICE

Pages 41-41

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of bord-lands, by which some lands are held of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the tenants pay sixpence per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, in lieu of sending provision anciently for their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>.

BORDER

Pages 42-42

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, is made to enclose par- terres, that they may not be injured by walking in them. Borders are made either circular, straight, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in cants; and are turned into knots, scrolls, volutes, and other compartments. They are rendered very orna- mental by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, yews, &c. that are raised in them. They are always laid with a sharp rising in the middle; because, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are flat, they are noways agreeable to the eye: and as for their breadth, the largest are allowed five or six feet, and the smallest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> four. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">WHITE</a> ORDER, p.459] e Order denotes the order of regular canons of St Augustine. See Augustines. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Order denoted the order of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>. These names were first given these two orders from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; but are disused since the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of several other orders, who wear the same colours. Gray Order was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the Cistercians; but since the change of the habit, the name suits them no more. Orders, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, are those instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and privileged to say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; and who are prohibited <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, &c. Of this kind are the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, or of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Such also were the knights <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a>, the knights of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALATRAVA">Calatrava</a>, knights of St Lazarus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> knights, &c. See Malta, Templar, &c. Father Putignani accounts those military orders where marriage is not allowed, real religious orders. Papebroch says, it is in vain to search for military orders before the 12th century. Orders, in a military <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, all that is lawfully commanded by superior officers. Orders are given out every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, whether in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, garrison, or on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, by the commanding officer; which orders are afterwards given to every officer in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> by their respective sergeants. Ordinal, a book containing the order or manner of performing divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">Ritual</a>. Ordinal Numbers, those which express order, as 1st, 2d, 3d, &c. Ordinance or Ordonnance, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, statute, or command of a sovereign or superior; thus the acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> are sometimes termed ordinances of parliament, as in the parliament rolls. Though in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> we find a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> made between the two; ordinances being only temporary things, by way of prohibition; and capable of being altered by the commons alone; whereas an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> is a perpetual law, and cannot be altered by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, lords, and commons. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> asserts, that an ordinance of parliament differs from an act, as the latter can only be made by the king, and the threefold consent of the estates; whereas the former may be made by one or two of them. Ordinance of the Forest, is a statute made in the 34th year of Henry I. relating to forest-matters. In the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, ordinances are such laws as are established by the king's authority alone. All ordinances begin with, à tous présens, et à venir salut.

BORDUNI

Pages 42-42
or BORDONE, Paris, an excellent Italian painter, was born at Venice about the year 1512; and, being of a noble family, had a polite educa- tion. He was the disciple of Titian; but has been admired more for the delicacy of his pencil than for the truth of his outlines. He was at the court of France in the reign of Francis I. who had a great esteem for him, and for whom he drew not only abundance of history-pieces, but the portraits of several court-ladies, in so fine a manner, that original nature was hardly more charming. He at length returned to Venice, laden with riches and honour; and having gained great reputation in all parts of Italy, died in 1587, aged 75.

BOREAS

Pages 42-42

a Greek name, now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Pezron observes, that anciently Bo- reas signified the north-east wind blowing at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice. The Greeks erected an altar to Boreas. He is represented on the temple at A- thens with his robe before his mouth, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he felt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> over which he presides, agreeably to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Ovid, who calls him gelidus tyran- nus, "the shivering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>," Met. vi. ver. 711. But he is usually described by the Roman poets as violent and impetuous; ibid. ver. 686—ver. 707. In paint- ing, he is generally represented like an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a horrible look, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> covered with snow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hoar <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, with the feet and tail of a dragon. M. Spierlingius has a treatise in praise of Boreas, wherein he shows the honours paid to him by antiquity. Bo- reas, according to this author, purifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, renders it calm and salubrious, preserves buildings from de- cay, drives away the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> and other noxious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- eases, and expels locusts and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> hurtful to the grounds.

BOREL

Pages 42-42
PETER, a learned physician, was the son of James Borel who published several poems, and was born at Castres in 1620. He applied himself to the study of physic, of which he was created doctor, and practised with great success in the city of Castres. To- wards the end of the year 1653, he went to Paris, and was soon after made physician in ordinary to the king. In 1674, he was received into the academy of sciences, and distinguished himself by writing a great number of works. The most esteemed are, 1. Historiarum et observationum medico-physicarum centuria quingue. 2. Bibliotheca chymica, duodecimo. 3. De vero telescopii inventore, cum brevi omnium conspiscillorum historia. He died in 1678.

BORELLI

Pages 42-42

JOHN ALPHONSO, a famous philoso- pher and mathematician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1608. He was professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in some of the most celebrated univer- sities of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, where he became highly in favour with the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Medicis; but having been engaged in the re- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLT">volt</a> of Messina, he was obliged to retire to Rome, where he spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> under the protection of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who ho- noured him with her friendship, and by her liberality towards him softened the rigour of his hard fortune. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two years in the convent of the regu- lar clergy of St Pantaleon, called the pious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, where he instructed the youth in mathematical stu- dies. He died there of a pleurisy, the 31st of De- cember 1679, in the 72nd year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote in Latin, 1. Euclid restored. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in medicine, deduced from physical causes. 3. Of percussive force. 4. Of natu- ral motions depending upon gravity. 5. An historical and meteorological account of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Mount Aetna, in the year 1669. 6. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of ani- mals; and several other works, some of which are in Italian.

BORGHIA

Pages 42-42

CESAR, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Pope Alexan- der VI. was a brave general, but a most abandoned vil- lain. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">ITALY</a>.—It is incredible what numbers he caused to be taken off by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and it is notorious that swarms of assassins were constantly kept in pay by him at Rome, for the sake of removing all who were either obnoxious or inconve- nient to him. He experienced various turns of fort- une; and was sometimes very prosperous, sometimes the reverse. He very narrowly escaped dying by poi- son, in 1503; for having concerted with the pope a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of poisoning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> newly created cardinals at once, for the sake of possessing their effects, the poison- ed wine, destined for the purpose, was by mistake brought to and drank by themselves. The pope died of it; but Cesar, by the vigour of his youth, and the force of antidotes, after many struggles, recovered. He only recovered to outlive his fortune and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, to see himself depressed, and his enemies exalted; for he was soon after divested of all his acquisitions, and sent a prisoner to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in order to free Italy from an incen- diary, and the Italian princes from those dangers which the turbulent and restless spirit of Cesar made them fear, even though he was unarmed. He escaped from thence; and got safe to Navarre to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John his bro- ther-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who was then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with his subjects. Cesar served as a volunteer in that war, and was killed in 1507.

BORGO

Pages 42-43

a town of Russia, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kymenegard. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. N. Lat. 60. 34. Borgo de St Sepulchro, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated in E. Long. 13. o. N. Lat. 43. 35. Borgo de Val de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, a town of Italy, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Parma, in E. Long. 10. 36. N. Lat. 44. 35. Borgo Forte, a town of the Mantuan in Italy, situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Po and Menzo. E. Long. 11. o. N. Lat. 44. 50. Borgo San Domino, a town of Italy, in the duchy of Parma, with a bishop's see. E. Long. 10. 31. N. Lat. 41. 53.

BORIA

Pages 43-43

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 2. N. Lat. 41. 50.

BORING

Pages 43-43

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the art of perforating, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making a hole through any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body. Boring of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The method of boring water-pipes is as follows. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of alder, which is a very useful wood in making pumps, water-pipes, &c., being laid on horses or trassels of a foot height, to rest the augre upon while they are boring, they set up a lathe to turn the least end of the poles, to fit them to the cavities of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end of the others. They turn the small ends of the poles about five or six inches in length, to the size they intend to bore the bigger ends about the same depth, viz. five or six inches. This is designed to make a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> to shut each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of poles together, the concave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> part, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of the joint. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the male part, they turn the channel in it, or a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> at a certain distance from the end; and in the female part they bore a small hole to fit over this channel. This being done, they bore the poles through; and to prevent them from boring out at the side, they stick great nails at each end to be a guide in boring. It is usual, however, to bore them at both ends; so that a crooked pole can be bored through and not spoil it. See Boring, Supplement. Boring, in Farriery, a cruel and absurd method of treating a wrenched shoulder. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.
