Had this education been confined to some limited sphere; had it embraced the prattling doctrines of casuistry and the unwieldy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of cloistered <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> alone; unfortunate and melancholy for the world would have been this zeal: no refuge for the venial penitent, no security against boisterous sectarianism would have remained; an unmannerly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> would have debased the mind, and the moral and the intellectual world would have sunk to a dread <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> of confusion. But the Jesuits knew well the benignant influence of literature, and the salutary elevation of science; they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that wealth, and power, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSCO">Bosco</a>, nour, followed philosophy; and that philosophy had driven famine, wretchedness, and vice, from their habitations. We dare not say that the interest and aggrandizement of their order were secondary considerations; but we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> avow it as our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the short reign of the Jesuits, and the objects at which they aimed, and above all the means which they employed, were more instructive, promised better, and effected more to humanity, than all the accumulated humility and sanctity of all the religious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. We have been led into this digression by the coincidence of certain considerations operating at the time on our minds. Bosco was of the order of Jesuits; that order is no more; its destruction took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in his life-time; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the delight and the instruction we have received from him and many others of the order; the present disposition among mankind to detract from its merits, to magnify its imperfections, and to confound it with the fanatical and enthusiastic groups of every persuasion which have disgraced the name and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. But to return; our author, on his arrival in Rome, entered the noviceship of the order, where his studies wore a new aspect, but were still pursued with diligence. Christian morality, the rules and constitutions of the order, claimed his attention for two years; after which he was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and became well versed in general literature, in a particular manner in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which at that time was very much cultivated. From the noviciate he was sent to the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and physics. It was in these sciences that his elevated genius and uncommon abilities shone forth so conspicuously, and procured to him the admiration of his superiors. In three years time he was able to give private <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> on mathematics; and was then exempted from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which the noviciates were bound to teach Latin and the belles lettres for five years before they commenced the study of theology. This exemption was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his great predilection to the mathematics, of which he was soon afterwards made public professor. It would appear to us, that the science of theology, as it was then inculcated, had little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for the mind of Bosco; for it is not likely that a mind intimately acquainted with truth, and accustomed to find her ever plain and undisguised, could relish the retiring obscurities of sophistry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the flimsy decorations of a mystical religion; nor can we wonder, that during the four years in which he was constrained to the study, he should become more familiar with Leibnitz, Maclaurin, and Newton, than with Loyola, and Laynez, and Aquaviva. For the professorship of mathematics he was eminently qualified, as besides a thorough knowledge of all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> productions in the science, he had acquired a pristine severity of demonstration by studying the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geometricians; and he conjoined withal an obliging accommodation of his own powers to the deficiencies of his pupils. It was for their benefit he at this time composed elementary treatises on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. But notwithstanding the arduous duties of his situation which he invariably fulfilled, he found time to instruct and enlighten more than boys; for about this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he entertained some of those original notions Bosco which were destined to grow up into system, and one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to astonish the whole world of science. These, as they grew, were strengthened by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> arguments in the public disputations, by anticipating obstacles, overcoming and removing them, and by mighty efforts in extending and applying them to the most remote and discursive actions of the universe. The animating spirit of discovery and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> led him to consider every portion of physical science; and indeed so versatile and so vigorous was his mind, we would be at a loss to specify one portion, which, within a few years, it did not comprehend, elucidate, and advance. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this we beg to present our readers with an enumeration of the principal subjects to which he turned his attention, and concerning which he published dissertations whilst he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the professorship. The transit of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; the spots in the sun; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of spheric trigonometry; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> to determine celestial objects; the ancient arguments for the rotundity of the earth; oscillating circles; on infinites and infinitely little quantities; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of bodies in unresisting spaces; the aberration of the fixed stars; the inequalities in terrestrial gravity; on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; on the limits of certainty in astronomical observations; on the solid of greatest attraction; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYCLOID">cycloid</a>; the logistic curve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVORA">evora</a> vivra; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>; the rainbow; the calculation of fractions; the centre of gravity; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; the law of continuity; lenses and dioptrical telescopes; the objective micrometer; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISIBILITY">divisibility</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Some of these are short, but all of them contain curious and valuable matter. It is only by perusing them we are able to discover the gradual progress of his mind; and to understand the manner in which he arrived at the theory of natural philosophy, which alone will render his name immortal. About this time a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for philosophical poetry was much prevalent amongst the learned, and some of our author's acquaintances had laboured in it with success. Of these we may mention Father Noceti, who wrote on the rainbow and the aurora borealis, and the justly celebrated Benedict Stay, whose poems on the philosophy of Descartes, and on the more modern philosophy, are excellent examples of fine Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and scientific <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. Bosco published their works with annotations and supplements, in which a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of information and learning is displayed. By such undertakings, the fame of our author was widely diffused, and he became an object of general admiration. The learned societies of many countries in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> conferred on him unsolicited honours, and several foreign princes invited him to their courts. His opinions on various subjects of civil <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, topography, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">hydrodynamics</a>, were asked and entertained by Pope Benedict XIV. John V. of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and others. These necessarily required his presence in different states, where he never failed to increase his reputation, and often terminated disputes which might otherwise have gone on to open warfare. He was employed to correct the maps of the papal dominions, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the meridian passing In this he was assisted by an English Jesuit, Christopher Mairé. An account of their expedition was printed at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and is interspersed with some curious anecdotes, concerning the opinions which the peasants of the Apennines formed of them, and the operations which they had to perform; but it is valuable on account of the accurate detail which is given of their observations. In the year 1757, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> by the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, to reconcile some differences concerning the draining of a lake, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Francis I., and that republic, were concerned. It was after he had succeeded in the object of his visit to that city, that he published there his *Theoria Philosophiae Naturalis* in 1758; and that he gained the esteem of the empress-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. Another occasion for his mediating powers soon presented itself, and which more nearly interested him, as his native city of Ragusa required them. It had been suspected by the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, that some ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> were fitted out at that port for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the French, thereby infringing the neutrality. Such a suspicion having no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> foundation, alarmed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Ragusa, and required speedy removal, as the consequences of it might be extremely prejudicial to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. Boscovich, who had often been successful in similar circumstances for other powers, appeared to them the most proper person for this purpose, and was accordingly entrusted with it. He repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and here also effected the object of his mission with honour to himself. He visited the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, which received him with distinguishing marks of respect, and which he soon afterwards complimented with an excellent Latin poem on the solar and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> eclipses. This was in the year 1762, when Dr Johnson was in London. Mr Murphy speaks of an interview which took place between our author and Johnson; but in order to magnify the unruly powers of the *tremendous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>*, he rather unhandsomely tells us of the easy cant with which a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> might travel through Italy and France. We are unwilling to mention what effects on some minds may have been produced by the formidable society of a Johnson; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are a contempt of elegant simplicity and ingenuous ease, and an affected <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to repulsive pomp and authoritative ostentation, be our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> far from his influence, amid the peace and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of social life. Boscovich was invited by the Royal Society to be of the party of their members sent to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, to observe the transit of Venus over the sun's disk, which happened in the year 1762. The nature of his embassy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of returning home, however, prevented his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the invitation. Soon after his return, and when his embassy was fulfilled, he was appointed by the senate of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> to the mathematical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and to superintend the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> of the royal college of Brera. He continued in this situation for six years, when he was made professor of astronomy and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> in the Palatine schools of Milan by the empress-queen; who also requested him to continue his attention to the observatory. This he expected to be the most agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life. Admired by the learned; beloved by his friends; having an adequate income; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and vigorous; he promised to himself, happy, because useful days, in the tranquil cultivation of the sciences: but a cloud <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> impending now burst over his head, and these bright days never came. The mysterious regulation in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> constitution of the Jesuits, though it had attracted the keen curiosity of the world, had, for very substantial reasons, never been explored; nay, such was the influence of the order over the minds of the most enlightened statesmen, that this impenetrable mystery was held sacred by the civil power in many countries, as if no danger could exist in what was not understood. But the rapid progress of science, and the gradual decay of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, required some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of security, and some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that it was ever necessary to conceal good intentions, and to cover virtuous principles with any other garb than what truth could bestow. These, it is well known, the Jesuits either could not, or were unwilling to give; and they, therefore, justly incurred the suspicion of men. The most trivial circumstances would augment this suspicion, and the least deviation from rectitude in any of the order would serve to justify it: these were not wanting, and soon became invincible; the interest of the Jesuits rapidly declined for many years, and at last, in 1773, their order was totally abolished. No exemption from the edict for its downfall could be procured; all who held offices were dismissed; and Boscovich sought refuge in the city of Paris. Thither indeed he was invited by the minister (we believe Turgot), by whose means he was made one of the directors of optics for the sea service, and received a pension: but it does not seem that his situation was agreeable to him; for it is well known that the peculiar nature of his circumstances was the sole cause of his long residence in Paris. Whether his dislike arose from the envy of some of the French, his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> of temper, or the incongruity of the prevailing manners with his own, we cannot determine: but it is reasonable to imagine, that the ruin of his order, and the subsidence of his own importance, would leave some indelible mark in his mind; and perhaps when he contemplated the apparent levity and the real scepticism of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he might be brought to fear that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> or the downfall of the world was concomitant. Sentiments very opposite to those of the French would thence naturally arise; morosity and discontent would invade him, and he wished to revisit the scenes of his youth. Be all this, however, as it may, certain it is, he applied for leave of absence for two years, after he had resided in Paris for ten years: this he easily procured, and accordingly set out for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASSANO">Bassano</a> in the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. At this place he published, in five vols. quarto, a collection of the works which he had finished in Paris. This forms a body of optical and astronomical knowledge, well worthy the attention of the philosophical and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> cultivators of the sciences. It may be worth mentioning, that by proceeding on the principles contained in one of the dissertations in this collection, an amiable philosopher of our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (Dr Robison) believed it possible to ascertain the motions of the earth, though the observer should be confined in a cellar; in prosecuting the subject, however, he found Boscovich found that an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> into which Boscovich had fallen, concerning the aberration of light, undermined the principles on which he had erected such a wonderful but legitimate problem. The candid and very interesting acknowledgment of the error, and his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> disappointment in the discovery of it, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> made in the 3rd vol. of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Transactions, is at once an evidence of his own liberality, and an undefeasible testimony to Boscovich's genius. We beg to recommend to our readers the perusal of the works which we have now mentioned; they would tend to form the mind to the true <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of investigating the phenomena of nature, and will satisfactorily shew that this mode is always rewarded by discovery. The following is a pretty just account of their contents: A new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for determining the refracting and diverging forces of diaphanous bodies; a demonstration of the falsehood of the Newtonian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between light and sound; the algebraic formulae regarding the focuses of lenses, and their applications for calculating the sphericity of those which are to be used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHROMATIC">achromatic</a> telescopes; the corrections to be made in ocular lenses, and the error of the sphericity of certain glasses; the causes which hinder the exact union of the solar rays by means of the great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> glasses, and the determination of the loss arising from it; the method of determining the different velocities of light passing through different mediums by means of two dioptrical telescopes, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, the other of a new kind, containing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> between the objective glass and the place of the image: a new kind of objective micrometers; the defects and inutility of a dioptrical telescope proposed and made at Paris, which gives two images of the same object, the one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the other inverse, with two contrary motions of moveable objects; masses floating in the atmosphere, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> of an extraordinary size, seen on the sun with the telescope, and resembling spots; the astronomical refractions, and various methods for determining them; various methods for determining the orbits of comets and of the new planet, with copious applications of these doctrines to other astronomical subjects, and still more generally to geometry and to the science of calculation; the errors, the rectifications, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of quadrants, of sextants, of astronomical sectors, of the meridian line, of telescopes called the instruments of transits, of the meridian, and of the parallactic machine; the trigonometrical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> formulae, which are of so much use in astronomy; the use of the micrometrical rhombus, extended to whatever oblique position; the error arising from refractions in using the astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> for a sundial, and the correction to be made; the appearing and the disappearing of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>'s ring; the methods of determining the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of the sun by means of the spots, proposed formerly by the author, and now perfected; the greatest exactness possible in determining the length of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> oscillating every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of middle time by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of terrestrial and celestial gravity; a compend of astronomy for the use of the marine, containing the elements of the heavenly motions, and of the astronomical instruments, to be explained to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the course of one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; a method for determining the altitudes of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> with the greatest exactness, by means of a gnomon alone, where other instruments are not to be had; the determination of the illuminated edge of the moon to be observed on the meridian; a method of using the retrograde return of Venus to the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, for determining the less certain elements of her orbit; a method for correcting the elements of a comet, of which the longitude of the node is given, and the inclination of the orbit has been found nearly; another method for the same purpose, and for finding the elliptical orbit, when the parabolic one does not agree with the observations; a method for correcting the elements of a planet by three observations; the projection of an orbit inclined in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic; the projection of an orbit inclined in any other plane; the calculation of the aberration of the stars, arising from the successive propagation of light; some beautiful theorems belonging to triangles, which are of great use in astronomy, reduced to the most simple demonstrations. After the publication of these works, our author left Bassano, and went to Rome to visit the companions of his youth. From Rome, he proceeded to Milan, where he revised some of his own works, and prepared for publication the two last volumes of Stay's poems. In such occupations, and amidst friends whom equal misfortune and temporary separation had still more endeared, he had remained happy, and might perhaps have been still further useful to the world; but his leave of absence was now nearly expired, and his dislike to a residence in Paris was augmented by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> which his present abode afforded. He was too delicate to apply for more leave of absence; and though he was sensible of the gratitude which he owed to France, he could not reconcile it with the destruction of his own repose. About this time also he had several attacks of gout, but he would admit no medical aid. Under these distresses, and others which we have before mentioned, our illustrious author at last sunk: a melancholy despondency seized on and subjugated his mind, so that for five months he remained perfectly factious; and an imposthume having burst in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, terminated his existence on the 13th of February 1787, in the 76th year of his age. The following inscription was composed by Benedict Stay, and engraved on marble by order of the senate of Ragusa, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their useful citizen the illustrious Boscovich. ROGERIO. NICOLAI. F. BOSCOVICHIO, Summi: Ingenii. Viro. Philosopho. Et Mathematico. Prestantissimo Scriptori. Operum. Egregiorum Res. Physicas. Geometricas. Astronomicas Plurimis. Inventis. Suis. Auctas. Continentium Celebriorum. Europae. Academiarum. Socio Qui. In. Soc. Jesu. Cum. Esset. Ac. Romae. Mathesim. Profiteretur. Benedicto XIV. Mandante. Multo. Besides the works which we have mentioned, he wrote several others on various subjects, as, on the project of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to Rome from Fiumicino to Maccarese; a third on two torrents in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>; a fourth on the bulwarks on the river Ponaro; a fifth on the river Sidone in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>; a sixth on the entrance into the sea of the Adige. He wrote other such works on the bulwarks of the Po; on the harbours of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>, of Magna Vacca, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVONA">Savona</a>, besides others, almost all which were printed. He had likewise received a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from Clement XIII. to visit the Pompit <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, on the draining of which he drew up his opinion in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to which he added further elucidations at the desire of Pius VI. We have spoken of Boscovich as the founder of a new system of natural philosophy, which has occupied much of the attention of the learned, and which alone will render the name of its author immortal. It becomes us therefore to give such a synopsis of it, as may satisfy the general reader, or induce the student to search for more information in the work from which we ourselves have derived it. In a subject so abstruse and remote from observation as many of the principles which we have to consider in this theory, much difficulty in investigation is to be expected, and perhaps the metaphorical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we are constrained to employ, will tend not a little to embarrass and mislead us. We are also aware of the many obstacles which a theory of such magnitude has to encounter in the improved mode of philosophising of the present day; we are aware that at the bare mention of a new theory in natural philosophy, some of our readers will revolt from our page, affect a contempt of our labours, and call to their aid the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>. But we would ask such, from whence does their spirit arise? we have found it in those who never studied a page of Bacon; and we have known it accompanied by indolence, and by a supine indifference to aught that dignifies and elevates humanity. It is surely no hard matter to condemn a theory, merely because it is a theory: nor is it at all demonstrable that such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> requires any great effort of genius or understanding. Now the spirit of Bacon is a spirit of zeal, and labour, and perseverance, and above all, of investigation. Not then from his writings has this contempt arisen, but from a total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of them; not from his doctrine, but from an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of his principles. We have reason to believe that the theory of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>- covich would have received the sanction of the illus- trious Bacon; because the foundation on which it is erected is consecrated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRADIATION">irradiation</a> from his works. Be this, however, as it may, we are convinced that such an example of true genius will be acceptable to every friend of humanity, and to every cultivator of science. That we may do <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to our author in giving a synopsis of his theory, we shall follow the order which he himself has adopted; and shall subjoin some gene- ral observations and remarks which have occurred to us in the course of the work. Boscovich's Theoria Philosophiae Naturalis is divid- ed into three parts; of which the first contains the ex- plication of the theory, its analytic deduction, and its vindication. The second contains the application of the theory to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and The third the application of the theory to physics. Of these in order, and first of the explication of the theory. This theory has something in common with the Leibnitzian and the Newtonian. With the former it admits that the elements of mat- ter are simple and inextended; but it differs from it, in denying the continued <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the elements, and in asserting that the elements are perfectly homogeneous. Like the Newtonian, it allows the existence of mu- tual powers or forces, which vary according to the distance by certain laws; but it goes further, in that it asserts these powers are both repulsive and attrac- tive, and that when either of these terminates the other begins; but it differs from the Newtonian in explain- ing by one principle phenomena to which the latter applies three. This one principle may be expressed by an algebraic formula, or by one continued geometrical curve; and it is the law by which the powers of repulsion and at- traction <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. As continued extension of bodies is re- jected from this theory, it is obvious, that, as on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> a repulsive power must render it impossible, so on the other an attractive power must give rise to the apparent examples of it, to the phenomena of cohe- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>: this accordingly is one essential characteristic of the theory. From these few remarks we may deduce the princi- ples of the theory. The first elements or atoms of matter are indivisi- ble, inextended, but simple, homogeneous, and finite in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. They are dispersed in an immense space, in such a manner as that any two or more may be distant from each other any assignable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>. This inter- val may be indefinitely augmented or diminished, but cannot entirely vanish. Actual contact of the atoms is therefore impossible, seeing that the repulsive power which prevents the entire vanishing of the interval, must be sufficient to destroy the greatest velocities by which the atoms tend to unite. The repulsive power must encircle every atom, must be equal at equal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- tances from the atoms, and moreover, must increase as the distance from the atoms diminishes. On the contrary, if the distance from the atoms increases, the repulsive power will diminish, and at last become equal to nothing, or vanish; then, and not till then, an at- tractive power commences, increases, diminishes, va- nishes. But the theory does not stop here; for it sup- poses, that a repulsive power succeeds to the second or attractive, increases, diminishes, vanishes; and that there are several alternations of this kind, till at the last an attractive power prevails, and though diminish- ing sensibly, as the squares of the distances increase, extends to the most distant regions of our system. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> as we have now mentioned may seem a geo- metrical and confused; but the curve line which tri- cal cur- ves expresses it so simple, that we are persuaded, our readers, though unacquainted with geometry, will com- prehend, and hence will be able to understand the theory itself. We shall now proceed therefore to exhibit this curve, and to show in what manner it elucidates the principles of the theory. The axis CAC has an asymptote of a curve in the point A, viz. the indefinite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>; on each side of which are placed two equal and similar branc- hes of a curve, viz. DEFG', &c. and DEFGHIKL MNOPQRSTV: the latter of these having the asym- ptotical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> ED, though indefinitely produced towards the right line AB, will never touch it; but it accedes to the axis CAC, and touches it in some point E. From this point it recedes on the opposite side of the axis to some point F, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> again to the axis CAC, and cuts it in the point G; from this it recedes in a similar manner, on the side of the axis from whence it originated, and arrives at the point H. From the point H it bends to the axis CAC, and cuts it in the point I, and so on in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> fits of accession and recession till it has com- pleted the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> IKL,LMN,NOP,PQR, RST; after which it becomes asymptotical, forming the arch T p s V, which approaches the axis CAC on the side opposite that from which it originated, in such a manner as that the distances from the axis shall be in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> duplicate ratios of the distances from the asymptote BA. Now, if we raise and let <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> perpendiculars on the axis CAC in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> a, b, d, &c. the segments of the axis so formed, viz. A a, A b, A d, &c. are ab- scisses, and will represent the distances between any two atoms or points of matter; and the perpendiculars so constructed, viz. a g, b r, d h, are ordinates, and will represent the intensity of the repulsive or attractive powers, according to their situation with respect to the axis CAC; for if on the same side with the asymptote

BOSHIES-MEN

Pages 69-69

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Hottentots, so called, according to Dr Sparrman, from their dwelling in woody <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mountainous places. They are sworn enemies to a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Some of their maxims are, to live on hunting and plunder, and never to keep any animal alive for the space of one night. By this means they render themselves odious to the rest of the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>; and are pursued and exterminated like the wild beasts, whose manners they have assumed. Others of them again are kept alive, and made slaves of. Their weapons are poisoned arrows, which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out of a small bow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> fly to the distance of 200 paces, and will <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> a mark with a tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of certainty at the distance of 50 or even 100 paces. From this distance they can by stealth, as it were, convey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> they hunt for food, as well as to their foes, and even to so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and tremendous a beast as the lion; this noble animal thus falling by a weapon which perhaps it despised, or even did not take notice of. The Hottentot, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, concealed and safe in his ambush, is absolutely certain of the operation of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, which he always culls of the most virulent kind; and it is said he has only to wait a few minutes in order to see the wild beast languish and die. The dwellings of these foes to a pastoral life are generally not more agreeable than their maxims and manners. Like the wild beasts, bushes and cliffs in rocks by turns serve them instead of houses; and some of them are said to be so far worse than beasts, that their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> has been found <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by their habitations. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of them are entirely naked; but such as have been able to procure the skin of any sort of animal, great or small, cover their bodies with it from the shoulders downwards as far as it will reach, wearing it till it falls off their back in rags. As ignorant of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> as apes and monkeys, like them they are obliged to wander about over hills and dales after certain wild roots, berries, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> (which they eat raw), in order to sustain a life that this miserable food would soon extinguish and destroy, were they used to better fare. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, however, is sometimes composed of several other dishes, among which may be reckoned the larvae of insects, or that kind of caterpillars from which butterflies are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>; and in like manner a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ants (the termites), grasshoppers, snakes, and some sorts of spiders. With all these changes of diet, the Boshies-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is nevertheless frequently in want, and famished to such a degree as to waste almost to a shadow. "It was with no small astonishment (says Dr Sparrman), that I for the first time <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in Lange Kloof a lad belonging to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men, with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, arms, legs, and body, so monstrously small and withered, that I could not have been induced to suppose but that he had been brought to that state by the fever that was epidemic in those parts, had I not seen him at the same time run like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPWING">lapwing</a>. It required but a few weeks to bring one of these starvelings to a thriving state, and even to make him fat; their stomachs being strong enough to digest the great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of food with which they are crammed, as they may rather be said to bolt than eat. It sometimes happens indeed that they cannot <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> retain what they have taken in; but this circumstance, it is said, does not hinder them from beginning again upon a new score."

BOSNA SERAGO

Pages 71-71

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bosnia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 57. N. Lat. 44. 40.

BOSNIA

Pages 71-71

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, seated between Slavonia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. It belongs entirely to the Turks; but they were on the point of being expelled from it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, when the Spaniards invaded <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and obliged the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to conclude the peace of Passarowitz in 1718, by which he gave up Bosnia to the Turks. It is 200 miles in length, and 75 in breadth. It is a barren <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and but little cultivated: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue arising chiefly from the silver <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> there are falcons, which are held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem.

BOSPHORUS

Pages 71-71
or Bosporus, in Geography, a long and narrow sea, which it is supposed a bullock may swim over. In a more general sense, it is a long narrow sea running in between two lands, or separating two continents, and by which two seas, or a gulf and a sea, are made to communicate with each other: In which sense, bosphorus amounts to the same with what we otherwise call an arm of the sea, channel, or strait; the Italians, furo; the Latins, fretum; and the French pas, manche. The word is Greek, βόσπορος, formed from βόστην, "bullock," and πέρα, "passage." The name bosphorus, is chiefly confined to two straits in the Mediterranean sea, viz. the bosphorus of Thrace, commonly called the straits of Constantinople, or channel of the "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black sea; and the Cimmerian or Scythian bosphorus, so called, it seems, from its resemblance to the Thracian; now more commonly the straits of Kophu, or Kiderleri, from two cities standing on it. The origin of the name is better agreed on than the reason why it was first given to the Thracian bosphorus. Nymphius tells us, on the authority of Accarion, that the Phrygians, desiring to pass the Thracian strait, built a vessel, on whose prow was the figure of a bullock; and which was hence called βόστην, "bullock;" and served them for a ferry-boat. Dionysius, Valerius Flaccus, Callimachus, Apollodorus, Martialinus, &c., say, that Io, being transformed into a cow by Juno, passed this strait swimming, which hence was called bosphorus. Arrian tells us, that the Phrygians were enjoined by the oracle, to follow the route which a bullock should mark out to them; and that, upon stirring one up, it jumped into the sea to avoid their pursuit, and swam over this strait. Others say, that an ox, tormented by a gad-fly, threw itself in, and swam over: and others, that anciently the inhabitants of these coasts, when they would pass over, joined little boats together, and had them drawn over by bullocks, &c.

BOSQUETS

Pages 71-71

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, groves so called from boschetto, an Italian word which signifies a little wood. They are compartments in gardens formed by branches of trees disposed either regularly in rows, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wildly and irregularly, according to the fancy of the owner. A bosquet is either a plot of ground enclosed with palisadoes of hornbeam, the middle of it being filled with tall trees, as elm or the like, the tops of which make a tuft or plume; or it consists of only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trees, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut, elm, &c. The ground should be kept very smooth and rolled, or else covered with grass, after the manner of green plots. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> bosquets, care should be taken to mix the trees which produce their leaves of different shapes, and various shades of green and hoary or mealy leaves, so as to afford an agreeable prospect. Bosquets are only proper for spacious gardens, and require a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense to keep them up.

BOSSAGE

Pages 71-71

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> that has a projection, and is laid rough in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, to be afterwards carved into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>, capitals, coats of arms, &c. Bossage is also that which is otherwise called rustic-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and consists of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which advance beyond the naked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the building, by reason of indentures or channels left in the joinings. These are chiefly used in the corners of edifices, and thence called rustic quoins. The cavities or indentures are sometimes round, sometimes chain-framed, or bevelled, sometimes in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> form, sometimes enclosed with a cavetto, and sometimes with a listel.

BOSSE

Pages 71-71
ABRAHAM, an able engraver, born at Tours, was well skilled in perspective and architecture. He wrote two treatises, which are esteemed; the one on the manner of designing, and the other upon engraving.

BOSSINEY

Pages 71-71
or BOSS-CASTLE, a town of Cornwall, in England, which sends two members to parliament. W. Long. 5. O. N. Lat. 50. 40.

BOSSU

Pages 71-71

RENE LE, born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1631, was admitted a canon regular in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Genevive, in 1649; and after a year's probation, took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. He taught polite literature with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success in several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses for 12 years, when he gave up the task for retirement. He then published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> betwixt the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and those of Des Cartes, with a view to reconcile them; which was but indifferently received. His next treatise was on epic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; which Boileau declared one of the best compositions on that subject in the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and which produced a great friendship between them. He died in 1680, and left a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of MSS. which are kept in the abbey of St John de Chartres.

BOSSUET

Pages 71-71

JAMES BENIGNE, bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, was born at Dijon, on the 27th of September, 1627. He distinguished himself by his preaching, and the zeal he discovered in his endeavours to bring over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> of France to the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; by his opposition to quietism; and by his numerous writings both in French and Latin, which have been collected together, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 17 vols 4to. This famous divine died at Paris, in 1704, aged 77.

BOSSUPT

Pages 71-71

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brabant. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 30. N. Lat. 50. 52.

BOSSUS

Pages 71-71

MATTHEW, distinguished by his virtue and his learning, was born in 1427. He devoted himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state in 1451, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of regular canons of Lateran, and afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. His orations, his sermons, and his letters, have been often printed. He also wrote a sort of an apology for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a>, and other works. He died at Padua in 1502, aged 75.

BOSTANGIS

Pages 71-72

in the Turkish affairs, persons employed in the garden of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>, out of whose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are collected those that are to row in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior's brigantines, when he has a mind to divert himself with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> upon the canal. They who row upon the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> are only capable of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> employments in the gardens; but they who row on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand may be promoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of bostangi-bachi, who has the general intendency of all the grand signior's gardens, and commands above 10,000 bostangis.

BOSTON

Pages 72-72

a corporation town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is commodiously seated on both sides the river Witham, over which it has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wooden <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and, being near the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, enjoys a good trade. It has a spacious market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the largest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> aisles in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the steeple of which serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-mark to sailors. Boston is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the Irby family. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 8113. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 15'. N. Lat. 53° 3'. Boston, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the state of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a>, and of New England, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, built in 1630, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of about four miles in circumference, at the bottom of Massachusetts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in a very convenient situation for trade. The town stands in W. Long. 71° 5'. N. Lat. 42° 24', about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from the mouth of the bay. At the entrance of this bay are several small rocks which appear above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, some of which are inhabited. There is but one safe channel to approach the harbour, and that so narrow, that two ships can hardly sail through abreast; but within the harbour there is room for 500 sail to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a good depth of water. On one of the islands stands a fort. At the bottom of the bay is a noble pier near 2000 feet in length; along which on the north side extends a row of warehouses for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and to this pier ships of the greatest burden may come and unload without the help of boats. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town lies round the harbour in the form of a half-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> beyond it rising gradually and affording a delightful prospect. The neck of land which joins the peninsula to the continent is but 40 yards over. Boston contained about 40,000 inhabitants in 1817; and the tonnage of the vessels belonging to it in 1815, amounted to 137,008 tons, which is greater than that of any other American port, except <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. The merchants are remarkably <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and enterprising, and the inhabitants in general bear the character of being well-informed, sober, and industrious, but sharp and overreaching. The austerity of the old Puritans is less relaxed here than in any of the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in America. Boston is the headquarters of federalism, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of aristocracy, in politics, and of unitarianism in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Though professing republicanism, they are ridiculously vain of those titles which are still retained. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a> are the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, and have twelve churches here. There are besides three Baptist churches, two Episcopalians, one Quaker, one Universalist, one Catholic, and two Methodist. Besides the churches, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are the statehouse, courthouse, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, jail, almshouse, workhouse, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a>. The town is well paved, and has excellent flagged footpaths. The streets, though generally narrow, are for the most part clean, and in good order. Boston is connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> towns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a>, by two handsome wooden bridges, the one 1503 feet in length, the other 3483 feet. Boston has frequently suffered by fire, but the houses that were thus destroyed have always been rebuilt to advantage. The late American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> began here by the attack at Bunkers-hill, when many brave men lost their lives.

BOSWORTH

Pages 72-72

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a> in England, containing 791 inhabitants in 1811. It has a lofty situation on a hill, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it is fertile in corn and grass. It is memorable for the decisive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near it between Richard III. and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, afterwards Henry VII. wherein the former lost his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 24'. N. Lat. 52° 25'.

BOTALLUS

Pages 72-73

Leonard, physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alençon, and to Henry III. was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTI">Asti</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. He introduced at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the practice of frequent letting of blood; which was condemned by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>; but soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> it came into practice with all the physicians. He published several books in physic and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>; and the best edition of his works is that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1665, octavo. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Is that science which arranges, distinguishes, and names all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and vegetables, to enable us to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> their properties and uses. Vegetables consist of an innumerable succession of individuals which it is impossible to examine, and would be useless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were possible. It is therefore necessary to diminish the labour by forming them into groups <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> classes, that the same name may apply to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of individuals. Now certain individual plants have so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> a resemblance to others in their flower, fruit, leaves, and general appearance, that almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at first sight would give them the same name. Thus every man who has seen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> daisy once, and knows its name, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably apply the same name without mistake to every other individual of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. This forms the first step in botany, or what is called arranging and naming plants according to their species. Nor is it only the first, but the easiest step in botany. It is also the most important; for all the individuals of the same species must in similar circumstances possess the same qualities. For example, we have no reason to doubt that each individual plant of common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>, or of foxglove, possesses the same medical qualities, though from their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of growth these qualities may differ in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. It is therefore the individuals of the species alone that are useful; and the whole value of any arrangement consists in enabling the botanist to distinguish and name the individuals, with the greatest ease and accuracy. If the number of species were small, definitions or descriptions To shorten the labour, it has been found very expedient to arrange plants into various divisions; first into some very general divisions which may reduce them into a small compass, then to subdivide these general divisions into others less comprehensive, and these into others, till we arrive at the particular species which we are in search of. Thus the arrangement descends from a general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of all plants to every particular species. Many plans of this kind have been attempted by various botanists, but the arrangement of the celebrated Linnæus is incomparably the most ingenious, most accurate, as well as the simplest and easiest. That illustrious botanist divided all plants into classes, the classes into orders, the orders into genera, and the genera into species. The orders, too, and the species, when numerous, he frequently subdivided into sections. Objections have been made to the arrangement of Linnæus, because it admits divisions which do not appear <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. But such persons, though distinguished botanists, seem to us to have misunderstood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and intention of that arrangement. It is not, and ought not to be, its object to give what has been called a natural arrangement; for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> does not class her productions. She places before us innumerable individuals, and leaves us to classify them according to the purpose which we have in view. If nature had formed plants into classes, orders, and genera, the botanist would have nothing to do but to study these. But in none of her works has nature done this. Classification is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of man; and it is necessary for man merely on account of the limited nature of the faculties of his mind. Classification enables us to accomplish by several steps or operations what we cannot accomplish by one. But were our faculties much more exalted, were our penetration much more acute, and our memories perfectly retentive; could we at once survey all the qualities of objects, discern their relations to one another, and retain the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of these accurately, we should have no occasion to generalize at all. As generalization or classification is necessary to aid our limited faculties, the best classification is that which leads us without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and by the easiest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, to the particular object which we have occasion to investigate. The arrangement of Linnæus is therefore the best: It is, however, not so perfect in some of its parts as it may yet be rendered. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in some of the genera which are distinguished by marks that are too minute. But when we consider the indefatigable mind of that illustrious man, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> in which he found botany, and the beautiful arrangement which he gave to it, we may justly enroll the name of Linnæus in the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, and Newton, and Locke. A botanical system is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> by which a person who has studied the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the science may find out the name of every plant which he meets with. This dictionary has been much enlarged by the labours of the great many eminent botanists of the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. We shall therefore point out the method of consulting it, after giving a very concise view of the principles upon which it is founded. We will give a concise view, because we think most or perhaps all the elementary books of this science tend to confound and disgust beginners by physiological definitions, and by the multiplicity of terms which they require to be studied at the very first outset. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as if a teacher of Latin was to require his pupils first to make themselves masters of a Latin dictionary before he allowed them to translate. Our plan is to require of a beginner no more elementary knowledge than what is sufficient to enable him to consult the system as he would a dictionary. The meaning of the rest of the botanical terms we think can best be learned by having recourse to an explanation in an alphabetical form, as they occur in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. This we intend to add to the present article. And we wish sincerely that every man who publishes a system of botany would do the same; for we have strong reasons to believe that different writers use the same words in different senses from one another. Linnæus, indeed, has defined his botanical terms; but in his two works, Delineatio Plantarum and Philosophia Botanica, he sometimes defines the same word differently. Now we ought to know which of his definitions succeeding botanists have adopted. Besides almost every botanist introduces terms of his own, which we shall look for in vain in the definitions of Linnæus.

BOTANOMANCY

Pages 412-412

(from garam, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and μαντεία, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>), an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of divination, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; especially sage and fig leaves. The manner of performing it was thus: the persons who consulted wrote their own names and their questions on leaves, which they exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and as many of the letters as remained in their own places were taken up, and being joined together, contained an answer to the question.

BOTANY. 954. ASTER, or Starwort. 38 species; viz. taxifolius, reflexus, crinitus, fruticulosus, tenellus, alpinus, sibiricus, tripolium, amelus, divaricatus, hispidifolius, dumosus, ericoides, tenuifolius, linearifolius, linifolius, acris, concolor, rigidus, novae-angliae, undulatus, grandiflorus, cordifolius, puniceus, annuus, vernus, indicus, laevis, mutabilis, tradescanti, novi-belgii, tardiflorus, miser, macrophyllus, chinensis, tataricus, hispidus, scaber. Europe, Cape, Asia, N. America. * S. leaves strap-spear-shaped, fleshy, smooth, 3-fibred; calyx scales blunt, somewhat membranaceous.—Goats and horses eat this species. Cows and swine refuse it. Sheep are not fond of it. 955. SOLIDAGO, or Golden Rod. 14 species; viz. sempervirens, canadensis, altissima, lateriflora, bicolor, lanceolata, caesia, mexicana, flexicaulis, latifolia, virgaurea, minuta, rigida, noveboracensis. Europe, N. America. * S. stem serpentine, branched; leaves mostly sitting; flowers in crowded panicles.—This plant is found wild on heaths and in woods, producing spikes of yellow flowers in August. The leaves have a moderately astringent bitter taste; and hence prove serviceable in debility and laxity of the viscera, and disorders proceeding from that cause. 957. CINERARIA, or Sky-flower. 26 species; viz. geifolia, cynamarifolia, sibirica, glauca, sonchifolia, cordifolia, crispa, integrifolia, longifolia, palustris, aurea, maritima, canadensis, capitacea, linifolia, purpurata, ameloides, americana, alata, elongata, cacacloides, denticulata, perfoliata, lineata, hastifolia, japonica. Europe, Africa, N. America, Jamaica. 956. INULA, or Eleocharis. 29 species; viz. helelenium, odora, susacolens, odoratus-christi, britannica, dysenterica, undulata, indica, pelicaria, arabica, spiracifolia, squarrosa, bubenion, salicina, hirta, mariana, germanica, japonica, dubia, ensifolia, crithmifolia, provincialis, montana, vestuans, bifrons, coronula, aromatica, pinifolia, foetida. Europe, Cape, E. Indies, N. America. * I. leaves embracing the stem, egg-shaped, wrinkled, cottony underneath; scales of the calyx egg-shaped.—This is a large downy plant, sometimes found wild in moist rich soils. The eleocharis, or root, especially when dry, has an agreeable aromatic smell; its taste on first chewing, is glutinous, and as it were, somewhat rank; in a little time it discovers an aromatic bitterness, which by degrees becomes considerably acid and pungent. Eleocharis root possesses the general virtues of alexipharmics; it is principally recommended for promoting expectoration in humoral asthmas and coughs; liberally taken, it is said to excite urine, and loosen the belly. In some parts of Germany large quantities of this root are candied and used as a stomachic, for strengthening the tone of the viscera in general, and for attenuating tenacious juices; spirituous liquors extract its virtues in greater perfection than watery ones; the former scarcely elevate anything in distillation; with the latter an essential oil arises, which concretes into white flakes: this possesses at first the flavour of the eleocharis, but is very apt to lose it on keeping. An extract made with water, possesses the bitterness and pungency of the root, but in a less degree than one made with spirit. The root is esteemed a good pectoral. Dr Hill says, he knows, from his own experience, that an infusion of the fresh root, sweetened with honey, is an excellent medicine in the hooping-cough. A decoction of the root cures sheep that have the scab. Horses and goats eat it. Cows, sheep, and swine refuse it. 958. ARNICA, or Leopard's Bane. 11 species; viz. montana, piloselloides, scorpioides, doronicum, maritima, crocea, ciliata, japonica, palma-ta, gerbera, coronopifolia. Europe, Africa, Japan. The arnica montana had formerly a place in our pharmacopoeias, under the title of doronicum germanicum. Then, however, it was little known or used; and being justly considered as one of the deleterious vegetables, it was rejected; but it has again been introduced into the list both of the London and Edinburgh colleges on the authority of fresh observations, particularly of those of Dr Collins of Vienna, who lately published a dissertation on the medical virtues of the arnica. This plant grows in different parts of Europe, particularly Germany. It has an acrid bitter taste, and when bruised, emits a pungent odour, which excites sneezing. On this account the country people in some parts of Germany use it in snuff, and smoke it like tobacco. It was formerly represented as a remedy of great efficacy against effusions and suffusions of blood from falls, bruises, and the like; and it was then also mentioned as a remedy in jaundice, gout, nephritis, &c., but in these affections it is now very little if at all employed. Of late it has been principally recommended in paralytic affections, or in cases where a loss or diminution of sense arises from an affection of the nerves, as in instances of amaurosis. In those it has chiefly been employed under the form of infusion. From a dram to half an ounce of the flowers has been directed to be infused in a pint of boiling water, and taken in differ- ent doses in the course of the day; sometimes it produces vomiting, sometimes sweating, sometimes diuresis: but frequently its use is attended with no sensible operation, unless it can be considered as such, that in some cases of paralysis, the cure is said to be preceded by a peculiar prickling, and by shooting pains in the affected parts. Besides being employed in paralytic affections, it has also been of late represented as a very powerful antispasmodic; and it is said to have been successfully employed in fevers, particularly those of the intermittent kind, and likewise in cases of gangrene. In those diseases it has been said to prove as efficacious as the Peruvian bark, when employed under the form of a pretty strong decoction, taken in small doses frequently repeated, or under the form of an electuary with honey. But these alleged virtues of the arnica have not been confirmed by any trials made in Britain, with which we are acquainted; and we are of opinion that its real influence still remains to be determined by future observations. It is, however, one of those active substances from which something may be expected. 959. Doronicum, or Leopard's Bane. Three species; viz. *pallidianches, plantagineum, bellidiastrium. Europe, N. It may be destroyed by dunging the ground in autumn, followed by a summer fallow, and harrowing the land about five days after sowing the grain. Both the leaves and flowers possess very considerable antiseptic properties, and are therefore used in antiseptic fomentations and poultices. From their antispasmodic powers they are frequently found to relieve pain, either applied externally or taken internally. Ray recommends the flowers in calculous cases. Centaurea, or Blue-bottle, Knapweed. 66 species; viz. erupina, moschata, crucifolia, lippii, alpina, centaureum, purygia, capitata, uniflora, linifolia, pectinata, nigra, pullata, montana, *cyanus, paniculata, spinosa, ragusa, cineraria, argentea, sibirica, sempervirens, *scabiosa, tatarica, stoebe, acaulis, orientalis, behen, repens, jacea, amara, alba, splendens, rhapontica, babylonica, glastifolia, confera, sonchifolia, seridis, romana, spherocephala, isardi, napifolia, aspera, benedicta, eriophora, egyptica, *calcitrata, calcitrapoides, *solstitialis, meltemis, sicula, centauroides, collina, rupestris, verutum, salmantica, cichoraceae, muricata, peregrina, radiata, nudicaulis, crocodilum, pumila, tingitana, galactites.
