He afterwards became fellow of the same college; in which station he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the university till he was invited to London by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Hodges, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretary of state, in the year 1700, who made him his chaplain, and recommended him to Dr Tenison archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; but his first preferments were owing to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sunderland, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and influence he was promoted to the parsonage of St Olave in Southwark, and the archdeaconry of Surry. Here he continued discharging very faithfully and diligently every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his pastoral office, till he was recommended to attend George I. as his chaplain when he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> in 1719. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to teach <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Frederic the English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and by his conduct he so won the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s favour, that he promoted him to the deanery of Christ-church, and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, in the same year. As he was visiting his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> five years afterwards, he received a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the secretary of state, acquainting him that his majesty had nominated him to the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> and primacy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. This honour he would gladly have declined; and desired the secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his good offices with his majesty to excuse him from accepting it. Ireland happened to be at this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, occasioned by Wood's ruinous project; and the ministry thought that the bishop would greatly contribute to quench it by his judgment, moderation, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. The king therefore laid his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> commands upon him; to which he submitted, but with some reluctance. As soon as he had taken possession of the primacy, he began to consider that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as his own; and to promote its true interest with the greatest zeal and assiduity. Accordingly, in innumerable instances, he exerted himself in the noblest acts of beneficence and public spirit. In seasons of the greatest scarcity, he was more than once instrumental in preventing a famine which threatened that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. On one of these occasions he distributed vast quantities of corn throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons passed a vote of public thanks; and at another time 2500 persons were fed at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, every morning, and as many every evening, for a considerable time together, mostly at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>'s expense. When schemes were proposed for the advantage of the country, he encouraged and promoted them not only with his counsel but his purse. He had great compassion for the poor clergy of his diocese, who were disabled from giving their children a proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and he maintained several of the children of such in the university. He erected four houses at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a> for the reception of clergymen's widows, and purchased an estate for the endowment of them. His charities for augmenting small livings and buying glebes amounted to upwards of 30,000l. besides what he devised by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> for the like purposes in England. In short, the instances he gave of his generosity and benevolence of heart, his virtue, his piety, and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, are almost innumerable, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his life is his noblest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. This excellent prelate died at London, on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1742, and was interred in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, where a beautiful monument of finely polished marble is erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

BOULTINE

Pages 419-419

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> which workmen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for a moulding, the convexity of which is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> one-fourth of a circle; being the member just below the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a> in the Tuscan and Doric <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

BOULUKE

Pages 419-419

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> orders of the Turks, a body of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a>, with an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> at their head, sent upon some particular enterprise.

BOUM SOLIS STABULA

Pages 419-419

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the territory of Mylae, so called: A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>; remarkable for its fertility and rich pastures (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>); and hence arose the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the oxen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> feeding there (Scholiast on Apollonius). Pliny and Seneca say, that something like dung is thrown out on the coast of Mylae and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MESSANA">Messana</a>, which gave rise to the fable of the oxen of the sun being stalled there; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the inhabitants affirm the same thing (Cluverius).

BOUNCE

Pages 419-419

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of squalus. See SQUALUS.

BOUND

Pages 419-419

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from one foot to the other; by which it differs from a hop, where the spring is from one foot to the same. It also differs from a half coupee, as in the latter the body always bears on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, either on one foot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the other; whereas, in the bound, it is thrown quite from the floor. BOUND-Bailiffs, are sheriffs officers for executing of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. The sheriffs being answerable for their misdemeanors, the bailiffs are usually bound in a bond for the due execution of their office; and thence are called bound-bailiffs, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people have corrupted into a much more homely appellation. BOUNDS OF LANDS. See ABUTTALS.

BOUNTY

Pages 419-421

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a premium paid by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the exporters of certain British commodities, as sail-cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings, fish, corn, &c. The happy influence which bounties have on trade and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> is well known; nor can there be a more convincing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the good intentions of the government under which we live, than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care that is taken to give all possible encouragement to those who shall establish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> improve any hazardous branch of trade. All undertakings, in respect either to mercantile enterprises, or in the establishment of manufactures, are weak and feeble in their beginnings; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> unsuccessful, either sink entirely, or at least are seldom revived in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Accidents of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are not only destructive to private persons, but exceedingly detrimental to the public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. On this principle, more especially especially since trade, for which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> designed us, hath been attended to, such attempts have been thought deserving, and have been favoured, with public support. This in former times usually flowed from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, in the form of letters-patent, charters, or other grants of privileges, which, however requisite they might be, were notwithstanding very frequently objects of censure. If such as obtained them failed in their endeavours, they were reputed projectors; if, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they succeeded, they were considered as monopolizers. Corporations, which imply the uniting certain individuals into a body, that they may thereby become more useful to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, are created by the crown. Many of these were formed for promoting trade; and, according to the old system of our government, were necessary and useful. On the same principle, privileges were granted to private persons, on a suggestion, that what was immediately of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to them would terminate in public utility. These also did good in bringing in many arts and manufactures; though, in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, tending to private interest more than public emolument, they were liable to legal correction. In later times, and in concerns of moment, a much better method has been adopted, as often as it hath been found practicable, by rejecting private or particular interest, and proposing the designed advantages to such as should perform the stipulations on which they are granted. These bounties, as they are paid by the public, so they are solely calculated for the benefit of the public. They are sometimes given to encourage industry and application in raising a necessary commodity; which was intended by the bounty on exporting corn. The intention of this bounty was to encourage <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> hath been, that we now grow more than twice as much as we did at the establishment of the bounty; we even consume twice as much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> as we then grew; yet in A.D. 1697, we exported a fifteenth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of what we grew, of late years a twenty-ninth part only. The bounty on this twenty-ninth part amounted to somewhat more than 50,000l. and the produce to more than 400,000l. It is evident that all this is so much clear <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. But this is far from being all that we have annually gained. For if our cultivation is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, as indeed it is, then the rent of lands, the subsistence of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the profits of the tradesmen supplying them with utensils, clothes, the value of horses employed, &c., must all be taken into the account. Besides this, we must add the freight (amounting to half the bounty), to make the idea of the advantages complete. Sometimes bounties are given with a view to promote manufactures, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of those made of silk. Many laws are to be found in our statute books in favour of the silk manufacture, made with great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and propriety, for the encouragement and support of many thousands of industrious persons employed therein. By statute 8 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 15. § 1. a bounty was given on the due <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of ribbons and stuffs, of silk only, of three shillings upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; silk, and ribbons of silk, mixed with gold and silver, four shillings a-pound; on silk gloves, silk stockings, silk fringes, silk laces, and sewing silk, one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> and threepence a-pound; on stuffs of silk and grogram yarn, eightpence a-pound; on silks mixed with inkle or cotton, one shilling; on stuffs of silk mixed with worsted, sixpence a-pound, for three years; and, from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of their utility, these were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by subsequent statutes. Sometimes bounties are given to support a new manufacture against foreigners already in possession of it, as in making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and sail-cloth. The promoting of the manufacture of British sail-cloth was undoubtedly a very important national object, as the consumption was very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and of consequence the purchase of it from foreigners a heavy expense on the public. Many methods were therefore devised, and countenanced by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, both here and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, for introducing and encouraging our own in preference to that of strangers, more especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. By stat. 12 Ann. cap. 16. § 2. a bounty was given of one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> per ell on all that was exported for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, and continued by subsequent statutes. By 4 Geo. II. cap. 27. § 4. an additional bounty of another penny an ell is granted. These bounties were to be paid out of an additional duty on imported sail-cloth. By the same statute every ship built in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or in the plantations, is under the penalty of 50l. to be furnished with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of sails of British manufacture. The amounts of these bounties mark the progress of the manufacture, which is also assisted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> on which the payment is assigned. The assistances, however, are never bestowed but on mature deliberation, in virtue of strong proofs, and with a moral certainty of a national benefit. The great intention of bounties is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the British trader on such ground as to render his commerce beneficial to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In order to this, some profit must accrue to himself; otherwise he would not embark therein; but this, whatever it be, must prove inconsiderable in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what results to the public. For if, by the help of such a bounty, one or many traders export to the value of 1000l., 10,000l., or 100,000 pounds worth of commodities or manufactures, whatever his or their profit or loss (for the latter, through avidity and overloading the market, sometimes happens) may be, the nation gains the 1000l., 10,000l., or 100,000l.; which was the object of the legislature in granting the bounty. Upon this consideration, that the entire produce of what is exported accrues to the nation, the legislature, when an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of circumstances required it, have made no scruple of augmenting a bounty; as in the case of refined <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> exported, from three to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings per hundred weight. In like manner, the original bounty of one pound per ton in favour of vessels employed in the whale-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> hath been doubled, and many new regulations made, in order to render this fishery more advantageous to the public. As a bounty is given on malt when allowed to be exported, so an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> of 30 shillings per ton hath been granted on all British-made malt-spirits when exported, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> benefit to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, manufactures, and commerce. It is indeed true, that on whatever account, or to whatever amount, this reward is given, the public seem to pay, and private persons seem to receive. But these private persons receive it as the hire from the public, for performing a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> which otherwise they would not perform, the benefit of which accrues to the public, and who can therefore very well afford to pay that reward in reality, which, as we have stated it, she on- ly seems to do. For, looking a little closer, we cannot help observing, that the bounty is paid to individuals, who, as such, make a part of the public. But the commodities or manufactures exported are sold to foreigners, and the whole produce of them, be it what it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, comes into the purse of the public. By attending to this self-evident doctrine, every reasonable and public-spirited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> will be easily reconciled to bounties; and the three following considerations will be sufficient to obviate the most common objections that have been made to the practice of giving them. 1. That no bounty can be desired but on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of national utility, which always deserves notice, and cannot be mistaken. It must likewise be alleged and proved, that this is the only means whereby the national benefit can be attained. 2. The sums issued on this account not only show the clear expense of the bounty, but also indicate the profit gained by the public; for as the one cannot exist without the other, that amount must be the incontestable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of both. 3. It must be remembered (and of this too some instances might be given), that if bounties should be improperly bestowed, they will of course prove ineffectual, and after a few fruitless trials will remain unclaimed, and consequently produce no expense. There is indeed another objection which hath been made against the giving of bounties. This is grounded on the frauds to which they are supposed to be liable; and particularly the relending of the goods on which the bounty hath been paid, and thereby deceiving and cheating the public. But whoever peruses the laws made on this head, and attentively considers the numerous precautions taken to fix every circumstance relative to the obtaining the bounty, the checks on the shipping of goods, the securities taken for their due exportation, the certificates required to ascertain their being actually delivered and sold in a foreign market, must be convinced, that to discharge all those securities, in case of an intended fraud, is a thing very difficult, if not impossible. To these remarks we may add, that bounties are usually granted only for a limited <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and then expire; are always liable to be suspended; and of course can never be the cause of any great national loss. There is no doubt that, exclusive of frauds, the immoderate thirst of gain may tempt interested men to aim at converting what was calculated for public benefit to its detriment, for their own private advantage. Thus, on a prospect of short crops in other countries, men may take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, but directly against the spirit, of the law, to send so much of our corn abroad as to endanger a famine at home. For this the wisdom of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> provides, not barely by suspending the bounty, but by prohibiting exportation and opening the ports for foreign supplies. We cannot with any shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> ascribe scarcity to the bounty on the exportation. If this was the case, suspensions would be frequent, whereas there have been but five in a course of 70 years. If the bounty had any share, the larger the exportation, the greater would be the scarcity. In A.D. 1750 we exported more than one fifth of our growth of wheat, which was notwithstanding but at four shillings per bushel; whereas a century before, A.D. 1650, when we had neither bounty nor exportation, wheat was at nine shillings and sixpence per bushel. The causes of scarcity are unkindly seasons; which though <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> policy cannot prevent, yet their sad effects have been evidently lessened by our increased growth, since the taking place of bounty and exportation. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s Bounty, for augmenting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> livings under 50l. per annum, consists of the produce of the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and tenths, after the charges and pensions payable out of the same are defrayed. A corporation for management of the same was settled, &c. in 1704. See Augmentation.

BOURBON

Pages 421-423
or Mascarenhas, Isle of, an island in the Indian ocean, lying on the east of Madagascar, in E. Long. 58° 30'. S. Lat. 21° 23'. This island has no port, and is in some places inaccessible. Its length and breadth have not been well determined; but the circumference, according to the account of a person who resided there some time, is about 57 leagues. It is for the most part mountainous, but in some places there are very beautiful and fertile plains. In the south part of the island there is a burning mountain, which has thrown out vast quantities of bitumen, sulphur, and other combustible materials; neither does it cease throwing them out still, so that the country about it is useless, and is called by the inhabitants pays brûlés, that is, burnt land. The shore is high and rocky all round; but though on this account it hath no ports, there are several good roads, particularly one on the west, and another on the north-east. As to its form, this island is irregular, so that it is difficult to judge from the maps whether it is round or long. The air is equally pleasant and wholesome, insomuch that the people live to a great age without feeling either infirmities or diseases. This is occasioned by the hurricanes, of which they have one or two every year. These purge and cleanse the air so as to render it highly salubrious; the certainty of which is thus distinguished, that when they fail of making their annual visits, as sometimes they do, diseases and death find an entrance into the island, which otherwise would soon be overstocked with inhabitants. The climate is hot, but not to such a degree as might be expected from its situation, the breezes from the mountains being constant and very refreshing. The tops of these mountains are in winter covered with snow; which, melting in the summer, furnishes abundance of rivers and rivulets, with which the country is plentifully watered: so that the soil, though not very deep, is wonderfully fruitful, producing Turkey corn and rice twice a-year, and the latter in great abundance. Most sorts of cattle are found here, good in their kind, and are very cheap; wild goats and wild hogs are found in the woods and on the tops of the mountains; here also are vast quantities of wild fowl of different kinds, fish, and land tortoises, affording at once the most delicate and wholesome food. As to fruits, they have bananas, oranges, citrons, tamarinds, and other kinds; neither does it want valuable commodities, particularly ebony, cotton, white pepper, gum benzoin, aloes, and tobacco; all excellent in their kind, when compared with those of other countries. This island is also happy in its deficiencies; for no animals that are venomous are to be found therein, and only two sorts that are disagreeable to the sight, viz. spiders of the size of a pigeon's egg, which weave nets of a surprising strength, reckoned by some capable of being treated so as to become as va- lable as silk; and bats of a most enormous size, which are not only skinned and eaten, but esteemed also the greatest delicacy that they have. The island of Bourbon was discovered by the Portuguese in 1545, as appears by a date inscribed by them upon a pillar when they first landed; but when the French settled in Madagascar, this island was totally desolate. Three Frenchmen being banished thither, and left there for three years, made such a report of it at their return as surprised their countrymen. They lived most of that time upon pork; and though they were in a manner naked, yet they affirmed that they never had the least pain or sickness whatever. This tempted one Anthony Taureau to go over thither in 1654, accompanied by seven French and six negroes, who carried with them the cattle from which the island has been stocked ever since. The first thing they did was to erect the arms of France, by order of M. Falcourt who was governor of Madagascar, and to bestow upon the island a new name. Then they set up huts, and laid out gardens, in which they cultivated melons, different sorts of roots, and tobacco; but just as the last became ripe, the whole plantation was destroyed by a hurricane. The French, however, went to work again; and by having some acquaintance with the climate, succeeded better, and added aloes to the rest of their plantations; but receiving no succour from Madagascar, and being tired of living by themselves in the isle of Bourbon, they very readily embraced the offer of an English captain, and in the year 1658 embarked for Madras. When the last great blow was given to the French at Madagascar by the natives, who surprised and cut them off in one night, there escaped as many men as, with their wives, who were natives, filled two canoes; and these being driven by the wind on the isle of Bourbon, were the next set of people who inhabited it. This last colony, for want of an opportunity to remove, were constrained to cultivate this new country of theirs, and to remain in it. It was not long before a further stock of inhabitants arrived. A pirate that had been committing depredations in the Indies, returning to Europe, ran ashore and was split to pieces on the rocks, so that the crew was forced to join themselves to the former inhabitants; and as they had on board their vessel a great many Indian women whom they had made prisoners, they lived with them, and in process of time had a numerous posterity. As East India ships touched frequently here, when too late to double the Cape, many of the sailors, for the sake of the women, deserted at the time of their departure, and staying behind became planters in the isle of Bourbon. As the place grew more populous, the people naturally became more civilized, and desirous of living in a more commodious manner; which induced them to build small vessels, that in these they might sometimes make a trip to Madagascar, in order to purchase slaves, whom they employed in their plantations to cultivate aloes, tobacco, and other things, with which they drove a small trade, when ships of any nation anchored in their roads for the sake of refreshments. In this situation they were, when the French East India Company put in their claim; and assuming the property of the island, sent thither five or six families and a governor. At first the inhabitants expected to reap some benefit from their new masters; but finding very little, and thinking the governor took too much upon him, they revolted at the instigation of a priest, seized their governor and put him into a dungeon, where he died of hunger and grief. For this some of the ring-leaders were punished, a kind of fort was erected, some guns placed on it, and the French flag kept flying; but in other respects, so little care was taken, that, till within these 40 years, the island was in no state of defence. The number of inhabitants in the year 1717 was computed at 2000; viz. 900 free, and 1100 slaves. Amongst these people the usual distinction of whites and blacks entirely fails: for even the free are of different colours; and a French writer assures us, that he saw in a church one family, consisting of five generations, of all complexions. The eldest was a female, 108 years of age, of a brown black, like the Indians of Madagascar; her daughter, a mulatto; her grand-daughter, a mestizo; her great grand-daughter, of a dusky yellow; her daughter again, of an olive colour; and the daughter of this last, as fair as an English girl of the same age. These people are, general speaking, of a gentle quiet disposition, very industrious, and submissive enough to authority, provided it is exercised with a tolerable degree of equity and decency; for otherwise the whole of them are apt to rise in rebellion at once; and the slaves have so little reason to complain of their masters, that they are always on the same side. The island is divided into four quarters. The first is that of St Paul, which is the largest and best peopled: their houses are built at the foot of a steep mountain, on both sides of a fresh water lake. As for the plantations, they are on the top of a mountain, which they ascend by a very rough and troublesome passage. On the summit there is a spacious plain, a great part of which is divided into plantations of rice, tobacco, corn, sugar, and fruits. The quarter of St Dennis lies seven leagues from that of St Paul, towards the east, and there the governor resides. It is not so well peopled as the former; but the country is more pleasant, and the situation better. At two leagues distance, proceeding along the sea-coast, is the quarter of St Mary's, which is but thinly peopled. The last and most fertile quarter is that of St Susannah, which is at the distance of four leagues from St Dennis. The road between these two quarters is tolerable, though part of it has been cut with much difficulty through a wood; but the passage from St Dennis to St Paul is only by sea. When the present company of India became, by their perpetual establishment, possessed of the island of Bourbon, they began to improve it exceedingly; raising new forts and batteries, so as to render it in a manner inaccessible; and importing coffee-trees from Arabia; which have succeeded so well, that it is believed they produce an eighth, according to some a sixth, part as much coffee as is raised in the kingdom of Yemen in Arabia, and it is likewise held next in goodness to that. In 1763, the population amounted to 4627 white people, and 15,149 blacks; the cattle consisted of 8702 beeves, 4084 sheep, 7405 goats, and 7619 hogs. Upon an extent of 125,909 acres of cultivated land, they gathered as much cassava as would feed their slaves, 1,135,000 pounds weight of corn, 844,100 pounds of rice, rice, 2,879,100 pounds of maize, and 2,535,100 pounds of coffee; which last the company bought up at about 3d. per pound. In 1811 the population was 16,400 Europeans, 3,496 free negroes, and 62,450 slaves. In 1738, Admiral Boscowen appeared before this island with a British fleet; but found it too strong to be attacked. See Bourbon, Supplement. Bourbon, Nicholas, a famous Latin poet in the 16th century, was a native of Vendeuvre near Langres, and the son of a wealthy man who was master of several forges. Margaret de Valois appointed him preceptor to her daughter Jane d'Albert of Navarre, the mother of King Henry IV. At length he retired to Conde, where he had a benefice, and died about the year 1550. He wrote eight books of Epigrams; and a poem on the forge, which he has entitled Ferraria. He had great knowledge of antiquity, and of the Greek language. Erasmus praises his Epigrams. Bourbon, Nicholas, a celebrated Greek and Latin poet, was nephew of the preceding. He taught rhetoric in several colleges of Paris; and the cardinal de Perron caused him to be nominated professor of eloquence in the Royal College: he was also canon of Langres, and one of the 40 of the French academy. At length he retired to the fathers of the oratory, where he died in 1644, aged 70. He is esteemed one of the greatest Latin poets France has produced. His poems were printed at Paris in 1630. Bourbon-Lancy, a town of France, in the department of Saone and Loire. It is remarkable for its castle and baths; and there is a large marble pavement, called the great bath, which is a work of the Romans. It is seated near the river Loire, in E. Long. 3° 46'. N. Lat. 46° 37'. Bourbon L'Archambaud, a town of France, in the department of Allier, remarkable for its baths, which are exceedingly hot. E. Long. 3° 28'. N. Lat. 46° 35'. Family of Bourbon, the present royal family of France. Henry IV. in 1589, though of the 10th generation, was the nearest heir, and succeeded Henry III. (the last of the Valois race), whose brother Francis II. married Mary queen of Scots, and both died without issue. Louis XVI. was the fifth king of this family in succession. This family also mounted the throne of Spain in 1700, by Philip V., grandson to Louis XIV., which was the occasion of the long and bloody war that ended in the peace of Utrecht. A branch of the Spanish family likewise mounted the throne of the two Sicilies in 1734. These three branches entered into a treaty offensive and defensive in 1761, which goes by the name of the family-compact. Bourbonne-le-Bains, a town of France, in Champagne, and in the Bassigny, famous for its hot baths. E. Long. 5° 45'. N. Lat. 47° 54'. Bourbonnois, a province of France, with the title of a duchy; bounded on the north, by Nivernois and Berry; on the west, by Berry and a small part of Upper Marche; on the south, by Auvergne; and on the east, by Burgundy and Forez. It abounds in corn, fruits, pastures, wood, game, and wine. Its principal town is Moulins; and the rivers are the Loire, the Allier, and the Cher. Bourbourg, a town in French Flanders, whose fortifications are demolished. It is seated on a canal that goes to Dunkirk, in E. Long. 2° 15'. N. Lat. 50° Bourbourg 55'.

BOURCHIER

Pages 423-423

John, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bemars, grandson and heir of a lord of the same name, who was descended from Thomas of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, and had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>-castle. Under Edward IV. our Lord John was created a knight of the Bath, at the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Edward IV., and was first known by quelling an insurrection in Cornwall and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, raised by Michael <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> a blacksmith, in 1495, which recommended him to the favour of Henry VII. He was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a> at the siege of The-ronne, under Henry VIII., by whom he was made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a> and the Marches, appointed to conduct the lady <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s sister, into France on the marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII., and had the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of continuing in favour with Henry VIII., for the space of 18 years. He died at Calais in 1532, aged 63. He translated, by King Henry's command, Froissart's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>; which was printed in 1532, by Richard Pinson, the scholar of Caxton, and the fifth on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of English printers. His other works were a whimsical medley of translations from French, Spanish, and Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, which seem to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> then, as they were afterwards in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. These were, The life of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, an Armorican knight; The famous exploits of Sir Hugh <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURDEAUX">Bourdeaux</a>; Marcus Aurelius; and, The Castle of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>. He composed also a book of the duties of the inhabitants of Calais; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> entitled Ite in Vineam, which is mentioned in none of our catalogues of English plays. Anthony Wood says it was usually acted at Calais after vespers.

BOURDALOUE

Pages 423-423
Lewis, a celebrated preacher among the Jesuits, and one of the greatest orators France has produced, was born at Bourges on the 20th of August 1632. After having preached in Provence, he in 1669 went to Paris; and there met with such applause, that the king resolved to hear him; on which he was sent for to court, and frequently preached before Louis XIV. He assisted the sick, visited the prisoners and hospitals, and was very liberal in giving alms. He died at Paris on the 13th of May 1704. The best edition of his sermons is in octavo.

BOURDEAUX

Pages 423-424

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and rich town in France, in the department of Gironde, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Guienne, and an archbishop's see; has an university and an academy of arts and sciences. It is built in the form of a bow, of which the river Garonne is the string. This river is bordered by a large quay, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> rises four yards at full tide, for which reason the largest vessels can come up to it very readily. The castle called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a> is seated at the entrance of the quay, and the river runs round its walls. Most of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> streets <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the quay. The town has 12 gates; and near another castle are fine walks under several rows of trees. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bordeaux, though considerable in point of size, was ill built, badly paved, dangerous, without <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any of those municipal regulations indispensably requisite to render a city splendid or elegant. It has entirely changed its appearance within these last thirty years. The public edifices are very noble, and all the streets newly built are regular and handsome. The quays are Bourdeaux, four miles in length, and the river itself is considerably broader than the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. On the opposite side, a range of hills covered with woods, vineyards, churches, and villas, extends beyond the view. Almost in the centre of the town is a fine equestrian statue in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> erected to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. in 1743, with the following inscription: *Ludovico quindecimo, Siue victori, semper pacificatoris; Suos omnes, quam latè regnum patet, Paterno pectori gerenti; Suorum in animis penitus habitanti.* The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the river Garonne, and the fertility of the adjoining <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, were probably the causes which induced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to lay the foundations of this city. The ruins of a very large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> yet remain, constructed under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Gallienus; it is of brick, as are most of the edifices of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when the empire was verging to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and the arts began rapidly to decline. During the irruptions of the barbarous nations, and particularly in those which the Normans repeatedly made, Bourdeaux was ravaged, burnt, and almost entirely destroyed. It only began to recover again under Henry II. of England, who having united it to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Eleanor of Aquitaine, rebuilt it, and made it a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of his policy to restore the city again to the lustre from which it had fallen. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> received all Guienne, Gascony, and many inferior provinces, in full sovereignty from his father Edward III. He brought his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> captive, John <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, to this city, after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Poictiers in 1356; and held his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> and residence here during eleven years. His exalted character, his uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, his victories, his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, his affability, and his munificence, drew strangers to Bourdeaux from every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but all this splendour soon disappeared. He lived to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the ingratitude of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Cruel, to whom he had restored the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Castile; he became a prey to distempers in the vigour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his dominions reunited again in many of their branches to the crown of France, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V.; he lost his eldest son Edward, a prince of the highest expectations; and at length, overcome with sorrow at this last affliction, he quitted Bourdeaux, and re-embarked for England, there to expire a memorable example of the hasty revolution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> greatness! In 1453, Charles VII., king of France, re-entered the city, and subjected the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guienne, which had been near three centuries under the English <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Conscious of the importance of such a conquest, he ordered the Chateau Trompette to be built to defend the passage of the river; and Louis XIV. afterwards employed the celebrated Vauban to erect a new fortress in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> style of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, on the same spot.—Madame de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAINTENON">Maintenon</a>, whom fortune seemed to have chosen as the object of her extremest rigour and extremest bounty, was removed from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIORT">Niort</a> in Poictou, where she was born, with her father the Baron d'Aubigne, to this castle, where she used to play with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the turnkey, in the greatest indigence. Bourdeaux presents few remains of antiquity. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> appears to be very old, and has suffered considerably from the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Guienne, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Louis XI. who was poisoned in 1473, lies buried before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar. The adjacent country is exceedingly pleasant, and at the season of the vintage forms one of the most delicious landscapes in the world. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1815 was 92,374. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 39. N. Lat. 44. 50.

BOURDELOT

Pages 424-424

JOHN, a learned French critic, who lived at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 16th and beginning of the 17th centuries. He distinguished himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> notes on Lucian, Petronius, and Heliodorus; by an Universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>; Commentaries on Juvenal; a Treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">Etymology</a> of French words; and by some other works which were never published.—There was also an abbe Bourdelot, his sister's son, who changed his name from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Michon to oblige his uncle. He was a celebrated physician at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, who gained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by a Treatise on the Viper, and other works. He died in 1685.

BOURDINES

Pages 424-424

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. o. N. Lat. 50. 35.

BOURDON

Pages 424-424

SEBASTIAN, a famous painter, born at Montpelier, in 1619. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years at Rome; and acquired such a reputation, that at his return to France he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being the first who was made rector of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He succeeded better in his landscapes than in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painting. His pieces are seldom finished; and those that are so, are not always the finest. He once laid a wager with a friend, that he should paint twelve heads after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and as big as the life, in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He won it: and these are said not to be the worst things he ever did. His most considerable pieces are, The gallery of M. de Bretonvilliers, in the aisle of Notre Dame; and, The seven works of mercy, which he etched by himself. But the most esteemed of all his performances is, The martyrdom of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, drawn for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Notre Dame: It is kept as one of the choicest rarities of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. Bourdon was a Calvinist; much valued and respected, however, in a Popish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, because his life and manners were good. We have also by this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of etchings; which are executed in a bold masterly style, and much more finished than those we generally meet with from the point of the painter. They are justly held in the highest estimation by the generality of the collectors. He died in 1673, aged 54.

BOURG

Pages 424-424

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAYENNE">Cayenne</a>, a French colony on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 52. o. N. Lat. 5. o. BOURG-en-Bresse, a town in France, and capital of Bresse, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. It is seated on the river Ressouze, almost in the centre of Bresse, in E. Long. 4. 19. N. Lat. 46. 13. BOURG-sur-Mer, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of France in Guienne, and in the Bourdelois, with a tolerable good harbour: seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORDOGNE">Dordogne</a> and Garonne, in W. Long. 3. 35. N. Lat. 45. o.

BOURGES

Pages 424-425

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France, in the department of Cher, and formerly an archbishop's see, with a famous university. The archbishop assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> title of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">Patriarch</a> of the Aquitains, and enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of primacy with regard to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBI">Albi</a>. It is seated between two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Every and the Orron, upon a hill that has a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to these rivers, by which it is almost surrounded, for there is but one avenue to it by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which is that of Port Bourbonnoux. It stands upon a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground; but one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is without houses; and the rest is but thinly peopled with gentlemen, students, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of souls amounting only to about 16,450. They have no manner of trade but for their own necessaries. It is divided into the old and new town. The walls of the old are almost entire, and the new town is almost as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the old. There are several churches, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and nunneries. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, dedicated to St Stephen, is a fine old Gothic structure: it is seated in the highest part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> are two handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers. The new one, which is built in the room of one which fell down, is almost 200 feet high. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is the largest in the city, where there was formerly an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and now a market. There is a fine walk from St Michael's gate into the fields, and three alleys, formed by four ranks of trees, the middlemost of which is spacious; besides which, there is a very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> mall. The university is famous for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. This city stands almost in the centre of France. E. Long. 2° 30'. N. Lat. 47° 10'.

BOURGET

Pages 425-425

a town of Savoy, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, seated at the southern extremity of a lake of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 55'. N. Lat. 44° 45'.

BOURGOGNE

Pages 425-425
or Burgundy, as it is called; a considerable province of France, with the title of a duchy. It is 130 miles in length, and 75 in breadth. It is bounded on the east, by the Franche Compte; on the west, by Bourbonnois and Nivernois; on the south, by Lyonnais; and on the north by Champagne. It is very fertile in corn and fruit, and produces excellent wine. It is watered by the rivers Seine, Dehune, Bresse, Armancon, Ouche, Souzon, Tille, and Saone. There are four mineral springs, at Apoigny, Primeau, Bourbon-Lancy, and St Reine. The first are obscure, and the two last in high reputation. In the canton of Bresse, there are two subterranean lakes which often overflow in times of the greatest drought, and lay a large tract of ground under water: one of them has no apparent spring or opening; and yet in a dry season, it throws out water enough to overflow the meadow-land near it. The grottoes or caves of Arcy are seated about 18 miles from Auxerre, and over them is soil about 10 feet deep. The entrance into these cavities is 200 paces long, but narrow. Twenty paces from the entrance is a lake, which seems to be formed by that part of the water that will not petrify. The highest of these vaults is not above eight feet. About 80 paces from the entrance there is a kind of hall, with a coffee-coloured ceiling, wherein there are a thousand odd figures, which have a very agreeable effect. Dijon is the capital town.

BOURGUIGNONS

Pages 425-426
or Burgundians, one of the northern nations who overran the Roman empire, and settled in Gaul. They were of a great stature, and very warlike; for which reason the emperor Valentinian the Great engaged them in his service against the Germans. They lived in tents which were close to each other, that they might the more readily unite in arms on any unforeseen attack. These conjunctions of tents they called burgs; and they were to them what towns are to us. Sidonius Apollinaris tells us that they wore long hair, took great pleasure in singing, and were fond of praise for their vocal talents. He adds, that they ate great quantities; and anointed their hair with butter, deeming that unction very ornamental. Their crown was at first elective, and the authority of their kings expired with their success. They were not only accountable for their own misconduct, but likewise for the calamities of nature, and the caprice of fortune. They were deposed if they had lost a battle; if they succeeded ill in any enterprise; or if, in short, any great event had not corresponded with the hopes of the public. They were not more favourably treated in case of a bad harvest or vintage, or if any epidemical distemper had ravaged the state. At first they were governed by many kings, and henden was the title of the royal dignity. But in latter times they were subject to one sovereign; and they grew humane and civilized, especially when Christianity was propagated in their country. Before that epocha their religion was much the same with that of the other northern nations. They had many priests, the chief of whom was distinguished by the name of sinistrus. He was perpetual, and they paid him great respect and veneration.

BOURIGNON

Pages 426-426

ANTONIETTA, a famous enthusiastic preacher and pretended prophetess, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISLE">Lisle</a> in 1616. At her birth she was so deformed, that it was debated some days in the family whether it was not proper to stifle her as a monster; but her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> diminishing, she was spared; and afterwards attained such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, that she had her admirers. From her childhood to her old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> she had an extraordinary turn of mind. She set up for a reformer, and published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books filled with very singular notions; the most remarkable of which are entitled The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the World, and The Testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a>. She was an enemy to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which she maintained ought to give <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the illumination of divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and asserted, that whenever any one was born again by embracing her doctrine, she felt the pains and throws of a woman in labour. Of her pretended visions and revelations we shall give one instance as a sample. In one of her ecstasies she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> in the same form in which he appeared before his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and the manner in which he was capable of procreating other men, since he himself possessed in himself the principles of both sexes*. Nay she pretended it was told her that he had carried this procreating <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> so far as to produce the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. "The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (says she), whom Adam brought forth without any concurrent assistance in his glorified state, was chosen by God to be the throne of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>; the organ and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by which God would communicate himself externally to men: This is Christ the first born united to human nature, both God and man." Besides these and such like extravagancies, she had other forbidding qualities: her temper was morose and peevish, and she was extremely avaricious and greedy of amassing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. She dressed like a hermit, and travelled to France, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, England, and Scotland. In the last she made a strong party, and some thousand sectarians, known by the name of Bourignonists. She died at Franeker in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Frise, October 30, 1680. Her works have been printed in 18 vols. 8vo.

BOURN

Pages 426-426

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, in England, seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 17. N. Lat. 52. 40. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, has a good market for corn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and is noted for the coronation of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edmund.

BOURNE

Pages 426-426
or BORN, an appellation anciently given to all little brooks or rivulets, and still used in the same sense in Scotland and in the north of England.

BOURO

Pages 426-426

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, between the Moluccas and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>. It is well cultivated; and is now subject to the Dutch, who have built a fortress here. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in it are exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on one side is uncommonly deep. It produces nutmegs and cloves, as well as cocoa and banana trees; besides many vegetables introduced by the Dutch. It is about 50 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 129. S. Lat. 4. 30.

BOUTANT

Pages 426-426
or ARCH-BOUTANT, in Architecture, an arch, or part of an arch, abutting against the reins of a vault to prevent its giving way. A Pillar Boutant, is a large chain or pile of stone, made to support a wall, terrace, or vault. BOUTÉ, in the manege. A horse is called bouté, when his legs are in a straight line from the knee to the coronet: short-jointed horses are apt to be bouté, and on the other hand long-jointed horses are not.

BOUTON

Pages 426-426

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, about 12 miles distant from the south-east <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>. The inhabitants are small but well shaped, and of a dark olive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Callasujung, which is about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the top of a small hill, and round it a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall. The houses are not built upon the ground, but on posts. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the inhabitants is Mahometanism. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 122. 30. S. Lat. 4. 30.

BOUTS-RIMES

Pages 426-426

a popular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the French <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; signifying certain rhymes, disposed in order, and given to a poet together with a subject, to be filled up with verses ending in the same words, and the same order. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the bouts-rimes is owing to one Du <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, a poet, in the year 1649. In fixing the bouts, it is usual to choose such as seem the remotest, and have the least connexion. Some good authors fancy that these rhymes are of all others the easiest, that they assist the invention, and furnish the most new thoughts of all others. Sarasin has a poem on the defeat of the bouts-rimes. The academy of Lanternists at Thoulouse have contributed towards keeping in countenance the bouts-rimes, by proposing each year a set of fourteen, to be filled up on the glories of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> monarque; the victorious sonnet to be rewarded with a fine medal. An instance hereof may be given in the following one, filled up by P. Commire. Tout est grand dans le roi, l'aspect seul de son buste Rend nos fiers ennemis plus froids que des glaçons. Et Guillaume n'attend que le temps des moissons, Pour se voir succomber sous un bras si robuste. Qu'on ne nous vante plus les <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> d'Auguste; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> de bien régner lui ferroit des leçons: Horace en vain l'égale aux dieux dans ses chansons: Moins que mon héros il étoit sage et juste, &c.

BOUVILLON

Pages 426-426

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Luxemburg in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 0. N. Lat. 40. 55.

BOVEY COAL

Pages 415-415

an inflammable fossil found in England, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brownish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and of a laminar structure. It is composed of wood, penetrated with petrol or bitumen; and frequently contains pyrites, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, and copperas.

BOVINA AFFECTO

Pages 417-417

a distemper of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, caused by a worm lodging between the skin and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and perforating the same. This distemper is not mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks, and is but little known in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

BOVINES

Pages 417-417

a small town of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, seated on the river Maese, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 50'. N. Lat. 49° 45'.

BOVINO

Pages 417-417

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, seated at the foot of the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 15'. N. Lat. 41° 17'. ROVUM (Itinerary); a town of the Silures, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, fifteen miles to the south of Isca Silurum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>: Now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COWBRIDGE">Cowbridge</a>; according to Baudrand, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>.

BOW

Pages 426-428

(arcus), a weapon of offence made of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which, after being strongly bent, by means of a string fastened to its two ends, in returning to its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state throws out an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force. It is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-bow, by way of distinction from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow or arbalest. The bow is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and the most universal of all weapons. It has been found to obtain among the most barbarous and remote people, and who had the least <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the rest of mankind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bow and arrow was first abolished in France under <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. in 1481; and in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were introduced the Swiss arms, that is, the halberd, pike, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The long-bow was formerly in great vogue in England; most of our victories in France were acquired by it; and many laws were made to regulate and encourage its use. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> under Henry VIII. complain "of the disuse of the long-bow, heretofore the safeguard and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and the dread and terror of its enemies." 33 Hen. VIII. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. The art of using bows is called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>, and those practised therein, archers or bowmen. See ARCHERY. The strength of a bow may be calculated on this principle, that its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, i.e. the power whereby it restores itself to its natural position, is always proportionate to the distance or space it is removed therefrom. The most barbarous nations often excel in the fabric of the particular things which they have the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Laplanders, who support themselves almost entirely by hunting, have an art of making bows, which we, in these improved parts of the world, have never arrived at. Their bow is made of two pieces of tough and strong wood, shaved <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the same size, and flatted on each side; the two flat sides of the pieces are brought closely and evenly together, and then joined by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> made of the skins of perch, which they have in great plenty, and of which they make a glue superior in strength to any which we have. The two pieces, when once united in this manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never separate, and the bow is of much more force to expel the arrow, than it could possibly have been under the same dimensions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made only of one piece. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the bow-string, called τριχων, was made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; and hence also called λευκος; though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s bow-strings are frequently made of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> cut into small thongs: whence τριχων. The uppermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bow, to which the string was fastened, was called ξαρτης, being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and the last thing towards finishing the bow. The Grecian bows were frequently beautified with gold or silver; whence we have mention of αυριον αριστος; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> is called Αγγελοποιος. But the matter of which they were ordinarily composed, seems to have been wood: though they were anciently, Scythian-like, made of horn, as appears from that of Pandarus in Homer, Iliad, 8. v. 105. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the bow is usually ascribed to Apollo, and was communicated to the primitive inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, who are said to have been the first of mortals who understood the use of bows and arrows. And hence, even in later ages, the Cretan bows were famous, and preferred by the Greeks to all others. Some, however, rather choose to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> Perseus, the son of Perseus, with the invention of the bow; while others ascribe it to Sothus, son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and progenitor to the Scythians, who were excellent at this art, and by many reputed the first masters of it. From them it was derived to the Grecians, some of whose ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were instructed by the Scythians in the use of the bow, which in those days passed for a most princely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. It was first introduced into the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The Indians still retain the bow. In the repository of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> we see a West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bow two yards long. The Scythian bow was famous for its incurvation, which distinguished it from the bows of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and other nations; being so great as to form a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>: whence the shepherd in Athenaeus, being to describe the letters in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>'s name, and expressing each of them by some apposite resemblance, compares the third to the Scythian bow; meaning not the more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> character Σ, but the ancient Ω, which is semicircular, and bears the third place in ΩΗΓΕΩΣ. Cross-Bow, is also called arbalet or arbaliet; which word is derived from arbalista, i.e. arcubalista, "a bow with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLING">sling</a>." The arbalet consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> bow set in a shaft of wood, furnished with a string and a trigger; and is bent with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> fitted for that purpose. It serves to throw bullets, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> arrows, darts, &c. The ancients had large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> for throwing many arrows at once, called arbalets or ballistas.
