The collar being thus rolled up, it is to be boiled in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kettle, till it is so tender, that you can run a straw through it; then set it by till it is thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and put it into the following pickle. To every gallon of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, put a handful or two of salt, and as much wheat-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>: Boil them together, then drain the bran as clear as you can from the liquor; and when the liquor is quite cold, put the brawn into it.

BRAY

Pages 464-464

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, seated on St George's channel, eight miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 16' N. Lat. 53° 8'. BRAY sur <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, a town of France, in Champagne, and in Senonos, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIE">Brie</a>. E. Long. 2° 15' N. Lat. 48° 35'.

BRAYLE

Pages 464-464

among sportsmen, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> slit to put upon the hawk's wing, to tie it up.

BRAZED

Pages 464-464

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> serving to describe three cheverons, one clasping another.

BRAZEN

Pages 464-464

something consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> formed out of it. See BRASS. BRAZEN <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">Age</a>. See AGE. BRAZEN <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">Dish</a>, among miners, is the standard by which the other dishes are gauged, and is kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRAZEN_SEA">BRAZEN <a </a>class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in Jewish antiquity, one of the sacred utensils in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. It was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in the plain of Jordan, and removed from thence into the inner <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the temple; where it was placed upon 12 oxen, three of which looked towards each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the world. It was ten cubits from the one brim to the other, five cubits in height, and 30 cubits in circumference, and contained 3000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The brim of it was perfectly round, and so it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the two upper cubits; but below the brim, in the three lower cubits, it was <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. It was a handbreadth thick, and the brim was wrought like the brim of a cup, with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of lilies. About the body of this huge vessel there were two borders of engravings, being the heads of oxen in demi-relief: out of which some suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> issued, and that they were made as cocks and conveyances for that purpose.—This brazen or molten sea, was designed for the priests to wash themselves in before they performed the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the temple. The supply of water was through a pipe out of the well Etam; though some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was constantly supplied with water by the Gibonites.

BRAZIER

Pages 464-465

BRAZIER, an artificer who makes and deals in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. This trade, as exercised in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, may be reckoned a branch of the smithery, though they seldom keep forges, except for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAZING">brazing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soldering, and tinning the insides of their vessels, which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> up chiefly out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and brass prepared rough to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. They consist of a working <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and a shop-keeping part, which latter many carry on to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, dealing as well in all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, as copper and brass goods for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture; and lately have fallen much into selling what is called French plate, made of a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> metal, silvered and polished to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that the eye cannot soon distinguish it from real silver. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">BRAZIL</a>. See BRASIL.

BRAZING

Pages 465-465

the soldering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> joining two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> together by means of thin plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, melted between the pieces that are to be joined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> be very fine, as when two leaves of a broken <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> are to be brazed together, they cover it with pulverized <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, melted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it may incorporate with the brass powder, which is added to it: The piece is then exposed to the fire without touching the coals, and heated till the brass is seen to run. Brazing is also the joining two pieces of iron together by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them hot, the one upon the other, which is used for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces by farriers, &c.

BRAZZA

Pages 465-465

a town and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>, and subject to Venice. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28°. N. Lat. 43°.

BREACH

Pages 465-465

in a legal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is where a person breaks through the condition of a bond <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covenant; on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> upon which, the breach must be assigned: And this assignment must not be general, but particular, as, in an action of covenant for not repairing houses, it ought to be assigned particularly what is the want of reparation: and in such certain manner, that the defendant may take an issue.

BREAD

Pages 465-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of dough kneaded and baked in an oven. See BAKER, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">BAKING</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARM">BARM</a>. The grains of all vegetables are almost entirely composed of substances very proper for the nourishment of animals; and amongst grains those which contain a farinaceous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> are the most agreeable and most nutritive. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, who appears to be designed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to eat of all substances which are capable of nourishing him, and still more of vegetables than animals, has, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial, and in all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, used farinaceous grains as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> basis of his food: but as these grains cannot be without difficulty eaten by men in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and intelligent animal has gradually found means not only to extract the farinaceous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, that is, the only nutritive part of these grains, but also to prepare it so that it becomes a very agreeable and wholesome aliment, such as the bread we now generally eat. Nothing appears so easy at first sight as to grind corn, to make a paste with the flour and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to bake this paste in an oven. They who are accustomed to enjoy the advantages of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> inventions, without reflecting on the labour it has cost to complete them, think all these operations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and trivial. However, it appears very certain, that for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time men no otherwise prepared their corn than by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> and forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> viscous cakes, not very agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and of difficult digestion. Before they were able to make bread of good taste and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as we have now, it was necessary to invent and complete ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn, and separating the pure flour with little trouble and labour; and that inquiries, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather some happy chance, which some observing person availed himself of, should discover, that flour, mixed with a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water, is susceptible of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> which almost entirely destroys its viscosity, heightens its taste, and renders it proper to make a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> bread, very agreeable to the taste, and of easy digestion. This essential operation, on which the good quality of bread depends, is entirely of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. It would add to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cultivators of chemistry, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them so useful and important a discovery; but, unhappily, it is too probable that they had no share in it. The ancient chemists were engaged in other pursuits than that of bread and other common objects. They hoped to make <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and what is bread in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with gold? However that be, to the fortunate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of raising the paste before baking we owe the perfection of the art of making bread. This operation consists in keeping some paste or dough, till by a peculiar spirituous fermentation it swells, rarefies, and acquires a smell and taste quick, pungent, spirituous, somewhat sour, and rather disagreeable. This fermented dough is well worked with some fresh dough, which is by that mixture and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> disposed to a similar but less advanced fermentation than that above mentioned. By this fermentation the dough is attenuated, and divided; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is introduced into it, which being incapable of disengaging itself from the tenacious and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> paste, forms in it small cavities, raises and swells it; hence the small quantity of fermented paste which disposes the rest to ferment, is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a>, from the French word <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, signifying to raise. When the dough is thus raised, it is in a proper state to be put into the oven; where, while it is baked, it dilates... Bread dilates itself still more by the rarefaction of the air, and of the spirituous substance it contains, and it forms a bread full of eyes or cavities; consequently light, and entirely different from the heavy, compact, viscos, and indigested masses, made by baking unfermented dough. The invention of beer, or wine of grains, furnishes a new matter useful in the making of bread. This matter is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> which forms upon the surface of these liquors during fermentation. When it is mixed with dough, it raises it better and more quickly than ordinary leaven. It is called yeast or barm. By means of this, the finest lightest bread is made. It often happens, that bread made with leaven dough has a sourish and not agreeable taste; which may proceed from too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a quantity of leaven, or from leaven in which the fermentation has advanced too far. This inconvenience does not happen to bread made with yeast; because the fermentation of this substance is not too far advanced, or because more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is given to that finer bread. It may be asked, Why, since dough is capable of fermenting spontaneously and singly, as we see from the leaven, a substance is added to dispose it to ferment? The true reason is, That all the parts of a fermenting substance do not ferment at the same time, nor to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; so that some parts of this substance have finished their fermentation, while others have not yet begun. The fermentable liquors which contain much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HYDROMEL">hydromel</a>, and most of wines, give proofs of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; for, after these liquors have become very vinous, they have still very distinctly a saccharine taste: but all saccharine matter is still susceptible of fermentation; and, in fact, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> vinous hydromel, or must, or even new beer, be distilled, so that all their ardent spirit shall be separated, and the residues diluted with water, we shall see a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fermentation take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and a new quantity of ardent spirit formed. The same thing precisely happens to dough, and still more sensibly, from its viscosity and want of fluidity; so that if it be left to ferment alone, and without the help of leaven, as the fermentation proceeds very slowly and successively, the parts which ferment first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have become sour and vapid before all the rest be sufficiently attenuated and changed, by which the bread will acquire a disagreeable taste. A mixture of a small quantity of leaven with dough effectually prevents this inconvenience; because the effect of this leaven, and of all fermenting substances, is to dispose to a similar fermentation all matters capable of it, with which it is mixed; or rather, by means of leaven, the fermentation of all the parts of such substances is effected more nearly at the same time. Bread well raised and baked differs from unfermented bread, not only in being less compact, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, and of a more agreeable taste, but also in being more easily miscible with water, with which it does not form a viscous mass, which circumstance is of great importance in digestion. It is observable, that without bread, or somewhat of this form, no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> seems to live. Thus the Laplanders, having no corn of their own, make a sort of bread of their dried fishes, and of the inner rind of the pine, which seems to be used, not so much for their nourishment as for supplying a dry food. For this mankind seem to have an universal appetite, rejecting bland, slippery, and mucilaginous foods. This is not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> accounted for, but seems to depend on very simple principles. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of our food depends on the mixture of the animal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> in every stage. Among others the saliva is necessary, which requires dry food as a necessary stimulus to draw it forth, as bland, slippery, fluid aliments are too inert, and make too short stay in the mouth, to produce this effect, or to cause a sufficient degree of manducation to emulge that liquor. For this reason we commonly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> dry bread along with animal food, which otherwise would be too quickly swallowed. For blending the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and water of our food nothing is so fit as bread, assisted by a previous manducation. For which purpose, bread is of like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> in the stomach, as it is proper that a substance of solid consistence should be long retained there. Now the animal fluids must be mixed with our aliment, in order to change the acceescency it undergoes. But liquid foods would not attain this end, whereas the solid stimulates and emulges the glands of the stomach. The bread then appears to be exceedingly proper, being bulky without too much solidity, and firm without difficulty of solution. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> we meet with various denominations of bread; as, 1. Panis siligenus, called also mundus, athleticus, isungua, coliphine, and robus, answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bread; being made of the purest flour of the best wheat, and only used by the richer sort. 2. Panis secundus or secundarius, called also smilacetus or smilaginicus, the next in purity; being made of fine flour, only all the bran not sifted out. 3. Autopyrus, called also syncomistus and confusans, made of the whole substance of the wheat, without either retrenching the finer flour or coarser bran; answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> bread. 4. Cocabaceus, apparently the same with what was otherwise denominated sordidus, as being given to dogs; furfuraceus, furfureus, or furfuratus, because made in great part of bran; and, in the middle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, bissex, on account of its brownness; sometimes also leibo. There were other sorts of bread, denominated from the manner in which they were made, or the uses they were applied to; as, 1. The militaris, which was prepared by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and officers in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; for which purpose some had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, others pounded the corn in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and baked it on the coals. 2. Clibanites, that baked in an oven, by way of contradistinction from that baked on the hearth or under the embers. 3. That called subcineritius, or sub cinere coctus; sometimes also reversatus, because it was to be turned in the baking. 4. Nauticus, answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-biscuit, and denominated accordingly bis coctus, because baked several times over to make it keep the longer. Other kinds of bread were denominated from their qualities and accidents; as, 1. The panis siccus, that which had been long baked; such as were the bis coctus, naval and buccellated bread. 2. Madidus, a sort made of rye or bear, sometimes also made of fine flour, wherewith they smeared their faces, by way of a cosmetic, to render them smooth. 3. Acidus, or sour bread, which was acidulated with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>. 4. Asymus, that unleavened or unfermented. The French have also a great variety of breads; as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s queen's bread, alamode bread, bread de Segovie, de Gentilly, quality-bread, &c. all prepared in peculiar manners by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. The brede de Gonesse excels all others, on account of the waters at Gonesse, a town three leagues from Paris. It is light, and full of eyes, which are the marks of its goodness. Pain de manège, is that which each family bakes for itself. Spice-bread, pain d'épice, denotes bread baked and iced over with the scam taken off sugar in refining houses; it is sometimes also made with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and other sorts of seasoning, and answers to what the ancients call panis mellitus. Among us, bread is chiefly divided into white, wheaten, and household; differing only in degrees of purity. In the first, all the bran is separated; in the second, only the coarser; in the third, none at all: so fine bread is made only of flour; wheaten bread of flour and a mixture of the finer bran; and household, of the whole substance of the grain, without taking out either the coarse bran or fine flour. We also meet with symmel bread, manchet or roll bread, and French bread: which are only so many denominations of the finest and whitest bread, made of the purest flour; except that in ill-roll bread there is an addition of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and in French bread, of eggs and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> also. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, and several of the northern counties of England, they have several sorts of oatmeal bread; as, 1. The bannock, which is an oat-cake, kneaded only with water, and baked on the embers. 2. Clap-bread, which is made into thin hard cakes. 3. Bitchiness bread, which is made of thin batter, and made into thin soft oat-cakes. 4. Riddle-cakes, which are thick and sour, have but little leaven, and are kneaded stiff. And, 5. Jannock, which is oatmeal bread made up into loaves. Add to these, pease-bread, much used in many parts of Scotland; being bread consisting either wholly of the flour of pease, or of this and oatmeal mixed: the dough, sometimes leavened, sometimes made only with water, is formed either into bannocks or cakes, and baked over the embers; or into what they call baps, i.e., a kind of flattish rolls, and baked in the oven. In the statute of assize of bread and ale, 51 Hen. III. mention is made of wastel-bread, cocket-bread, and bread of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREET">treet</a>; which answer to the three kinds of bread now in use, called white, wheaten, and household bread. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, they heretofore distinguished bread by the names esquires bread, panis armigerorum; monks bread, panis conventualis; boys bread, panis puerorum; and servants bread, panis famulorum, called also panis servientalis. A like distribution obtained in the households of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and princes; where, however, we find some other denominations; as messengers bread, panis nuncius, that given to messengers as a reward of their labour; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-bread, panis curialis, that allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> for the maintenance of his household; eleemosynary bread, that distributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by way of alms. It is for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> that the food of the poor should be as various as possible, that, in time of dearth and scarcity of the ordinary kinds, they may not be without ready and cheap resources. To the discovery of such resources several benevolent philosophers having successfully turned their inquiries, we shall lay before the reader the result of their experiments. 1. Bread of Potatoes*. Potatoes, previously deprived of their skin, cut into thin slices, and put between <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, will dry in a heat somewhat less than 35° des Pommes de Reaumur's thermometer; and, when thus dried, de Terre, they will preserve their white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. By this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> they lose about two thirds of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and they may then be reduced to a fine powder. A little of this powder thrown upon the fire sends out a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, accompanied with a smell resembling burnt bread. As this smell is perceived from all farinaceous vegetables when treated in the same manner, M. Parmentier thinks it may be considered as the characteristic of the presence of an amylaceous matter. This smell does not, however, he observes, arise from the amylaceous or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> part separately, but from both taken together. The powder of potatoes, obtained in the manner described above, has the smell and taste of wheat; and, like it, is devoured by rats and mice; but, even when most finely powdered, it has not the feel or brightness of the flour of wheat; although, on a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, it yields the same products. It is also nutritious, and keeps well for a long time. Finding so great a similarity between the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of wheat and what may be called the meal of potatoes, M. Parmentier next endeavoured to make bread of them when mixed in different proportions. His trials were made with one-fourth, one-third, one-half, and two-thirds, of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>-meal, the remainder being flour from wheat. These proportions, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and yeast, yielded bread which was well tasted, but which had fermented little, was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and covered with hard brown crusts. Bread made from the meal of potatoes alone, with the addition of salt and yeast, was eatable, but very heavy, unfermented, and exceedingly brown. This bread, from the meal of potatoes alone, was apt to crumble into powder. To give it more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a>, he mixed with the meal a decoction of bran, or a mixture of honey and water; either of which made it lighter and more fermented: it obtained also a crust of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> colour, became well tasted, and sufficiently adhesive. M. Parmentier obtained bread also, well fermented, and of a good colour and taste, from a mixture of raw potato-pulp with meal of wheat, or potato-meal, with the addition of yeast and salt. Potatoes, when used for making bread, are not readily disposed to ferment; without which, bread is very insipid, and not easily digested. But M. Parmentier found, from a variety of experiments, that good bread might be made from equal quantities of flour and potato-meal. He concludes, therefore, with recommending the mixture of potatoes, in times of scarcity, with the flour of wheat, instead of employing rye, barley, or oats, as has frequently been done. When grain is altogether wanting, he recommends the use of bread made from a mixture of the amylaceous powder of potatoes and of their pulp, this mixture being fermented with leaven or with honey. The meal of this root, when diluted with hot water, acquires a tenacious and gluey consistence. However fair the meal of potatoes may be, it always gives a gray colour to the bread made by mixing it with the flour of wheat. Bread: but a mixture of the pulp of potatoes with the flour of wheat does not produce brown-coloured bread. M. Parmentier made bread, very much like that of wheat, by a mixture of the following four substances, viz. four ounces of amylaceous powder of potatoes, one dram of mucilage extracted from barley, one dram of the bran of rye, and a dram and a half of glutinous matter dried and powdered. 2. Bread from different Vegetables not commonly in Use*. Although <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut has not hitherto been employed, yet it is certain that wholesome bread, without any bitterness, may be obtained from it. M. Parmentier advises, that the fruit, after the skin is taken off, and the juice pressed from it, be made into a paste, which must be diluted in water, and then strained through a sieve. A milky-coloured liquor is thus separated, which, on standing, deposits a fine powder. This, being dried, is without either smell or taste, and very fit for aliment; the mass from which it is procured retaining the bitterness of the fruit. The roots of the bryonia, when treated in the same manner, yielded a similar white powder. By the same treatment also, fine, white, insipid, inodorous powders may be procured from the roots of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, gladiolus, ranunculus, fumaria, arum dracunculus, mandragora, colchicum, filipendula, and helieborus; <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which grow spontaneously, and in great abundance. Of acorns bread has frequently been made; and to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in some countries, they are in common use. The method of preparation which M. Parmentier recommends is, that they be deprived of their cover by boiling, then dried and powdered, and afterwards baked in the same manner as the flour of wheat. When fully ripe, and made into a paste, they were deprived of their astringency by merely pressing their juice from them. The mass remaining after the pressure, when dried, was easily reduced to a fine powder by no means disagreeable. The gramin caninum arvense, in its appearance, approaches to corn; and some naturalists have considered it as the original <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> from which all our grain is produced. Its roots are sweet tasted, and have long been employed in making ptisans. In the preparation of them for bread, it is only necessary that the roots should be cleansed, cut small, dried, and pounded. This powder, M. Parmentier observes, does not dissolve in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water or spirits; but it does in boiling water, which it renders thick and cloudy, and, upon cooling, the whole mass obtains a gelatinous consistence. Upon a chemical analysis, it yields an acid empyreumatic oil, which possesses a singular odour, resembling that which is perceived on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the plant. The spongy residuum, calcined in the air, gives a fixed alkali. These properties incontestably prove, that it contains an amylaceous (A) matter similar to that of grain, which appears to be the nutritive part of vegetables. This amylaceous matter, formed into a jelly, and diffused in water, keeps for a long time without suffering any change; it then turns acid, and at length putrefies. The amylaceous matter of acid and poisonous plants, although innocent and nutritive, cannot be converted into bread without the addition of some mucilaginous substance. In times of great scarcity, common bran will answer the purpose; but when potatoes are to be had, the addition of a proper proportion of these is to be preferred. M. Parmentier gives an account of the bread which he obtained from the amylaceous powders of the different vegetables mentioned above, with the addition of potatoes and a small quantity of common leaven of grain. This bread appeared in general to be well fermented; it was of a good white colour, and free from any disagreeable odour; but to the taste, it was somewhat insipid; which, however, he imagines, might have been corrected by the addition of a proper quantity of salt. As the resources against scarcity here pointed out can be procured only at particular seasons, the author proposes a method for preserving the matter thus obtained. For this purpose, he advises, that bread prepared in the manner mentioned above should be carefully --- (A) M. Beccari of the Bolognian academy has discovered in the flour of wheat two distinct substances. The one he terms an animal or glutinous matter; the other, an amylaceous matter or vegetable paste. The gluten has been supposed to be the nutritive part of corn, from its not dissolving unless in vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; from its assuming a spongy form in boiling water; from its supposed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> to the animal lymph; and, lastly, from the similitude which the products it affords, on a chemical analysis, bear to those obtained from animal substances. M. Parmentier, however, from various experiments, was led to conclude, with the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">Model</a> of Petersburg, that the gluten or animal matter of Beccari exists in the bran, and is not the nutritive part of the wheat. Having made experiments with four different kinds of flour, it appeared that the quantity of animal matter was always proportioned to the coarseness of the flour. Hence, were this gluten the nutritive part, the coarsest bread, or that which contained most bran, would afford the greatest quantity of nourishment. The contrary of this, however, is now known to be fact. The amylaceous part, or, as some have termed it, the secula, of wheat and other vegetables, is a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, not soluble in spirit of wine, vinegar, or cold water. It contains more acid, and less water, than the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. It is found in many of those plants that make the nourishment of men and other animals. Hence M. Parmentier concludes it to be the nutritive matter. Though we are not to consider the glutinous matter as the nutritious part of vegetables, yet it is a very necessary ingredient. It is that which preserves the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the paste in fermenting bread; it is that which forms the viscid pellicle, and stops the air in fermentation; gives the savoury taste to bread; occasions it to be light, to ferment, and which forms the small cells seen in it. It is found especially near the cortical part of grain; and this accounts for its being found in the greatest quantity in coarse brown meal. It is this gluten which renders wheat a superior aliment to the other grains and roots. Bread, fully dried, reduced to powder, and then kept in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> cask. By this means, he is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it may be preserved for a very long time, and will always be ready to make an agreeable and wholesome panada by the addition of a little butter and salt. M. Parmentier, in order to discover the degree of power wherewith this alimentary powder nourished, made himself the subject of experiment; and found, that three ounces of it for dinner, and as much for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, made into panada with water, was a sufficient quantity of aliment for a day. From his discharge by stool while he used it, he had reason to believe that it is almost totally alimentary. He concludes with recommending it not only as useful in times of scarcity, but as a proper substitute for sea biscuit, and as a species of food well adapted for armies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. 3. Cheap method of making wholesome Bread, when wheat-flour is dear, by mixing turnip with it. "At the time I tried this method, bread was very dear, insomuch that the poor people, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where I live, could hardly afford themselves half a meal a-day. This put me upon considering whether some cheaper method might not be found than making it of wheat-meal. Turnips were at that time very plentiful. I had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them pulled, washed clean, pared, and boiled; when they were become soft enough to mash, I had the greatest part of the water pressed out of them, and afterwards had them mixed with an equal quantity in weight of coarse wheat meal; the dough was then made in the usual manner, with yeast or barm, salt, water, &c. It rose very well in the trough; and after being well kneaded, was formed into loaves, and put into the oven to be baked. I had at the same time some other bread made with common meal in the ordinary way. I baked my turnip bread rather longer than the other. When they were drawn from the oven, I caused a loaf of each sort to be cut; and found, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, the turnip-bread was sweeter than the other, to the full as light and as white, but had a little taste (though nowise disagreeable) of the turnip. Twelve hours afterwards I tasted my turnip-bread again, when I found the taste of the turnip in it scarcely perceptible, and the smell quite gone off. On examining it when it had been baked 24 hours, had I not known that there were turnips in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, I should not have imagined it: it had, it is true, a peculiar sweetish taste, but by no means disagreeable; on the contrary, I rather preferred it to the bread made of wheat-meal alone. After it had been baked 48 hours, it underwent another examination, when it appeared to me to be rather superior to the other; it ate fresher and moister, and had not at all abated in its good qualities: to be short, it was still very good after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>: and, as far as I could see, kept as well as the bread made of common wheat-meal. "In my trials of this bread by the taste, I was not satisfied with eating it by itself; I had some of it spread with butter; I tasted it with cheese; I ate of it toasted and buttered, and finally in boiled milk and in soup: in all these forms it was very palatable and good. Bread, in Medicine. Besides the alimentary, bread has also medical qualities.—Decoctions, creams, and jellies of bread, are directed in some dispensaries. Bread carefully toasted, and infused or lightly boiled in water, imparts a deep colour, and a sufficiently agreeable restringent taste. This liquor, taken as common drink, has done good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in a weak lax state of the stomach and intestines; and in bilious vomiting and purging; or the cholera morbus: examples are related in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> essays of several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of this kind cured by it, without the use of any other medicine.—In Westphalia there is a very coarse bread eaten, which still retains the opprobrious name given it by a French traveller of Bonpournikel, "good for his horse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICKEL">Nickel</a>." It is the same with what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called panis furfuraceus, or panis impurus, from its not being cleansed from the husk; and panis ater, from the blackness of its colour: though we learn from Pliny, that the Romans for 300 years knew no other bread. The Germans make two sorts of waters by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> from this bread; the one with, the other without, the addition of a spirituous liquor: to both which great virtues are ascribed. That without any thing spirituous, is made out of the juice of craw-fish, may-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, rose-water, nutmegs, and saffron, distilled from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of this bread. This is esteemed a great restorative, and given in hectic habits. The other is distilled from this bread and Rhenish wine, with nutmegs and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>. This is given in all the disorders of the stomach, vomiting, loss of appetite, and other complaints of the same kind: and besides these, there is a spirit distilled from it by the retort in the dry way, which, when separated from its fetid oil, is esteemed a powerful sudorific, and very valuable medicine in removing impurities of the blood. Bread is also medicinal, applied externally, as is vulgarly known. Mr Boyle assures us he drew a menstruum from bread stronger than aquafortis, and which would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> even upon glass itself. Bread-Fruit Tree. See Supplement. Bees-Bread. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>. Cassada Bread. See Jatropha, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Earth Bread. In the lordship of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> in the Upper Losatia, a sort of white earth is found, which the poor, urged by the calamities of the wars which raged in those parts, make bread. It is taken out of a hill where they formerly worked at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> has somewhat warmed this earth, it cracks, and small white globules proceed from it as meal; it does not ferment alone, but only when mixed with meal. Mr Sarlitz, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was pleased to inform us, that he has seen persons who in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> lived upon it for some time. He assured us that he procured bread to be made of this earth alone, and of different mixtures of earth and meal; and that he even kept some of this bread by him upwards of six years: he further says, a Spaniard told him, that this earth is also found near Gerona in Catalonia." Eucharist or Sacramental Bread, in the Protestant churches, is common leavened bread, in conformity to the ancient practice. In the Romish mass, azymeous or unleavened bread is used, particularly in the Gallican <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, where a sort is provided for this purpose, called pain à chanter, made of the purest wheaten flour pressed between two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates graven like wafer-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, being first rubbed with white wax to prevent the paste from sticking. The Greeks observe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ceremonies in their making the eucharist bread. It is necessary... Bread. the person who bakes it have not lain with his wife the day before; or, if it be a woman, that she have not conversed with her husband. The Abyssinians have an apartment in their churches for this service, being a kind of sacristy. F. Sirmond, in his disquisition on azymous bread, shows, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, that anciently there were as many ceremonies used in the Latin church in the preparation of the unleavened bread as are still retained in the eastern churches. He cites the example of Queen Radegonda, who distributed with her own hands in the church, the bread which she herself had made. It appears also from the dispute of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Humbert against the Greeks, that in the Latin church no bread was used for the eucharist, but what was taken out of the sacristy, and had been made by the deacons, subdeacons, and even priests, who rehearsed several psalms during the process. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> writers enumerate other species of bread allotted for purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; as, 1. Calendarius, that anciently offered to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>. 2. Prebendarius, the same with capitularis, that distributed daily to each prebendary or canon. 3. Benedictus, that usually given to catechumens before <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, in lieu of the eucharist bread, which they were incapable of partaking of. The panis benedictus, was called also panogium and eulogion, being a sort of bread blessed and consecrated by the priest, whereby they prepare the catechumens for the reception of the body of Christ. The same was used afterwards, not only by catechumens, but by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> themselves, as a token of their mutual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> and friendship. Its origin is dated from the 7th century, at the council at Nantz. In the Gallican church we still find panis benedictus, pain benit, used for that offered for benediction, and afterwards distributed to pious persons who attend divine service in chapels. 4. Consecrated bread is a piece of wax, paste, or even earth, over which several ceremonies have been performed with benedictions, &c., to be sent in an Agnus Dei, or relic-box, and presented for veneration. 5. Unleavened bread, panis azymus. The Jews eat no other bread during their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>: and exact search was made in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to see that no leavened bread was left. The usage was introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their hasty departure from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, when they had not leisure to bake leavened. 6. Shew-bread was that offered to God every Sabbath-day, being placed on the golden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in the holy of holies. Horse-Bread is made of wheat, oats, and beans; to which sometimes are added aniseed, gentian, liquorice, fenugreek, eggs, and ale; and sometimes rye and white wine are used. For <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>-horses three sorts of bread are usually given with success, for the second, third, and fourth nights feeding: they are all made of beans and wheat worked with barn; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> consisting chiefly in the proportion of the two former. In the first kind, three times the quantity of beans is used to one of wheat; in the second, equal quantities of both; in the third, three times the quantity of wheat to one of beans. Sago-Bread. See SAGO. Assize* of Bread. The price and weight of bread is regulated by the magistrates according to the price of wheat. We have divers tables of the weights of the loaves both of wheat, wheaten, and household bread, at every price of wheat. If bread want one ounce in 36, the baker formerly was to suffer the pillory: now, to forfeit 5s. for every ounce wanting; and for every defect less than an ounce, 2s. 6d.; such bread being complained of and weighed before a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> within 24 hours after it is baked or exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> within the bills of mortality, or within three days in any other place. It is to be observed, bread loses weight by keeping: in some experiments, recited by Bartholine, the diminution was near one-fourth in six months. The same author assures us, that in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, they make bread which keeps 30 or 40 years; and that they are there fonder of their old hard bread, than elsewhere of new or soft; since the older it is, the more agreeable it grows. For their great feasts, particular care is taken to have the oldest bread; so that, at the christening of a child, they have usually bread which had been baked perhaps at the christening of his grandfather. It is made of barley and oat-meal baked between two hollow <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Bread-Room, in a ship, that destined to hold the bread or biscuit. The boards of the bread-room should be jointed and caulked, and even lined with tin-plates or mats. It is also proper to warm it well with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> for several days before the biscuit is put into it; since nothing is more injurious to the bread than moisture. Breadth, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, one of the three dimensions of bodies, which multiplied into their length constitutes a surface. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">Break</a>, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies to divide a thing into several parts with violence. In the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to break ground, is to open the trenches before a place. Among sportsmen, to break a horse in trotting, is to make him light upon the hand in trotting, in order to make him fit for a gallop. To break a horse for hunting, is to supple him, to make him take the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of running. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">Breakers</a>, a name given by sailors to those billows that break violently over rocks lying under the surface of the sea. They are distinguished both by their appearance and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, as they cover that part of the sea with a perpetual foam, and produce a hearse and terrible roaring, very different from what the waves usually have in a deeper bottom. When a ship is unhappily driven among breakers, it is hardly possible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her. Breaking, in a mercantile style, denotes the becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">bankrupt</a>. See Bankrupt. Breaking-Bulk, in the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is the same with unloading part of the cargo. Breakspear, Nicholas. See Adrian IV. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKWATER">Breakwater</a>, a sort of rampart of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or wood, placed in the water before a harbour to break the force of the waves. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAM">Bream</a>. See Cyprinus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. To Bream, to burn off the filth, such as grass, ooze, shells, or sea-weed, from a ship's bottom, that has gathered to it in a voyage, or by lying long in a harbour. This operation is performed by holding kindled furze, faggots, or such materials to the bottom, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> incorporating with the pitch, sulphur, &c. that had formerly covered it, immediately loosens and throws off whatever filth may have adhered to the planks. After this, the bottom is covered anew with a composition of sulphur, tallow, &c. which not only makes makes it smooth and slippery, so as to divide the fluid more readily, but also poisons and destroys those <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> which eat through the planks in the course of a voyage. Breasting may be performed either when the ship lies <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> after the tide has ebbed from her, or by docking, or by careening.

BREAST

Pages 471-471

in Anatomy, denotes the fore-parts of the thorax. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Smiting the breast is one of the expressions of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>. In the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> beats his breast in rehearsing the general confession at the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>.

BREASTS

Pages 471-471
or Mammae**, in Anatomy. See Anatomy Index. The breasts are usually two; though we also meet with instances of trimamia or women with three breasts*, and even some with four, all yielding milk alike†. **BREAST-Hooks**, in Ship-Building, are thick pieces of timber incurvated into the form of knees, and used to strengthen the fore-part of the ship, where they are placed at different heights directly across the stem, so as to unite it with the bows on each side. The breast-hooks are strongly connected to the stem and hawse-pieces by tree-nails, and by bolts driven from without through the planks and hawse-pieces, and the whole thickness of the breast-hooks, upon whose inside those bolts are forelocked or clinched upon rings. They are usually about one-third thicker, and twice as long, as the knees of the decks they support. **BREAST-Plate**, in antiquity, a piece of armour worn to defend the breast, originally believed to be made of hides, or hemp, twisted into small cords, but afterwards made of brass, iron, or other metals, which were sometimes so exquisitely hardened, as to be proof against the greatest force. **BREAST-Plate**, in Jewish antiquity, one part of the priestly vestments anciently worn by the high-priests. It was a folded piece of the same rich embroidered stuff of which the ephod was made; and it was set with twelve precious stones, on each of which was engraven the name of one of the tribes. They were set in four rows, three in each row; and were divided from each other by little golden squares or partitions in which they were set. The names of these stones, and that of the tribes engraven on them, as also of their disposition on the breast-plate, are as follows: | Sardine | Emerald | Ligare | Beryl | |---------|---------|--------|-------| | Reuben | Judah | Gad | Zebulon | | Topaz | Sapphire | Agate | Onyx | |--------|----------|-------|------| | Simon | Dan | Asher | Joseph | | Carbuncle | Diamond | Amethyst | Jasper | |-----------|---------|----------|--------| | Levi | Naphtali| Issachar | Benjamin | This breast-plate was fastened at the four corners; those on the top to each shoulder by a golden hook or ring at the end of a wreathed chain; and those below, to the girdle of the ephod, by two strings or ribbons, which had likewise two rings and hooks. This ornament was never to be severed from the priestly garment; and, it was called the memorial, to put the high-priest in mind how dear those tribes ought to be to him, whose names he wore on his breast. It is also called the breast-plate of judgment, because it had the divine oracle of Urim and Thummim annexed to it. See URIM AND THUMMIM. **BREAST-Plate**, in the manege, the strap of leather that runs from one side of the saddle to the other, over the horse's breast, in order to keep the saddle tight, and hinder it from sliding backwards. **BREAST-Work**, in Fortification, the same with PARAFET.

BREATH

Pages 471-471

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> inspired and expelled again in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of respiration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were very watchful over the last breath of dying persons, which the nearest relations, as the mother, father, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, received in their mouths.

BRECHIN

Pages 471-472

a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 18'. N. Lat. 56° 40'. It consists of one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome street, and two smaller; and is on the side of a small hill, washed by the Southesk, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of two large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It contained 5000 inhabitants in 1811. At the foot of the town is a long row of houses independent of it, built on ground held in feu from the family of Northesk. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and, with four others, sends a member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It has a small share of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture, which has lately declined. It lies at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the harbour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>; and the tide flows within two miles of the town; to which a canal might be made, which perhaps might create a trade, but would be of certain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in conveying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the corn of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Brechin was a rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bishopric, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. about the year 1150. At the Reformation, its revenues, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and in kind, amounted to 700l. a-year; but, after that event, were reduced to 150l. chiefly by the alienation of lands and tythes by Alexander Campbell, the first Protestant bishop, to his chieftain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Argyll.—The Culdees had a convent here. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a> was witness to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> made by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> David to his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ABBEY">new <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Dunfermline. In after times, they gave way to the Mathurines <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Friars. The ruins of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, according to Maitland, are still to be seen in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> Wynd.—Here was likewise an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> called Maison de Dieu, founded in 1256, by William de Brechin, for the repose of the souls of the kings William and Alexander; of John earl of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> and Huntingdon his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>; of Henry his father, and Juliana his mother. Albino bishop of Brechin, in the reign of Alexander II. was witness to the grant. By the walls which are yet standing, behind the west end of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> street, it appears to have been an elegant little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a Gothic pile, supported by 12 pillars; is in length 166 feet, in breadth 6x: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is ruinous, and part serves as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The west end of one of the aisles is entire: its door is Gothic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> consists of many <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>; the window of it neat tracery. The steeple is a handsome tower, 120 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the four lower windows in form of long narrow openings; the belfry windows adorned with that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of opening called the quatrefoil: the top battlemented, out of which rises a handsome spire.—At a small Brechin, small distance from the aisle stands one of those singular round towers whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> has so long baffled the conjectures of antiquaries. These towers appear to have been peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; in the last they are frequent; in the former, only two at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> exist. That at Brechin stood originally detached from other buildings. It is at present joined near the bottom by a low additional aisle to the church, which takes in about a sixth of its circumference. From this aisle there is an entrance into it of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, approachable by a few steps, for the use of the ringers; two handsome bells are placed in it, which are got at by means of six ladders placed on wooden semicircular floors, each resting on the circular abutments within side of the tower. The height from the ground to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is 80 feet; the inner diameter, within a few feet of the bottom, is 8 feet; the thickness of the wall at that part, 7 feet 2 inches; so that the whole diameter is 15 feet 2 inches; the circumference very near 48 feet; the inner diameter at top is 8 feet 7 inches; the thickness of the walls 4 feet 6 inches; the circumference, 38 feet 8 inches; which proportion gives the building an inexpressible elegance: the top is roofed with an octagonal spire 23 feet high, which makes the whole 103. In this spire are four windows placed alternately on the sides, resting on the top of the tower; near the top of the tower are four others facing the four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: near the bottom are two arches, one within another, in relief; on the top of the outmost is a crucifixion: between the mouldings of the outmost and inner are two figures; one of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; the other of St John, the cup, and lamb. On each corner of the bottom of this arch is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of certain beasts; one possibly the Caledonian bear; and the other, with a long snout, the boar. The stone-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> within the inner arch has a small slit or peep-hole, but without the appearance of there having been a door within any modern <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; yet there might have been one originally; for the filling up consists of larger <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> than the rest of this curious rotund. The whole is built with most elegant masonry, which Mr Gough observed to be composed of 60 courses.—This tower hath often been observed to vibrate with a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The castle of Brechin was built on an eminence, a little south of the town; it underwent a long siege in the year 1393; was gallantly defended against the English under Edward III.; and, notwithstanding all the efforts of that potent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the brave governor Sir Thomas Maule, ancestor of the family of Panmure, held out this small fortress for 20 days, till he was slain by a stone <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> from an engine on the 20th of August, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was instantly surrendered. The family of Panmure have now a noble house on the site of the old castle.—Brechin is also remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the rebellion raised in 1452, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the earl of Douglas in Stirling castle. The victory fell to the royalists under the earl of Huntly. The malecontents were headed by the earl of Crawford, who, retiring to his castle of Finhaven, in the frenzy of disgrace declared, that he would willingly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> that fell to the share of his antagonist.

BRECKNOCK

Pages 472-472
or Brecon, a town of Brecknockshire in Wales, and capital of the county. It is called by the Welsh Aber Hondey, and is seated at the confluence of the rivers Hondey and Usk, over which there Brecknock is a handsome stone bridge. It is an ancient place, containing three churches, one of which is collegiate, and is seated at the west end of the town. The houses are well built. Here was formerly a stately castle, and a strong wall, through which there were three gates, that are all demolished. It sends one member to parliament. It is well inhabited, which is in some measure owing to its being the town where the assizes are kept; and there is here a considerable woollen manufactory. The markets are well supplied with cattle, corn, and provisions. W. Long. 3. 15. N. Lat. 52. 0.

BRECKNOCKSHIRE

Pages 472-472

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; Cardiganshire and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>, on the west; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, on the east; and by Glamorganshire and Monmouthshire, on the south. It is 35 miles in length, 30 in breadth, about 100 in circumference, and contained 37,735 inhabitants in 1811. It is surrounded with hills, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the valleys pretty temperate. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the hills is very stony, but the streams descending from thence into the valleys render them fruitful both in corn and grass. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities here are corn, cattle, fish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a>'s fur, besides <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth and stockings. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USK">Usk</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, and the Yvron. The chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Brecknock, Bealt, and Hay. Two miles to the east of Brecknock is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, called Brecknock Meer, and by the Welsh Llyn Savaiddan; it is two miles in length, and nearly the same in breadth, and contains otters, tench, &c. The county sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Landaff, and contains 61 parishes, and is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. See Breconshire, Supplement.

BREDA

Pages 472-474

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Dutch Brabant. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, well-built <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, regularly fortified after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way, and is one of the strongest places on the Dutch frontiers. It is seated on the river Merck, in a marshy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which may be overflowed and rendered inaccessible to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is 4000 paces in circumference, and contains upwards of 11,000 inhabitants. The town is of a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the ramparts are all planted round with elms. At every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> there is a gate built with brick. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a noble structure, remarkable for its fine spire, which is 362 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Angelbert II., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, is a curious piece, adorned with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> suitable to the occasion. In 1577, the garrison delivered this city to the states-general; but it was taken in 1581 by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> de Barlaamont, assisted by the baron de Fresin, who was prisoner therein. In 1590, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Maurice took it again from the Spaniards. In 1625 it was invested by Spinola; when it endured a siege too remarkable not to deserve a particular detail. The citadel, which formed the residence of the princes of that family, was surrounded by a ditch of prodigious depth filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a strong wall defended by three great bastions; and the arsenal was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the vast quantities of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores it contained. Spinola, perfectly acquainted with the strength of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, thought he should expose his whole army to immediate destruction, should he attempt an assault before he had regularly carried carried on his approaches. He even resolved upon reducing the city by famine, as the method attended with least danger to his army; and accordingly began with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> trenches round, for the space of four miles, erecting forts and redoubts at certain distances. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the garrison, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> thousand infantry, and several troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, composed of English, French, and Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, took the most vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. The English were under the command of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Morgan, who had frequently distinguished his valour in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the States: the French were directed by Colonel de Hauterive; and the Dutch troops were subject to the immediate orders of Colonel Lohre, though the whole received their instructions from Justin de Nassau, the governor. The first advantage was gained by Baglioni, who seized a large convoy of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and stores coming up the river, converting the boats into a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. This loss dispirited the besieged, and reduced them to a stated allowance of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and what added to their misfortunes, though they were ignorant of it, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Maurice, from whom they were in hopes of receiving relief. Meanwhile Spinola prosecuted the siege with the utmost diligence and vigour. On his pushing his trenches near the bastions, the besieged began a terrible fire to retard his approaches, and kept it up with such vehemence and obstinacy, that Spinola was in hopes they must soon surrender for want of ammunition. But here he formed a false judgment of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of Justin de Nassau, who finding he could not accomplish his purpose by his firing, resolved to try the effect of water. With this view, he stopped up the course of the river Marek; and having formed a large basin of water, opened the sluices, swept away men, horses, and houses, in an inundation, and overflowed the whole country. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> force of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> fell upon Spinola's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and he exerted his utmost ability to remove the consequences. He dug large pits, and cut out ditches and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> to receive the water; but these being filled, and the whole ground covered over, so as to appear one uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of water, served only to entrap his cavalry. The inundation was augmented by the rains which happened to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; a mortality among the soldiers and horses ensued; and of his whole army, Spinola had scarce twelve thousand men fit for service by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. With these inconsiderable remains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of vast extent were to be defended, the works were to be advanced, the sallies from the garrison repulsed, and provisions to be conveyed into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, while Spinola, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, was confined to a sick-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. In the garrison, an epidemical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and scarcity likewise prevailed; but the excellent regulations made, and strictly observed, enabled the town to hold out three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four months beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> expected. The magistrates bought the corn for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>; obliging them to sell the bread to the inhabitants and garrison at a fixed price, and returning the surplus of their pay to the soldiers. A variety of other prudent regulations were established by the magistrates and governor, such as we do not find equalled by any instances recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> upon a similar occasion, and all evincing the steadiness, sagacity, courage, and ability of Justin de Nassau. A kind of rivalry appeared between him and Spinola, which should best fulfil their several duties. The Spanish general caused himself to be carried about the works in a litter; he inspected and directed every thing; and displayed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of full <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at the time his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was in imminent danger from an acute malady. He ordered several breaches in the lines to be repaired. These the Hollanders had made by sap, with a view of introducing succours to the besieged.
