It consists of two suspending ribs, one on each side of the bridge, which are to extend over the whole breadth of the river: if this distance is thought to be too great for one stretch, it is proposed to raise two other ribs on the opposite side, to meet and abut upon one another; on this account a pier is required, upon which the two abutting ends may rest, and as it bears only the perpendicular pressure, it may be so thin, as to make little obstruction to the current of the river. The suspending arch being erected, is to be understood to be of such strength as to bear the bridge suspended to it from the arch; bars descend on each side to which cross beams or bars of iron are fixed on each side of the bridge at proper distances; along these others are extended in a direction across the river, and covered in such a way as to form a passage for carriages and passengers of every description. It has this particular advantage, that it admits of a drawbridge. The advantages proposed by the patentee are: That the span may be greater by this than by other constructions, and that the distances between the abutresses and intermediate pier, may be greater than heretofore, or if more piers are requisite, between pier and pier: more particularly, 1. A bridge of this construction requires less time to execute, it not being subject to the interruption of tides. 2. That it is done at less expense. 3. The ascent is easier. 4. They are not so liable to decay. 5. They may be repaired with more certainty and facility, and at less expense. 6. They will not be subject to the accidents which have destroyed others. 7. They may be erected at any extent, in regard to length and width. 8. They can be secured so as to form one entire piece. 9. They can be preserved in their parts from decays of an accidental nature, and assisted in their durability, by the application of different preservatives. 10. And lastly, It is clearly evident on inspection of the figure, that bridges of this construction, whatever their length be, are in no respect subject to the continual accidents which arise to bridges on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> construction, from currents, tides, swells, inundations, &c. &c. In this bridge, there is much ingenuity displayed; and very considerable advantages attached to the use of it; as it is a level, the passage over it is easy; it being well adapted for a draw-bridge where requisite, renders it worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and in several situations it might be advisable to adopt it; but at the same time, we are not certain, that so many advantages would accrue from the use of it, as is proposed by the patentee; for instance the suspending arch must be raised by scaffolding as well as other arches; and this scaffolding, we apprehend, must be preserved till the whole of the bridge is finished. On the other hand, if piers are to be raised, they may be slender, having only the perpendicular weight to sustain, and will on that account be little interruption to the course of the river. The other patent is obtained by Mr John Nash, architect, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>-street, London, for his invention of an iron bridge, Feb. 7, 1797, on a new and improved construction. What the patentee here proposes, is that in forming the arches and piers for a bridge, in place of archstones, that boxes of cast iron, or plate iron, be formed to the size and figure of the arch stone; and that these boxes be cast with a bottom, or that the bottom may be put in before using. The piers are raised by like boxes, the first row of boxes being laid for the found of the bridge, and fixed to the bed of the river by piles driven into the ground; the boxes are then filled with clay, sand, sand mixed with lime, stone of any kind, small or great, brick, with or without lime; being thus filled, another row of boxes is placed, and bedded as if stone; filled up in the same manner till prepared for throwing the arch. The arch-boxes being prepared as already mentioned, are placed in the same manner as arch-stones are placed in an arch; and being filled as before directed, the arch is completed and formed of solid materials cased with iron; and that iron may not abut on iron, he proposes plates of lead laid between each box, and in this manner the bridge is finished, forming one solid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> cased with iron. In some parts of this, and other countries, the situation is such, that neither stone nor lime can be procured, but at an enormous expense; in such a situation the invention would be meritorious; as a bridge could be erected forming a convenient passage, the boxes being filled with such earthy or stony materials as the place could supply, and if filled with small or round stones, the interstices might be filled with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, to render them solid. In some places so situated, that although stone is to be got in quantity and quality sufficient, yet lime cannot easily be procured, the invention might succeed; but we suppose that when both stone and lime can be procured, few would think of casing it with iron, which is less durable than stone, when constantly exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, in wet and dry. A body of solid iron is very different from a thin plate, exposed on both sides to materials different from itself. We come now to the description of the greatest undertaking of this kind, that ever graced the British annals, or was accomplished in Europe or the world, that we have accounts of, except in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, as formerly mentioned. The London Bridge, which, though clumsily This interesting project has so far engaged the attention of the legislature, that a select committee has been appointed of such members as were no ways concerned in any of the plans brought forward; they have made three valuable reports, that respecting this bridge being contained in the third report, viz. the rebuilding of London bridge, by which colliers, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> vessels, and all vessels of light burdens, are to be admitted to pass the new London bridge, and to ship and discharge goods immediately at wharfs, and warehouses, to be constructed along the banks of the river, and opposite to the centre of the city; for which purpose this new bridge is to be formed of cast iron 65 feet high, clear above high water, with inclined planes connecting it with the present streets, and such other improvements as may grow out of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. The bed of the river is to be deepened, so as to admit ships of 200 tons lying afloat at low water; and that no encroachment may be made on the property of those connected with the shore, it is proposed to contract the course of the river to 600 feet, according to Mr Jesson's report, by which room will be procured for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, or wharfs and warehouses. The plan of the bridge is projected by Messrs Telford and Douglas; the span 600 feet, equal to the width of the river when contracted, which is now accomplished, and we understand the plan is far advanced in the execution; but a plan of so great extent must be subject to many unavoidable interruptions. A short account of the plan of the bridge will not be unacceptable to our readers, as it will enable them to form a more perfect judgment of this magnificent structure. The whole is of cast iron, which is less liable to corrode than hammered iron; the ribs are cast in as large portions, as can conveniently be moulded; they are connected together by cross and diagonal tie-braces, in such a manner, that any of the pieces of the ribs or braces can be taken out, and replaced, without injuring the whole, or interrupting the passage, thus the bridge can be kept in repair with ease, and convenience; all the frames are so connected vertically and horizontally, from the soffit of the arch to the roadway, that the whole will act as one solid frame; and are so disposed from the middle of the arch, to the abutment, as to give a greater width to the bridge at entrance from the shore, from the different inclined planes, which enter to the bridge from three different directions, by which the public will be accommodated by three different bridges, as to entrance and egress. The inclined planes which afford entrance to the bridge from the shore, and streets, will give ample room for warehouses, vaults, and other conveniences for depositing the goods, before they can be put on board, or after they are unshipped, till they can be conveniently carried off by the proprietors. We come now, as proposed, to ascertain the strength of an abutment that will support, or counteract the pressure of any number of arches, abutting upon one another, in the manner we have proposed. Throw up the contents of the number of feet in all the arch-stones, from the one end of the bridge to the other; divide this between the two abutments, and find what base is necessary to contain a number of feet equal to the half, upon each pier from the spring of the arch to the height of the road-way, with one-fourth or one-third added, for allowance made for superincumbent weight upon the bridge, or any default in equilibration or otherways, care being always taken to secure a proper found to abutments. To find the abutments of iron bridges, being of so great extent as those now raised, or may be raised; take a base that will contain a weight of stone, equal to half the weight of the bridge from the spring to the road-way, with what is thought necessary to add for extra weight upon the bridge; here it is still more necessary to attend to a proper found, and further it may be necessary in large arches of stone, or an iron arch, to bolt the stones together according to Mr Mylne's method; as the great pressure is laid upon them before the cement has fastened the stones, this may be the cause of the failure in the abutment in the Shropshire bridges, and also of others. Such magnificent structures are worthy of every attention. We have already treated, and we hope with satisfaction to our readers, of the principles upon which this theory is founded. We shall now adduce some undeniable instances, from the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> and ancient architects. First, upon a small scale, we find vaults thrown, of 8, 10, or more feet, of arches abutting upon one another, upon thin walls; some not exceeding 10 inches, and 6 feet in height; and arches from 18 to 20 feet, the supporting wall from which the arch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> not exceeding 14 inches, the arches below the semicircle, the main abutments being of sufficient strength. Upon a larger scale, in the Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, it has universally been practised to support the arches by abutments on the outside of the wall, but not without exception, and where this exception has been made, we find the arch equally well secured, and with much superior grandeur and elegance. In that superb structure of Gothic architecture, St Giles's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of the High Church, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, the steeple stands upon four columns, not stronger in proportion to its weight than the six feet pier we propose for an arch of 75 feet span; this central part of the building is supported by the parts to the east and west, and by arcades, forming aisles in the other direction, none of them exceeding half its height or thereby; it rises above them with its majestic head, adorned with an imperial crown; and for supporting the stately arches that form this crown, no outside abutments are prepared; in this, the exception above referred to consists; it seems as if by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> intended for the support of our theory. The weight is laid upon the shoulder at the spring of the arch, but with so much elegance as if it were only intended to form an ornamental part of the proposed figure; and under the appearance of an ornament concealing its real use. Some of the arch-stones likewise are projected outward, in the horizontal direction, ornamented at their extremity, and, at the same time that they enrich the crown with an additional ornament, they are a counterpoise to the arch at that place. To complete the con- Bridge. ception, to adorn the proposed figure throughout, and to finish a well proportioned and elegant crown, the summit is put upon it, at the same time securing the keystone, which without this precaution would by the side pressure have sprung upwards, and have brought the whole arches to ruin. That these arches are as well protected by the weight placed at the spring of the arch, as any that are supported by abutments, we need only as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> produce their stability, in resisting, notwithstanding of its great height and exposure in situation, the boisterous effects of the elements, and the concussion arising from the vibration of large bells, suspended in it, and so frequently rung. From the principles formerly laid down, and the authority now adduced in support of our theory, we hope that it has received ample <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>. And we venture to conclude, that we have pointed out a method to every mason, and engineer, how in drawing his plan, he may be able to ascertain the weight to be laid on the shoulder of his arch, to counterpoise the weight, according to the intended span, and what thickness he has occasion to make his pier, without encumbering it, not only with useless matter, but what is materially injurious to the strength of his bridge, by choking the current, and causing it act with ten times more force upon it, than it otherwise would do, as we have formerly shown. We cannot pass the instance of ancient architecture last mentioned, without observing what attention has been paid to the principles of equilibration; and, although the architects have not communicated the principles upon which they executed their plans, they give evident proofs of their having followed some regular theory. Can we suppose that the projector of St Giles's church, Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, and innumerable others, could have produced such elegant and well-proportioned structures accidentally, without a well regulated principle to act upon, or that the projector of this imperial crown we have been describing, had not thoroughly digested all its parts and ornaments, before it began to be erected. The ancient architects have, however, thought proper to leave to posterity to collect their principles from the works that have been executed. The moderns are actuated with more liberality of sentiment, in laying down their principles, as well as executing their projects, many of which will do honour to the age, and leave posterity both principles and examples to follow and improve upon. After having treated upon the rise and progress of bridges, from what we know, from the most early periods, it may appear somewhat awkward that the foundation is neglected, and the manner of preparing; but when it is considered that this must be regulated by the superstructure to be raised upon it; that although it must be the first part with which we begin, it must be the last in the plan, and in founding a bridge there is indeed much to be considered; and as we propose to offer some methods for founding, which so far as we know have not appeared, we will be attentive to lay them before our readers, under the article Foundation. We have described bridges of different materials, but have mentioned none of wood; this will come properly to offer itself under the article Centre, in which we intend to offer some concise and simple construction, and some forms of wooden bridges, that in point of elegance and strength, may not only vie with, but supersede the use of iron bridges in many instances. From the spring of the arch (fig. 10.), parallel lines are drawn from the divisions of the arch, to the perpendicular db, being each two feet at the outer part of the arch-stone. These divisions are marked in the figure 1, 2, 3, &c.; the measures of each of these lines are inserted in column 2d; the first and second are added together as marked in column 1st, their sum is inserted in column 3d, the half or arithmetical mean in column 4th. In the same manner the 2d and 3d, the 3d and 4th, &c. The sum of the means when added make 72.75, being each 2 feet distant; 143.5 superficial feet × 3 in depth is 436.5 solid feet; but as these parallel divisions decrease in breadth as they ascend from the spring of the arch, the mean deficiency in solid measure, as above, in the work, 3937.5, being deducted from the 436.5, leaves the remainder 436.1 solid feet. Between the 10th and 13th division the deficiency is greater, as above, amounting to 265.5 solid feet, to be deducted from 229.5; there remains 226.845 solid feet, which, added to 436.1 is 662.945, the resisting force, to counteract the lateral pressure of the arch-stones 374.75, reckoned from a; but reckoned from c, which the counterpoise is raised to, there being only 25 divisions, the lateral pressure only amounts to 347.55 solid feet, little more than one half of the opposing force. The arch then must be sufficiently secured without any addition to the pier, more than furnishing a base for this weight. We have chosen to express both forces by solid feet, in place of weight, as the weight will differ according to the quality of the stone; whereas the solid foot is applicable to every quality of stone of which an arch is raised, stones from the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> being nearly of the same specific gravity, and of consequence a solid foot will be as nearly of the same weight. If from different quarries, the weight of a solid foot of each can be easily ascertained. The above table, and work of means and deficiency, we might have expressed in algebraic and fluxionary equations, the small increment of deficiency being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>. We should have had the appearance of being more learned, but whether we should have been more useful to the generality of our readers, we leave them to judge; but we think it becoming in every learned man, to express himself so, as to be universally understood. See the article BRIDGE in the Supplement.

BRIDGE

Pages 509-509

in Music, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a stringed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> over which the strings are stretched. The bridge of a violin is about one inch and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and near an inch and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Bridge-Town, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Barbadoes, situated in W. Long. 61°, N. Lat. 13°. It stands in the inmost part of Carlisle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. This originally was a most unwholesome situation, and was chosen entirely for its convenience for trade; but is now deemed to be as healthy as any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the island. The town itself would make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in any European <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is said to contain 1500 houses, and some contend that it is the finest the British possess in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The houses in general are well built and finished, and their rents as high as such houses would let for in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The wharfs and quays are well defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and very convenient. The harbour is secured from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which is the constant trade-wind there; and Carlisle bay is capable of containing 500 ships, and is formed by Needham and Pelican <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. But what renders Bridge-town the finest and most desirable town in the West Indies, is its security against any attacks from foreign enemies. It is defended on the westward by James-fort, which mounts 18 guns. Near this is Willoughby's fort, which is built upon a tongue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> running into the sea, and mounts 12 guns. Needham's fort has three batteries, and is mounted with 20 guns; and St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s fort, which is the strongest in the island, stands more within land. In short, according to Mr Douglas, there is all along the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-shore, a breastwork and trench, in which, at proper places, were 29 forts and batteries, having 328 cannon mounted, while the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> shore is secured by high rocks, steep cliffs, and foul ground. Such was the state of the fortifications in 1717; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they have been much strengthened. Bridgetown is destitute of few elegancies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conveniences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> that any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> can afford. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Michael exceeds many English cathedrals in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, largeness, and conveniency; and has a fine organ, bells, and clock. Here also is a free-school for the instruction of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> boys, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The latter was erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for propagating the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, in pursuance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Christopher Codrington, who left about 2000l. a-year for its endowment, for maintaining professors and scholars to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and practise <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, and physic. See CODRINGTON.

BRIDGENORTH

Pages 509-510

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a> in England, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, which divides it into two parts; but they are united by a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and these are called the upper and the lower town. It is said to have been built by Ethelfleda, widow of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Mercians, about the year 675. Robert de Belizma, son of Robert de <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>, built the castle, and maintained it against King Henry I., by which means it was forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and remained so till the reign of Richard III., who gave it to John Sutton <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>. This town has undergone several sieges; and in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> it suffered very much, many fine buildings, and the whole town, being almost destroyed by fire, when Sir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Kirke defended the citadel for King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. There are now no other remains of the castle than a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the towers, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> yet called the castle, within the walls of the old one; within which stands one of the churches, dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Magdalen, which was made a free chapel, and exempted from episcopal jurisdiction. The other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the town, on the highest part of the hill, near to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> stood a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which was destroyed by fire in the civil wars, together with the church <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned; which has been since rebuilt by the inhabitants. In this town is a free-school which sends and maintains eighteen scholars at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. On the west banks of the river are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and magnificent convent, under which were several remarkable vaults and caverns running to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length. length. Part of the Cowgate street is a rock, rising perpendicularly, in which are several houses and tenements that form a very agreeable though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a>. In many other places there are also caves and dwellings for families in the rocks; and indeed the whole town has a very singular appearance. This town sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 4179 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 30. N. Lat. 52. 40.

BRIDGEWATER

Pages 510-510

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in England, seated on the river Parret, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, near which ships of 100 tons burden may ride with ease. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well frequented <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. There are in it several large inns, and the market is well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 4911 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 0. N. Lat. 51. 15.

BRIDLE

Pages 510-510

in the manege, a contrivance made of straps <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, in order to keep a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> in subjection and obedience. The several parts of a bridle are the bit or snaffle; the head-stall, or leathers from the top of the head to the rings of the bit; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, over the fore-head and under the fore-top; the throat-band, which buttons from the head-band under the throat; the reins, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> thongs of leather that come from the rings of the bit, and being <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> over the horse's head, the rider holds them in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; the nose-band, going through loops at the back of the head-stall, and buckled under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>; the trench; the covesan; the martingal; and the chaff-halter. Pliny assures us that one Pelethronius first invented the bridle and saddle; though <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> ascribes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to the Lapithae, to whom he gives the epithet Pelethronii, from a mountain in Thessaly named Pelethronium, where horses were first begun to be broken. The first horsemen, not being acquainted with the art of governing horses with bridles, managed them only with a rope or a switch, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. This was the practice of the Numidians, Getolians, Libyans, and Massilians. The Roman youth also learned the art of fighting without bridles, which was an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> or lesson in the manege; and hence it is, that on Trajan's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are represented riding at full speed without any bridles on. Scolding BRIDLE. See BRANK.

BRIDLINGTON

Pages 510-510

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in the east riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in England. It is seated on a creek of the sea near Flamborough-head, having a commodious quay for ships to take in their lading. It has a safe harbour, and contained 3731 inhabitants in 1811. It is more generally known by the name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, as it gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of that name, though the earldom is now extinct. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 10. N. Lat. 54. 15.

BRIDON

Pages 510-510
or SNAPPLE, after the English fashion, is a very slender bit-mouth without any branches. The English make great use of them, and scarcely use any true bridles except in the service of war. The French call them bridons, by way of distinction from bridles.

BRIDPORT

Pages 510-510

a seaport town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in England. It has a low situation between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which unite a little lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Its inhabitants amounted to 3666 in 1814. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, who are chosen by the inhabitants who are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-keepers. It is noted for making of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> for shipping; whence arises a proverb of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that is hanged, that he is stabbed with a Bridport dagger. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 0. N. Lat. 50. 40.

BRIEF

Pages 510-510

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ issued from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, directed to any judge-ordinary, commanding and authorizing that judge to call a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> to inquire into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> mentioned in the brief, and upon their verdict to pronounce <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. Apostolical BRIEFS, letters which the pope dispatches to princes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other magistrates, relating to any public affair.—These briefs are distinguished from bulls, in regard the latter are more ample, and always written on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, and sealed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or green wax; whereas briefs are very concise, written on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, sealed with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wax, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of a fisherman, or St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>.

BRIEG

Pages 510-510

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> in Germany, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 35. N. Lat. 50. 40. It might have passed for a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> before the last siege; the castle, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and the arsenal, being very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ornaments, and most of the houses very well built. But the Prussians, who besieged it in 1741, threw 2172 bombs into it, and 4714 cannon bullets, which reduced a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town to ashes, and quite ruined a wing of the castle. It was obliged to surrender, after sustaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days continual fire. The Prussians, to whom this place was ceded by the peace, have augmented the fortifications, and built a new suburb.—The town stands upon the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>; on the other side of which there are plenty of fallow-deer, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forests of beech and oak trees. They have a yearly fair, at which they sell above 12,000 horned cattle. Since 1728, they have begun to manufacture fine cloth.

BRIEL

Pages 510-510

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of the United Provinces, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Veorn. It was one of the cautionary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> which were delivered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and garrisoned by the English during her reign and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the next. The Dutch took it from the Spaniards in 1572, which was the foundation of their republic. It is seated at the mouth of the river Meuse, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 56. N. Lat. 52. 53.

BRIESCIA

Pages 510-510

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Lithuania, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. The name given to it by some is Polesia. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Novogrode, and Troki; on the west, by those of Bielsko and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUBLIN">Lublin</a>; on the south by that of Chelm and Upper Volhnia; and on the east, by the territory of Rzeczica. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from east to west, and is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Bug and Pripose: it is full of woods and marshes; and there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> that yield <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fish, that are salted by the inhabitants, and sent into the neighbouring provinces.

BRIEUX

Pages 510-511

ST, a town of France, in Upper Brittany, now called the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">Coast</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated in a bottom, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which deprive it of a prospect of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, though it is not above a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from from it, and there forms a small port. The churches, streets, and squares, are tolerably handsome; but the town is without walls and ditches. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Michael is in the suburb of the same name, and is the largest in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The convent of the Cordeliers is well built, and the garden is spacious. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which is very near, is maintained by the town for the instruction of youth. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 6250 in 1815. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 58. N. Lat. 48. 33.

BRIG

Pages 511-511
or BRIGANTINE, a merchant-ship with two masts. This term is not universally confined to vessels of a particular construction, or which are masted and rigged in a manner different from all others. It is variously applied, by the mariners of different European nations, to a peculiar sort of vessel of their own marine. Amongst British seamen, this vessel is distinguished by having her main-sails set nearly in the plane of her keel; whereas the main sails of larger ships are hung athwart, or at right angles with the ship's length, and fastened to a yard which hangs parallel to the deck: but in a brig, the foremost edge of the mainsail is fastened in different places to hoops which encircle the mainmast, and slide up and down it as the sail is hoisted or lowered: it is extended by a gaff above and a boom below.

BRIGADE

Pages 511-511

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a party <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a body of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or foot, under the command of a brigadier.—An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> is divided into brigades of horse and brigades of foot: a brigade of horse is a body of eight or ten squadrons; a brigade of foot consists of four, five, or six battalions. The eldest brigade has the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the first line; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the right of the second; the two next take the left of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and the youngest stand in the centre. BRIGADE-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, is an officer appointed by the brigadier, to assist him in the management and ordering of his brigade.

BRIGADIER

Pages 511-511

is the general officer who has the command of a brigade. The eldest colonels are generally advanced to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>. He that is upon duty is brigadier of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> at the head of their own brigades, and are allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> and ten men of their own brigade for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>.—But the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of brigadier-general in the British <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is now abolished.

BRIGANDINE

Pages 511-511

a coat of mail, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> defensive armour, consisting of thin pointed scales of plate, pliant and easy to the body.

BRIGANTES

Pages 511-511

(Tacitus), a people of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, reaching from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to sea, the whole breadth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>). Now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> (Camden.) Also a people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, of uncertain position.

BRIGANTIA

Pages 511-511
or BRIGANTIUM, in Ancient Geography, a town of Vindelicia; now Bregenz, in Tyrol, at the east end of the lake of Constance.—Another Brigantium in the Alpes Cottiae; which last is probably Briancon, a town on the borders of Dauphiny.

BRIGANTINUS LACUS

Pages 511-511

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a lake of Rhaetia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Vindelicin, which Tacitus includes in Rhaetia. Ammian calls the lake Brigantia. It took its name either from the Brigantii, the people Brigantinus inhabiting on it, or from the adjoining town. Now the lake of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> or Bodensee. BRIGANTINUS Portus, in Ancient Geography, a port of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; so called from Flavius Brigantium. Now El Puerto de la Corunna, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the Grogne.

BRIGG

Pages 511-511

by some called Clamford Bridges, a town of England, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, seated on the river Anka. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 20. N. Lat. 53. 40.

BRIGGS

Pages 511-511

William, an eminent physician in the latter end of the 17th century, was the son of Augustin Briggs, Esq. four times member for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, where our author was born. He studied at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and his genius leading him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic, he travelled into France, where he attended the lectures of the famous anatomist M. Vieussens at Montpelier. After his return, he published his Ophthalmographia in 1676. The year following he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine at Cambridge, and soon after was made fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1682, he quitted his fellowship to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>; and the same year, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of Vision was published by Hooke. The ensuing year he sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> a continuation of that discourse, which was published in their Transactions; and the same year, he was by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. appointed physician to St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. In 1684, he communicated to the Royal Society two remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> relating to vision, which were likewise printed in their Transactions; and in 1685 he published a Latin version of his Theory of Vision, at the desire of Mr Newton, afterwards Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Cambridge, with a recommendatory epistle from him pre-

BRIGHTHELMSTONE

Pages 511-512

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> in England. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous town, has a pretty good harbour, and contained 12,012 inhabitants in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 10'. N. Lat. 50° 50'. It was at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. embarked for France in 1651, after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. It has lately been considerably extended and embellished, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its having become a place of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>. It is a favourite residence of the present king.

BRIGITTINS

Pages 512-512
or BRIDGETINS, more properly Brigittins, a religious order, denominated from their founder, St Bridget or Birgit, a Swedish lady in the 14th century; whom some represent as a queen; but Fabricius, on better grounds, as a princess, the daughter of King Birgenes, legislator of Upland, and famous for her revelations. The Brigittins are sometimes also called the Order of our Saviour; it being pretended, that Christ himself dictated the rules and constitutions observed by them to St Bridget. In the main, the rule is that of St Augustin; only with certain additions supposed to have been revealed by Christ, whence they also denominate it the Rule of our Saviour.—The first monastery of the Bridgetin order was erected by the foundress about the year 1344, in the diocese of Linconen; on the model of which all the rest were formed. The constitution of these houses was very singular: though the order was principally intended for nuns, who were to pay a special homage to the holy Virgin, there are also many friars of it, to minister to them spiritual assistance. The number of nuns is fixed at 60 in each monastery, and that of friars to 13, answerable to the number of apostles, of whom St Paul made the 13th; besides which there are to be four deacons, to represent the four doctors of the church, St Ambrose, St Augustin, St Gregory, and St Jerome; and eight lay-brothers; making together, says our author, the number of Christ's 72 disciples.—The order being instituted in honour of the Virgin, the direction is committed to an abbess, who is superior not only of the nuns, but also of the friars, who are obliged to obey her. Each house consists of two convents or monasteries, separately enclosed, but having one church in common; the nuns being placed above, and the friars on the ground. The Bridgetins profess great mortification, poverty, and self-denial, as well as devotion; and they are not to possess any thing they can call their own, not so much as a half-penny; nor even to touch money on any account. This order spread much through Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands, &c. In England we read but of one monastery of Brigittins, and this built by Henry V. in 1415, opposite to Richmond, now called Sion house; the ancient inhabitants of which, since the dissolution, are settled at Lisbon. The revenues were reckoned at £495l. per annum.

BRIGNOLES

Pages 512-512

a town of France, in the department of Var, formerly Provence, famous for its prunes. It is seated among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in a pleasant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 275 miles S. S. E. of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and had 9000 inhabitants in 1815. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 15'. N. Lat. 43° 24'.

BRIHUEGA

Pages 512-512

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in New Castile, where General Stanhope with the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were taken prisoners, after they had separated themselves from that commanded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Staremberg. It is seated at the foot of the mountain Tajuna, 43 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 20'. N. Lat. 41° 0'.

BRILL

Pages 512-512

MATTHEW and PAUL, natives of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and good painters.—Matthew was born in the year 1550, and studied for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> at Rome. He was eminent for his performances in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and landscape, in the galleries of the Vatican; where he was employed by Pope Gregory XIII. He died in 1584, being no more than 34 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—Paul was born in 1554; followed his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Matthew to Rome; painted several things in conjunction with him; and, after his decease, brought himself into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by his landscapes, but especially by those which he composed in his latter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of them was more pleasing, the disposition more noble, all the parts more tender, agreeable, and painted with a better gusto than his earlier productions in this way; which was owing to his having studied the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> Carrache, and copied some of Titian's works in the same kind. He was much in favour with Pope Sixtus V.; and for his successor Clement VIII., painted the famous piece, about 68 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, wherein the saint of that name is represented <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> about his neck. He died at Rome the year 1626, aged 72.

BRILLIANT

Pages 512-512

in the Ménage. A brisk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-metalled stately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is called brilliant, as having a raised neck, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and excellent haunches, upon which he rises, though ever so little put on.

BRILLIANTS

Pages 512-512

a name given to diamonds of the finest cut. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">DIAMOND</a>.

BRIM

Pages 512-512

M denotes the outmost verge <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> edge, especially of round things. The brims of vessels are made to project a little over, to hinder liquors, in pouring out, from running <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the side of the vessel. The briming of vessels was contrived by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> potters, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the supercilium or drip of the cornices of columns: it is done by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> over some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is on the wheel.

BRIN

Pages 512-512

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and well built: the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states is held alternately there and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLMUTZ">Olmutz</a>. The castle of Spilberg is on an eminence, out of the town, and is its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It was invested by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1742, but he was obliged to raise the siege. It is near the river Swart, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 8'. N. Lat. 49° 8'.

BRINDISI

Pages 512-514

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> celebrated town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Terra d'<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, with an archbishop's see. Its walls are still of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; but the inhabited houses do not fill above half the enclosure. The streets are crooked and rough; the buildings <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and ruinous; no very remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> edifice. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, dedicated to St Theodore, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Roger, but not equal in point of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> to many churches founded by that monarch, who had a strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Little remains of ancient Brundusium, except innumerable broken pillars fixed at the corners of streets to defend the houses from carts; fragments of coarse mosaic, the floors of former habitations; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> marble basin, into which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> runs from brazen heads of deer; some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, coins, and other small furniture of an antiquary's cabinet. Its castle, built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederick II., to protect the northern branches of the harbour is large and stately. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. repaired it. The port is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and the finest in the Adriatic. The outer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is formed by two promontories, which stretch off gradually from each other as they advance into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, leaving a very narrow channel at the base of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Andrew, on which Alphonsus I. built a fortress, lies between the capes, and secures the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from the fury of the waves. In this triangular space, large ships may ride at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. At the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> the hills recede in a semicircular shape, to leave room for the inner haven; which, as it were, clasps the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in its arms, or rather encircles it, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a stag's head and horns. This form is said to have given rise to the name of Brundusium, which, in the old Messapian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signified the head of a deer. In ancient days, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the two havens was marked by lights placed upon columns of the Corinthian order, standing on a rising ground, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line with the channel. Of these one remains entire upon its pedestal. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is adorned with figures of Syrens and Tritons, intermingled with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACANTHUS">acanthus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and upon it a circular vase, which formerly held the fire. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> inscription has been cut upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a>. Near it is another pedestal of similar dimensions, with one piece of the shaft lying on it. The space between these pillars answered to the entrance of the harbour. The whole kingdom of Naples (says Mr Swinburne) cannot show a more complete situation for trade than Brindisi. Here goodness of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, depth of water, safety of anchorage, and a central position, are all united; yet it has neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, husbandry, nor populousness. From the obstructions in the channel which communicates with the two havens, arises the tribe of evils that afflict and desolate this unhappy town. Julius Caesar may be said to have begun its ruin, by attempting to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> up Pompey's fleet. He drove piles into the neck of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> between the two ridges of hills; threw in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, trees, and ruins of houses; and had nearly accomplished the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a>, when Pompey sailed out and escaped to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. In the 16th century, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARANTO">Taranto</a> sunk some ships in the middle of the passage, to prevent the royalists from entering the port, and thereby provided a resting <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for sea weeds and sand, which soon accumulated, choked up the mouth, and rendered it impracticable for any vessels whatsoever. In 1752 the evil was increased, so as to hinder even the waves from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> through; and all communication was cut off, except in violent easterly winds, or rainy seasons, when an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh water raises the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. From that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the port became a fetid green lake, full of infection and noxious insects; no fish but eels could live in it, nor any boats ply except canoes made of a single tree. They can hold but one person, and overset with the least irregularity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The low grounds at each end were overflowed and converted into marshes, the vapours of which created every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> a real pestilence; and in the course of very few years, swept off or drove away the largest portion of the inhabitants. From the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eighteen thousand, they were reduced in 1766 to that of five thousand livid wretches, tormented with agues and malignant fevers. In 1775 above fifteen hundred persons died during the autumn; a woeful change of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>! Thirty years ago, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Brindisi was esteemed so wholesome and balsamic, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of Naples were wont to send their consumptive friars to this city for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. This state of misery and destruction induced the remaining citizens to apply for relief to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Carlo Demarco, one of the king's ministers, and a native of Brindisi. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this application, Don Vito Caravelli was ordered to draw up plans, and fix upon the means of opening the port afresh: Don Andrea Pigonati was last year sent to execute his projects; and, by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and the labour of galley-slaves, has succeeded in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. The channel has been partly cleared, and has now two fathom of water. It can admit large boats, a great step towards the revival of trade; but what is of more immediate importance, it gives a free passage to the sea, which now rushes in with impetuosity, and runs out again at each tide; so that the water of the inner port is set in motion, and once more rendered wholesome. The canal or gut is to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred yards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and drawn in a straight line from the column. At present its parapets are defended by piles and fascines; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the original <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> be pursued, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> piers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be erected on both sides. When the canal shall be scooped out to a proper depth, and its piers solidly established, vessels of any burden may once more enter this land-locked port, which affords room for a whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. Docks wet and dry may be dug, goods may be shipped at the quay, and convenient watering-places be made with great ease. If <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> should think it a place of rising trade, and worthy of their notice, there is no want of space in the town for any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> whatever. Circulation of cash would give vigour to husbandry, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> would soon abound in this market. The sands at the foot of the hills, which form the channel, are to be laid out in beds for muscles and oysters. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> are raising nurseries of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and lemon trees; and other citizens intend introducing the cultivation of mulberry-trees, and brooding of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The engineer would have done very little for the health of Brindisi, had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> only opened a passage, and given a free course to the waters; the marshes at each extremity of the harbour would still have infected the air; he, therefore, at the expense of about a thousand ducats, had the fens filled up with earth, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> raised to con- Brindisi, line the waters, and prevent their flowing back upon Brindisi the meadows. The people of Brindisi, who are sensible of the blessings already derived from these operations, who feel a return of health, and see an opening for commerce and opulence, seem ready to acknowledge the obligation. They intend to erect a statue to the king, with inscriptions on the pedestal in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the minister and agents. The workmen, in cleaning the channel, have found some medals and seals, and have drawn up many of the piles that were driven in by Caesar. They are small oaks stripped of their bark, and still as fresh as if they had been cut only a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, though buried above eighteen centuries seven feet under the sand. The soil about the town is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and good. It produces excellent cotton, with which the Brindisians manufacture gloves and stockings. "It is impossible to determine who were the founders of Brundusium, or when it was first inhabited. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> took early possession of a harbour so convenient for their enterprises against the nations dwelling beyond the Adriatic. In the year of Rome 509, they sent a colony thither. Pompey took refuge here; but finding his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> untenable, made a precipitate retreat to Greece. In this city Octavian first assumed the name of Caesar, and here he concluded one of his short-lived peaces with Antony. Brundusium had been already celebrated for giving birth to the tragic poet Pacuvius, and about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> became remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. The barbarians, who ravaged every corner of Italy, did not spare so rich a town; and, in 836, the Saracens gave a finishing blow to its fortune. The Greek emperors, sensible of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of having such a port as this in Italy, would have restored it to its ancient strength and splendour, had the Normans allowed them time and leisure. The Greeks struggled manfully to keep their ground; but, after many varieties of success, were finally driven out of Brindisi by William I. The frenzy for expeditions to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, though it drained other kingdoms of their wealth and subjects, contributed powerfully to the re-establishment of this city, one of the ports where pilgrims and warriors took shipping. It was also benefited by the residence of the emperor Frederick, whose frequent armaments for the Holy Land required his presence at this place of rendezvous. The loss of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Grecian empire, and the ruin of all the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> trade after the Turks had conquered the East, reduced Brindisi to a state of inactivity and desolation, from which it has never been able to emerge." E. Long. 18. 5. N. Lat. 40. 52.

BRINDLEY

Pages 514-515

James, a most uncommon genius for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> inventions, and particularly excellent in planning and conducting inland navigations, was born, in 1716, at Tunsted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>: Through the mismanagement of his father (for there was some little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>) his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was totally neglected; and, at seventeen, he bound himself apprentice to a mill-wright, near Macclesfield, in Cheshire. He served his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>, and, afterwards, setting up for himself, advanced the mill-wright business, by inventions and contrivances of his own, to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection which it had not attained before. His fame, as a most ingenious mechanic, spreading widely, his genius was no longer confined to the business of his profession: for, in 1752, he erected a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-engine at Clifton, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, for the purpose of draining coal-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and, in 1755, was employed to execute the larger <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> for a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> mill, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGLETON">Congleton</a>, in Cheshire. The potteries of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> were also, about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, indebted to him for several valuable additions in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> used by them for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> flint-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. In 1756, he undertook to erect a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> under Line upon a new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; and it is believed that he would have brought this engine to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree of perfection, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> some interested engineers had not opposed him. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, however, was soon afterwards called off to another object, which, in its consequences, hath proved of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> importance to trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; namely, the projecting and executing "Inland navigations." By these navigations the expense of carriage is lessened; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> is opened from one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to another, and from each of these parts to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and hence products and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are afforded at a moderate price. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bridgewater hath, at Worsley, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estate abounding with coal, which had hitherto lain useless, because the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-carriage was too great to find a market for consumption. The duke, wishing to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> these mines, perceived the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a canal from Worsley to Manchester; upon which occasion Brindley, now become famous, was consulted; and declaring the scheme practicable, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> for this purpose was obtained in 1758 and 1759. It being, however, afterwards discovered, that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> would be more beneficial, if carried over the river Irwell to Manchester, another act was obtained to vary the course of the canal agreeably to the new plan, and likewise to extend a side-branch to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGFORD">Longford</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> in Stretford. Brindley, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, had begun these great works, being the first of the kind ever attempted in England, with navigable subterraneous tunnels and elevated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>; and as, in order to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water, it should be free from the usual obstructions of locks, he carried the canal over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and many large and deep valleys. When it was completed as far as Barton, where the Irwell is navigable for large vessels, he proposed to carry it over that river, by an aqueduct of thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet above the surface of the water; and though this project was treated as wild and chimerical, yet, supported by his noble <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, he began his work in Sept. 1760, and the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> sailed over it in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1761. The duke afterwards extended his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>; and obtained, in 1762, an act for branching his canal to the tideway in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>; this part of the canal is carried over the rivers Mersey and Bolland, and over many wide and deep valleys. The success of the duke of Bridgewater's undertakings encouraged a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gentlemen and manufacturers in Staffordshire, to revive the idea of a canal-navigation through that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and Brindley was, therefore, engaged to make a survey from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> to the Mersey. In 1766, this canal was begun, and conducted under Brindley's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived; but finished after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Mr. Marshall, of whom he had a great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, in May 1777. The proprietors called it, "the canal from the Trent to the Mersey;" but the engineer, more emphatically, "the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">Trunk</a> Navigation," Brindley, on account of the numerous branches, which, as he justly supposed, would be extended every way from it. It is 93 miles in length; and, besides a large number of bridges over it, has 76 locks and five tunnels. The most remarkable of the tunnels is the subterraneous passage of Harecastle, being 2880 yards in length, and more than 70 yards below the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The scheme of this inland-navigation had employed the thoughts of the ingenious part of the kingdom for upwards of 20 years before; and some surveys had been made: but Harecastle hill, through which the tunnel is constructed, could neither be avoided nor overcome by any expedient the most able engineers could <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a>. It was Brindley alone who surmounted this and other the like difficulties, arising from the variety of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> and quicksands, as no one but himself would have attempted to conquer. Brindley was engaged in many other similar undertakings; for a fuller account of which, not being consistent with our plan, we refer the reader to the "Biographia Britannica;" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather to a curious and valuable pamphlet, published some years since, and entitled, "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inland Navigations, particularly that of the duke of Bridgewater." He died at Turnhurst in Staffordshire, September 27, 1772, in his 56th year; somewhat immaturely, as it should seem; but he is supposed to have shortened his days by too intense application, and to have brought on a hectic fever, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on him for some years before it consumed him. For he never indulged and relaxed himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> diversions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as not having the least relish for them; and though once prevailed on to see a play in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, yet he declared that he would on no account be present at another; because it so disturbed his ideas for several days after, as to render him unfit for business.
