As it was feared that a dissolution of parliament would instantly take place, the house resolved, upon the motion of the honourable Thomas Erskine, That they would consider any person as an enemy to his country, who should advise his majesty, in any manner, to interrupt their discharging the important duty of providing a remedy for the abuses which prevailed in the East Indies. They also resolved to form themselves into a committee on the state of the nation on Monday the 22d. In the mean while, on Wednesday the 17th of December, Mr Fox's India bill was rejected in the house of lords, on a division of 95 to 76, and, at 12 o'clock on the night of the 18th, a message was delivered to the secretaries of state, requiring them to transmit to his majesty the change of seals of their offices, by the under secretaries, as a personal sonal interview would be disagreeable. Early the next morning, letters of dismission, signed Temple, were sent to the other members of the cabinet, and a general resignation of offices took place. A new administration was immediately formed, in which Mr William Pitt was appointed first lord of the treasury and chancellor of the exchequer. The marquis of Caernarvon, and Mr Townshend, who had been created Lord Sidney, were made secretaries of state; Lord Thurlow became lord-high-chancellor; the privy-seal was transferred to the duke of Rutland; Earl Gower became president of the council; the duke of Richmond was made master of the ordnance, and Lord Howe first lord of the admiralty; Mr Grenville and Lord Mulgrave were appointed joint-paymasters of the forces, and Mr Henry Dundas, treasurer of the navy. The office of lord advocate of Scotland, which this gentleman had formerly held, was now transferred from the honourable Henry Erskine to Mr Lay Campbell. A spectacle was now about to be exhibited, which had long been unknown in Britain, that of an administration appointed by the crown, in direct opposition to the house of commons. This, however, was no longer that house of commons which had subdued the royal prerogative, and contended with success against our ablest and most ambitious monarchs. The late coalition had produced throughout the nation a general distrust of the character of those who formed the majority of its members; and it was soon found, that a representative body possesses little power or influence, and may safely be disregarded, when it ceases to render itself the organ of the sentiments of the public. It was expected that an immediate dissolution of parliament would take place; but the change of the highest officers of the crown having been hastily made, it is probable that the new ministry dreaded entering instantly upon the business of an election against the powerful parties coalesced in opposition to them; perhaps also they might wish to observe the effect of the late measures upon the public mind, and act as circumstances should direct. The majority, however, of the house of commons, feared a dissolution; and, on Monday the 22d of December, voted an address to the king, stating the inconveniences to the public credit and the affairs of India, which would attend a prorogation or dissolution of parliament. His majesty returned an answer on the 24th, acquiescing, in general terms, in the sentiments contained in the address, and assuring the house, that after a short adjournment, their meeting would not be interrupted by any prorogation or dissolution. This answer was regarded as ambiguous; and a dissolution was expected to take place immediately after the usual adjournment at Christmas. When the house met on the 12th of January, Mr Fox attempted to introduce, previous to any other business, the discussion of certain resolutions, which had been prepared by the opposition; while the new ministers endeavoured to be heard first, by means of a stratagem, which consisted of a declaration of Mr Pitt, that he had a message to deliver from the king. After some tumult, Mr Fox was allowed to proceed. He called upon Mr Pitt to give the house satisfactory assurances that no dissolution would take place; but this last gentleman having declined to comply with this requisition, Mr Fox moved, that the house should resolve itself into a committee on the state of the nation. The motion was carried, on a division of 232 to 713. Various resolutions were then carried: 1. That to issue public money after a prorogation or dissolution of parliament, unless an act shall have previously passed, appropriating the supplies to specific services, will be a high crime and misdemeanor; a breach of public trust, derogatory to the privileges of parliament and to the constitution of the country. Accounts of money already issued were ordered, and the farther issuing of any money was prohibited till three days after this account should be presented. It was farther resolved, on the motion of the earl of Surrey, that, in the present state of his majesty's dominions, an administration was necessary that should have the confidence of that house and the public, and that the recent appointments did not engage the confidence of the house. It was lastly resolved, on the motion of Mr Fox, that the second reading of the mutiny bill should be deferred to the 23d of February. Warm debates took place upon these resolutions, in which the most pointed personalities were cast out and retorted from both sides of the house. The coalition was branded, as a corrupt confederacy of two desperate factions to seize upon the government of the country; and the India bill was represented as having been an experiment made by the late secretary of state, with a view, if not to place the crown on his own head, at least to raise himself to a degree of power superior to that of the sovereign. On the other hand, the party composing the new administration was described as a coalition, not indeed of parties, but of the shreds and remnants, of the dregs and outcasts of parties; as a body collected for the purpose of fighting the battles of secret and unconstitutional influence, of trampling on the power and dignity of the house of commons, of establishing a government of cabal, intrigue, and favoritism, and of destroying the very principles of laudable ambition and honourable service in the state. On the 14th of January, Mr Pitt obtained leave to bring in a bill for the better government and management of the affairs of the East India Company. By this bill, commissioners were appointed by his majesty, authorized to superintend and control all operations of the courts of directors and proprietors of the East India Company, relative to the civil and military government or revenues of the territories and possessions of the company. This board of control was to have access to all papers belonging to the company; and the court of directors was on no pretence to send out orders to India, without the previous approbation of the board, which was also authorized to alter and amend the orders of the directors. His majesty was authorized to name the commanders in chief in India, and to remove any governor, general, or member of the councils, of any British settlement in India; and all nominations by the court of directors to these offices, were declared to be subject to the approbation of his majesty; nor was the court of proprietors allowed, for the future, to revoke any proceeding of the court of directors which had been approved of by his majesty. It was chiefly objected to this bill, that it disfranchised the East India Company or violated their charter no less than Mr Fox's bill.

BRITANNICUS

Pages 807-807
or BRITTANICO, John, an eminent Italian scholar of the 15th century, was born in the Brescian territory, of a family originally from Britain. He published notes on Persius, Juvenal, Terence, Statius, and Ovid, with annotations on Pliny's href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, which last were published after his death. He died in 1510. BRITÉ, or BRIGHT, in Husbandry. Wheat, barley, or any other grain, is said to brité, when it grows over ripe and shatters.

BRITTANY

Pages 807-807
or BRETAGNE, a considerable province of France, which is 150 miles in length and 112 in breadth. It is a peninsula, surrounded on all sides by the ocean except on the east, where it joins to Anjou, Maine, Normandy, and Poitou. It is divided into the upper and lower; and therein are large forests. It carries on a great trade, by reason of the many harbours on its coasts. It was united to the crown of France in 1532. Rennes is the capital town. According to the new division of France, Brittany is divided into several departments.

BRITTLENESS

Pages 807-807

that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of bodies on account of which they are denominated brittle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which subjects them to be easily broken by pressure or percussion. Brittle bodies are extremely hard; a very small percussion exerts a force on them <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the greatest pressure, and thus may easily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them. This effect is particularly remarkable in glass suddenly cooled, the brittleness of which is thereby much increased. Tin, though in itself tough, gives a brittleness to all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> when mixed therewith. The brittleness of glass has been said to arise from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEITY">heterogeneity</a> of the parts whereof it is composed, as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and sand can never bind sufficiently together; but this cannot be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; for the pure calces of metals, or any other simple substances, when vitrified, become brittle also. In timbers, brittleness seems to be connected with durability; the more brittle any sort of wood is, the more durable it is found. Thus oak is of very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>: while beech and birch, as being tough, presently rot, and are of little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>.

BRITTON

Pages 807-808

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, on the river Isara <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Oyse; now Pont-ouye.

BRIVATES

Pages 808-808

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a port of Gallia Celtica, now Brest, in Brittany.

BRIVES-LA-GALLARD

Pages 808-808

a town of France, in lower Limosin, now the department of Correze. It stands in a fruitful plain, opposite to an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> formed by the river Correze, over which there are two handsome bridges. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a> and cotton <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are established here. It is 220 miles south by west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. Gallard <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. N. Lat. 45. 15.

BRIXELLUM

Pages 808-808

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia Cispadana; remarkable for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where Otho killed himself after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDRIACUM">Bedriacum</a>; now Bersello <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bresello, in the territory of Rhoigo.

BRIXEN

Pages 808-808

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the bishopric of the same name, and where the bishop <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> resides, is seated on the river Eisache, at some distance from the mountain Brenner. It is surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, where there are plenty of vineyards, which yield good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine. It is a populous town; and the houses are well built, with piazzas, and are painted on the outside. The public buildings are very handsome, and there are several spacious squares. It is much frequented, on account of the mineral waters that are near it. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 30. N. Lat. 46. 35.

BRIXIA

Pages 808-808

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cenomani in the Regio Transpadana; now Brescia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Bresciano.

BRIZE VENTS

Pages 808-808

shelters used by gardeners who have not walls on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, to keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> winds from damaging their beds of melons. They are inclosures about six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and an inch or more thick; made of straw, supported by stakes fixed into the ground, and props across on both inside and outside; and fastened together with willow-twigs, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wire.

BROACH

Pages 808-808

BROCHA (from the French broche), denotes an awl <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BODKIN">bodkin</a>; also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> packing-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>. A spit, in some parts of England, is called a broach; and from this word comes to pierce or broach a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>. In Scotland, broach, broche, or brotchie, is the name of an utensil which the Highlanders used, like the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIBULA">fibula</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, to fasten their vest. It is usually made of silver, of a round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, with a tongue crossing its diameter, to fasten the folds of the garment; sometimes with two tongues, one on each side of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in the middle. There are preserved, in several families, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> broaches of very elegant workmanship, and richly ornamented. Some of them are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with names, to which particular virtues used to be attributed; others are furnished with receptacles for relics, supposed to preserve from harm. So that these broaches seem to have been worn not only for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> but as amulets. One or two of this sort are figured and described by Mr Pennant, Tour in Scotland, i. 90. iii. 14. edit. 3d.

BROADCAST

Pages 808-811

as opposed to the drill-husbandry, denotes the method of cultivating corn, turnips, pulses, clover, the foreign grasses, and most other field <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, that are not transplanted, by sowing them with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; in which method they are scattered over the ground at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and thence said to be sown in broadcast. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. This is called the old husbandry, to distinguish it from the drill, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoeing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> new husbandry. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">Broad</a>-Piece, a denomination given to certain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> pieces broader than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>; particularly Caroluses and Jacobuses. Broad-Side, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a discharge of all the guns on one side of a ship at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. A broad-side is a kind of volley of cannonade, and ought never to be given at a distance from the enemy above musket-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at point-blank. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCADE">Brocade</a>, or Brocado, a stuff of gold, silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, raised and enriched with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, foliages, and other ornaments, according to the fancy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> or manufacturers. Formerly the word signified only a stuff wove all of gold, both in the warp and in the woof, or all of silver, or of both mixed together; thence it passed to those stuffs in which there was silk mixed, to raise and terminate the gold or silver flowers: but at present all stuffs, even those of silk alone, whether they be programs of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a> or of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, satins, and even taffeties or lustrings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they be but adorned and worked with some flowers or other figures, are called brocades. In manufacturing brocades, the flatted gilt wire is spun on threads of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> silk approaching as near as may be to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of gold itself. The wire, winding off from a bobbin, twists about the thread as it spins round; and, by means of curious machinery, too complex to be described here, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of threads are thus twisted at once by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of one wheel. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> art consists in so regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, that the several circumvolutions of the flatted wire on each side may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> touch one another, and form, as it were, one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> covering. It is said, that at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> there is made a sort of flatted wire, gilt only on one side, which is wound upon the thread so that only the gilt side appears; and that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of this wire is kept a secret, and has been attempted in other places with little success. There is also a gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> wire, made in the same manner as the gilt silver: Savary observes, that this kind of wire, called false gold, is prepared chiefly at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>; and that the ordinances of France require it to be spun, for its distinction from the gilt silver, on flaxen or hempen threads. One of our writers takes notice, that the Chinese, instead of flatted gilt wire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> slips of gilt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, which they both interweave in their stuffs and twist upon silk threads: this practice he inconsiderately proposes as a hint to the British weaver. But, whatever be the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of stuffs of this kind of manufacture, it is obvious that they must want durability. The Chinese themselves, according to Du Halde's account, sensible of this imperfection, scarcely use them any otherwise than in tapestries, and such other ornaments as are not intended to be much worn, or exposed to moisture. The Venetians have carried on a large trade to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> in a kind of brocade called damasquete, which, though it has only about half the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold or silver as that made among us, looks far more beautiful. The flatted wire is neither wound <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together on the silk threads, nor the threads stuck close in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>; yet by passing the stuff betwixt rolls, the disposition and management of which is kept a secret, the tissue or flower is made to appear one entire brilliant plate of gold or silver. The French ministry, ever vigilant for the advancement of arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, judged this manufacture important enough to deserve their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and accordingly, for contriving the machinery, they engaged the ingenious M. Vaucanson, known throughout <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for his curious pieces of mechanism, who, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the academy for the year 1757, lately printed, gives an account of his success, and of the establishment of such a manufacture at Lyons. The lower roll is made of wood, 32 inches in length and 14 in diameter; the upper one of copper, 36 inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 8 in diameter: this last is hollow, and open at one end, for introducing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> heaters. For making the rolls cylindrical, he has a particular kind of lathe, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> tool, which the most dexterous hand could not guide in a straight line through such a length as 36 inches, is made to slide by means of a screw, on two large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>-rulers, perfectly straight, and capable of being moved at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, nearer, and always exactly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, to the axis of the roll. He first disposed the rolls nearly as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> flating mill. In this disposition, ten men were scarcely sufficient for turning them with force enough to duly extend the gilding: and the collars, in which the axes of the rolls turned at each end, wore or gulled so fast, that the pressure continually diminished, insomuch that a piece of stuff of ten ells had the gilding sensibly less extended on the last <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> than on the first. He endeavoured to obviate this inconvenience by screwing the rolls closer and closer in proportion as the stuff passed through, or as the wearing of the collars occasioned more play between them; but this method produced an imperfection in the stuff, every turn of the screw making a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> across it. To lessen the attrition, each end of the axis, instead of a collar, was made to turn between three iron cylinders called friction <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>: but even this did not answer fully, for now another source of unequal pressure was discovered. The wooden roll, being compressible, had its diameter sensibly diminished: it likewise lost its roundness, so that the pressure varied in different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of its revolution. On trying different kinds both of European and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> woods, all the hard ones split, the soft ones warped without splitting, and of more than 20 rolls, there was not one which continued round for 24 hours even without being worked in the machine. These failures put him upon contriving another method of pressing the rolls together, so that the force should always accommodate itself to whatever inequalities might happen. The axis of the copper roll being made to turn between friction wheels as before, that of the wooden one is pressed upwards by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> at each end furnished with a half-collar for receiving the end of the axis. Each lever has the end of its short arm supported on the frame of the machine, and the long arm is drawn upwards by an iron rod communicating with the end of the short arm of another lever placed horizontally: to the long arm of this lever is hung a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and the levers are so proportioned, that a weight of 30 pounds presses the rolls together with a force <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 17,536 pounds, which was found to be the proper force for the sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>. Brocade, tension of the gilding. By this contrivance four men can turn the rolls with more ease than ten can turn those which are kept together by screws; and the same weight acting uniformly in every part, the pressure continues always equal, though the wooden roll should even become oval, and though the stuff be of unequal thickness. A piece of cloth, of about two ells, is sewed to the beginning and end of the stuff, to keep it out to its width when it enters and parts from the rolls, which could not be done by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for fear of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> or bruising them; as it would take too much time to sew these cloths to every small piece of an ell or two, a number of these is sewed together. The stuff is rolled upon a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which is placed behind the machine, and its axis pressed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> to keep the stuff tight as it comes off. Four iron bars, made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, are introduced into the copper roll, which in half an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> acquires the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or nearly such a one as is used for the ironing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>: the wooden roll is then laid in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the machine set to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. If more than 30 ells are to be passed at once, the wooden roll must be changed for another, for it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not bear a long continuance of the heat without danger of splitting: and therefore the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> should be provided with several of these rolls, that when one is removed, another may be ready to supply its room: as soon as taken off from the machine, it should be wrapt in a cloth and laid in a moist place. The principal inconvenience attending the use of this machine, it that the heat necessary for extending the gilding, though it improves the brightness of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and yellow silks, is injurious to some colours, as crimson and green. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> pressure will not supply the place of heat; and the only method of preventing this injury, or rendering it as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as possible, appeared to be, to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the stuff through with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celerity. Method of clearing Brocade when sullied. For this purpose neither alkali nor <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> must be used; because the former, while they clean the gold, corrode the silk, and change or discharge its colour; and the latter also alters the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and even the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of certain colours. But spirit of wine may be used without any danger of its injuring either the colour or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the subject; and in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> proves as effectual for restoring the lustre of the gold as the most corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETERGENTS">detergents</a>. A rich brocade flowered with a variety of colours, after being disagreeably tarnished, had the lustre of the gold perfectly restored by washing it with a soft <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> dipt in warm spirit of wine, and some of the colours of the silk which were likewise soiled became at the same time remarkably bright and lively. Spirit of wine seems to be the only material adapted to this intention, and probably the boasted secret of certain artists is no other than this spirit disguised. As to powders, however fine, and however cautiously used, they scratch and wear the gold, which here is only superficial and of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> tenacity. Brocade-Shell, the English name of a species of Limax. Brocadel, or Brocadel, a kind of coarse brocade; chiefly used for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCCOLI">Broccoli</a>, a kind of cabbage cultivated for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. See Brassica. Broche, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROACH">Broach</a>. See Broach. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCK">Brock</a>, among sportsmen, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote a badger.—A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HART">hart</a>, too, of the third year, is called a brock, or brocket; and a hind of the same year, is called a brocket's sister. Brocklesby, Richard, an eminent English physician. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROD">Brod</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Possegia in Slavonia, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a>. It was once more considerable than at present; and is memorable for a victory obtained over the Turks in 1668. E. Long. 18. 36. N. Lat. 45. 20. Brodeau, John, in Latin Brodeus, a great critic, on whom Lipsius, Scaliger, Grotius, and all the learned, have bestowed great encomiums, was descended from a noble family in France, and born at Tours in 1500. He was liberally educated, and placed under Alciat to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but soon forsaking that, he gave himself up wholly to languages and the belles lettres. He travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he became acquainted with Sadolet, Bembus, and other famous wits: and here (says Thuanus) he applied himself to the study of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the sacred languages, in which he made no small proficiency. Then, returning to his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he led a retired, but not an idle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as his many learned lubrications abundantly testify. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> free from all ambition and vain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and suffered his works to be published rather under the sanction and authority of others than under his own. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> works are, 1. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the Anthologia. 2. Ten books of miscellanies. 3. Notes on Oppian, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, &c. He died in 1563, aged 63. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRODERA">Brodera</a>, or Brodra, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the empire of the Great Mogul. It stands in a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain, on the little river Wasset; and is fortified, after the old way, with pretty good walls and towers. It is inhabited by Banians and callico-weavers. The country about it produces plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-lac and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>. E. Long. 72. 30. N. Lat. 22. 10. Brogling for eels; the same with Snigling. Broglia, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> in Italy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a county of the same name, situated near the frontiers of Provence, in E. Long. 6. 42. N. Lat. 44. 12. Broke, Sir Robert, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chief <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>, was the son of Thomas Broke, Esq. of Claverly in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; from whence he removed to the middle temple, and soon became a very eminent lawyer. In the year 1542, he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> reader, and double reader in 1550. In 1552, he was made serjeant at law; and in the year following (first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>), lord chief justice of the common pleas; about which time he received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. Stow says he was recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons; which is confirmed by a manuscript in the Ashmolean library. He died and was buried at Claverly in Shropshire, the place of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, in 1558. Wood gives him the character of a great lawyer and an upright judge. His works are, 1. An abridgement containing an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of of the year-books till the time of Queen Mary. 2. Certain cases adjudged in the reign of Henry VIII. Edward VI. and Queen Mary. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a> on the statute of limitations, 32 Hen. VIII. c. 2.

BROKEN WIND

Pages 811-812

among farriers. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">BROKER</a>. The origin of the word is contested; some derive it from the French broier, "to grind;" others from brocarder, "to cavil, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> triggle;" others deduce broker from a trader broken, and that from the Saxon broc, "misfortune," which is often the true reason of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s breaking. In which view, a broker is a broken trader by misfortune; and it is said none but such were formerly admitted to that employment. Brokers are of three kinds; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>-brokers, stock-brokers, and pawn-brokers. Exchange-Brokers, are a sort of negotiators, who contrive, make, and conclude bargains between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and tradesmen, in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or merchandise, for which they have a fee or premium. These, in old English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, are called brokers, and in Scotland, broccarit, i.e. according to Skene, mediators or intercessors in any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, &c. They make it their business to know the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of the course of exchange, to inform merchants how it goes, and to notify to those who have money to receive or pay beyond <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, who are proper persons for negotiating the exchange with; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is accomplished, that is, when the money is paid, they have for brokerage 2s. per 100l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. These, by the statute of 8 and 9 William III., are to be licensed in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor, who gives them an oath, and takes bond for the faithful execution of their offices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any person shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a broker without being thus licensed and admitted, he shall forfeit the sum of 500l.: and persons employing him, 3l.; and brokers are to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> contracts, &c. under the like penalty: also brokers shall not <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> for themselves, on pain of forfeiting 200l. They are to carry about with them a silver medal, having the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s arms and the arms of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and pay 40s. a-year to the chamber of the city. In France, till the middle of the 17th century, their exchange brokers were called courtiers de change; but by an arrêt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in 1639, the name was changed for that more creditable one of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> de change, banque, et finance; and in the beginning of the 18th century, to render the office still more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king's counsellors was added. At <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, and several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, the Arabs, who do the office of exchange-brokers, are called consuls; the manner of whose negotiating with the European merchants has something in it so very particular, that we have referred it to a distinct article. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a>. The exchange-brokers at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, called makelers, are of two kinds: the one, like the English, called sworn-brokers, because of the oath they take before the burgomasters; but the others negotiate without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and are called walking-brokers. The first are in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 395; whereof 375 are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and 20 Jews: the others are near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that number; so that in Amsterdam there are near 1000 exchange-brokers.—The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two consists in this: The books and persons of the former are allowed as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; whereas, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of dispute, the latter are disowned, and their bargains annulled. The fee of the sworn exchange-brokers of Amsterdam is fixed by two regulations, of 1613 and 1623, with regard to matters of exchange, to 18 sols for 100 livres de gros, or 600 florins; i.e. three sols for 100 florins; payable, half by the drawer and half by the person who pays the money. But <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has made considerable alterations herein. The Jews, Armenians, and Banians, are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> brokers throughout most parts of the Levant and the Indics. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> all affairs are transacted by a sort of brokers whom they call delat, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> talkers. Their manner in making their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> is very singular: after the brokers have launched out into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and usually impertinent discourses, coming towards a conclusion, they only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with their fingers. The buyer's and seller's broker each takes the other by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, which they cover with their coat or a handkerchief: the finger stretched out stands for six; bent for five; the tip of the finger for one; the whole hand for 100l.; and the hand clinched for 1000l. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> express even pounds, shillings, and pence, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. During all this mystic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the two brokers appear as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and composed as if there were nothing passing between them. The French distinguish two kinds of brokers; one for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of merchants, the other of manufacturers, artificers, and workmen. The business of the former is to facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of goods in the wholesale and mercantile way; that of the other, to procure the goods wanted for manufacturers, artificers, &c. or to sell their goods when made. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> there is scarce a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of tradesmen, or even <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, but have their brokers, who are usually taken out of their body, and make it their sole business to negotiate in the particular kinds of goods to which such company is by statutes restrained. There are brokers for drapery, brokers for grocery, brokers for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, &c. There are even brokers for tanners, curriers, cutlers, and the like. Stock-Brokers, are those who are employed to buy and sell shares in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock of a company or corporation, and also in the public funds. As the practice of stock-jobbing has been carried to such an excess as became not only ruinous to a great number of private families, but even affected, or at least might soon affect, the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, the legislature thought fit to put a stop to it, or at least to bring it within certain bounds, and under some regulation. The negotiations, &c. of these brokers are regulated by stat. 6 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 18. and 7 and 10 Geo. II. cap. 8. which, among other things, enacted, that contracts in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of wagers, &c. incur a penalty of 500l. and by the sale of stock, of which the seller is not possessed, a forfeit of 100l. and that brokers keep a book, in which all contracts, with their dates, and the names of the parties concerned, shall be entered, on pain of 50l. Pawn-Brokers, persons who keep shops, and lend money upon pledges to necessitous persons, and most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> at an exorbitant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. They are more properly styled pawn-takers, or tallymen; sometimes fripers, or friperers. These are meant in 1 Jac. I. cap. Brokers, Brome. xxi. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 5, where it is declared, that the sale of goods wrongfully taken to any broker, or pawn-broker, in London, Westminster, Southwark, or within two miles of London, does not alter the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. And (sect. 7) if a broker, having received such goods, shall not, upon request of the owner, discover them, how and when he came by them, and to whom they are conveyed, he shall forfeit the double value thereof. See BROKER, Supplement. In the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there are companies established by authority for the letting out money on pawns, called mounts of piety; a title little becoming such institutions. In some parts of Italy, they have also mounts of piety of another kind, wherein they only receive ready money, and return it again with interest, at a certain sum per annum. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, they have several such mounts, which are distinguished into frank and perpetual: the interest of the former is only four per cent.; that of the latter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. Brokers are also those who sell old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture, and wearing apparel, &c.

BROME

Pages 812-812

Richard, a dramatic writer who lived in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Decker, Ford, Shirley, &c. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, he having been originally no better than a menial <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to the celebrated Ben Johnson. He wrote himself, however, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation, as is testified, not only by various commendatory verses written by his contemporaries and prefixed to many of his plays, but also by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> which his quondam <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> addressed to him on account of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called The Northern Lass. Brome, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of his master, laid it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as his first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> point, to apply closely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of men and manners. His genius was entirely turned to comedy; and therefore his proper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was observation more than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>. His plots are all his own, and are far from being ill conducted; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, which for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> are strongly marked, were the offspring of his own judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the foibles of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart. In a word, his plays in general are good ones; met with great applause when first acted; and as Langbain informs us, were thought by the players worthy to be revived, to their own profit and the author's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, in that critical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> which he himself lived in. Nay, we have had a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, even in our own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, of the merit of one of his comedies, which with a very little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> has lately been revived, and with great success, viz. The Jovial Crew, which for no less than three seasons running brought crowded audiences to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> in Covent Garden at all the frequent repetitions of its performance. The comedies which the author left behind him are 15 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; ten of which are collected together, as above mentioned, in two volumes octavo. He joined also with Thomas Heywood in a play called The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> Witches.

BROMELIA

Pages 812-814

the Pine-apple: for the classification see <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method it ranks under the 10th order, Coronariae. As the pine apple, on account of its highly flavoured fruit, is a desirable object to those who can afford the expense of raising it, we shall here enter somewhat into the detail of the most approved method of cultivation.—The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the crowns which grow on the fruit, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the suckers which are produced either from the sides of the plants or under the fruit: both which are found to be equally good; although by some persons the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is thought preferable to the suckers, as supposing it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce fruit sooner than the suckers, which is certainly a mistake. The suckers and crowns must be laid to dry in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for four or five days, or more (according to the moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which adhered to the old plant or fruit); for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are immediately planted, they will rot. The certain rule of judging when they are fit to plant, is by observing if the bottom is healed over and become hard; for if the suckers are drawn off carefully from the old plants, they will have a hard skin over the lower part, so need not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the crowns of those whose bottoms are moist. But whenever a crown is taken from the fruit, or the suckers from old plants, they should be immediately divested of their bottom-leaves, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to allow depth for their planting; so that they may be thoroughly dry and healed in every part, lest when they receive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and moisture they should perish, which often happens when this method is not observed. If these suckers or crowns are taken off late in the autumn, or during the winter, or early in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, they should be laid in a dry place in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a> for a fortnight or three weeks before they are planted; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, they will be fit for planting in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> at farthest. These should be planted in a rich good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden mould, not too heavy so as to detain the moisture too long, nor over <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; but where this is wanting, you should procure some fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from a good pasture, which should be mixed with about a third part of rotten neats dung, or the dung of an old melon or cucumber <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> which is well consumed. These should be mixed six or eight months before they are used, but if it be a year it will be the better; and should be often turned, that their parts may be the better united, as also the clods well broken. This earth should not be screened very fine; for if you only clear it of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, it will be better for the plants than when it is made too fine. You should always avoid mixing any sand with the earth, unless it be extremely stiff, and then it will be necessary to have it mixed at least six months or a year before it is used; and it must be frequently turned, that the sand may be incorporated in the earth so as to divide its parts: but you should not put more than a sixth part of sand; for too much sand is very injurious to these plants. In the summer season, these plants must be frequently watered; but you should not give them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: you must also be very careful that the moisture is not detained in the pots by the holes being stopped, for that will soon destroy them. If the season is warm, they should be watered twice a-week; but in a cool season, once a-week will be often enough: and during the summer season you should once a-week <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> them gently all over their leaves; which will wash the filth from off them, and thereby greatly promote the growth of the plants. There are some persons who frequently shift these plants from pot to pot. But this is by no means to be practised by those who propose to have large well-flavoured fruit: for unless the pots be filled with the roots, by the time the plants begin to show their fruit, they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> produce small fruit, which have generally large crowns on them; therefore the plants will not require to be new potted oftener than twice in a season. The first time should be about the end of April, when the suckers and crowns of the former year's fruit (which remained all the winter in those pots in which they were first planted) should be shifted into larger pots; i.e. those which were in halfpenny or three-farthings pots, should be put into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> or at most three halfpenny pots, according to the size of the plants; for you must be very careful not to over-pot them, nothing being more prejudicial to these plants. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time for shifting of them is in the beginning of August; when you should shift those which are of a proper size for fruiting the following spring into twopenny pots, which are full large enough for any of these plants. At each of these times of shifting the plants, the bark-bed should be stirred up, and some new bark added, to raise the bed up to the height it was at first made: and when the pots are plunged again into the bark-bed, the plants should be watered gently all over their leaves, to wash off the filth, and to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the earth to the roots of the plants. If the bark-bed be well stirred, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of good fresh bark added to the bed, at this latter shifting, it will be of great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the plants; for they may remain in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> until the beginning of November, or some time latter, according to the mildness of the season, and will require but little fire before that time. During the winter, they will not require to be watered oftener than once a-week, according as you find the earth in the pots too dry: nor should you give them too much at each time; for it is much better to give them a little water often, than to over-water them. You must observe never to shift those plants which show their fruit into other pots; for if they are removed after the fruit appears, it will stop the growth, and thereby cause the fruit to be smaller, and retard its ripening, so that many times it will be October or November before the fruit is ripe: therefore you should be very careful to keep the plants in a vigorous growing state from the first appearance of the fruit, because upon this depends the goodness and the size of the fruit; for if they receive a check after this, the fruit is generally small and ill-tasted.—When you have cut off the fruit from the plant whose kind you are desirous to propagate, you should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> the leaves, and plunge the pots again into a moderate hot-bed, observing to refresh them frequently with water, which will cause them to put out suckers in plenty; so that a person may be soon supplied with plants enough of any of the kinds, who will but observe to keep the plants in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The most dangerous thing that can happen to these plants is their being attacked by small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> insects, which appear at first like a white <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILDEW">mildew</a>, but soon after have the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>; these attack both root and leaves at the same time; and if they are not soon destroyed, will spread over a whole stove in a short time, and in a few weeks entirely stop the growth of the plants by sucking out the nutritious juice, so that the leaves will appear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and sickly, and have generally a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of yellow transparent spots all over them. These insects, after they are full grown, appear like bugs, adhering so closely to the leaves as not to be easily washed off, and seem to have no local <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. They were originally brought from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> upon the plants which were imported from thence; and are probably the same insects which have destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-caness of late in some of the Leeward <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, for upon some sugar-caness which were sent Mr Miller from Barbadoes he observed great numbers of these insects. Since they have been in England, they have spread greatly in such stoves where there has not been more than ordinary care taken to destroy them. They have also attacked the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-trees in many gardens near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and have done them incredible damage; but they do not endure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in winter, so that they are never found on such plants as live in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The only method yet discovered for destroying these insects, is by frequently washing the leaves, branches, and stems, of such plants as they attack, with water in which there has been a strong infusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> stalks. But this method cannot be practised on the ananas plants, because the insects will fasten themselves so low between the leaves, that it is impossible to come at them with a sponge to wash them off; so that if all those which appear to sight are cleared off; they will soon be succeeded by a fresh supply from below, and the roots will be also equally infested at the same time. Therefore, whenever these insects appear on the plants, the safest method will be to take the plants out of the pots, and clear the earth from the roots; then prepare a large tub, which should be filled with water in which there has been a strong infusion of tobacco stalks; into this tub you should put the plants, placing some sticks across the tub to keep them immersed in water. In this water they should remain 24 hours; then take them out, and with a sponge wash off all the insects from the leaves and roots, and dip the plants into a tub of fair water, washing them therein, which is the most effectual way to clear them from the insects. After which, you should pot them in fresh earth; and, having stirred up the bark-bed, and added some new tan to give a fresh heat to the bed, the pots should be plunged again, observing to water them all over the leaves, and this should be repeated once a-week during the summer season; for these insects always multiply much faster where the plants are kept dry, than where they are sometimes sprinkled over with water, and kept in a growing state. As these insects are frequently brought over from America on the ananas plants which come from thence, those persons who procure their plants from thence should look carefully over them when they receive them, to see they have none of these insects on them; for if they have, they will soon be propagated over all the plants in the stove where they are placed; therefore, whenever they are observed, the plants should be soaked (as before directed) before they are planted into pots. Such are the directions generally given with regard to the culture of the pine-apple in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Of late, however, some very considerable improvements have been made in that article. The leaves of the oak have been substituted to the more expensive bark; and by treating the pines with them, they are found to thrive as well, and to produce as good fruit, as in the other method. Of the proper way of managing these leaves for the rearing of exotic plants, an account is given under the article Oak-Leaves. But the most considerable improvement is that mentioned in the 67th volume of the Philosophical Transactions, where a method is shown by William <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>, Esq. of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, of raising these <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> in Water. His account of this method is as follows. "Before I enter into the particulars of raising pine-apples in water, it will be necessary to tell you that my hot-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is covered with the best crown-glass, which I apprehend gives more heat than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort of green glass generally used for hot-houses. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> part of the house, and indeed anywhere in the lowest parts of it, the pine-apple plants will not thrive well in water. The way in which I treat them is as follows. I place a shelf near the highest part of the back wall, so that the pine-plants may stand without absolutely touching the glass, but as near it as can be; on this shelf I place pans full of water, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight inches deep; and in these pans I put the pine-apple plants, growing in the same pots of earth as they are generally planted in to be plunged into the bark-bed in the common way; that is, I put the pot of earth, with the pine-plant in it, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a> full of water, and as the water decreases I constantly fill up the pan. I place either plants in fruit, or young plants as soon as they are well rooted, in these pans of water, and find they thrive equally well: the fruit reared this way is always much larger, as well as better flavoured, than when ripened in the bark-bed. I have more than once put only the plants themselves without any earth, I <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> after they had roots, into these pans of water, with only water sufficient to keep the roots always covered, and found them flourish beyond <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. In my house, the shelf I mention is supported by irons from the top, and there is an intervening space of about ten inches between the back wall and the shelf. A neighbour of mine has placed a leaden cistern upon the top of the back flue (in which, as it is in contact with the flue, the water is always warm when there is a fire in the house), and finds his fruit excellent and large. My shelf does not touch the back flue, but is about a foot above it; and consequently the water is only warmed by the air in the house. Both these methods do well. The way I account for this success is, that the warm air always ascending to the part where this shelf is placed, as being the highest part of the house, keeps it much hotter than in any other part. The temperature at that place is, I believe, seldom less than what is indicated by the 73rd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Fahrenheit's thermometer, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> shines it is often at above 100°: the water the plants grow in seems to enable them to bear the greatest heat, if sufficient air be allowed; and I often see the roots of the plants growing out of the holes in the bottom of the pot of earth, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> vigorously in the water. "My hot-house (the dimensions of which it may be proper to know) is 60 feet long and 11 feet wide, the flues included; six feet high in the front, and 11 feet at the back of the inside of the house. It is warmed by two fires. A leaden trough or cistern on the top of the back flue is preferable to my shelf, as in it the pine plants grow much faster in the winter, the water being always warmed by the flue: of this I have seen the great benefit these last two months in my neighbourhood. It is not foreign to this purpose to mention, that as a person was moving a large pine-plant from the hot-bed in my house last-summer, which plant was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> showing fruit, by some accident he broke off the plant just above the earth in which it grew, and there was no root whatever left to it: by way of experiment I took the plant, and fixed it upright in a pan of water (without any earth whatever) on the shelf; it there soon threw out roots, and bore a pine-apple that weighed upwards of two pounds."

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an incision made in the aspera arteria, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe, which is necessary in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and especially in a violent quinsy, to prevent suffocation from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inflammation or tumor of the parts. It is also called laryngotomy and tracheotomy. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRONKHORST

Pages 814-814

JOHN VAN, an eminent painter who flourished about the middle of the last century. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>: and after having studied under several masters, entered the school of Cornelius Poelenberg, whose style of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> he imitated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. He painted both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and landscapes; and his pictures, which are very highly finished, are held in great estimation. He amused himself with the point; and some landscapes from Poelenberg, together with other subjects from his own compositions, are attributed to him.

BRONTIAE

Pages 814-815
or Thunder-stones, in href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History. These were supposed, according to the opinion of many philosophers, to have only an imaginary existence. But of late years the attention of naturalists has been much directed to stones that have fallen from the clouds. The fact seems to be sufficiently established; but whether the stones are formed in the atmosphere during the thunder storm which generally accompanies their fall, are ejected from a volcano, or projected, as some suppose, from the moon, there is great difference of opinion.

BRONTIUM

in Grecian antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> underneath the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, in which were kept brazen vessels full of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and other materials, with which they imitated the noise of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>.

BRONTOLOGY

Pages 815-815

denotes the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an explanation of its causes, phenomena, &c. together with the presages drawn from it. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>.

BRONZE

Pages 815-815

also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> prepared by the colourmen of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, wherewith to imitate bronze.—There are two sorts, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> bronze, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a>. The latter is made solely of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-dust, the finest and brightest that can be got: the former is made of the same, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of red ochre well pulverized. They are both applied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. To prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> greenish, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> must be dried over a chafing-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">dish</a> as soon as bronzed.

BRONZES

Pages 815-815

a name given by antiquarians to figures either of men <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beasts, to urns, and in general to every piece of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made of that metal. We likewise give the name of bronzes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> or busts <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, whether these pieces be copies of antiques or original subjects.—Among medallists, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> medals bear the name of bronze.

BRONZING

BROODING

BROOKE

Pages 815-816

Mrs., <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a clergyman of the name of Moore, was a lady as remarkable for her virtue and suavity of manners as for her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> literary accomplishments. Her first performance, which introduced her to the notice and consequent esteem of the public, was Julia Mandeville; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> concerning which there were various opinions, but which everybody read with eagerness. It has been often wished that she had made the catastrophe less melancholy; and we believe that she afterwards was of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, but she thought it beneath her character to alter it. She soon afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> with her husband, who was chaplain to the garrison at Quebec; and here she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and loved those romantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and scenes which gave birth to Emily Montague, a work most deservedly in universal esteem, which has passed through several editions, and which is now not easily met with. On her return to England, accident introduced her, and congenial sentiments attracted her, to Mrs Yates; and an intimacy was formed which terminated only with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of that lady. Mrs Brooke, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this connexion, formed an acquaintance with Mr Garrick, and wrote some pieces for the stage. She had, however, great reason to be dissatisfied with his behaviour as a manager; and she made The Excursion, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> which she wrote at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the vehicle by which she exhibited to the public her complaints and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Drury. Her anger, we believe, was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, but the retribution was too severe. She herself afterwards thought so, for she lamented and retracted it. Her first dramatic performance was the tragedy of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, 1746. Her next effort in that line was, The Siege of Synope, a tragedy, introduced by Mr Harris, and written principally with a view of placing Mrs Yates in a conspicuous character. This did not altogether fail, but it did not become popular; it wanted energy, and it had not much originality; there was little to disapprove, but there was nothing to admire. Her next and most popular production was Rosina, which, in a most liberal manner, she presented to Mr Harris. Few <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> pieces have been equally successful. Her last musical piece, entitled Marion, which was introduced by Shield, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some time to be occasionally exhibited. Mrs Brooke was also the translator of various books from the French. She was esteemed by Dr Johnson, valued by Miss Seward, and her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> courted by all the first characters of her time. She died in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1789, two days after her husband. Her husband enjoyed the rectory of Colney in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, to which he had been preferred after his arrival from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">BROOM</a>. See Genista, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">Butcher</a>'s Broom. See Ruscus, Botany Index. Spanish Broom. See Spartium, Botany Index.

BROOM ALSO

Pages 816-816

m also denotes a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> besom <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> implement wherewith to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> away dirt, dust, and the like. We say, a birch-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-broom, a rush-broom, a heath-broom. The primitive kind of brooms, from whence the denomination is given to all the rest, was made of the genista or wild broom growing on commons. Broom-flower gives the denomination to an order of knights instituted by St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> of France, on occasion of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The motto was, Exaltat humiles, and the collar of the order made up of broom <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and husks, enamelled and intermixed with fleurs de lys of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, set in open lozenges, enamelled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, chained together; and at it hung a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">florence</a> of gold. This answers to what the French called Ordre de la Geneste, from the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of broom so called; different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> broom, as being lower, the stalk smaller, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> narrow; the flower is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and bears a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> husk.
