I found my confidence not abated, that still the same Guide was able to conduct me to my wished-for home. I immediately resumed my former fortitude, considered the Nile as indeed no more than rising from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> as all other rivers do, but widely differing in this, that it was the palm for 3000 years held out to all the nations of the world as a detur dignissimo, which in my cool hours I had thought was worth the attempting at the risk of my life, which I had long either resolved to lose, or lay this discovery a trophy in which I could have no competitor, for the honour of my country, at the feet of my sovereign, whose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> I was." The object of Mr Bruce's wishes being now gratified, he bent his thoughts on his return to his native country. He arrived at Gondar 19th November 1770; but found, after repeated solicitations, that it was by no means an easy task to obtain permission to quit Abyssinia. A civil war in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time breaking out, several engagements took place between the king's forces and the troops of the rebels, particularly three actions at a place called Serbraxos on the 16th, 20th, and 23rd of May 1771. In each of them Mr Bruce acted a considerable part, and for his valiant conduct in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> received, as a reward from the king, a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, of 184 links, each link weighing 3½dwt., or somewhat more than 25lbs. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> in all. At Gondar, after these engagements, he again preferred the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties to be allowed to return home, entreaties which were long resisted; but his health at last giving way, from the anxiety of his mind, the king consented to his departure, on condition of his engaging by oath to return to him in the event of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, with as many of his kindred as he could engage to accompany him. After a residence of nearly two years in that wretched country, Mr Bruce left Gondar on the 16th of December 1771, taking the dangerous way of the desert of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, in place of the more easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of Masuah, by which he entered Abyssinia. He was induced to take this rout, from his knowledge and former <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of the cruel and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> temper of the natives of Masuah. Arriving at Teawa the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1772, Mr Bruce had the misfortune to find the sheikh Fidele at Atbara, the counterpart of the maybe of Masuah, in every bad <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; by his intrepidity and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, however, and by making good use of his foreknowledge of an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, which happened on the 17th of April, he was permitted to depart next day, and he arrived at Sennaar on the 29th of the same month. Mr Bruce was detained upwards of four months at that miserable and inhospitable place; the inhabitants of which he describes in these expressive words: "War and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> seem to be the only employment of these horrid people, whom heaven has separated by almost impassable deserts from the rest of mankind, confining them to an accursed spot, seemingly to give them an earnest in time of the only other worse which he has reserved to them for an eternal hereafter." This delay was occasioned by the villany of those who had undertaken to supply him with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but at last, by disposing of 178 links of his gold chain, the well-earned trophy of Serbraxos, he was enabled to make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for his dangerous journey through the deserts of Nubia. He left Sennaar on the 5th of September, and arrived on the 3d of October at Chendi, which he quitted on the 20th, and travelled through the desert of Gooz, to which village he came on the 26th of October. On the 9th of November he left Gooz, and entered upon the most dreadful and dangerous part of his journey; the perils attending which he has related with a power of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> not unworthy of the greatest masters. All his camels having perished, Mr Bruce was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of abandoning his baggage in the desert, and with the greatest difficulty reached Assouan upon the Nile on the 29th of November. After some days rest, having procured fresh camels, he returned into the desert, and recovered his baggage, among which is particularly to be remarked a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> (of three feet radius) supplied by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> academy at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>; by means of which noble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, now deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at Kinmaird, Mr Bruce was enabled with precision and accuracy to fix the relative situations of the several remote places he visited. On the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1773, after more than four years absence, he arrived at Cairo, where, by his manly and generous behaviour, he so won the heart of Mahomet Bey, that he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRMAN">firman</a>, permitting the commanders of English vessels belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> to bring their ships and merchandise to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, a place far preferable in all respects to Jidda, to which they were formerly confined. Of this permission, which no European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> could ever before acquire, many English vessels have since availed themselves; and it has proved peculiarly useful both in public and private dispatches. Such was the worthy conclusion of his memorable journey through the desert; a journey which, after many hardships and dangers, terminated in obtaining this great national benefit. At Cairo Mr Bruce's earthly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> had nearly been concluded by a disorder in his leg, occasioned by a worm in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. This accident kept him five weeks in extreme agony, and his health was not re-established till a twelvemonth afterwards, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of Porretta in Italy. On his return to Europe, Mr Bruce was received with all the admiration due to so exalted a character. After passing some considerable time in France, particularly at Montbard, with his friend the comte de Buffon, by whom he was received with much hospitality, and is mentioned with great applause, he at last revisited his native country, from which he had been upwards of twelve years absent. It was now expected that he would take the earliest opportunity of giving to the world a narrative of his travels, in which the public curiosity could not but be deeply interested. But several circumstances contributed to delay the publication; and what these were will be best related in his own words: "My friends at home gave me up for dead; and as my death must have happened in circumstances difficult to have been proved, my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> became as it were a hereditas jacens, without an owner, abandoned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to those whose original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> extended no further than temporary possession. "A number of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits were the inevitable consequence of this upon my return. To these disagreeable avocations, which took up much time, were added others still more unfortunate. The relentless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>, caught at Bengazi, maintained its ground, at times, for a space of more than 16 years, though every remedy had been used, but in vain; and what was worst of all, a lingering distemper had seriously threatened the life of a most near relation (his second wife), which, after <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years constant alarm, where every duty bound me to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and attendance, conducted her at last, in very early life, to her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>." Amidst the anxiety and the distress thus occasioned, Mr Bruce was by no means neglectful of his private affairs. He considerably improved his landed property, inclosing and cultivating the waste grounds; and he highly embellished his paternal seat, making many additions to the house, one in particular of a noble museum, filled with the most precious stores of oriental literature, large collections of drawings made, and curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> obtained, during his far-extended peregrinations. The termination of some law-suits, and of other business, which had occupied much of his time, having at length afforded leisure to Mr Bruce to put his materials in order, his greatly desired and long expected <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> made its appearance in 1790, in five large quarto volumes embellished with plates and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a>. It is unnecessary to enter into any critic or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of this celebrated work. It is universally allowed to be replete with curious and useful information; and to abound in narratives which at once excite our admiration and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> our feelings. The very singular and extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> which it gives of Abyssinian manners, startled the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of some; but these manners, though strange in the sight of an European, are little more than might be expected in such a barbarous country. A more serious objection to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of Mr Bruce's narrative was started by an anonymous critic, in an Edinburgh newspaper, soon after the publication, from the account of two astronomical phenomena, which it is asserted could not possibly have happened as Mr Bruce asserts. The first of these is the appearance of the new moon at Fursbouth, during Mr Bruce's stay in that place, which he mentions to have been from 25th Dec. 1768, to the 7th of Jan. 1769; and on a particular day in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> interval asserts, that the new moon was seen by a fakir, and was found by the ephemerides to be three days old; whereas it is certain that the moon changed on the 8th of January 1767. The other phenomenon appears equally impossible. At Teawa Mr Bruce says he terrified the sheikh by foretelling that an eclipse of the moon was to take place at four o'clock afternoon of the 17th of April 1772; that accordingly, soon after that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the eclipse was begun; and when the shadow was half over, told the sheikh that in a little time the moon would be totally darkened. Now, by calculation, it is certain, that at Teawa this eclipse must have begun at 36 minutes past four, and the moon have been totally covered at 33 minutes past five; while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> set there a few minutes past six, before which time the moon, then in opposition, could not have risen: so that as the moon rose totally eclipsed, Mr Bruce could not see the shadow half over the disk, nor point it out to the sheikh. To these objections, which appear unsurmountable, Mr Bruce made no reply, though in conversation he said he would do it in the second edition of his book. The language of the work is in general harsh and unpolished, though sometimes animated. Too great a display of vanity runs through the whole, and the apparent facility with which the traveller gained the most familiar access to the courts, and even to the harams, of the sovereigns of the countries through which he passed, is apt to create in readers some doubts of the accuracy of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>. Yet there appears upon the whole such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of manly veracity, and circumstances are mentioned with a minuteness so unlike deceit, that these doubts are overcome by the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of truth, which the whole detail irresistibly fastens upon the mind. This first impression being almost wholly disposed of within a short time, Mr Bruce had stipulated for a second edition, which was preparing for the press, when death removed the author from this transitory stage. That event happened on the 26th of April 1794. In the evening of that day, when some company were departing, Mr Bruce attended them down stairs; on the steps his foot slipped, and he fell down headlong. He was taken up speechless, and remained in a state of insensibility for eight or nine hours, when he expired, on the 27th of April 1794, in the 65th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He married, for his second wife, at Carronhall, 20th May 1776, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, eldest daughter of Thomas Dundas of Fingask. Mrs Bruce died, after a long and lingering indisposition, during which she was attended with the most affectionate assiduity by her husband, in 1784, having had issue two sons and one daughter. There never, perhaps, existed a man better qualified for the hazardous enterprise he undertook, than Mr Bruce. His person was of the largest size, his height exceeding six feet, and the bulk as well as the strength of his body was proportionally great. He excelled in all corporeal accomplishments, being a hardy, practised, and indefatigable swimmer, trained to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and fatigue of every kind, and his long residence among the Arabs had given him a more than ordinary facility in managing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. In the use of fire arms he was so unerring, that in innumerable instances he never failed to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> the mark; and his dexterity in handling the spear and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> on horseback was also uncommonly great. He was master of most languages, understanding the Greek perfectly; and was so well skilled in oriental literature, that he revised the New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in the Ethiopic, Samaritan, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and Syriac, making many useful notes and remarks on difficult <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>. He had applied from early youth to mathematics, drawing, and astronomy; and had acquired some knowledge of physic and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was astonishingly retentive, his judgment <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and vigorous. He was dexterous in negotiation, a master of public business, animated with the warmest zeal for the glory of his king and country, a physician in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> or city, a soldier and horseman in the field, while, at the same time, his breast was a stranger to fear, though he took every precaution to avoid danger. Such, at least, is his own representation of his character; and though an impartial judge would probably make considerable abatement for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bias of a man drawing his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>, yet it cannot be denied, that in personal accomplishments, Mr Bruce equalled, if not exceeded, most of his contemporaries; was uncommonly distinguished for vigour of understanding, as well as great literary attainments; and in active persevering intrepidity may be classed with the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in any age or country. Thus accomplished, Mr Bruce could not but be eminently fitted for an attempt so full of difficulty and danger as the discovery of the sources of the Nile: no one who peruses his account of the expedition, can fail to pay an unsought tribute of admiration to his intrepidity, manliness, and uncommon dexterity in extricating himself out of situations the most dangerous and alarming, in the course of his long and hazardous journey. Not to mention his conduct during his residence in Abyssinia, his behaviour at Massah, Teawa, and Sennar, evinces the uncommon vigour of his mind; but it was chiefly during his passage through the Nubian desert that his fortitude, courage, and prudence, appeared to the greatest advantage. Of his learning and sagacity, his delineation of the course of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s fleet from Tarshish to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPHIR">Ophir</a>, his account of the cause of the inundations of the Nile, and his comprehensive view of the Abyssinian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, afford ample proofs. He expresses throughout all his works a deep and lively <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the care of a superintending Providence, without whose influence, he was convinced of the futility of all human ability and foresight to preserve from danger. He appears to have been a serious believer of the truth of Christianity; and his illustrations of some parts of the sacred writings are original and valuable. (Edin. Mag.)

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and bishopric of Spire, situated on the river Satz, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 30'. N. Lat. 49° 15'. BRUCHUS. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRUCKER

JAMES, a German theologian and historian. See Supplement. BRUEGHEL. See Breughel.

BRUGES

Pages 836-836

John of, (real name, John van Eick), a celebrated Flemish painter, and the first who discovered the method of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, flourished in the 15th century. He found in the course of his chemical experiments (to which science he also applied himself), that, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> colours with linseed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> oil, he could form them into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body which would resist the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and not need the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> used in painting the water colours or in fresco. He presented the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> painted in this manner to Alphonsus I. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, who was much pleased with it.

BRUIN

Pages 836-836

John de, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, was born at Gorcum in 1620. He had uncommon skill in dissecting animals, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lover of experiments. He made also observations in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He published dissertations De vi attrice; De corporum gravitate et levitate; De cognitione Dei naturalis; De lucis causa et origine, &c. He had a dispute with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius, to whom he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> printed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1693; where-in he criticises Vossius's book De natura et proprietate lucis; and strenuously maintains the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of Descartes. He died in 1675, after he had been professor 23 years; and his funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> was pronounced four days after by M. Grevis.

BRUMALES PLANTAE

Pages 836-836

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> (from bruma, winter); <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which flower in our winter; such are plants from southern tropical regions, which retain in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their former habits, and observe the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of flowering, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in those regions being at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year with our winter.

BRUMALIA

Pages 836-836

in Roman antiquity, festivals of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> celebrated twice a-year; the first on the 12th of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and the other on the 18th of the kalends of November. They were instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, who during these feasts used to entertain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. Among other heathen festivals which the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were much inclined to observe, Tertullian mentions the brume <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brumalia.

BRUMOY

Pages 836-836
Peter, a learned Jesuit, born at Rouen in 1668, distinguished himself in his youth by his talents for the belles lettres; and during his whole life was beloved for his probity, his virtue, and the goodness of his heart. He wrote many works, the most considerable of which is his Theatre of the Greeks. He died at Paris in 1742.

BRUN

Pages 836-836

Anthony le, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, famous for his skill in negotiating, was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at Dole in the year 1600. He was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Dole; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in all the state negotiations which concerned the provinces. He was sent afterwards by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> IV. to the diet of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATISBON">Ratisbon</a>, and from thence to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand III. He was one of the plenipotentiaries of his Catholic majesty, at the conferences of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> held in 1643; where, though all the other plenipotentiaries took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of him, yet it is said that he far exceeded them all in capacity. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain was particularly beholding to him for the peace which the Dutch made at Munster, exclusively of France; and the intriguing turn which he showed upon this occasion made him dreaded ever after by French ambassadors. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters as well as of politics; and therefore employed his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> as well as tongue in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He died at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, during his embassy, in the year 1654.

BRUNDISIUM

Pages 836-837
or Brundusium, in Ancient Geography, a town of Calabria, with the best harbour in Italy. It was a very ancient town, and belonged originally to the Salentines; but was taken by the Romans about 256 years before Christ. Now Brindisi. BRUNIA. See Botany Index.

BRUNO

Pages 837-837

JORDANO, an atheistical writer, was born at Nola in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; and about the year 1582 began to call in question some of the tenets of the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which occasioned his retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>: but after two years stay there, he expressed his aversion to Calvinism in such a manner that he was expelled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. After having staid some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Lyons, Thonlouse, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of M. Castlenau the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>. He was very well received by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and the politer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> friends were Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Sidney and Sir Fulk Greville. With these and some others of their club, Bruno held assemblies; but as they treated of subjects of a very delicate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which could not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> capacity of every body, they kept the door always shut, and none but select persons were admitted into their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. At Sir Philip's request, he composed his Spaccio della Bestia Triumphant, which was printed in 8vo, 1584, and dedicated to that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is remarkable for nothing but its impiety, we are told in one of the Spectators (No. 389.), sold at an auction in London for 30l. From England he went to Wittemberg, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, where he printed some tracts, in which he openly avowed his atheistical principles. After visiting some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Germany, he made a tour to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. Here he was apprehended by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>; tried; condemned; and refusing to retract, was burnt at the stake, February 9th 1600.

BRUNSBUTTLE

Pages 837-837

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, seated at the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 42. N. Lat. 44. 30. It is a subject to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. BRUNSFELSIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRUNSWICK

Pages 837-839

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is composed of five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. the Old Town, the New Town, the Hagen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Burg, the Old Wieck, and the Sack, which makes it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> are almost all built of wood. There are several churches, one of which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, but the appearance of its antiquity is almost absorbed by the repairs it has undergone. Brunswick is a fortified place, and would require a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to besiege, and not a few men to defend it. It is of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, divided in the middle by the river Ocker. It is about two miles in circumference, and is strongly fortified. On the ramparts is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, ten feet six inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet two inches in circumference, weighing 1800 quintals, and has 93 quintals of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of 730 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to the distance of 33,000 paces, and throw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> of a thousand weight; but it requires 52 pounds of powder for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. This city is the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> whom we style the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttle. The inhabitants Brunswick, of the city and parts adjacent carry on a considerable trade with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. Brunswick rum is well known in England; a small sort of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink of the inhabitants of the city. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> here is the Lutheran, and they observe it very strictly. The peasants are sober and laborious, but clownish and heavy; however, as they are robust and strong, they make good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> is styled duke of Brunswick, though he has no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in, nor dominion over, this city, which belongs to the duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttle. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is about 30,000; and the whole income of the duchy is estimated at 170,000l. The academy of Brunswick, Dr Moore informs us, has been new-modelled, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> improved, by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> prince. Students now <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to this academy from many parts of Germany; and there are generally some young gentlemen from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> who are sent to be educated here. Such of them as are intended for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, will not find so many advantages united at any other place on the continent as at the academy of Brunswick. They will here be under the protection of a family partial to the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>—every branch of science is taught by masters of known abilities—the young students will see garrison duty regularly performed, and may by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the prince obtain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to attend the reviews of the Prussian troops at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. They will have few temptations to expense, in a town where they can see no examples of extravagance—have few opportunities of dissipation, and none of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> debauchery. The fortifications at Brunswick were sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility, and on one occasion they saved the town from being pillaged, and afforded Prince Frederick, who is now in the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, an opportunity of performing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which it is imagined gave him more joy than twenty victories. This happened in the year 1761, soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Kirch-Denkern, when Duke Ferdinand protected Hanover, not by conducting his army into that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and defending it directly, as the enemy seemed to expect, and probably wished; but by diversion, attacking with strong detachments, commanded by the hereditary prince, their magazines in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, and thus <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> their attention from Hanover to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. While the duke lay encamped at Willhemstall, watching the motions of Broglio's army, the maréchal being greatly superior in numbers, sent a body of 20,000 men, under Prince Xavier of Saxony, who took possession of Wolfenbuttle, and soon after invested Brunswick. Prince Ferdinand, anxious to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his native city, ventured to detach 5000 of his army, small as it was, under his nephew Frederick, assisted by General Luckner, with orders to harass the enemy, and endeavour to raise the siege. The young prince, while on his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, sent a soldier with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the governor, which was wrapped round a bullet, and which the soldier was to swallow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of his being taken by the enemy.—He had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to get safe into the town. The letter apprised the commander of the garrison of the prince's approach, and particularised the night and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> when he expected to be at a certain place near the town, requiring him to favour his entrance. In the middle of the night appointed, the prince fell suddenly on the enemy's cavalry, who, unsuspicious of Brunswick's approach, were encamped carelessly within a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the town. They were immediately dispersed, and spread such an alarm among the infantry, that they also retreated with considerable loss. Early in the morning the young prince entered Brunswick, amidst the acclamations of his fellow-citizens, whom he had relieved from the horrors of a siege. The hereditary prince having destroyed the French magazines in Hesse, had been recalled by his uncle, and ordered to attempt the relief of Brunswick. While he was advancing with all possible speed, and had got within a few leagues of the town, he received the news of the siege being raised. On his arrival at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, he found his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Frederick at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, entertaining the French officers, who had been taken prisoners the preceding night. Brunswick, the duchy of, is a country of Germany, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a>; on the west, by the circle of Westphalia, from which it is separated by the river Weser; on the south by Hesse, and the little territory of Pieschfeld; and on the east by Thuringia, with the principalities of Anhalt and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a>, and the duchy of Magdeburg. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are, the Weser, the Öcker, and the Lyne; and it is fertile both in corn and pastures. It is divided into three principalities, Wolfenbuttle, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRUBENHAGEN">Grubenhagen</a>, and Calenberg, which also comprehends the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>. The principality of Wolfenbuttle has its own dukes, and constitutes what is now called the duchy of Brunswick; but the other two belong to the elector of Hanover. The territories of the house of Brunswick occupy a space of 1340 square English miles, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 209,000 souls in 1816. At the new arrangements made in 1815 by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, Brunswick was left in possession of its independence. Brunswick, the family of. The illustrious and ancient house of Brunswick owes its origin to Azo IV. of the family of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, son of Hugo III. marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Azo, who died in 1055, left by his wife Conegonde, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heiress to Guelf III. duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, a son who was Guelf IV. great-grandfather to Henry the Lion. His son, Guelf V. surnamed the Valiant, was created duke of Bavaria by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Henry II. His son, Guelf VI. married Matilda, the richest heiress in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but having no issue, his brother Henry the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> succeeded to his dominions. He died in 1125, having married Wulphild, daughter of Magnus, last duke of Saxony of the Bulling family, by whom he had Henry the Proud, who succeeded to Bavaria in 1137; and he having married a daughter of the emperor Letharius, his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> granted him <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of Saxony, and meant him for his successor in the empire; but this last he was disappointed of. Dying in 1139, both Saxony and Bavaria devolved on his son Henry V. surnamed the Lion. He married Maude, eldest daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II. of England, and is always looked upon as the founder of the Brunswick family: it is therefore extremely remarkable, that his present majesty should be descended from one of our worthiest monarchs, in whom were united the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> Anglo-Saxon and Norman blood. The dominions possessed by Henry the Lion were the most extensive of any prince of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but having refused to assist the emperor Frederick Frederick Barbarossa in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Pope Alexander III. this drew the emperor's resentment on him; and being already jealous of his power and abilities, all his former services were forgotten; and in the diet of Wurtzburg in 1179 or 1180, he was proscribed. The duchy of Bavaria was given to Otho <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Whittlepatch, from whom is descended the present electoral family of Bavaria; the duchy of Saxony to Bernard <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a>, founder of the house of Anhalt; and all his other territories disposed of to different persons. On this he retired to England; and by his father's intercession, Brunswick and Lunenburg were restored to him. His wife Maude died in 1189, and he in 1195. He left three sons: but the two oldest not leaving any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue, William, the third son, carried on the line of the family; and his son Otho was created duke of Brunswick and Lunenburg in 1235, by the emperor Ferdinand II. From him all the succeeding dukes of this family have descended; and no family can boast of a line of princes who have more distinguished themselves, both by their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> abilities and martial achievements; and they are allied to all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> families in Europe. The house of Brunswick has divided into several branches. The late duke of Brunswick had a command in the Prussian army, and fell in the attack made by the French on the 16th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, two days before the battle of Waterloo.

BRUNTISLAND

Pages 839-839

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a> in Scotland, situated on the frith of Forth, eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 5'. N. Lat. 56° 12'. It has the best harbour on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which is formed by a rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> caked out with piers, for there are none on this side the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> entirely <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. This is dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a steeple rising in the centre. The old castle, built by the Dukes, commanded both town and harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has a natural strength, which, with the conveniency of a port opposite to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, made it, during the troubles of 1560, a most desirable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>. The French, allies of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> regent, fortified it strongly. In 1715, it was surprised and possessed by the rebels, who here formed the bold <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of passing over a body of troops to the opposite shore, which was in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> executed under the command of Brigadier Macintosh, notwithstanding all the efforts of the men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to prevent it. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1934 in 1811.

BRURUS

Pages 846-846

Stephen Junius, the disguised author of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Vindiciae contra tyrannos. See Languet.

BRUSCHIUS

Pages 839-839

GASPARD, a Latin historian and poet, was born at Egra in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in 1518. He was devoted to books from his childhood, and especially to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in which he gained so much reputation, that he attained to the poetical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of poet laureat, and of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine. He wrote with prodigious facility; and his verses are extremely flowing, easy, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. He published Latin poems on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of subjects; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and bishoprics of Germany; history of German monasteries, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other works, of which a catalogue is given in Gesner's Bibliotheca. Bruschius was far from being rich, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather he was very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, subsisting almost entirely by the benefactions of his poetical patrons, and by presents from the abbots and abbesses whose monasteries he described. The liberality of some abbots, while he was with Oporin at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, enabled him to buy a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of clothes; but when he found that appearing well dressed in the streets procured him many marks of respect from the vulgar, he tore his new finery to pieces, "as slaves that had usurped their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s honours." Bruschius seems to have been too great a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he lived in, or indeed for any age. He was murdered in the forest of Scalingenbach, between Rottemberg on the Tauber and Winshelm; and it was believed that this assassination was concerted and carried into execution by some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> against whom Bruschius was about to write something.

BRUSH

Pages 839-839

an assemblage of hairs and hogs bristles, fastened in the holes of a wooden handle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> board, pierced for that purpose, serving to cleanse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> bodies by rubbing therewith. The manner of making brushes is by folding the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> or bristle in two; and bringing it by means of a packthread, which is engaged in the fold, through the holes with which the wood is pierced all over, being afterwards fastened therein with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>. When the holes are thus filled, the ends of the hair are cut to make the surface even. Shearmen's Brush, is made of wild boar's bristles; and serves to lay the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> or nap of cloth, after shearing it for the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Brush, among painters, a larger and coarser kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, made of hogs bristles, wherewith to lay the colours on their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces. The Chinese painters brush consists of the stalk of a plant; whose fibres being fretted at both ends, and tied again, serve for a brush. Wire-Brushes, are used by silversmiths and gilders, for scrubbing silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> pieces, in order to the gilding of them. There is a method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> or colouring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, performed by only rubbing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the skin with a brush. This the French leather-gilders call broussure; being the lowest of all the sorts of dye allowed by their statutes. Brush of a Fox, among sportsmen, signifies his drag or tail, the tip or end of which is called the chape. Brush is also used in speaking of a small thicket or coppice. In this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word is formed from the middle-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> Latin bruscia, bruscius, which signifies the same.

BRUSH-WOOD

Pages 839-839

d denotes small slender wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spray. See Browsz. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">Brush</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> appearance of the electric <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> issuing in a parcel of diverging rays from a point. Beccaria ascribes this appearance to the force with which the electric fluid, going out of a point, divides the contiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and passes through it to that which is more remote. BRUSHING. Among jockies, a brushing gallop denotes a brisk one: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> should have his brushing gallop in a morning before watering.

BRUSSELS

Pages 840-840

the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> district of, is one of the four parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Brabant. This quarter is bounded on the east by that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; and on the south by Hainault. Brussels is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of this quarter, and of all Brabant.

BRUTE

Pages 840-845

a general name for all animals except mankind. Among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, the monkey kind bear the nearest resemblance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> shape and internal structure, but more in the former than in the latter. In the monkey kind, the highest and the nearest approach to the likeness of man is the ouran outang, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Homo Sylvestrus*.—The structure and economy of brutes make the objects of what is called <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">Comparative Anatomy</a>. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Philosophers have been much puzzled about the essential characteristics of brutes, by which they may be distinguished from man. Some define a brute to be an animal not <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RISIBLE">risible</a>, or a living creature incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>; others call them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> animals. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> allowed them a sensitive power, but denied them a rational one. The Platonists allowed them reason and understanding, though in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> less pure and refined than that of men. Lactantius allows every thing to brutes which men have, except a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and even this has been ascribed to them by some sceptics. Descartes maintained, that brutes are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> inanimate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, absolutely destitute not only of reason, but of all thought and perception, and that all their actions are only consequences of the exquisite mechanism of their bodies. This system, however, is much older than Descartes; it was borrowed by him from Gomez Pereira, a Spanish physician, who employed 30 years in composing a treatise which he entitled Antoniana <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARGARITA">Margarita</a>, from the Christian names of his father and mother. It was published in 1554; but his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> had not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of gaining partizans, or even of being refuted; so that it died with him. Even Pereira seems not to have been the inventor of this notion; something like it having been held by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as we find from Plutarch and St Augustin. Others, who rejected the Cartesian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, have maintained that brutes are endowed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> essentially inferior to that of men; and to this soul some have allowed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>, others not. And, lastly, in a treatise published by one Bougeant a Jesuit, entitled, A Philosophical Amusement on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a> of Beasts, he affirms that they are animated by evil spirits or devils. The opinion of Descartes was probably invented, or at least adopted by him, to defeat two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> objections: one against the immortality of the souls of brutes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were allowed to have any; the other against the goodness of God, in suffering creatures who had never sinned to be subjected to so many miseries. The arguments in favour of it may be stated as follow: 1. It is certain, that a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> actions are merely <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>; because they are done imperceptibly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, and without any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>; which are to be ascribed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of objects and the primordial disposition of the machine, wherein the influence of the soul has no share; of which number are all habits of the body acquired from the reiteration of certain actions. In all such circumstances, human beings are no better than automata. 2. There are some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> movements so involuntary, that we cannot restrain them; for example, that admirable mechanism ever on the watch to preserve an equilibrium, when we stoop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, or incline our bodies in any way, and when we walk upon a narrow plank. 3. The natural liking for, and antipathy against, certain objects, which in children precede the power of knowing and discriminating them, and which sometimes in grown persons triumph over all the efforts of reason, are all phenomena to be accounted for from the wonderful mechanism of the body, and are so many cogent proofs of that irresistible influence which objects have on the human frame. 4. Every one knows how much our passions depend on the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> into which the blood is put, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> impressions caused by the animal-spirits between the heart and brain, that are so closely connected. connected by their nerves; and if such effects may be produced by such simple mechanical means as the mere increase of motion in the blood, without any direction of the will, we are not to wonder at the actions of brutes being the effects only of a refined mechanism, without thought or perception. A farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> will arise from a consideration of the many wonderful effects which even the ingenuity of men has contrived to bring about by mechanical means; the androide, for instance, of Mr Kempel, which plays at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>. Now, it is not to be questioned, but that the mechanism of the body of the meanest animal infinitely surpasses that of Mr Kempel's machine; and what can be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, but that the actions of that animal must be proportionably more surprising than those of the wooden chess-player? See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROIDES">ANDROIDES</a> and AUTOMATON. The above is a short <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of all the arguments that are brought in favour of the Cartesian system: but they are evidently very far from being conclusive. They are deficient, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, because, though we allow them in the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> the Cartesians themselves can desire, they prove only the possibility of brutes being inanimate, and that the power of God actually could produce such and such actions from inanimate machines; but that he actually hath done so, they have not the least tendency to prove. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> place, the Cartesian argument is insufficient, because it hath no limits, and knows not where to stop; as, by the same method of arguing, every man might prove his neighbour to be an inanimate machine: for though every individual be conscious of his own thoughts, he is not so of those of his neighbours; and it no more exceeds the power of God to cause an inanimate machine perform the actions of a man than those of a beast. Neither are the two objections which the hypothesis is calculated to answer, to be at all admitted as arguments in its favour. They are, 1. That if we allow brutes to have souls, they must be immaterial, and consequently immortal: and, 2. It seems a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the goodness of Good to think that he should subject innocent creatures to such a multitude of evils as we see the brute <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> endure in this world. The first of these is productive of no bad consequences to us, though it should be granted; and if it is supposed that the brute creatures are really immortal, the second objection vanishes; because, in the enjoyment of endless felicity, all temporary afflictions, how severe soever, must be swallowed up as though they had never been. As to a positive proof on the other side, viz. that brutes are really endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and consciousness, there is undoubtedly the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of brutes that there is for that of mankind. We see brutes avoid pain as much as we do; and we likewise see them seek for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and express their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in the enjoyment of certain things by signs not at all equivocal. Therefore, though we <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the possibility of all this being the effect of mere mechanism; yet, as we are conscious that in ourselves similar effects are produced by a sentient principle, we have all the reason in the world to conclude that in brutes they are likewise derived from a principle of sensation; especially seeing we know of no kind of mechanism in any other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> that produces anything like the effects <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned: and until we see that a mechanism of this kind does take place in some part of nature, we have no reason to suppose it in any. As to those actions of the human body in which it seems to move spontaneously, like an automaton, without the direction of the mind or will, it is almost superfluous to observe, that they were not performed in this manner originally, but required very great exertions of the will and intellectual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> before the body could be brought to perform them easily; so that from this nothing can be inferred. Add to this, that divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> sets forth to us in many places the brute creation as objects of mercy; which could not be done without the highest absurdity, if they were not really capable of feeling pleasure and pain as well as we. The most rational opposers of the Cartesian scheme maintain, that brutes are endowed with a principle of sensation as well as we; though of an inferior nature to ours. Great disputes, however, have arisen on this subject; some maintaining, that the soul of brutes is merely sensitive, and that they are altogether destitute of reflection and understanding; others, that they not only reason, but make a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it than men do. That the brutes are endowed only with sensation, and totally destitute of all power of reflection, or even reasoning, is what can by no means be maintained on good grounds: neither can it be asserted that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> entirely from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> propensity to certain things, without knowing why or wherefore. In numberless instances, needless to be mentioned here, but which will readily occur to every reader, it is evident, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> will get the better of many of the natural instincts of brutes; which could never be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> were they absolutely incapable of reasoning. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is equally certain, that they are by no means capable of education in the same degree that men are; neither are the rational exertions of beasts at all to be compared even with those of the meanest savages. One remarkable instance of this is in the use of the element of fire. The most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations have known how to make this element subservient to their purposes; or if some have been found who have been entirely ignorant of its existence, they have quickly learned its uses on seeing it made use of by others; but though many of the brute creatures are delighted with warmth, and have opportunities every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of seeing how fire is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and by that means preserved, it never was known that one of them attempted to preserve a fire by this means. This shows a strange defect of rationality, unaccountable upon any other supposition than that the soul or sentient principle of brutes is somehow or other inferior in its nature to that of man; but still it is a sentient principle, capable of perceptions as quick, and in many instances much more so than our own. Father Bougeant supports his opinion of the spirits of brute creatures being devils in the following manner: Having proved at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> that beasts naturally have understanding, "Reason (says he) naturally inclines us to believe that beasts have a spiritual soul; and the only thing that opposes this sentiment is, the consequences that might be inferred from it. If brutes have a soul, that soul must be either <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> or spirit; it must You dare not say it is matter, because you must then necessarily suppose matter to be capable of thinking; nor will you say that it is spirit, this opinion bringing with it consequences contrary to the principles of religion; and this, among others, that man would differ from beasts only by the degrees of plus and minus; which would demolish the very foundation of all religion. Therefore, if I can elude all these consequences; if I can assign to beasts a spiritual soul, without striking at the doctrines of religion; it is evident, that my system, being moreover, the most agreeable to reason, is the only warrantable hypothesis. Now I shall, and can do it, with the greatest ease imaginable. I even have means, by the same method, to explain many very obscure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Holy Scripture, and to resolve some very great difficulties which are not well confuted. This we shall unfold in a more particular manner. "Religion teaches us, that the devils, from the very moment they had sinned, were reprobate, and that they were doomed to burn for ever in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has not yet determined whether they do actually endure the torments to which they are condemned. It may then be thought that they do not yet suffer them, and that the execution of the verdict brought against them is reserved for the day of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> judgment.—Now what I pretend to infer from hence is, that, till doomsday comes, God, in order not to suffer so many legions of reprobate spirits to be of no use, has distributed them through the several spaces of the world, to serve the designs of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, and make his omnipotence to appear. Some, continuing in their natural state, busy themselves in tempting men, in seducing and tormenting them; either immediately, as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, and those that lay hold of human bodies; or by the ministry of sorcerers or phantoms. These wicked spirits are those whom the Scripture calls the powers of darkness, or the powers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. God, with the others, makes millions of beasts of all kinds, which serve for the uses of men, which fill the universe, and cause the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and omnipotence of the Creator to be admired. By that means I can easily conceive, on the one hand, how the devils can tempt us; and on the other, how beasts can think, know, have sentiments, and a spiritual soul, without any way striking at the doctrines of religion. I am no longer surprised to see them have forecast, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and judgment. I should rather have occasion to wonder at their having no more, since their soul very likely is more perfect than ours. But I discover the reason of this; it is because, in beasts as well as in ourselves, the operations of the mind are dependent on the material organs of the machine to which it is united; and those organs being grosser and less perfect than in us, it follows, that the knowledge, the thoughts, and the other spiritual operations of the beasts, must of course be less perfect than ours: And if these proud spirits know their own dismal state, what a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> must it be to them thus to see themselves reduced to the condition of beasts! But, whether they know it or not, so shameful a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> is still, with regard to them, the primary effect of the divine vengeance, I just mentioned; it is an anticipated hell." Having mentioned the prejudices against this hypothesis, such particularly as the pleasure which people of sense and religion take in beasts and birds, especially all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals: he proceeds, "Do we <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> beasts for their own sakes? No. As they are altogether strangers to human <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, they can have no other appointment than that of being useful and amusing. And what care we whether it be a devil or any other creature that amuses us? The thought of it, far from shocking, pleases me mightily. I with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> admire the goodness of the Creator, who gave me so many little devils to serve and to amuse me. If I am told that these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> devils are doomed to suffer eternal tortures, I admire God's decrees, but I have no manner of share in that dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>; I leave the execution of it to the sovereign Judge: and, notwithstanding this, I live with my little devils as I do with a multitude of people, of whom religion informs me that a great number shall be damned. But the cure of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> is not to be effected in a moment: it is done by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and reflection: give me leave then lightly to touch upon this difficulty, in order to observe a very important thing to you. "Persuaded as we are that beasts have intelligence, have we not all of us a thousand times pitied them for the excessive evils which the majority of them are exposed to, and in reality suffer? How unhappy is the condition of horses! we are apt to say upon seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> whom an unmerciful carman is murdering with blows. How miserable is the dog whom they are breaking for hunting? How dismal is the fate of beasts living in woods! they are perpetually exposed to the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; always seized with apprehensions of becoming the prey of hunters, or of some wilder animal; for ever obliged, after <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fatigue, to look out for some poor insipid food; often suffering cruel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>; and subject, moreover, to illness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! If men are subject to a multitude of miseries that overwhelm them, religion acquaints us with the reason of it; viz., the being-born sinners. But what crimes can beasts have committed by birth to be subject to evils so very cruel? What are we, then, to think of the horrible excesses of miseries undergone by beasts? miseries, indeed, far greater than those endured by men. This is, in any other system, an incomprehensible mystery; whereas nothing is more easy to be conceived from the system I propose. The rebellious spirits deserve a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> still more rigorous, and happy it is for them that their punishment is deferred. In a word, God's goodness is vindicated, man himself is justified: for what <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> can we have, without <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, and often in the way of mere diversion, to take away the lives of millions of beasts, if God had not authorised us so to do? And beasts being as sensible as ourselves of pain and death, how could a just and merciful God have given man that privilege, if they were not so many guilty victims of the divine vengeance? "But hear still something more convincing, and of greater consequence: beasts, by nature, are extremely vicious. We know well that they never sin, because they are not free; but this is the only condition wanting to make them sinners. The voracious birds and beasts of prey are cruel. Many insects of one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> devour one another. Cats are are perfidious and ungrateful; monkeys are mischievous; and dogs envious. All beasts in general are jealous and revengeful to excess; not to mention many other vices we observe in them: and at the same time that they are by nature so very vicious, they have, say we, neither the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, nor any helps to resist the bias that hurries them into so many bad actions. They are, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, necessitated to do evil, to disconcert the general order, to commit whatever is most contrary to the notion we have of natural <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and to the principles of virtue. What monsters are these in a world originally created for order and justice to reign in? This is, in good part, what formerly persuaded the Manicheans, that there were of necessity two orders of things, one good, and the other bad; and that the beasts were not the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the good principle: a monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>! But how then shall we believe that beasts came out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of their Creator with qualities so very strange? If man is so very wicked and corrupt, it is because he has himself through sin perverted the happy nature that God had given him at his creation. Of two things, then, we must say one: either that God has taken delight in making beasts so vicious as they are, and of giving us in them models of what is most shameful in the world; or that they have, like man, original sin, which has perverted their primitive nature. "The first of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> finds very difficult access to the mind, and is an express contradiction to the holy scriptures; which say, that whatever came out of God's hands, at the time of the creation of the world, was good, yea very good. What good can there be in a monkey's being so very mischievous, a dog so full of envy, a cat so malicious? But then many authors have pretended, that beasts, before man's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, were different from what they are now; and that it was in order to punish man that they became so wicked. But this opinion is a mere supposition, of which there is not the least footstep in holy Scripture. It is a pitiful subterfuge to elude a real difficulty: this at most might be said of the beasts with whom man has a sort of correspondence; but not at all of the birds, fishes, and insects which have no manner of relation to him. We must then have recourse to the second proposition, That the nature of beasts has, like that of man, been corrupted by some original sin: Another hypothesis, void of foundation, and equally inconsistent with reason and religion, in all the systems which have been hitherto espoused concerning the souls of beasts. What party are we to take? Why, admit my system, and all is explained. The souls of beasts are refractory spirits which have made themselves guilty towards God. The sin in beasts is no original sin; it is a personal crime, which has corrupted and perverted their nature in its whole substance; hence all the vices and corruption we observe in them, though they can be no longer criminal, because God, by irrevocably reproving them, has at the same time divested them of their liberty." These quotations contain the strength of Father Bougeant's hypothesis, which also hath had its followers; but the reply to it is obvious.
