a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>, eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 30. N. Lat. 52. 31.

BRYANT

Pages 846-846

Sir Francis, a soldier, statesman, and a poet of no inconsiderable fame in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born of a genteel family, educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards spent some time in travelling abroad. In the year 1522, the 14th of Henry VIII., he attended in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a> in his expedition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Brittany; and commanded the troops in the attack of the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORLAIX">Morlaix</a>, which he took and burnt. For this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he was knighted on the spot by the earl. In 1528, he was in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but on what service is doubtful. In 1529, he was sent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to France; and the year following to Rome, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s divorce. He had also been there in 1522, in the same capacity, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> to the holy...

BRYE

Pages 847-847

JOHN THEODORE DE, an excellent engraver, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>; but he resided chiefly at Franckfort, where he carried on a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>. It does not appear when he was born, nor to what <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> he owed his instructions in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and engraving. He worked almost entirely with the graver, and seldom called in the assistance of the point. He acquired a neat free style of engraving, excellently well adapted to small subjects, in which many figures were to be represented; as funeral parades, processions, and the like, which he executed in a charming manner. He also drew very correctly. His heads in general are spirited and expressive, and the other extremity of his figures well marked. His back-grounds, though frequently very slight, are touched with a masterly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He died, as his sons inform us in the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Boissard's collection of portraits, on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 27th, 1598; the two first parts of which collection were engraved by himself, assisted by his sons, who afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it.

BRYENNIUS

Pages 847-847

MANUEL, a Greek writer on music, is supposed to have flourished under the elder Paleologus, viz. about the year of Christ 1120. He wrote three books of Harmonics; the first whereof is a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on Euclid, as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third are on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. He professes to have studied perspicuity for the sake of young men. Meibomius had given the public expectations of a translation of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but not living to complete it, Dr Wallis undertook it; and it now makes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the third volume of his works, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in three volumes folio, 1699. Bryennius, Nicephorus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> distinguished by his courage, probity, and learning, was born at Orechia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; where his father by rebellion provoked the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to send his general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Comnenus against him, who ordered his eyes to be pulled out; but being charmed with his son Bryennius, he married him to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Comnena his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, so famous by her writings. When Alexis came to the throne, he gave Bryennius the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Caesar; but would not declare him his successor, though solicited to it by the empress Irene; and was therefore succeeded by his son John Comnenus, to whom Bryennius behaved with the utmost fidelity. Being sent, about the year 1137, to besiege Antioch, he fell sick; and, returning, died at Constantinople. This prince wrote the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Alexis Comnenus, which he composed at the request of his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> the empress Irene.

BRYGMUS

Pages 847-847

among physicians, a grating noise made by the gnashing of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>.

BRYONIA

Pages 847-847

BRYONY. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>-Bryony. See Tamus, Botany Index. BRYUM. See Botany Index.

BUA

Pages 847-847

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, near the town of Trau; called likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">Partridge</a>-island, because frequented by those birds. It is called Babus by Pliny. In the times of the decay of the empire it was called Boas; and several illustrious men that fell under disgrace at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> were banished to this island; among whom were Florentius, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the offices of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, Immentius de Valenti, and the heretic Jovian. The emperors of Constantinople either were not much acquainted with this pretended <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were willing to treat the banished with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. It is certain that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this island is exceedingly mild; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> perfectly good; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and fruit excellent; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> around it abounds in fish, and the port is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and secure. Neither is it so small that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has not room to walk and ride about as much as he pleases; for it is ten miles in length, and about 25 in circuit; nor can it be said to be rugged, though rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous.

BUANEER

Pages 848-856

one who dries and smokes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fish after the manner of the Indians. The name was particularly given to the first French settlers on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Domingo, whose sole employment consisted in hunting bulls or wild boars, in order to sell their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and flesh. The name has also been applied to those famous piratical adventurers, chiefly English and French, who joined together to make depredations on the Spaniards of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Of both these we shall give an account. I. The Bucaneers of St Domingo. The Spaniards had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the possession of the West Indies and the continent of America, when other nations, especially the English and French, began to follow them there. But though the Spaniards were unable to peo- ple such extensive countries themselves, they were resolved that no others should do it for them; and therefore made a most cruel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on all those of any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> who attempted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in any of the Antilles or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The French, however, were at last lucky enough to acquire some footing in the island of St Christopher's; but by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they began to subside into a regular form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the Spaniards found means to dislodge them. Upon this the wretched fugitives, considering at how <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a distance they were from their mother-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and how near to the island of Hispaniola or St Domingo, the northern parts of which were then uninhabited and full of swine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, immediately resolved to take possession of that country, in conjunction with several other adventurers of their own and the English nation; especially as the Dutch, who now began to appear in these seas, promised to supply them plentifully with all kinds of necessaries they might require, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for the hides and tallow they should procure by hunting. These new settlers obtained the name of buccaneers, from their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of buccaneering their beef and pork in order to keep it for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, or for their own consumption, the method of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be presently described. But some of them soon grew tired of this new way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and took to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a>; while many more chose to turn pirates, trusting to find among those who remained on shore a quick sale for all the plunder they could make at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This new body of adventurers were called freebooters, from their making free prey or booty of whatever came in their way. The colony now began to thrive at a great rate, by the cheap and easy manner in which the freebooters acquired the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and the profusion with which they distributed them among their old companions, the buccaneers and planters, for the merest trifles. This brought numbers of settlers from Old France in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of indented servants, though they toiled rather like slaves during the three years for which they generally bound themselves. One of these men presuming to represent his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who always fixed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> for sending him with skins to the port, that God had forbidden such a practice, when he had declared, "Six days shalt thou labour, and on the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> shalt thou rest;" "And I (replied the brutish buccaneer) say to thee, Six days shalt thou kill bulls, and strip them of their skins, and on the seventh day shalt thou carry their hides to the sea-shore." This command was followed by blows, which sometimes enforce obedience, sometimes disobedience, to the laws of God. Thus the colony consisted of four classes: buccaneers; freebooters; planters; and indented servants, who generally remained with the buccaneers or planters. And these four orders composed what they now began to call the body of adventurers. These people lived together in a perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> under a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>: every freeman had a despotic authority over his own family; and every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> was a sovereign in his own ship, though liable to be discarded at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the crew. The planters settled chiefly in the little island of Tortuga on the northern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Hispaniola: but it was not long before some of them going to the great island to hunt with the buccaneers, the rest were surprized by the Spaniards; and all, even those who had surrendered at discretion in hopes of mercy, were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or hanged. The next care of the Spaniards was to rid the great island of the buccaneers; and for this reason they assembled a body of 500 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>-men, who, by their seldom going fewer than 50 in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, obtained the name of the Fifties from their enemies, whose manners and customs we shall now enter upon. The buccaneers lived in little huts built on some spots of cleared ground, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to dry their skins on, and contain their buccaneering houses. These spots they called Boucanes, and the huts they dwelt in Ajoupas, a word which they borrowed from the Spaniards, and the Spaniards from the natives. Though these ajoupas lay open on all sides, they were very agreeable to the hardy inhabitants, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> are so very desirable things. As the buccaneers had neither wife nor child, they associated by pairs, and mutually rendered each other all the services a master could reasonably expect from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, living together in so perfect a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, that the survivor always succeeded his deceased partner. This kind of union or fellowship they called s'ematelotet [insailoring], and each other matalot [sailor], whence is derived the custom of giving, at least in some parts of the French Antilles, the name matalotage [sailorage], to any kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> formed by private persons for their mutual advantage. They behaved to each other with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and openness of heart: it would have been a crime to keep any thing under lock and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the least pilfering was unpardonable, and punished with expulsion from the community. And indeed there could be no great temptation to steal, when it was reckoned a point of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, never to refuse a neighbour what he wanted; and where there was so little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, it was impossible there should be many disputes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any happened, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> friends of the parties at variance interposed, and soon put an end to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. As to laws, the buccaneers acknowledged none but an odd jumble of conventions made between themselves, which, however, they regarded as the sovereign rule. They silenced all objections by coolly answering, that it was not the custom of the coast; and grounded their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of acting in this manner, on their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> under the tropic, which freed them, in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, from all obligations antecedent to that marine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. The governor of Tortuga, when that island was again settled, though appointed by the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, had very little authority over them; they contented themselves with rendering him from time to time some slight homage. They had in a manner entirely shaken off the yoke of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and thought they did a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in not wholly forgetting the God of their fathers. We are surprised to meet with nations, among whom it is a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to discover any trace of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship: and yet it is certain, that had the buccaneers of St Domingo been perpetuated on the same footing they subsisted at the time we are speaking of, the third or fourth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of them would have had as little religion as the Caffres and Hottentots of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, or the Topinambous and Cannibals of America. They even laid aside their surnames, and assumed nick-names, or martial names, most of which have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. tinued in their families to this day. Many, however, on their marrying, which seldom happened till they turned planters, took care to have their real surnames inserted in the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; and this practice gave occasion to a proverb, still current in the French Antilles, *a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is not to be known till he takes a wife.* Their dress consisted of a filthy greasy shirt, dyed with the blood of the animals they killed; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of trousers still more nasty; a thong of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> by way of belt, to which they hung a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> containing some Dutch knives, and a kind of very short sabre called *manchette*; a hat without any brim, except a little flap on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> to take hold of it by; and shoes of hogskin all of a piece. Their guns were four feet and a half in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, and of a bore to carry balls of an ounce. Every man had his contract servants, more or fewer according to his abilities; besides a pack of 20 or 30 dogs, among which there was always a couple of beagles. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment at first was ox-hunting; and, if at any time they chased a wild <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, it was rather for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>, or to make provision for a feast, than for any other advantage. But in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, some of them took themselves entirely to hunting of hogs, whose flesh they bacanned in the following manner: First, they cut the flesh into long pieces, an inch and a half thick, and sprinkled them with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which they rubbed off after 24 hours. Then they dried these pieces in stoves over a fire made of the skin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the beast, till they grew as hard as a board, and assumed a deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Pork prepared in this manner will keep in casks a twelvemonth and longer; and when steeped but a little while in lukewarm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, becomes plump and rosy, and yields moreover a most grateful smell, either broiled or boiled, or otherwise dressed, enough to tempt the most languid appetite and please the most delicate palate. Those who hunt the wild boar, have of late been called simply *hunters*. In hunting, they set out at day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, preceded by the beagles, and followed by their servants with the rest of the dogs; and as they made it a point never to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALK">balk</a> their beagles, they were often led by them over the most frightful precipices, and through places which any other mortal would have deemed absolutely impassable. As soon as the beagles had roused the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, the rest of the dogs struck up and surrounded the beast, stopping it, and keeping a constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">barking</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCANEER">bucaneer</a> could get near enough to shoot it; in doing this, he <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> aimed at the pit of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; when the beast fell, he hamstringed it, to prevent its rising again. But it has sometimes happened that the creature, not wounded enough to tumble to the ground, has run furiously at his pursuer, and ripped him open. But, in general, the bucaneer seldom missed his aim; and when he did, was nimble enough to get up the tree behind which he had the precaution to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself. What is more; some of them have been seen to overtake the beast in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, and hamstring it without any further ceremony. As soon as the prey was half-skinned, the master cut out a large bone, and sucked the marrow for breakfast. The rest he left to his servants, one of whom always remained behind to finish the skinning, and bring the skin with a choice piece of meat for the huntsman's dinner. They then continued the chase till they had killed as many beasts as there were heads in the company. The master was the last to return to the boucan, loaded bucaneer-like the rest with a skin and a piece of meat. Here the bucaniers found their tables ready: for every one had his separate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; which was the first thing, any way fit for the purpose, that came in their way, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree, and the like. No table-cloth, no napkin, no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> or wine, graced their board; not even potatoes or bananas, unless they found them ready to their hand. When this did not happen, the fat and lean of the game, taken alternately, served to supply the place. A little pimento, and the squeeze of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, their only sauce; contentment, peace of mind, a good appetite, and abundance of mirth, made everything agreeable. Thus they lived and spent their time, till they had completed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hides for which they had agreed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; which done, they carried them to Tortuga, or some port of the great island. As the bucaniers used much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and fed only on flesh meat, they generally enjoyed a good state of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. They were indeed subject to fevers, but either such as lasted only a day, and left no sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> the day following; or little slow fevers, which did not hinder them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and were of course so little regarded, that it was usual with the patient, when asked how he did, to answer "Very well, nothing ails me but the fever." It was impossible, however, they should not suffer considerably by such fatigues, under a climate to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of which few of them had been early enough inured. Hence the most considerate among them, after they had got <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> enough for that purpose, turned planters. The rest soon spent the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their labour in taverns and tippling-houses; and many had so habituated themselves to this kind of life, as to become incapable of any other. Nay, there have been instances of young men, who having early embarked through <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> in this painful and dangerous profession, persisted in it afterwards, merely through a principle of libertinism, rather than return to France and take possession of the most plentiful fortunes. Such were the bucaniers of St Domingo, and such their situation, when the Spaniards undertook to extirpate them. And at first they met with great success; for as the bucaniers hunted separately, every one attended by his servants, they were easily surprised. Hence the Spaniards killed numbers, and took many more, whom they condemned to a most cruel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. But whenever the bucaniers had time to put themselves into a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, they fought like lions, to avoid falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a nation from whom they were sure to receive no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; and by this means they often escaped: nay, there are many instances of single men fighting their way through numbers. These dangers, however, and the success of the Spaniards in discovering their boucans, where they used to surprise and cut the throats of them and their servants in their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, engaged them to cohabit in greater numbers, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively, in hopes that by so doing they might at last induce the Spaniards to let them live in peace. But the fury with which they behaved whenever they met any Spaniards, served only to make their enemies more intent on their destruction; and assistance coming to both parties, the whole island was turned into a slaughter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and so much blood spilt on both sides, that many places, on account of the carnage of which Bucaniers, which they had been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, were entitled, of the massacre; such as the hill of the massacre; the plain of the massacre; the valley of the massacre; which names they retain to this day. At length the Spaniards grew tired of this way of proceeding, and had recourse to their old method of surprise, which, against enemies of more courage than vigilance, was like to succeed better. This put the bucaniers under a necessity of never hunting but in large parties, and fixing the bucaniers in the little islands on the coast, where they retired every evening. This expedient succeeded; and the bucaniers, by being more fixed, soon acquired the air and consistency of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. When the bucaniers had once fixed themselves, as related, each bucan ordered scouts every morning to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, in order to reconnoitre the coast, and see if any Spanish parties were abroad. If no enemy appeared, they appointed a place and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of rendezvous in the evening, and were never absent if not killed or prisoners. When therefore any one of the company was missing, it was not lawful for the rest to hunt again till they had got intelligence of him if taken, or avenged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> if killed. Things continued in this situation for a long time, till the Spaniards made a general hunt over the whole island; and, by destroying their game, put the bucaniers under a necessity of betaking themselves to another course of life. Some of them turned planters; and thereby increased some of the French settlements on the coast, and formed others. The rest, not relishing so confined and regular a life, entered among the freebooters, who thereby became a very powerful body. France, who had hitherto disclaimed for her subjects these ruffians whose successes were only temporary, acknowledged them, however, as soon as they formed themselves into settlements; and took proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for their government and defence. See the article St Domingo. The hunting both of the bull and boar is at this day carried on, and proves of considerable importance. That of the former furnishes France with the finest hides brought from America. The bucaniers put the hides in packs which they call loads, mixing together hides of full grown bulls, of young bullocks, and of cows. Each of these loads is composed of two bull-hides, or of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>; that is to say, either of two real bull hides, or of one bull-hide and two cow-hides, or of four cow-hides, or of three young bullocks hides; three bullocks hides being reckoned equivalent to two full-grown bulls hides, and two cows hides equivalent to one bull's hide. These bulls they commonly call oxen in France, though they be not gelt. Each load is commonly sold for six pieces of eight reals, which is a Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, the French coin being but little current, or not at all, in the island of St Domingo. The boar meat buccanned in the manner above mentioned is sold by the bundle or pack, weighing commonly 60 pounds, at the rate of six pieces of eight per pack. The palmetto leaves serve to pack it up in; but their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is deducted, so that there must be in each pack 60 pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> flesh. These bucaniers have also a great trade of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> of boars, which they melt, and gather in large pots called potiches. This lard, which is called mantegua, is also sold for about eight pieces of eight per pot. There is a great trade, and a great consumption of each of these merchandises in the French settlements of the island of St Domingo, and in those of Tortuga: besides which, they used to send great quantities of them to the Antilles, and even into the continent of French America. There is also a great deal of it sold for the support of the crews of the ships that come from France for trading, or which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> of Tortuga fit out for cruising against the Spaniards. The Spaniards, who have large settlements in the island of St Domingo, have also their bucaniers there, whom they call matadores or monteros. Their chase has something noble, which savours of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>: the huntsman being on horseback uses the lance to strike the bull, thinking it beneath his courage to shoot him at a distance. When the servants who are on foot, have discovered the beast, and with their dogs have driven it into some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVANNAH">savannah</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, in which the master waits for them on horseback, armed with two lances, the matadore goes and hamstring it with the first lance, the head of which is made like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> or half-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and extremely sharp, and kills it afterwards with the other lance, which is a common one. The chase is very agreeable; the huntsman making commonly, in order to attack the bull, the same turns and the same ceremonies which are practised in those festivals so famous in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, wherein the greatest lords expose themselves sometimes to the view of the people, to make them admire their dexterity and intrepidity in attacking those furious animals: but then it is a very dangerous chase; those bulls, in their fury, often running directly against the huntsman, who may think himself very happy if he comes off only with the loss of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and if he himself is not mortally wounded. The Spaniards dress their hides like the French, who have learned it from them; and these hides being carried to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>, a famous harbour in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, are a part of the trade of that celebrated town. The flota and the galleons scarce ever fail touching there, on their return from Vera Cruz and Porto Bello, and load there those hides which they carry into Spain, where they are sold for Havannah hides, the most esteemed of any that are brought from America into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. II. Buccaneers, the Pirates. Before the English had Raynal's made any settlement at Jamaica, and the French at St Domingo, some pirates of both nations, who have since been so much distinguished by the name of Buccaneers, had driven the Spaniards out of the small island of Tortuga; and, fortifying themselves there, had with an amazing intrepidity made excursions against the common enemy. They formed themselves into small companies, consisting of 50, 100, or 150 men each. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, of a greater or smaller size, was their only armament. Here they were exposed night and day to all the inclemencies of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; having scarce room enough to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> independence, the greatest blessing to those who are not proprietors of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, rendered them averse from those mutual restraints which the members of society impose upon themselves for the common good; some of them chose to sing, while others were desirous of going to sleep. As the authority they had conferred on their captain was confined Bucaneer, to his giving orders in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, they lived in the greatest confusion. Like the savages, having no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of want, nor any care to preserve the necessaries of life, they were constantly exposed to the severest extremities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst. But deriving, even from their very distresses, a courage superior to every danger, the sight of a ship transported them even to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of frenzy. They never deliberated on the attack, but it was their custom to board the ship as soon as possible. The smallness of their vessels, and the skill they showed in the management of them, screened them from the fire of the greater ships; and they presented only the fore-part of their little vessels filled with fusileers; who fired at the port-holes with so much exactness, that it entirely confounded the most experienced gunners. As soon as they threw out the grappling, the largest vessel seldom escaped them. In <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> necessity, they attacked the people of every nation, but fell upon the Spaniards at all times. They thought that the cruelties the latter had exercised on the inhabitants of the new world justified the implacable aversion they had sworn against them. But this was heightened by a personal pique, from the mortification they felt in seeing themselves debarred from the privileges of hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, which they considered as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>. Such were their principles of justice and religion, that, whenever they embarked on any expedition, they used to pray to heaven for the success of it; and they never came back from the plunder, but they constantly returned thanks to God for their victory. The ships that sailed from Europe to America seldom tempted their avidity. The merchandise they contained would not easily have been sold, nor been very profitable to those barbarians in these early times. They always waited for them on their return, when they were certain they were laden with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, jewels, and all the valuable productions of the new world. If they met with a single ship, they never failed to attack her. As to the fleets, they followed them till they sailed out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bahama; and as soon as any one of the vessels was separated by accident from the rest, it was taken. The Spaniards, who trembled at the approach of the buccaneers, whom they called devils, immediately surrendered. Quarter was granted, if the cargo proved to be a rich one; if not, all the prisoners were thrown into the sea. The buccaneers, when they had got a considerable booty, at first held their rendezvous at the island of Tortuga, in order to divide the spoil; but afterwards the French went to St Domingo, and the English to Jamaica. Each person, holding up his hand, solemnly protested that he had secreted nothing of what he had taken. If any one among them was convicted of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, a case that seldom happened, he was left, as soon as an opportunity offered, upon some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> island, as a traitor unworthy to live in society. Such brave men among them as had been maimed in any of their expeditions, were first provided for. If they had lost a hand, an arm, a leg, or a foot, they received 26l. An eye, a finger, or a toe, lost in fight, was valued only at half the above sum. The wounded were allowed 2s. 6d. per day for two months, to enable them to have their wounds taken care of. If they had not money enough to answer these several demands, the whole company were obliged to engage in some fresh expedition, and to continue it till they had acquired a sufficient stock to enable them to satisfy such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> contracts. After this act of justice and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, the remainder of the booty was divided into as many shares as there were buccaneers. The commander could only lay claim to a single share with the rest; but they complimented him with two or three, in proportion as he had acquitted himself to their satisfaction. Favour never had any influence in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the booty; for every share was determined by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Instances of such rigid justice as this are not easily met with; and they extended even to the dead. Their share was given to the man who was known to be their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> when alive, and therefore their heir. If the person who had been killed had no intimate, his part was sent to his relations when they were known. If there were no friends or relations, it was distributed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and to the churches, which were to pray for the person in whose name these benefactions were given. When these duties had been complied with, they then indulged themselves in all kinds of profusion. Unbounded licentiousness in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, wine, women, every kind of debauchery, was carried to the utmost pitch of excess, and was stopt only by the want which such profusion brought on. These men who were enriched with several millions, were in an instant totally ruined, and destitute of clothes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. They returned to sea; and the new supplies they acquired were soon lavished in the same manner. The Spanish colonies, flattering themselves with the hopes of seeing an end to their miseries, and reduced almost to despair in finding themselves a perpetual prey to these ruffians, grew weary of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. They gave up all the power, conveniences, and fortune, which their connections procured them, and formed themselves almost into so many distinct and separate states. They were sensible of the inconveniences arising from such a conduct, and avowed them; but the dread of falling into the hands of rapacious and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> men, had greater influence over them than the dictates of honour, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and policy. This was the rise of that spirit of inactivity which continues to this time. This despondency served only to increase the boldness of the buccaneers. As yet they had only appeared in the Spanish settlements, in order to carry off some provisions when they were in want of them. They no sooner found their captures begin to diminish, than they determined to recover by land what they had lost at sea. The richest and most populous countries of the continent were plundered and laid waste. The culture of lands was equally neglected with navigation; and the Spaniards dared no more appear in their public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, than sail in the latitudes which belonged to them. Among the buccaneers who signalized themselves in this new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of excursions, Montbar, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, particularly distinguished himself. Having by chance, in his infancy, met with a circumstantial account of the cruelties practised in the conquest of the new world, he conceived an aversion which he carried to a degree of frenzy against that nation which which had committed such enormities. The enthusiasm this spirit of humanity worked him up to, was turned into a rage more cruel than that of the religious fanaticism, to which so many victims had been sacrificed. The manes of these unhappy sufferers seemed to rouse him, and call upon him for vengeance. He had heard some account of the buccaneers, who were said to be the most inveterate enemies to the Spanish name: he therefore embarked on board a ship, in order to join them. In the passage they met with a Spanish vessel; attacked it; and, as it was usual in those times, immediately boarded it. Montbar, with a sabre in his hand, fell upon the enemy; broke through them; and, hurrying twice from one end of the ship to the other, levelled every thing that opposed him. When he had compelled the enemy to surrender, leaving to his companions the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of dividing so rich a booty, he contented himself with the savage <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of contemplating the dead bodies of the Spaniards, lying in heaps together, against whom he had sworn a constant and deadly hatred. Fresh opportunities soon occurred, that enabled him to exert this spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, without extinguishing it. The ship he was in arrived at the coast of St Domingo; where the buccaneers on land immediately applied to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> some provisions for brandy. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> they offered were of little value, they alleged in excuse, that their enemies had overrun the country, laid waste their settlements, and carried off all they could. "Why (replied Montbar) do you tamely suffer such insults?" "Neither do we (answered they in the same tone); the Spaniards have experienced what kind of men we are, and have therefore taken advantage of the time when we were engaged in hunting. But we were going to join some of our companions, who have been still worse treated than we: and then we shall have warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." "If you approve of it (answered Montbar), I will head you, not as your commander, but as the foremost to expose myself to danger." The buccaneers perceiving from his appearance that he was such a man as they wanted, cheerfully accepted his offer. The same day they overtook the enemy, and Montbar attacked them with an impetuosity that astonished the bravest. Scarce one Spaniard escaped the effects of his fury. The remaining part of his life was equally distinguished as on this day. The Spaniards suffered so much from him, both by sea and land, that he acquired the name of the Exterminator. His savage disposition, as well as that of the other buccaneers who attended him, having obliged the Spaniards to confine themselves within their settlements, these freebooters resolved to attack them there. This new method of carrying on the war required superior forces; and their associations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> became more numerous. The first that was considerable was formed by L'Olonois, who derived his name from the sands of Olones the place of his birth. From the abject state of a bondsman, he had gradually raised himself to the command of two canoes, with 22 men. With these he was so successful as to take a Spanish frigate on the coast of Cuba. He then repaired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_AU_PRINCE">Port-au-<a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, in which were four ships, fitted out purposely to sail in pursuit of him. He took them, and threw all the crews into the sea, except one man, whom he saved, in order to send him with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the governor of Bucaner, the Havannah, acquainting him with what he had done, and assuring him that he would treat in the same manner all the Spaniards that should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into his hands, not excepting the governor himself, if he should be so fortunate as to take him. After this expedition, he ran his canoes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-ships <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>, and sailed with his frigate only to the island of Tortuga. Here he met with Michael de Basco, who had distinguished himself by having taken, even under the cannon of Porto-Bello, a Spanish ship, estimated at 218,500l. and by other actions equally brave and daring. These two gave out, that they were going to embark together on an expedition equally glorious and profitable; in consequence of which they soon collected together 440 men. This body of men, the most numerous the buccaneers had yet been able to muster, sailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Venezuela, which runs up into the country for the space of 50 leagues. The fort that was built at the entrance of it for its defence was taken; the cannon were nailed up; and the whole garrison, consisting of 250 men, put to death. They then reembarked, and came to Maracaybo, built on the western coast of the lake of the same name, at the distance of ten leagues from its mouth. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which had become flourishing and rich by its trade in skins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and cocoa, was deserted. The inhabitants had retired with their effects to the other side of the bay. If the buccaneers had not lost a fortnight in riot and debauch, they would have found at Gibraltar, near the extremity of the lake, every thing that the inhabitants had secreted to secure it from being plundered. On the contrary, they met with fortifications lately erected, which they had the useless satisfaction of making themselves masters of, at the expense of a great deal of blood; for the inhabitants had already removed to a distance the most valuable part of their property. Exasperated at this disappointment, they set fire to Gibraltar. Maracaybo would have shared the same fate, had it not been ransomed. Besides the sum they received for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, they also carried off with them all the crosses, pictures, and bells of the churches; intending, as they said, to build a chapel in the island of Tortuga, and to consecrate this part of their spoils to sacred purposes. Such was the religion of these barbarous people, who could make no other offering to heaven than that which arose from their robberies and plunder. While they were idly dissipating the spoils they had made on the coast of Venezuela, Morgan, the most renowned of the English buccaneers, sailed from Jamaica to attack Porto-Bello. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of operations was so well contrived, that he surprised the city, and took it without opposition. The conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> was an object of much greater importance. To secure this, Morgan thought it necessary to sail in the latitudes of Costa-Ricca, to procure some guides in the island of St Catharine's, where the Spaniards confined their malefactors. This place was so strongly fortified, that it ought to have held out for ten years against a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Notwithstanding this, the governor, on the first appearance of the pirates, sent privately to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> measures how he might surrender himself without incurring the imputation of cowardice. The result of this consultation was, that Morgan, in the nighttime, should Bucaneer attack a fort at some distance, and the governor should sally out of the citadel to defend a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of so much consequence; that the assailants should then attack him in the rear, and take him prisoner, which would consequently occasion a surrender of the place. It was agreed that a smart firing should be kept on both sides, without doing mischief to either. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> was admirably carried on. The Spaniards, without being exposed to any danger, appeared to have done their duty; and the bucaniers, after having totally demolished the fortifications, and put on board their vessels a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of warlike ammunition which they found at St Catharine's, steered their course towards the river Chagre, the only channel that was open to them to arrive at the place which was the object of their utmost wishes. At the entrance of this considerable river, a fort was built upon a steep rock, which the waves of the sea constantly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> against. This bulwark, very difficult of access, was defended by an officer whose extraordinary abilities were equal to his courage, and by a garrison that deserved such a commander. The bucaniers, for the first time, here met with a resistance that could only be equalled by their perseverance: it was a doubtful point, whether they would succeed or be obliged to raise the siege, when a lucky accident happened that proved favourable to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and their fortune. The commander was killed, and the fort accidentally took fire; the besiegers then taking advantage of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> calamity, made themselves masters of the place. Morgan left his vessels at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, with a sufficient number of men to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> them; and sailed up the river in his sloops for 33 miles, till he came to Cruces, where it ceases to be navigable. He then proceeded by land to Panama, which was only five leagues distant. Upon a large and extensive plain that was before the city, he met with a considerable body of troops, whom he put to flight with the greatest ease, and entered into the city, which was now abandoned. Here were found prodigious treasures concealed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and caves. Some valuable commodities were also taken upon the boats that were left aground at low water; and in the neighbouring forests were also found several rich deposits. Having burnt the city, they set sail with a great number of prisoners, who were ransomed a few days after, and came to the mouth of the Chagre with a prodigious booty. In 1603, an expedition of the greatest consequence was formed by Van <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, but who had served all his life among the French. His intrepidity would never let him suffer the least signs of cowardice among those who associated with him. In the heat of an engagement, he went about his ship; successively observed his men; and immediately killed those who shrank at the sudden report of a pistol, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, or cannon. This extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> had made him become the terror of the coward and the idol of the brave. In other respects, he readily shared with the men of spirit and bravery the immense riches that were acquired by so truly warlike a disposition. When he went upon these expeditions, he generally sailed in his frigate, which was his own property. But these new designs requiring greater numbers to carry them in- to execution, he took to his assistance Gramont, Bucaneer, Godfrey, and Jonqué, three Frenchmen distinguished by their exploits; and Lawrence de Graff, a Dutchman, who had signalized himself still more than they. Twelve hundred bucaniers joined themselves to these famous commanders, and sailed in six vessels for Vera Cruz. The darkness of the night favoured their landing, which was effected at three leagues from the place, where they arrived without being discovered. The governor, the fort, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, and the posts of the greatest consequence, every thing, in short, that could occasion any resistance, was taken by the break of day. All the citizens, men, women, and children, were shut up in the churches, whither they had fled for shelter. At the door of each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> were placed barrels of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> to blow up the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. A bucanier, with a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, was to set fire to it upon the least appearance of an insurrection. While the city was kept in such terror, it was easily pillaged; and after the bucaniers had carried off what was most valuable, they made a proposal to the citizens who were kept prisoners in the churches to ransom their lives and liberties by a contribution of 437,500l. These unfortunate people, who had neither ate nor drank for three days, cheerfully accepted the terms that were offered them. Half of the money was paid the same day: the other part was expected from the internal parts of the country; when there appeared on an eminence a considerable body of troops advancing, and near the port a fleet of 17 ships from Europe. At the sight of this armament, the bucaniers, without any marks of surprise, retired quietly, with 1500 slaves they had carried off with them as a trifling indemnification for the rest of the money they expected, the settling of which they referred to a more favourable opportunity. Their retreat was equally daring. They boldly sailed through the midst of the Spanish fleet; which let them <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without firing a single gun, and were in fact rather afraid of being attacked and beaten. The Spaniards would not probably have escaped so easily and with no other inconvenience but what arose from their fears, if the vessels of the pirates had not been laden with silver, or if the Spanish fleet had been freighted with any other effects but such merchandise as was little valued by these pirates. A year had scarce elapsed since their return from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, when, on a sudden, they were all seized with the rage of going to plunder the country of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. It is probable that the hopes of finding greater treasures upon a sea little frequented, than on one long exposed to piracies of this kind, was the cause of this expedition. But it is somewhat remarkable, that both the English and French, and the particular associations of these two nations, had projected this plan at the same time, without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, intercourse, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of acting in concert with each other. About 4000 men were employed in this expedition. Some of them came by Terra Firma, others by the straits of Magellan, to the place that was the object of their wishes. If the intrepidity of these barbarians had been directed, under the influence of a skilful and respectable commander, to one single uniform end, it is certain that they would have deprived the Spaniards of this import- But their natural character was an invincible obstacle to so rare an union; for they always formed themselves into several distinct bodies, sometimes even so few in number as ten or twelve, who acted together, or separated, as the most trifling caprice directed. Grognier, Lecuyer, Picard, and Le Sage, were the most distinguished officers among the French; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Samms, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Wilner, and Towley, among the English. Such of these adventurers as had got into the South sea by the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, seized upon the first vessel they found upon the coast. Their associates, who had sailed in their own vessels, were not much better provided. Weak, however, as they were, they beat several times the squadrons that were fitted out against them. But these victories were prejudicial to them, as they interrupted their navigation. When there were no more ships to be taken, they were continually obliged to make descents upon the coasts to get provisions, or to go by land in order to plunder those cities where the booty was secured. They successively attacked Seppa, Puebla-Nuevo, Leon, Realejo, Puebla-Viejo, Chiriquita, Lesparso, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, Villia, Nicoy, Tecanteca, Mucmeluna, Chiloteica, New-Segovia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUAYAQUIL">Guayaquil</a>, the most considerable of all these places. Many of them were taken by surprise; and most of them deserted by their inhabitants, who fled at the sight of the enemy. As soon as they took a town, it was directly set on fire, unless a sum proportioned to its value was given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it. The prisoners taken in battle were massacred without mercy, if they were not ransomed by the governor or some of the inhabitants: gold, pearls, or precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, were the only things accepted of for the payment of their ransom. Silver being too common, and too weighty for its current value, would have been troublesome to them. The chances of fortune, that seldom leave guilt unpunished, nor adversity without a compensation for its suffering, atoned for the crimes committed in the conquest of the new world, and the Indians were amply revenged of the Spaniards. While such piracies were committed on the southern ocean, the northern was threatened with the same by Gramont. He was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, by birth a gentleman, and had distinguished himself in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity in Europe; but his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for wine, gaming, and women, had obliged him to join the pirates. He was, however, affable, polite, generous, and eloquent; he was endued with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, and was a person of approved valour; which soon made him be considered as the chief of the French buccaneers. As soon as it was known that he had taken up arms, he was immediately joined by a number of brave men. The governor of St Domingo, who had at length prevailed upon his master to approve of the project, equally wise and just, of fixing the pirates to some place, and inducing them to become cultivators, was desirous of preventing the concerted expedition, and forbade it in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s name. Gramont, who had a greater share of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than his associates, was not on that account more inclined to comply, and sternly repelled: "How can <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> disapprove of a design he is unacquainted with, and which has been planned only a few days ago?" This answer highly pleased all the buccaneers; who directly embarked, in 1685, to attack <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPEACHY">Campeachy</a>. They landed without opposition. But at some distance from the coast, they were attacked by 800 Spaniards, who were beaten and pursued to the town; where both the parties entered at the same time. The cannon they found there was immediately levelled against the citadel. As it had very little effect, they were contriving some stratagem to enable them to become masters of the place, when intelligence was brought that it was abandoned. There remained in it only a gunner, an Englishman; and an officer of such signal courage, that he chose rather to expose himself to the greatest extremities, than basely to fly from the place with the rest. The commander of the buccaneers received him with marks of distinction, generously released him, gave him up all his effects, and besides complimented him with some valuable presents: such influence have courage and fidelity even on the minds of those who seem to violate all the rights of society. The conquerors of Campeachy spent two months in searching all the environs of the city, for 12 or 15 leagues, carrying off every thing that the inhabitants, in their flight, thought they had preserved. When all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> they had collected from every quarter was deposited in the ships, a proposal was made to the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, who still kept the field with 900 men, to ransom his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. His refusal determined them to burn it, and demolish the citadel. The French, on the festival of St Louis, were celebrating the anniversary of their king; and in the transports of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>, intoxication, and national love of their prince, they burnt to the value of a million of logwood; a part, and a very considerable one too, of the spoil they had made. After this singular and extravagant instance of folly, of which Frenchmen only could boast, they returned to St Domingo. In 1697, 1200 buccaneers were induced to join a squadron of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ships that sailed from Europe under the command of Pointis, to attack the famous city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. This was the most difficult enterprise that could be attempted in the new world. The situation of the port, the strength of the place, the badness of the climate, were so many obstacles that seemed insurmountable to any but such men as the buccaneers were. But every obstacle yielded to their valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>: the city was taken, and booty gained to the amount of 1,750,000l. Their rapacious commander, however, deprived them of the advantages resulting from their success. He scrupled not, as soon as they set sail, to offer 5250l. for the share of those who had been the chief instruments in procuring him so considerable a spoil. The buccaneers, exasperated at this treatment, resolved immediately to board the vessel called the Sceptre, where Pointis himself was, and which at that time was too far distant from the rest of the ships to expect to be assisted by them. This avaricious commander was upon the point of being massacred, when one of the malecontents cried out: "Brethren, why should we attack this rascal? he has carried off nothing that belongs to us. He has left our share at Carthagena, and there we must go to recover it." This proposal was received Buccina received with general applause. A savage joy at once succeeded that gloomy melancholy which had seized them; and without further deliberation all their ships sailed towards the city. As soon as they had entered the city without meeting with any resistance, they shut up all the men in the great church; and exacted payment of £18,750l. the amount of their share of booty which they had been defrauded of; promising to retreat immediately upon their compliance, but threatening the most dreadful vengeance if they refused. Upon this, the most venerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in the city mounted the pulpit, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all the influence his character, his authority, and his eloquence gave to him, to persuade his hearers to yield up without reserve all the gold, silver, and jewels they had. The collection which was made after the sermon, not furnishing the sum required, the city was ordered to be plundered. At length, after amassing all they could, these adventurers set sail; when unfortunately they met with a fleet of Dutch and English ships, both which nations were then in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Spain. Several of the pirates were either taken or sunk, with all the cargo they had on board their ships; the rest escaped to St Domingo. Such was the last memorable event in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the buccaneers. The separation of the English and French, when the war, on account of the prince of Orange, divided the two nations; the successful means they both made use of to promote the cultivation of land among their colonies, by the assistance of these enterprising men; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> they showed in fixing the most distinguished among them, and entrusting them with civil and military employments; the protection they were both under the necessity of affording to the Spanish settlements, which till then had been a general object of plunder: all these circumstances, and various others, besides the impossibility there was of supplying the place of these remarkable men, who were continually dropping off, concurred to put an end to a society as extraordinary as ever existed. Without any regular system, without laws, without any degree of subordination, and even without any fixed revenue, they became the astonishment of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which they lived, as they will be also of posterity.

a town of France, in Gascony, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAHUS">Bahus</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 5. N. Lat. 43. 47.

BUAT-NANCAY

Pages 847-847

L. G. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> du, a French writer on politics and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. See Supplement.

BUBALIS

Pages 847-847

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of the buffalo, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">bos</a>. See Bos.

BUBASTIS

Pages 847-848

in the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, one of the names of Isis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. The Egyptians bestowed different names on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, either to characterize his effects or his relations with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; they followed the same method respecting the moon. Cheiremon, a sacred writer of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, leaves no doubt on this subject. "Every thing which is published of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and Isis, all the sacerdotal fables, allude only to the phases of the moon, and the course of the sun." Bubastis was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> attributes of Isis. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a> having personified her, formed of her a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of that name was built, as described by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, and where the people collected from all parts of Egypt, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the year. A cat was the symbol of this deity. The priests fed it with sacred food; and when it died, they embalmed its body, and carried it in pomp to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> prepared for it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have explained this worship variously. The Greeks pretend that when Typhon declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the gods, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> transformed himself into a vulture, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> into an ibis, and Bubastis into a cat, and that the veneration of the people for the latter animal took rise from that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>; but they ascribe their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to the Egyptians, who thought very differently. However that may be, the cat was greatly honoured in Egypt, and a Roman soldier having imprudently killed one, was immediately put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the populace. Bubastis, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the priests, was deemed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Isis, and even represented her in cer- BUB <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> circumstances. It is for this reason that the Greeks, who honoured the moon by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, bestowed it also on this Egyptian divinity. Bubastis, says Herodotus, is called Diana by the Greeks. The Egyptians attributed to her the virtue of assisting pregnant women. The Greeks and Latins, disciples of the Egyptians, ascribed the same power to Diana; and Horace does not think it unworthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the following strophe to her: Montium custos nemorumque, Virgo, Quae laborantes utero puellas Ter vocata audis, adimisque lethe, Diva Triformis. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> seek for the origin of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> worship in the laws imposed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> on women, and which in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> follow the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> revolutions. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophers and the poets buried it under allegories unintelligible to the people. A perfect resemblance, however, does not exist between the two deities we have been speaking of. The Greeks constituted Diana <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> and of the forests; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the Egyptians did not acknowledge in Bubastis. The former added, that she was the daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, and Bubastis was produced by Osiris and Isis. A barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was introduced at the festivals celebrated in honour of Bubastis, called by the Greeks also Ilithyia, or Lucina, to mark her presiding over childbirth. The Egyptians adored her under this name in the city of Ilithyia, situated near Latopolis. It remains to resolve a question which naturally arises here: How could Bubastis be called the daughter of Isis, since she also was a symbol of the moon? The Egyptian theology easily explains these apparent contradictions. Isis was the general appellation of the moon, Bubastis a particular attribute. The sun, in conjunction with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the night, formed the celestial <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Osiris and Isis; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> which appears three days after was allegorically called their daughter. It is in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> that the Hebrews called this same phenomenon the birth of the moon, and that Horace says, Celo supinas si tuleris manus, Nascente <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">lund</a> rustica Phidyle, &c. &c. These observations inform us, why in the city of Ilithyia, where Bubastis was adored, the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the lunar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> was consecrated by a particular worship. In fact, it is three days after the conjunction, that the moon, disengaged from the rays of the sun, appears as a crescent, and is visible to us. The Egyptians celebrated therefore a solemnity in honour of Bubastis, which in their tongue signified new moon. The crescent with which her head was crowned, expresses palpably the intention of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in creating this symbolical divinity.

BUBBLE

Pages 848-848

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a cant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> given to a kind of project for raising <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on imaginary grounds, much practised in France and England in the years 1719, 1720, and 1721. The pretence of those schemes was the raising a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> for retrieving, setting on foot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carrying on, some promising and useful branch of trade, manufacture, machinery, or the like. To this end proposals were made out, showing the advantages to be derived from the undertaking, and inviting persons to be engaged in it.
