The sum necessary to manage the affair, together with the profits expected from it, were divided into shares or subscriptions, to be purchased by any disposed to adventure therein. Bubbles, by which the public have been tricked, are of two kinds, viz. 1. Those which we may properly enough term trading bubbles; and, 2. Stock or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> bubbles. The former have been of various kinds; and the latter at different times, as in 1719 and 1720.

BUBONOCELF

Pages 848-848
or Hernia inguinalis, in Surgery, a tumour in the inguen, formed by a prolapsus of the intestines, omentum, or both, through the processes of the peritoneum and rings of the abdominal muscles. See SURGERY Index.

BUC

Pages 848-848

GEORGE, a learned English antiquarian, flourished in the beginning of the 17th century. In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. he was made one of the gentlemen of his majesty's privy-chamber, and knighted; he was also constituted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the revels. What he mostly distinguished himself by was his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reign of Richard III.; in which he takes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to wipe off the bloody stains that have blotted his character, and represents the person and actions of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in a much less odious <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than other historians have done. He also wrote, 2. A Treatise of the Art of Revels; and, 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled The Third Universitie of England.

BUCCELLARIUS

Pages 856-856

an order of soldiery under the Greek emperors, appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and distribute the ammunition <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; though authors are somewhat divided as to their office and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Among the Visigoths buccellarus was a general name for a client <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vassal who lived at the expense of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. Some give the denomination to parasites in the courts of princes, some make them the body-guards of emperors, and some fancy they were only such as emperors employed in putting persons to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> privately.

BUCCELLATUM

Pages 856-856

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> writers, denotes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> biscuit baked hard and dry, both for lightness and keeping. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a> always carried with them enough for a fortnight, and sometimes much longer, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that military <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> was kept up.

BUCCINA

Pages 856-856

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musical and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. It is usually taken for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is confirmed by Festus, by his defining it a Buccina crooked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, played on like a trumpet. Vegetius observes, that the buccina was bent in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, in which respect it differed from the tuba <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trumpet. It is very hard to distinguish it from the cornu or horn, unless it was something less, and not quite so crooked; yet it certainly was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, because we never read of the cornu in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with the watch, but only the buccina. Besides, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the buccina was sharper, and to be heard much farther than either the cornu or the tuba. In Scripture, the like instrument, used both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and in the temple, was called ramshorns, kiren jobel, and sepheroth haggigobelin. This instrument was in use among the Jews to proclaim their feast-days, new-moons, jubilees, sabbatic years, and the like. At Lacedæmon, notice was given by the buccina when it was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the like was done at Rome, where the grandees had a buccina blown both before and after they sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. The sound of the buccina was called buccinum, or bucinus; and the musician who played on it was called buccinator.

BUCCLEUGH

Pages 856-856

a village in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Selkirk in Scotland, from which the noble family of Scott have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>.

BUCENTAUR

Pages 856-856

a galeas <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> galley of the doge of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, adorned with fine pillars on both sides, and gilt over from the prow to the stern. This vessel is covered over head with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, made of purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. In it the doge receives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords and persons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that go to Venice, accompanied with the ambassadors and counsellors of state, and all the senators seated on benches by him. The same vessel serves also in the magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of Ascension <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, on which the doge of Venice throws a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to espouse it, and to denote his dominion over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice. Bucentaurs is also the name of a ship, as great and as magnificent as that of the Venetians, built by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and launched on a lake which is six leagues in length.

BUCEPHALA

Pages 856-856
or BUCEPHALOS, in Ancient Geography, a town built by Alexander, on the west side of the Hydaspis, a river of the Hither India, in memory of his horse Bucephalus, which was killed in the action with Porus, after crossing that river. Others say, this horse died of age, 30 years old; and not in the battle, but some time after. His being branded or marked on the buttock with the head of an ox, gave rise to his name (Hesychius).—This generous animal, who had so long shared the toils and dangers of his master, had formerly received signal marks of royal regard. Having disappeared in the country of the Uxii, Alexander issued a proclamation, commanding his horse to be restored, otherwise he would ravage the whole country with fire and sword. This command

BUCER

Pages 856-857

MARTIN, one of the first authors of the reformation at Strasburg, was born in 1491, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>; and took the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of St Dominic, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but meeting afterward with the writings of Martin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, and comparing them with the Scriptures, he began to entertain doubts concerning several things in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. After some conferences with Luther at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a> in 1521, he adopted most of his sentiments; but in 1532, he gave the preference to those of Zwinglius. He assisted in many conferences concerning religion; and in 1548 was sent for to Augsburg to sign the agreement between the Papists and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, called the interim. His warm opposition to this project exposed him to many difficulties and hardships; the news of which reaching England, where his fame had already arrived, Cranmer archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> gave him an invitation to come over, which he readily accepted. In 1549, a handsome apartment was assigned him in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and a salary to teach <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward VI. had the greatest regard for him. Being told that he was very sensible of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and suffered much for want of a German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, he sent him 100 crowns to purchase one. He died of a complication of disorders in 1551; and was buried at Cambridge with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> funeral pomp. Five years after, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, his body was dug up, and publicly burnt, and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> demolished; but it was afterwards set up by order of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. He composed many works, among which are commentaries on the evangelists and gospels.

BUCHAM

Pages 859-859

a small town of Swabia in Germany, seated on the lake of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 20'. N. Lat. 47° 41'.

BUCHAN

Pages 857-857

a district of Scotland, lying partly in the shire of Aberdeen and partly in that of Banff: it gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Erskine.

BUCHANAN

Pages 857-858

GEORGE, the best Latin poet of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, perhaps inferior to none since the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born in February 1506. This accomplished scholar and distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> was not descended of a family remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. He had no occasion for the splendour of ancestry. He wanted not a reflected greatness, the equivocal, and too often the only ornament of the rich and noble. The village of Killearn, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a>, Scotland, was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>; and the abject poverty in which his father died might have confined him to toil at the lowest employments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the generosity of an uncle had not assisted him in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and enabled him to pursue for two years his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. But that short space was scarcely elapsed, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his benefactor made it necessary that he should return to his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and forsake, for a time, the paths of science. He was yet under his 20th year, and surrounded with the horrors of indigence. In this extremity, he enlisted as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier under John <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, who commanded the troops which France had sent to assist Scotland in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> it waged, at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, against England. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had not destined him to be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. He was disgusted with the fatigues of one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; and, fortunately, John <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, then Buchanan professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at St Andrew's, hearing of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> and his merit, afforded him a temporary relief. He now became the pupil of John Mair, a celebrated teacher in the same university, under whom he studied the subtleties of logic; and contracting an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he followed him to Paris. There, after having encountered many difficulties, he was invited to teach <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARBE">Barbe</a>. In this slavish occupation he was found by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Cassillis; with whom having remained five years at Paris, he returned to Scotland. He next acted as preceptor to the famous earl of Murray, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of James V. But while he was forming this nobleman for public affairs, he found that his life was in danger; and from enemies, whose vindictive rage could suffer no abatement, and who would not scruple the most dishonourable means of gratifying it. The scandalous lives of the clergy had, it seems, excited his indignation; and, more than reasoning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> argument, had estranged him from the errors of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. The Franciscan monks, in return to the beautiful but poignant satires he had written against them, branded him with the appellation of atheist; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of all denominations are too apt indiscriminately to lavish where they have conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>; and, not satisfied with the outrage of abuse and calumny, they conspired his destruction. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Beaton gave orders to apprehend him, and bribed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James with a very considerable sum to permit his execution. He was seized upon accordingly; and the first genius of his age was about to perish by the halter, or by fire, to satisfy a malignant resentment, when, escaping the vigilance of his guards, he fled into England. Henry VIII. at all times the slave of caprice and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, was then <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and at the same stake, the Lutheran and the Papist. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> or a satirist. After a short stay, Buchanan crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to France; and, to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> disappointment, found at Paris, Cardinal Beaton, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from Scotland. He retired privately to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURDEAUX">Bourdeaux</a>, dreading, perhaps, new misfortunes, and concerned that he could not prosecute his studies in obscurity and silence. Here he met Andrew Govea, a Portuguese of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and worth, with whom he had formerly been acquainted during his travels, and who was now employed in teaching a public school. He disdained not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as the assistant of his friend; and during the three years he resided at this place, he composed the tragedies which do him so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. It was here, also, that he wrote some of the most pleasant of those poems, in which he has rallied the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, and threatened to forsake them, as not being able to maintain their votary. About this time, too, he presented a copy of verses to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. who happened to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through Bourdeaux. His enemies, meanwhile, were not inactive. Cardinal Beaton, wrote about him to the archbishop of Bourdeaux; and by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which a cunning and a wicked heart can invent, he invited him to punish the most pestilential of all heretics. The archbishop, however, was not so violent as the cardinal. On inquiring into the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, he was convinced that the poet had committed a very small impropriety; and allowed Buchanan lowed himself to be pacified. But fortune was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> to continue her smiles. Andrew Govea being called by the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, his master, to establish an academy at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, he entreated Buchanan to accompany him. He obtained his request; and had not been a year in his own country, when he died, and left his associate exposed to the malice of his invertebrate enemies the monks. They loudly objected to him, that he was a Lutheran; that he had written poems against the Franciscans; and that he had been guilty of the abominable crime of eating <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. He was confined to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> till he should learn what these men fauced to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: and they enjoined him to translate the Psalms of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> into Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; a task which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> knows with what admirable skill and genius he performed. On obtaining his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he had the offer of a speedy promotion from the king of Portugal: the issue of which, his aversion to the clergy did not allow him to wait. He hastened to England; but the perturbed state of affairs during the minority of Edward VI. not giving him the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of any lasting security, he set out for France. There he had not been long, when he published his Jephtha, which his necessities made him dedicate to the marshal de Brissac. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> did not want generosity, and could judge of merit. He sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, as preceptor to his son Timoleon de Cossi. In this employ he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years; and during the leisure it afforded him, he fully examined the controversies which now agitated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and put the last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to many of the most admired of his smaller poems. When his pupil had no longer any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for him, he passed into Scotland, and made an open profession of the reformed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. But he soon quitted his native country for France; which appears to have been more agreeable to his taste. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, however, having determined that he should have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of educating her son, recalled him: and till the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> should arrive at a proper age, he was nominated to the principality of St Andrew's. His success as James's preceptor is well known. When it was reproached to him, that he had made his majesty a pedant; "It is a wonder (he replied) that I have made so much of him." Mackenzie relates a story concerning his tutelage of his pedantic majesty, which shows under what authority Buchanan held his pupil, and at the same time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of his veneration for royalty. The young king being one day at play with his fellow pupil the master of Erskine, Buchanan, who was then <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, desired them to make less noise. Finding that they disregarded his admonition, he told his majesty, if he did not hold his tongue, he would certainly whip his breech. The king replied, he would be glad to see who would <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> the cat, alluding to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. Buchanan, in a passion, threw the book from him, and gave his majesty a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> flogging. The old countess of Mar, who was in the next apartment, rushed into the room, and taking the king in her arms, asked how he dared to lay his hand on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s anointed. Buchanan's answer is too indelicate to be repeated. On the misfortunes that befell the amiable but imprudent Mary, he went over to the party of the earl of Murray; and at his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire he was prevailed upon to write his "Detection;" a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which his greatest admirers have read with regret. Having been Buchanan sent with other commissioners to England, against his mistress, he was, on his return, rewarded with the abbacy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> Regal; made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; and some time after lord <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and privy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. He was likewise rewarded by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> with a pension of 100l. a-year. The last twelve years of his life he employed in composing his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. After having vied with almost all the more eminent of the Latin poets, he contested with Livy and Sallust the palm of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sagacity. But it is to be remembered with pain, that, like the former of these historians, he was not always careful to preserve himself from the charge of partiality. In the year 1582, he expired at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in the 76th year of his age. Various writers who have mentioned this author, speak of him in very different <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, according to their religious and political principles. From his works, however, it is evident, that, both as a Latin poet and prose writer, he hath been rarely equalled since the reign of Augustus; nor is he less deserving of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> as a friend to the natural liberties of mankind, in opposition to usurpation and tyranny. "The happy genius of Buchanan (says Dr Robertson), equally formed to excel in prose and verse, more various, more original, and more elegant, than that of almost any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> who writes in Latin, reflects, with regard to this particular, the greatest lustre on his country." To his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> an obelisk 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> was erected by subscription in 1788, at Killearn the place of his nativity, designed by Mr J. Craig, nephew to the celebrated poet Thomson. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his works. 1. Rerum Scoticorum, &c. 2. Psalmorum Davidis paraphrasis poetica. 3. De jure regni apud Scotos Dialogus. 4. Psalmus civ. cum judicio Barclaii, &c. 5. Psalmus exx. cum analysi organica Beuzeri. 6. Baptistes, sive Calumnia. 7. Alcestis, tragedia. 8. Tragedia sacra et extera. 9. De Caeto recepto carmen, opus Stephan. 10. Franciscanus et Fratres, &c. 11. Elegiae, Silvae, &c. 12. De spera Herborne. 13. Poemata. 14. Satyra in cardinalem Lotharingium. 15. Rudimenta grammatices, Tho. Linacrei ex Anglico sermone in Latinum versae. 16. An admonition to the true lords. 17. De prosodia. 18. Chameleon, 1572. 19. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">Ad</a> viros sui seculi epistolae. 20. Literae reginae Scoticae ad com. Bothwell. 21. A detection of the doings of Mary queen of Scots, and of James earl of Bothwell, against Henry Lord Darnly. 22. Vita <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> ipso scripta biennio ante mortem, cum commentario D. Rob. Sibbaldi, M.D. 23. Life of Mary queen of Scots. These have been severally printed often, and in various countries. An edition of them all collected together was printed at Edinburgh in 1704, in 2 vols folio.

BUCHANNESS

Pages 858-858

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of Scotland, which is the farthest point of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETERHEAD">Peterhead</a>, and the most eastern of all Scotland. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 30. N. Lat. 57. 28.

BUCHAREST

Pages 858-859

a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, seated in the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, and the ordinary residence of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPODAR">hospodar</a>. The houses are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and very ill built, except a few that belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons. In 1716, a party of Germans sent from Transylvania entered this town, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> prisoner with all his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and carried them off. This expedition was the more easily performed, as several lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> had a secret intelligence with the governor of Transylvania. This prince had no other way to regain his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but by giving up that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Walachia, which lies between the river Aluth and Transylvania, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany, by the peace concluded at Passarowitz in 1718. The Germans again entered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his dominions, and levied excessive contributions. But affairs took another turn after the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Crotska in 1737; for the emperor was obliged to restore this part of Walachia to the hospodar. Bucharest contains about 69,000 inhabitants.

BUCHAW

Pages 858-858

a town of Germany, seated on the river Tederece, 22 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULM">Ulm</a>. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, whose abbeys had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diets of the empire. The town is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 37. N. Lat. 48. 5.

BUCHIOCHE

Pages 859-859

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of woollen cloth manufactured in Provence in France, which the French ships carry to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>.

BUCKENHAM

Pages 859-859

New, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, which formerly had a strong castle, but now demolished. It is seated in a flat, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 10'. N. Lat. 52° 30'. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 656 in 1811.

BUCKET

Pages 859-859

a small portable vessel to hold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, often made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> for its lightness and easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of fire. It is also the vessel let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a well, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the sides of ships, to fetch up water.

BUCKING

Pages 859-859

the first operation in the whitening of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> yarn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cloth.

BUCKINGHAM

Pages 859-859

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of Buckinghamshire in England, stands in a low ground, on the river Ouse, by which it is almost surrounded, and over which there are three handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-bridges. The town contained 3500 inhabitants in 1811, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It seems, however, to have been but an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the Conquest; for, according to Doomsday-book, it paid only for one hide, and had but 26 burgesses. Edward the elder fortified it in the year 918 against the incursions of the Danes, with a rampart and turrets. It also had formerly a castle in the middle of the town, of which no vestiges now remain. The shrine of St Rumald, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of fishermen, preserved in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-gaol stands in this town, and here the assizes are sometimes kept. It was formerly a staple for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, but that advantage it hath now lost. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and 12 burgesses, who are the sole electors of the members. In its neighbourhood are many <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> upon the Ouse.

BUCKINGHAM-SHIRE

Pages 859-859

(supposed to derive its name from the Saxon word Buc, denoting a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HART">hart</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> buck) an inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the landing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was included in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Catteuchlani; and after their conquest it was included in their third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Flavia Cassariensis. During the heptarchy it belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Mercia, which commenced in 582, and terminated in 827, having had 18 kings; and it is now included in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> circuit, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and the province of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; south by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>; east by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>; and west by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. It is of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, whose greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is from north to south. It contains 441,000 acres; has above 111,400 inhabitants, 185 parishes, 73 vicarages; is 49 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 18 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 109 in circumference. It has 15 market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYLESBURY">Aylesbury</a>, the county towns, Marlow, Newport-Pagnell, Winslow, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WENDOVER">Wendover</a>, Beaconsfield, Wiccomb, Chesham, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERSHAM">Amersham</a>, Stony <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a>, Colnbrook, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IVINGHOE">Ivinghoe</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OLNEY">Olney</a>, Risborough; besides the considerable villages of Eaton and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">Penny</a> Stratford, and 613 others inferior. It is divided into eight <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, provides 560 men for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, sends 14 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>-men; and pays 12 parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Ouse, Coln, Wicham, Amersham, Isis, Tame, and Loddon. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> produce is bone-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, corn, fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and breeding rams. The most noted places are the Chiltern Hills, Vale of Aylesbury, Bernwood Forrest, Wooburn-Heath, and 15 parks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is generally good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> mostly chalk or marle. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Buckinghamshire amounted to 117,650 in 1811. See Buckinghamshire, Supplement.

BUCKLE

Pages 859-859

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. The buckle was so much esteemed in former times, that few persons of repute and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> wore their girdles without it; and it may be considered, in coats of arms, as a token of the surety, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the bearer.

BUCKLER

Pages 859-860

a piece of defensive armour used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It was worn on the left arm, and composed of wickers woven together, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood of the lightest sort, covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and fortified with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or other metal. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> was sometimes round, sometimes oval, and sometimes almost <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Most of the bucklers were curiously adorned with all sorts of figures of birds and beasts, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, lions; nor of these only, but of the gods, of the celestial bodies, and all the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was derived from the heroic times, and from them communicated to the Grecians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Barbarians. The scutum, or Roman buckler, was of wood, the parts being joined together with little plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and and the whole covered with a bull's hide. An iron plate went about it without, to keep off blows; and another within, to hinder it from taking any damage by lying on the ground. In the middle was an iron boss or umbo jutting out, very serviceable to glance off <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and darts; and sometimes to press violently upon the enemy, and drive all before them. They are to be distinguished from the clypei, which were less, and quite round, belonging more properly to other nations, though for some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> used by the Romans. The scuta themselves were of two kinds; the ovata, and the imbricata: the former is a plain oval figure; the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> inward like half a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>. Polybius makes the scuta four feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and Plutarch calls them ἀποδεξίας, reaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the feet. And it is very probable that they covered almost the whole body, since in Livy we meet with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who stood on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, sometimes sleeping with their head on their shield, having fixed the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Votive Bucklers: Those consecrated to the gods and hung up in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, either in commemoration of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, or as a thanksgiving for a victory obtained over an enemy; whose bucklers, taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were offered as a trophy.

BUCKOR

Pages 860-860

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul. It is seated on the river Indos, on the banks of which there are corn and cattle; but the west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, which is bounded by Sagestan in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. The inhabitants are strong, robust, and apt to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a>; for which reason the Mogul has a garrison at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town called Buckor, which is seated in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> made by the river Indos. They are all Mahometans, and drive a great trade in cotton cloth and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> commodities. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 70° 5' N. Lat. 28° 20'.

BUCKRAM

Pages 860-860

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth stiffened with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, used in the making of garments to keep them in the form intended. It is also used in the bodies of women's gowns; and it often serves to make wrappers to cover cloths, serges, and such other merchandises, in order to preserve them, and keep them from the dust, and their colours from fading. Buckrams are sold wholesale by the dozen of small pieces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remnants, each about four ells <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> according to the piece from which they are cut. Sometimes they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> new pieces of linen cloth to make buckrams, but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> old sheets and old pieces of sails.

BUCKSTALL

Pages 860-860

a toil to take deer, which must not be kept by any body that has not a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> of his own, under penalties.

BUCOLIC

Pages 860-860

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a kind of poem relating to shepherds and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> affairs, which, according to the most generally received <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, took its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Bucolics, says Vossius, have some conformity with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. Like it, they are pictures and imitations of ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, however, that comedy represents the manners of the inhabitants of cities, and bucolics the occupations of country people. Sometimes, continues he, this last poem is in form of a monologue, and sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. Sometimes there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in it, and sometimes only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>; and sometimes it is composed both of action and narration. The hexameter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> is the most proper for bucolics in the Greek and Latin tongues. Moschus, Bion, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, are the most renowned of the ancient bucolic poets.

BUDA

Pages 860-861

the Beglerbegliec of, was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> governments of the Turks in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It included all the countries of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Teisse and Danube, and between <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AGRIA">Agria</a> and Novigrad; all all Lower Hungary from Gran and Canisca, the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Slavonia, and almost all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>: but a good part of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. BUDÆUS, WILLIAM, the most learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in France in the 15th century, was descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and illustrious family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1467. He was placed young under masters; but barbarism prevailed so much in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Paris, that Budæus took a dislike to them, and spent his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in idleness, till his parents sent him to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Here he passed three years without adding to his knowledge; for his parents sending for him back to Paris, found his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> no less than before, and his reluctance to study, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> and other useless pleasures, much greater. They talked no more to him of learning of any kind; and as he was heir to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune, left him to follow his own inclinations. He was passionately fond of hunting, and took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in horses, dogs, and hawks. The fire of youth beginning to cool, and his usual pleasures to pall upon his senses, he was seized with an irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for study. He immediately disposed of all his hunting equipage, and even abstracted himself from all business to apply himself wholly to study; in which he made, without any assistance, a very rapid and amazing progress, particularly in the Latin and Greek languages. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which gained him greatest reputation was his treatise de Asse. His erudition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> birth were not his only advantages; he had an uncommon share of piety, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, gentleness, and good-breeding. The French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, Francis I., often sent for him; and at his persuasion, and that of Du Bellay, founded the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of France, for teaching the languages and sciences. The king sent him to Rome with the character of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Leo X., and in 1522 made him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests. The same year he was chosen provost of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. He died at Paris in 1540. His works, making four volumes in folio, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1557. BUDDÆUS, JOHN FRANCIS, a celebrated Lutheran divine, and one of the most learned men Germany has produced, was born in 1667, at Anclam, a town of Pomerania, where his father was minister. He was at first Greek and Latin professor at Colburg; afterwards professor of morality and politics in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>; and at length, in 1705, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Jena, where he fixed, and where he died, after having acquired a very great reputation. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. A large historical German <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>. 2. Historia ecclesiastica Veteris Testamenti, 2 vols 4to. 3. Elementa philosophiae practicae, instrumentalis, et theoreticae, 3 vols 8vo, which has had a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of editions, because in most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Germany the professors take this work for the text of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>. 4. Selecta juris <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> et gentium. 5. Miscellanea sacra, 3 vols 4to. 6. Isagoge historico-theologica <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> theologiam universam, singulare ejus partes, 2 vols 4to; which is much valued by the Lutherans. 7. A treatise on atheism and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>.

BUDDLE

Pages 861-861

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> frame of boards, used in washing metallic ores. BUDDLEIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BUDELICH

Pages 861-861

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is seated on the little river Traen, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 55. N. Lat. 49. 52.

BUDGE-BARRELS

Pages 861-861

among engineers, small barrels well hooped, with only one head; on the other end is nailed a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, to draw together upon strings like a purse. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is for carrying powder along with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>; being less dangerous, and easier carried, than whole barrels. They are likewise used upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of mortars for holding <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> powder.

BUDGELL

Pages 861-862

EUSTACE, Esq., an ingenious and polite writer, was the son of Gilbert Budgell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and was born at St Thomas, near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, about the year 1685. He was educated at Christchurch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; from which he removed to the Inner Temple, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: but instead of studying the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for which his father intended him, he applied to polite literature; kept <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the gentlest persons in town; and particularly contracted a strict intimacy with the ingenious Mr Addison, who was first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to his mother, and who, on his being made secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wharton, lord <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, took him with him as one of the clerks of his office. Mr Budgell, who was about 20 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and had read the classics, and the works of the best English, French, and Italian authors, now became concerned with Sir Richard Steele and Mr Addison in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the Tatler, as he had, soon after, a share in writing the Spectators, where all the papers written by him are marked with an X; and when that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was completed, he had likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, where his performances are marked with an asterisk. He was afterwards made under secretary to Mr Addison, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> secretary to the lords justices of Ireland, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. Soon after, he was chosen a member of the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in 1717, Mr Addison, having become <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretary of state in England, procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of accountant and comptroller general of the revenue in Ireland. But the next year, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bolton being appointed lord-lieutenant, Mr Budgell wrote a lampoon against Mr Webster, his secretary, in which his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> himself was not spared; and upon all occasions treated that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> with the utmost contempt. This imprudent step was the primary cause of his ruin: for the duke of Bolton, in support of his secretary, got him removed from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of accountant-general; upon which, returning to England, he, contrary to the advice of Mr Addison, published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in a pamphlet, entitled, "A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the lord," &c. Mr Addison had now resigned the seals, and was retired into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for the sake of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: Mr Budgell Budgell had also lost several other powerful friends who had been taken off by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; particularly the lord <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sunderland: he, however, made several attempts to succeed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but was constantly kept <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the duke of Bolton. In the year 1720 he lost 20,000l. by the South-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> scheme, and afterwards spent 5000l. more in unsuccessful attempts to get into parliament. This completed his ruin. He at length employed himself in writing pamphlets against the ministry, and wrote many papers in the Craftsman. In 1733, he began a weekly pamphlet, called The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>; which he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for above 100 numbers, printed in eight volumes 8vo. During the progress of this work, Dr Tindal's death happened, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> Mr Budgell had 2000l. left him; and the world being surprised at such a gift from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> entirely unrelated to him, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the next heir, a nephew, and the continuator of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of England, immediately imputed it to his making the will himself. Thus the satirist: Let Budgell <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> low Grub-street on my quill, And write whate'er he please except my will. It was thought he had some hand in publishing Dr Tindal's Christianity as old as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>; for he often talked of another additional volume on the same subject, but never published it. After the cessation of the Bee, Mr Budgell became so involved in law-suits, that he was reduced to a very unhappy situation. He got himself called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and attended for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the courts of law; but finding himself unable to make any progress, and being distrest to the utmost, he determined at length to make away with himself. Accordingly, in the year 1736, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> at Somerset-stairs, after filling his pockets with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; ordered the waterman to shoot the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and, while the boat was going under, threw himself into the river. He had several days before been visibly distracted in his mind. Upon his bureau was found a slip of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, on which were these words: What Cato did, and Addison approv'd, Cannot be wrong. Besides the above works, he wrote a Translation of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>. He was never married; but left one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who afterwards assumed his name, and became an actress in Drury-lane.

BUDINUS

Pages 862-862

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain of Sarmatia Europaea, from which the more northern <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the Borysthenes is said to take its rise, according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. But this is contradicted by later accounts. Now Podolia. BUDNÆANS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, so called from the name of their leader, Simon Budnæus. They not only denied all kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, but asserted, that he was not begotten by any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of divine power; being born, like other men, in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> way. Budnæus was deposed from his ministerial functions in the year 1584, and publicly excommunicated, with all his disciples; but afterwards abandoning his peculiar sentiments, he was readmitted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Crellius ascribes the origin of the above <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Neuser. BUDOÀ, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, with a bishop's see, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It is seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CATTARO">Cattaro</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Dulugno, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>; and is an important fortress, where the Venetians formerly kept a strong garrison. In 1667, it suffered greatly by an earthquake; and in 1686 was besieged by Soliman, basha of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCUTARI">Scutari</a>; but General Cornaro obliged him to raise the siege. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 22. N. Lat. 42. 12.

BUDRIO

Pages 862-862

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Bolognese. The adjacent fields produce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, which renders the town of more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> than larger places. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 35. N. Lat. 44. 27.

BUDUN

Pages 862-862

is the name of one of the Ceylonese gods: he is supposed to have arrived at supremacy, after successive transmigrations, from the lowest state of an insect, through the various <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of living animals. There have been three deities of this name, each of which is supposed to reign as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> removes a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of sand, half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and six miles round, by a single grain in a thousand years. See SAKRADAWENDRA.

BUDWEIS

Pages 862-862

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built, surrounded with strong walls, fortified with a good rampart, and might be made an important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1744, but he did not keep it very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. E. Long. 14. 19. N. Lat. 42. 15. BUDZIAC <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Neister, Bog, and Nieper; having <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> and Russia on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Little Tartary on the east, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south, and Bessarabia on the west. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Oczzakow. It is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>.

BUENA VISTA

Pages 862-862

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying in N. Lat. 15. 56. It is also called Bonivista and Bonnevue; but the first is the true appellation, the others being only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> and corruptions of the original name, which signifies a good prospect, intimating the beautiful appearance it makes to ships at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is reckoned near 20 leagues in circumference, and is distinguished on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side by a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rocks that bound it. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> that stretches east and north-west is terminated with sundry banks to the sea; but the interior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is chiefly mountainous. From the northern point there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ridge of rocks projecting near a whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> into the sea, against which the waves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> with incredible fury. Another point of rocks stretches into the sea on the southern point of the island eastward, a league and a half beyond that point; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for shipping.

BUENOS AYRES

Pages 863-863

Neustra Senhora de, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Buenos Ayres, in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, was founded in the year 1535, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Pedro de Mendoza, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governor. It stands on a point called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, on the south side of the Plata, fronting a small river, in S. Lat. 34° 34' 38", according to the observations of Father Ferville. The situation is in a fine plain, rising by a gentle ascent from the river; and truly paradisaical, whether we regard the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that beautiful verdure which overspreads the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country, of which the inhabitants have a prospect as far as the eye can reach. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is very considerable in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, containing according to some 40,000, according to others 60,000 inhabitants. The streets are straight, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and pretty equal in the heights and dimensions of the buildings; one very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> adorns it, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> being a castle in which the governor holds his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and presides over a garrison of 3000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The city was taken by the British in 1826, but retaken by the inhabitants a few weeks after.

BUFF

Pages 863-863

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> prepared from the skin of the buffalo; which dressed with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, after the manner of shanny, makes what we call buffskin. This makes a very considerable article in the French, English, and Dutch commerce at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and all along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The skins of elks, oxen, and other like animals, when prepared after the same manner as that of the buffalo, are likewise called buff. Of buffskin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> buff-leather, are made a sort of coats for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or gens d'armes of France, bandoliers, belts, pouches, and gloves. In France, there are several manufactories designed for the dressing of those sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CORBEIL">Corbeil</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIORT">Niort</a>, at Lyons, at Rome, at Etanepus, at Cone.

BUFFALMACO

Pages 863-863

Boramico, an Italian painter; the first who put labels to the mouths of his figures, with sentences; since followed by bad masters, but more frequently in caricature engravings. He died in 1340.

BUFFALO

Pages 863-863

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>. BUFFET was anciently a little apartment, separated from the rest of the room by slender wooden columns, for the disposing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, glass-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c. It is now properly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in a dining-room, called also a side-board, for the plate, glasses, bottles, basins, &c., to be placed on, as well for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the table as for magnificence. In houses of persons of distinction in France, the buffet is a detached room, decorated with pictures relative to the subject, with fountains, cisterns, and vases. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> faced with marble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>.

BUFFIER

Pages 863-863
Claude, a French writer, born in 1661, became a Jesuit in 1679, and died at Paris in 1737. There are many works of this author, which show deep penetration and accurate judgment; the principal of which is, Un Cours des Sciences, &c.; that is, "A Course of Sciences upon principles new and simple, in order to form the language, the understanding, and the heart, 1732," in folio. This collection includes an excellent "French grammar upon a new plan; a philosophical and practical treatise upon eloquence; an art of poetry," which, however, is not reckoned the best part of this miscellany; "elements of metaphysics; an examination into vulgar prejudices; a treatise of civil society; and an exposition of the proofs of religion:" all full of reflections, just as well as new. He was the author of other works, in verse and prose, of which no great account is had; and it is remarkable, that his style in both is rather easy than accurate and correct, notwithstanding the precepts in his "Grammar," which is really philosophic.

BUFFON

Pages 863-864

George <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> Le Clerc, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of, a celebrated naturalist, was born at Montbard, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the 9th of September 1707; his father was a counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Dijon, and the son was destined to the same office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> science had not drawn him away from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He studied at Dijon; and his eager <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, his acuteness, penetration, and robust <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, fitted him to pursue business and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> with equal ardour. His early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> was for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and the young Le Clerc was never without Euclid in his pocket. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty, he went with an English nobleman and his governor to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; but he overlooked the choicest remains of art, and, amidst the ruins of an elegant and luxurious people, he first felt the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, whose zealous and successful admirer he afterwards proved. On his return to France, he fought, on some occasional quarrel, with an Englishman, whom he wounded, and was obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He there translated Newton's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a> from the Latin, and Hales's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATICS">Statics</a> from the English, into the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He afterwards came to England, at the age of 25; and this journey concluded his travels: he staid there about three months. At the age of 21, he succeeded to the estate of his mother, which was valued at about 300,000 livres (above 12,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>); and he was one of those whose easy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> affluent circumstances urge on to literary pursuits, and clear the path of some of its thorns. Perhaps this was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his retirement to Montbard, where he spent much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and where his leisure was little interrupted: while in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, his office of intendant of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s garden and cabinet engaged much of his time. He loved much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and was partial to the fair; but he loved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> more. He spent 14 hours every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; and, when we examine the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his knowledge, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his works, we wonder at his having executed so much much even in this time. At five in the morning he retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> in his vast gardens, and he was then inaccessible. This was, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> called it, the cradle of natural history; but she was indifferently accommodated. The walls were naked: an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and an elbow <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, were the only furniture of his study. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> were in a cabinet in another <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and he went occasionally from one to the other. The eras of Buffon's works are pretty well known. When each was finished it was put aside, in order that he might forget it, and he then returned to it with the severity of a critic. He was anxious to have it perspicuous; and if those to whom he read his works hesitated a moment, he changed the passage. The works of others he at last read like Magliabechi, the titles, the contents, and the most interesting parts; but he read M. Neckar's Compte Rendu, and the Administration of the Finances, at length; he spoke of them also with no little enthusiasm. His favourite authors were Fenelon, Montesquieu, and Richardson. M. de Buffon's conversation was unadorned, rarely animated, but sometimes very cheerful. He was exact in his dress, particularly in dressing his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. He sat <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> at table, and thus seemed at his ease. His conversation was, at this time, unembarrassed, and his guests had frequently occasion to notice some happy turn of phrase, or some deep reflection.
