His complaisance was very considerable: he loved praise, and even praised himself; but it was with so much frankness, and with so little contempt of others, that it was never disagreeable. Indeed, when we consider the extent of his reputation, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of his works, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> with which they were always received, we do not wonder that he was sensible of his own value. It would perhaps have displayed a stronger mind to have concealed it. His father lived to 93, and almost adored his son; his grandfather to 87; and the subject of the present article exceeded only 80. He died in April 1788. Fifty-six <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> were found in his bladder; but if he had consented to the operation, he might probably have lived longer. He left one son; who near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower in the gardens of Montbard has placed a low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, with the following inscription: Excellse Turri Humilis Columna, Parenti suo Fil. Buffon. This son fell a victim to the tyranny of Robespierre during the late revolution in France.

BUFFOON

Pages 864-864

a droll, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mimic, who diverts the public by his pleasantry and follies. Menage after Salmasius, derives the word from buffo; a name given to those who appeared on the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> with their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> blown up; that, receiving blows thereon, they might make the greater noise, and set the people a laughing. Others, as Rhodiginus, make the origin of buffoonery more venerable; deriving it from a feast instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Erechtheus, called euphonia. Buffoons are the same with what we otherwise find denominated scurræ, gelasiani, mimologi, ministelli, go-liardi, joculatores, &c. whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is laid at the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. Gallienus never sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to meat without a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of buffoons by him; Tiberinus also renders pantomimes by buffoons. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> he observes, the shows of the buffoons were taken away by Domitian, restored by Nerva, and finally abolished by Trajan.

BUFONITA

Pages 864-864

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the toad-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This has been received not only among the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of native <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> by the generality of authors, but even has held a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the gems, and is still worn in rings by some people; though undoubtedly it is an extraneous fossil. There has been a strong <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the world, that it was found in the head of an old toad; and that this animal voided it at the mouth, on being put on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cloth. The general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the bufonite is a deep dusky <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; but it varies greatly in this respect in several specimens, some of which are quite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, others of an extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> simple brown, a chestnut colour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> colour, black-gray, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whitish. The bufonite are usually found immersed in beds of stone; and so little doubt is there of what they have originally been, viz. the petrified <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the lupus piscis, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>-fish, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the jaw of the fish has sometimes been found with the teeth petrified in it. The bufonite are said to be cordial and astringent; many other fanciful virtues are ascribed to them, which the present practice has rejected.

BUG

Pages 864-865
or BUGG. See CIMEX, Entomology Index. Cheap, easy, and clean mixture for effectually destroying Bugs. Take of the highest rectified spirit of wine, (viz. lamp-spirits) that will burn all away dry, and leave not the least moisture behind it, half a pint; new distilled oil, or spirit, of turpentine, half a pint: mix them together; and break into it, in small bits, half an ounce of camphire, which will dissolve it in a few minutes; shake them well together; and with a piece of sponge, or a brush dipt in some of it, wet very well the bed or furniture wherein these vermin harbour and breed, and it will infallibly kill and destroy both them and their nits, although they swarm never so much. But then the bed and furniture must be well and thoroughly wet with it (the dust upon them being first brushed and shaken off), by which means it will neither soil, stain, nor in the least hurt, the finest silk or damask bed that is. The quantity here ordered of this mixture (that costs but about a shilling) will rid any one bed whatever, though it swarms with bugs. If any buggs should happen to appear after once using it, it will only be for want of well wetting the lacing, &c. of the bed, or the folding of the linens or curtains near the rings, or the joints or holes in and about the bed or head-board, wherein the buggs and nits nestle and breed; and then their being wetted all again with more of the same mixture, which dries in as fast as you use it, pouring some of it into the joints and holes where the brush or sponge cannot reach, will never fail absolutely to destroy them all. Some beds that have much wood-work can hardly be thoroughly cleared without being first taken down; but others that can be drawn out, or that you can get well behind, to be done as it should be, may. The smell this mixture occasions will be all gone in two or three days; which yet yet is very wholesome, and to many people agreeable. Remember always to shake the mixture together very well whenever you use it, which must be in the daytime, not by candle-light, lest the subtlety of the mixture should catch the flame as you are using it, and occasion damage. Early in the spring, even in February, the larva of this insect begins to burst from the egg; and it is at this season that attention is so very requisite. The bed ought to be stripped of all its furniture, which should be washed, and even boiled, if linen; if stuff, it should be hot-pressed. The bedstead should be taken to pieces, dusted, and washed with spirit of wine in the joints; for in those parts the females lay their eggs. This done, the joints, crevices, cavities, &c. should be well filled with the best soft soap mixed with verdigris and Scots snuff. On this substance, the larva, if any escape the cleansing, or any, which is common in old houses, creep into the bedstead, will feed at first, and of course be destroyed: this last will effect the purpose in houses where these vermin are not so numerous, by repeating the operation every three months.—Professor Kalm mentions, that, from repeated trials, he has been convinced, that sulphur, if it be properly employed, entirely destroys bugs, and their eggs in beds or walls, though they were ten times more numerous than the ants on an ant-hill. His translator, Dr Forster, adds, that a still more effectual remedy is, to wash all the infected furniture with a solution of arsene. See further the article CIMICIFUGA.

BUGEY

Pages 865-865

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the east by Savoy, on the west by Bresse, on the south by Dauphiny, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the territory of Gex and the Franche Compte. It is about 40 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Though it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> full of hills and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, yet it is fertile in some places, the rivers abound in trouts, and there is plenty of all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> places are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELLEY">Belley</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Seisel, St Rambert, Fort L'Ecluse, and Chateau Neuf.

BUGGERS

Pages 865-865

(Bulgarii) anciently signified a kind of heretics, otherwise called Paterini, Cathari, and Albigeneses. The word is formed of the French Bougres, and that from Bougria <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bulgaria, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where they chiefly appeared. Among other errors they held that men ought to believe no scripture but the New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> was not necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>; that husbands who conversed with their wives could not be saved; and that an oath was absolutely unlawful. They were strenuously refuted by Fr. Robert, a Dominican, surnamed the Bugger, as having formerly made profession of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. The Buggers are mentioned by Matthew <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in the reign of Henry III. under the name of Bugares. Circa dies autem illos invaluit haeretica pravitas corum qui vulgariter dicuntur Paterini et Bugares, de quorum erroribus malo tacere quam loqui. Bugger, or Buggerer, came afterwards to be used for a sodomite; it being one of the imputations laid, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or wrong, on the Bulgarian heretics, that they taught, or at least practised, this abominable crime. Bugger (Bulgarius), is also a denomination given to usurers; usury being a vice to which the same heretics are said to have been much addicted.

BUGGERY

Pages 865-865
or SODOMY, is defined by Sir Edward Coke to be a carnal copulation against nature, either by a confusion of species, that is to say, either a man or woman with a brute beast; or sexes, as a man with a man, or a man unnaturally with a woman. It is said this sin against God and nature was first brought into England by the Lombards. As to its punishment, the voice of nature and of reason, and the express law of God, determines it to be capital. Off: Levit. xx. this we have a signal instance, long before the Jewish dispensation, by the destruction of two cities by fire from heaven; so that this is an universal, not merely a provincial, precept. Our ancient law, in some measure, imitated this punishment, by commanding such miscreants to be burnt to death; though Flota says, they should be buried alive; either of which punishments was indifferently used for this crime among the ancient Goths. But now the general punishment of all felonies is the same, namely, by hanging: and this offence (being in the times of Popery only subject to ecclesiastical censures) was made felony without benefit of clergy by statute 25 Hen. VIII. c. 6. revived and confirmed by 5 Eliz. c. 17. And the rule of law herein is, that, if both parties are arrived at the years of discretion, agentes et consentientes pari pana plectonatur, "both are liable to the same punishment."

BUGIA

Pages 865-865

by the Africans called Bugeiah, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Algiers, and once the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of that name. It is supposed to be the Salde of Strabo, built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It hath a handsome port formed by a narrow neck of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> running into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of whose promontory was formerly faced with a wall of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; where was likewise an aqueduct, which supplied the port with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, discharging it into a capacious basin; all which now <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in ruins. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> itself is built on the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one, at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain that looks towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east; a great part of whose walls run up quite to the top of it; where there is also a castle that commands the whole town, besides two others at the bottom, built for a security to the port. The inhabitants drive a considerable trade in ploughshares, mattocks, and other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tools, which they manufacture from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The town is watered by a large river, supposed to be the Nasava of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is populous; and hath a considerable market for iron <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and wax, which is carried on with great tranquility; but is no sooner over than the whole place is in an uproar, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> seldom concludes without some flagrant instance of barbarity. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. N. Lat. 35. 30.

BUGIE

Pages 865-865

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, situated on the western shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> almost opposite to Ziden, the port town to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, and about 100 miles west of it. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36. N. Lat. 22. 15. BUGLE. See AJUGA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BUGLOSS. See ANCHUSA, BOTANY Index. Vipers Bugloss. See ECHIUM, BOTANY Index.

BUILDING

Pages 865-868

BUILDING, a fabric erected by art, either for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, magnificence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convenience. Building is also used for the art of constructing and raising an edifice; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it comprehends as well the expences as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and execution of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings are much more commodious, as well as beautiful, than those of former times. Of old they used to dwell in houses, most of them with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> staircase, low ceilings, and dark windows; the rooms built at random, without any thing of contrivance, and often with steps from one to another; so that one would think the people of former ages were afraid of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>: whereas the genius of our times is altogether for light staircases, fine sash-windows, and lofty ceilings. And such has been our builders industry in point of compactness and uniformity, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> after the new way <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford, on the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ground, almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the conveniences which could be had from an old one. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> 11 Geo. I. and 4 Geo. III. for the regulation of building within the weekly bills of mortality, and in other places therein specified, party walls are required to be erected of brick or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which shall be two bricks and a half thick in the cellar, two bricks thick upwards to the garret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, &c. and other limitations are enacted respecting the disposition of the timbers, &c. And every building is to be surveyed; and the person who offends against the statute in any of the particulars recited, is liable to a forfeit of £250l. to be levied by warrant of justices of the peace. The other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> statutes relating to building are 19 Car. II. c. 3. 22 Car. II. c. 11. 5 Eliz. c. 4. 33 Eliz. c. 6. 6 Ann. c. 31. 7 Ann. c. 17. 33 Geo. II. c. 30. and 6 Geo. III. c. 37. Building of Ships. See Ship-Building. Builth, or Bealt, a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> in Brecknockshire, pleasantly seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, over which there is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> that leads into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 52. 8. Buis, a territory of France, in Dauphiny. It is a small mountainous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but pretty fertile; and Buis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NIONS">Nions</a> are the principal places. Bukari, a small well-built town of Hungarian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, situated on the Golfo di Bikeriza, in E. Long. 25. 53. N. Lat. 45. 20. Bukharia, a general name for all that vast tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> lying between Karazm and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Kobi, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY_DESERT"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> bordering on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. It derives its name of Bukharia from the Mogul word Bukhor, which signifies a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; it being formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for those who wanted instruction in the languages and sciences to go into Bukharia. Hence this name appears to have been given to it by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> who under Jenghiz Khan conquered the country. It is nearly the same with that called by the Arabs Mawarainahr, which is little other than a translation of the word Transoxiana, the name formerly given to those provinces. This region is divided into Great and Little Bukharia. Great Bukharia (which seems to comprehend the Sogdiana and Bactriana of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, with their dependencies) is situated between the 34th and 46th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between the 76th and 92d degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is Bukharia bounded on the north by the river Seri, which separates it from the dominions of the Eluths or Kalmucs; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kashgar in Little Bukharia, on the east; by the dominions of the great Mogul and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the south; and by the country of Karazm on the west: being about 770 miles long from west to east, and 730 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from south to north. It is an exceeding rich and fertile country; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> abound with the richest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; the valleys are of an astonishing fertility in all sorts of fruit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>; the fields are covered with grass the height of a man; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with excellent fish; and wood, which is scarce over all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, is here in great plenty. But all these benefits are of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the Tartar inhabitants, who are naturally so lazy, that they would rather go rob and kill their neighbours than apply themselves to improve the benefits which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> so liberally offers them. This country is divided into three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> provinces, viz. Bukharia proper, Samarcan, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALK">Balk</a>; each of which generally has its proper khan. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bukharia proper is the most western of the three; having on the west Karazm, on the north a desert called by the Arabs Guzznah, on the east the province of Samarcan, and on the south the river Amu. It may be about 390 miles long, and 320 broad. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Bukhara, Zam, Wardansi, Karakal, Sionjbalza, Karshi, Zarnju, Nersem, Karmina, &c. Little Bukharia is so called, not because it is less in dimensions than the other, for in reality it is larger; but because it is inferior to it as to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its cities, goodness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, &c. It is surrounded by deserts; it has on the west, Great Bukharia; on the north, the country of the Kalmucs; on the east, that of the Moguls subject to China; on the south, Thibet, and the north-west corner of China. It is situated between the 93d and 118th degrees of east longitude, and between 35° 30' and 45° of north latitude; being in length from east to west about 850 miles, and in breadth from north to south 380: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> its dimensions be taken according to its semicircular course from the south to the north-east, its length will be 1200 miles. It is sufficiently populous and fertile; but the great elevation of its land, joined to the height of the mountains which bound it in several parts, particularly towards the south, renders it much colder than from its situation might naturally be expected. It is very rich in mines of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver; but the inhabitants reap little benefit from them, because neither the Eluths nor Kalmucs, who are masters of the country, nor the Bukhars, care to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in them. Nevertheless, they gather abundance of gold from the beds of the torrents formed by the melting of the snow in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and from hence comes all that gold dust which the Bukhars carry into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, China, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. Much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a> is likewise found in this country; and all sorts of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, even diamonds; but the inhabitants have not the art of either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> or polishing them. The inhabitants both of Great and Little Bukharia, are generally those people called Bukhars. They are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-burnt and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-haired; although some of them are very fair, handsome, and well made. They do not want <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and are addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; merce; which they carry on with China, the Indies, Persia, and Russia: but those who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with them will be sure of being overreached, if they do not take great care. The habits of the men differ very little from those of the Tartars. Their girdles are like those of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>. The garments of the women differ in nothing from those of the men, and are commonly quilted with cotton. They wear bobs in their ears 12 inches long; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> and twist their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in tresses, which they lengthen with black ribbands embroidered with gold or silver, and with great tassels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and silver, which hang <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to their heels; three other tufts of a smaller size cover their breasts. Both sexes carry about with them prayers written by their priests, which they keep in a small leathern purse by way of relics. The girls, and some of the women, tinge their nails <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> with the juice of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> called by them kena: they dry and pulverize it; then mixing it with powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, expose it in the air for 24 hours before they use it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> lasts a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Both sexes wear <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> breeches, and boots of Russia <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, very light, and without heels, or leather soles; putting on galoches, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-headed slippers like the Turks, when they go abroad. They wear also the same sort of bonnets and covering for the head; only the women set off theirs with trinkets, small pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and Chinese pearls. Wives are distinguished from maids by a long piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> worn under their bonnets; which, folding round the neck, they tie in a knot behind, so that one end of it hangs down to the waist. The Bukhar houses are of stone, and pretty good; but their moveables consist mostly of some China trunks plated with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Upon these, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time, they spread the quilts they have made use of at night, and cover them with a cotton carpet of various colours. They have likewise a curtain sprigged with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and various figures; also a sort of bedstead half a yard high, and four yards long, which is hidden in the daytime with a carpet. They are very neat about their victuals; which are dressed in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s chamber by his slaves, whom the Bukhars either take or buy from the Russians, Kalmues, or other neighbours. For this purpose there are in the chamber, according to the largeness of the family, several iron pots, set in a kind of range near a chimney. Some have little ovens, made, like the rest of the walls, with a stiff clay or bricks. Their utensils consist of some plates and porringers made of cagua wood or of china, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> vessels. A piece of coloured calico serves them instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-cloth and napkins. They use neither chairs nor tables, knives nor forks; but sit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged on the ground; and the meat being served up, they pull it to pieces with their fingers. Their spoons resemble our wooden ladles. Their usual food is minced meats, of which they make pies of the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: these serve for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> when the Bukhars go long journeys, especially in winter. They carry them in a bag, having first exposed them to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; and when boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they make very good broth. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink, of which they have a black sort prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; eating <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> with it, when they have any. As the Bukhars buy their wives, paying for them more or less according to their handsomeness; so the surest way to be rich is to have many daughters. The persons to be married must not see or speak to each other from the time of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> to the day of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. This is celebrated with three days feasting, as they do great annual festivals. The evening before the wedding, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of young girls meet at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>'s house and divert themselves till midnight, playing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and singing. Next morning the guests assemble, and help her to prepare for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. Then, notice being given to the bridegroom, he arrives soon after, accompanied by ten or twelve of his relations and friends. These are followed by some playing on flutes, and by an Abus (a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>), who sings, while he beats two little timbrels. The bridegroom then makes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; which being ended, he distributes the prizes, six, eight, or twelve, in number, according to his ability. They consist of damasks, sables, fox-skins, calico, or the like. The parties do not see each other while the marriage ceremony is performing, but answer at a distance to the questions asked by the priest. As soon as it is over, the bridegroom returns home with his company; and after dinner carries them to the bride's house, and obtains leave to speak to her. This done, he goes back, and returns again in the evening, when he finds her in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>; and in presence of all the women, lays himself down by her in his clothes, but only for a moment. The same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> is acted for three days successively; but the third night he passes with her entirely, and the next day carries her home. Although the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> throughout all Little Bukharia is the Mahometan, yet all others enjoy a perfect toleration. The Bukhars say, that God first communicated the Koran to mankind by Moses and the prophets; that afterwards Mahomet explained, and drew a moral from it, which they are obliged to receive and practise. They hold Christ to be a prophet, but have no notion of his sufferings. Yet they believe in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, but cannot be persuaded that any mortal shall be eternally damned: on the contrary, they believe, that as the demons led them into sin, so the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> will <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on them. They believe, moreover, that at the last day every thing but God will be annihilated; and, consequently, that all creatures, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, and Christ himself, will die. Likewise, that, after the resurrection, all men, excepting a few of the elect, will be purified or chastised by fire, every one according to his sins, which will be weighed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>. They say there will be eight different paradises for the good; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hells, where sinners are to be purified by fire; that those who will suffer most, are liars, cheats, and others of that kind: that the elect who do not feel the fire will be chosen from the good; viz. one out of 100 men, and one out of 1000 women; which little troop will be carried into one of the paradises, where they shall enjoy all manner of felicity, till it shall please God to create a new world. It is a sin, according to them, to say, that God is in heaven. God, say they, is everywhere; and therefore it derogates from his omnipresence to say that he is confined to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. They keep an annual fast of 30 days, from the middle of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the middle of August, during which time they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> nothing all day; but eat twice in the night, at sunset and midnight; Bukharia nor do they drink any thing but tea, all strong liquors being forbidden. Whoever transgresses these ordinances is obliged to emancipate his most valuable slave, or to give an entertainment to 60 people; he is likewise to receive 85 strokes on the back with a leathern strap called dura. The common people, however, do not observe this fast exactly, and workmen are allowed to eat in the daytime. The Bukhars say prayers five times a-day; before morning, towards noon, after noon, at sunset, and in the third <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night. Jenghis Khan, who conquered both the Bukharias from the Arabs, left the empire of them to his son Jagatay Khan. He died in the year 1240, and left the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to his son Kara Kulaku, and of Little Bukharia to Amul Khoja Khan. A long succession of khans is enumerated in each of these families, but their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is uninteresting. They are long since extinct, and the Kalmuc Tartars are masters of the country. See Bukhara, Supplement.

BULAC

Pages 868-868

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, situated on the eastern shore of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, about two miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, of which it is the port town, and contains about 4000 families. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, as all the vessels going up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Nile make some stay here. It is also at this place that they cut the banks of the river every year, in order to fill their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and overflow the neighbouring ground, without which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> would produce neither grain nor herbage. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. N. Lat. 30.

BULAFO

Pages 868-868

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, consisting of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of wood tied together with thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, so as to form a small interstice between each pipe. It is used by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>.

BULAM

Pages 868-869
or Bulama, an island on the western coast of Africa, at the mouth of the Rio Grande, in N. Lat. 11° and W. Long. 15°. This island, which is about 18 leagues long, and four broad, forms part of a cluster of islands, which have been known by the name of Bissagos, and are supposed to be the Hesperides of the ancients. This island was purchased in 1792 by a society instituted for similar purposes with those of the Sierra Leone association. The sum of 9000l. was subscribed for the establishment of the colony, and the management of it is intrusted to a committee who sailed from Spithead in April 1792, and having arrived at Bulama, took possession of the new purchase, and left a body of settlers consisting of 49 men, 13 women, and 25 children, under a superintendent, with a supply of stores and provisions necessary for an infant settlement. The following account of the climate, soil, and productions of Bulama, drawn up by Mr Johansen, gives a flattering picture of this island. The climate, says he, on the whole, may be deemed salubrious, and will become more so in proportion to the increase of cultivation. The mornings and evenings are temperate and pleasant; the middle of the day is hot, but the fine sea breeze which then sets in tends greatly to cool and refresh the air. The heat of the sun is not so excessive or intolerable as has been generally supposed; indeed nature has most admirably adapted our mechanical and physical qualities to the exigencies of different regions; and man, who is the inhabitant of every climate, may, in some measure, render himself indigenous to every soil. Here the only danger arises from too sudden an exposure to the operation of the vertical rays of the sun, or an excess of labour; both of which the first settlers ought most studiously to avoid. "It appears from Mr Beaver's observations at noon, between the 20th of July 1792, and the 28th of April 1793, that the thermometer, when lowest, was at 74; the medium heat 85; and that it never exceeded 96, except at one time when it rose to 100, during a calm that occurred in the interval between the north-east breeze in the morning and the south-west in the evening of the 19th of February 1793. The difference between the heat of noon and that of the morning and evening is from 20 to 30 degrees. On the 23d of October 1792, hail of the size of a pin's head fell during two minutes, although not a cloud was to be seen during this phenomenon. The mercury in the thermometer then stood at 85; the wind was at north-east in the morning and south-west in the evening. "Immediately after sunset a dew constantly begins to fall, which induces some to light a fire in their houses; they at the same time put on warmer clothing. There is little or no twilight; and night and day are nearly equal: the earth has therefore time to cool during twelve hours absence of the sun. "None of these terrible and destructive hurricanes so frequently experienced in the West Indies are to be met with here. The tornadoes, which arise chiefly from the eastern point of the compass, are but of short duration, seldom lasting above an hour, and may be readily foreseen some time previously to their commencement. They occur at the beginning and close of the wet season, and are highly beneficial, as they purify the air, and dispel the noxious vapours with which it would otherwise abound. "The rains set in about the latter end of May or the beginning of June, and discontinue in October or November. They do not fall every day, for there is often a considerable interval of clear weather, during which the atmosphere is beautifully serene; the showers in the first and last months occur but seldom; and are far from being violent; while, on the other hand, they sometimes resemble torrents, more especially towards the middle of the season. During the whole of this period, Europeans should, if possible, confine themselves to their habitations, as the rains prove injurious to health, more especially, if those exposed to them neglect to wipe their bodies dry, and to change their clothes immediately on their return home. It is deemed prudent also not to dig the earth until the expiration of a month after the return of fair weather, as this is considered to be unhealthy. "During the continuance of the dry season, a dew falls during the night, in sufficient quantity to answer all the purposes of vegetation. "Every stranger is generally here, as well as in the West Indies, subject to a fever or seasoning on his arrival. This is not infectious; it proceeds perhaps from an increased perspiration and a sudden extension of the pores of the human body, in consequence of the heat, by which means it is rendered more liable to imbibe the abundant exhalations that arise from the animal, vegetable, Bulama, getable, and mineral kingdoms; but even this, slight as it is, might doubtless be avoided by means of a proper regimen, and a short seclusion from the full action of the open air, more especially at noon, and during the evening, till the climate has been rendered familiar. "Bulama is admirably adapted for all the purposes of an extensive commerce, being not only happily situated at the mouth of the Rio Grande, but in the vicinity of several other navigable rivers; so that a trade with the internal parts of Africa is thereby greatly facilitated. The landing is remarkably easy and safe, there being no surge; the ebb and flow is regular, and there is an increase of 16 feet of water at spring tide. The bay opposite the Great Bulama is adorned with a number of islands, covered with trees, and forms a most excellent harbour, sufficiently capacious to contain the whole navy of Great Britain, which might ride there in safety. The settlement in general is well supplied with water. A number of springs have been lately discovered in different places; and besides a draw-well in the fort which was erected for the defence of the colony, there is a small stream, which runs into Lewis Bay, near the new settlement called Hesper Eleusis: this is admirably situated for the supply of shipping. "The island is beautifully surrounded and interspersed with woods: lofty fruit and forest trees, mostly free from underwood and brambles, form a verdant belt, in some places two or three miles broad, which entirely encircles it, in such a manner as to represent a plantation artificially formed around a park. Within this the fields are regularly divided by trees, so as to resemble the hedge-rows in England. The beach has in some places the appearance of gravel walks; it is fringed with mangrove-trees, which forming a line with the high-water mark dip their branches into the sea, and thus afford nourishment to the oysters that often adhere to their extremities. "The soil is abundantly rich and deep; stones do not here impede the labours of the farmer; and indeed none have hitherto been discovered, but a small sort, resembling pieces of ore, which are to be met with on the shore. There are many savannahs or natural meadows, so extensive that the eye can scarcely descry their boundaries. These are admirably adapted for the rearing of stock and feeding of cattle of every kind. "Cotton, indigo, rice, and coffee, grow spontaneously on this coast; the sugar cane is indigenous to many parts of Africa, and might be cultivated here by the labour of freemen, in equal perfection, and to much greater advantage than in the exhausted islands of the West Indies. All kinds of tropical productions, such as pine-apples, limes, oranges, grapes, plums, cassada, guava, Indian wheat, the papaw, water-melon, muskmelon, the pumpkin, tamarind, banana, and numbers of other delicious fruits, also flourish here. The adjoining territories produce many valuable sorts of spices, gums, and materials for dyeing: all of which, it is but fair to suppose, might be readily cultivated in a kindred climate and a congenial soil. "The neighbouring seas abound with a variety of fish, highly agreeable to the palate. The lion, tyger, jackal, &c. are natives of the continent; but in Bulama no animals have been discovered, the wolf, some buffaloes, a few elephants, and a species of the deer, excepted. "The woods abound with doves, guinea fowls, and a variety of birds, celebrated for the beauty of their plumage." The settlement was abandoned a short time after it was formed.

BULARCHUS

Pages 869-869

a Greek painter; the first who introduced (among the Greeks at least) different colours in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>. He flourished in 740 B.C.

BULB

Pages 869-870

in the anatomy of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bud, generally produced under the ground, upon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near the root of certain herbaceous plants, hence denominated bulbous. A bulb is defined by Linnæus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hybernaculum, produced upon the descending caudex or root; consisting of stipule, petioli, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the former leaves, and scales or bark. To elucidate this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, it is proper to remark, that every bud contains, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> or embryo, a plant, in every respect similar to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> upon which it is seated. Plants therefore are perpetuated in the buds, as well as in the seeds; and the species may be renewed with equal efficacy in either way. The tender rudiments of the future vegetable, of which the bud is composed, are inclosed, and during the severities of winter defended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> injuries, by a hard bark or rind, which generally consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scales placed over each other like tiles, and fastened together by means of a tenacious, resinous, and frequently odoriferous, substance. Thus defended, the buds remain upon different parts of the mother plant till the ensuing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and are, therefore, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety, denominated by Linnæus the hybernaculum or winter-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the future vegetable. With respect to their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, buds are situated either upon the stem and branches, or upon the roots: the former are styled gemmae, or buds properly so called; but as they subsist several years by their roots, may be furnished with the other species of hybernaculum called bulbs, which, according to the definition, are seated upon the descending caudex or root. Again, trees which are perennial, with a woody and durable stem or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, have generally proper buds or gemmae, but no bulbs. In bulbous plants, as the tulip, onion, or lily, what we generally call the root, is in fact a bulb or hybernaculum, which incloses and secures the embryo or future shoot. At the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this bulb may be observed a fleshy knob or tubercle, from whence proceed a number of fibres or threads. This knob, with the fibres attached to and hanging from it, is, properly speaking, the true root; the upper part being only the cradle or nursery of the future stem, which after the bulb has repaired a certain number of times, it perishes; but not till it has produced at its sides a number of smaller bulbs or suckers for perpetuating the species. One part of Linnæus's definition still remains obscure. The bulb, says he, is composed of the remains or rudiments of the former leaves of the plant; rudimenta foliorum praeteritorum. It is easy to comprehend that buds contain the rudiments of the future leaves; but how can bulbs be said to contain the radiments of leaves that, to all appearance, are already perished? To explain this, let it be observed, that, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of very eminent botanists, the root, in a very great number of perennial herbs, is annually renewed or repaired out of the trunk or stalk itself; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> only, roots are properly said to descend. In the perennials alluded to, the basis of the stalk continually, and by insensible degrees, descends below the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and is thus changed into a true root; which root, by the continuance of the said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the stalk, also descends; and thus, according to the durableness of its substance, becomes a longer or shorter root; the elder or lower part rotting off in proportion as the upper is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> out of the stalk. Thus, in brownwort, the basis of the stalk, sinking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by degrees till it is hid under the ground, becomes the upper part of the root; and continuing still to sink, the next year becomes the lower part, and the following year rots away. This is exactly what obtains in bulbous roots, as well as in the far greater number of other herbaceous perennials; as arum, valerian, tansy, samphire, primrose, wood <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, and others. The immediate visible cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> is the string-roots which this kind of trunks frequently puts forth; which descending themselves directly into the ground, serve like so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> for pulling the trunk after them. Hence the tuberous roots of iris are sometimes observed to reascend a little upon the rotting or fading away of the string roots which hang at them. In bulbous roots, where the stalk and former leaves of the plant are sunk below, and formed into what is called the bulb or wintering of the future vegetable, the radicles or small fibres that hang from the bulb are to be considered as the root; that is, the part which furnishes nourishment to the plant: the several rinds and shells, whereof chiefly the bulbs consist, successively perish, and shrink up into so many dry skins; betwixt which, and in their centre, are formed other leaves and shells, and thus the bulb is perpetuated. What has been said of the descent of roots by the sinking of the stalk, is further confirmed by the appearance of certain roots; as of valerian, plantago <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s bit, in which the lower part appears bitten or chopped off. In these the lower part rotting off as the upper descends, the living remainder becomes stumped, or seems bitten. All bulbous roots, says the learned Dr Grew in his anatomy of plants, may be considered as hermaphrodite roots, or root and trunk both together; for the radicles or strings only are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> roots; the bulb actually containing those parts which springing up make the body or leaves of the plant; so that it may be regarded as a large bud under ground. Bulbous roots are said to be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, when composed of one uniform lump of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: tunicated, when formed of multitudes of coats surrounding one another; squamosè, when composed of, or covered with, lesser flakes; duplicate, when there are only two to each plant: and aggregate, when there is a congeries of such roots to each plant. **BULBOCASTANUM.** See **BUNIUM**, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BULBOSE

Pages 870-870
or **BULBOUS**. See **BULB**. **BULEUTÆ**, in Grecian antiquity, were magistrates answering to the decurions among the Romans. See Decurius. **BULFINCH.** See Loxia, Ornithology Index.

BULGARIA

Pages 870-870

a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Wallachia, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south by Romania and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>. It is very narrow, but 325 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> on the side of the Danube, from Servia till it falls into the Black sea. The Bulgarians anciently inhabited the plains of Sarmatia that extended along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. Thence they migrated, about the middle of the 7th century of the Christian era, in quest of new settlements. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of them passed the Danube, and took possession of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> adjacent to the western <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Euxine sea. Several attempts were made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to dispossess and extirpate them: But they defended themselves with equal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and success. Constantine III. being defeated and intimidated, concluded an ignominious peace with them (A.D. 78), and purchased their friendship by the payment of an annual tribute. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> II. refused to comply with these dishonourable terms, and invaded their territories (A.D. 687); but he was defeated, and constrained to renew the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a> was carried on, almost without interruption, between them and the eastern emperors, during the course of several centuries. After a long and doubtful struggle, the Romans prevailed; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> reduced Bulgaria to the form of a province (A.D. 1019). From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Bulgarians remained in subjection, and were governed by Roman dukes, until the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Angelus, when they revolted (A.D. 1186). The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Bulgaria, in the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, scarcely merits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Stephen IV. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, having defeated the Bulgarians, obliged them to acknowledge him as their sovereign. His successors were styled kings of Hungary and Bulgaria; and this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was transmitted, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Hungary, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. By the aid of the eastern emperors they threw off the Hungarian yoke; and, in return, they assisted their ally in an attempt to recover <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a> (A.D. 1369). Provoked by this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, Amurath invaded their country; and Bajazet, his successor, completed the conquest of it (A.D. 1396). Bulgaria still remains a province of the Ottoman empire. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but extremely ignorant, insomuch that they seem to know nothing of Christianity but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and fasting. It is divided into four sangiacates; Byden, Sardice, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a>, and Silistria. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are of the same names, except Sardice, which is now called Sophia. **BULGARIAN <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>**, the same with the Slavonic.

BULIMY

Pages 870-870

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> in which the patient is affected with an insatiable and perpetual desire of eating; and, unless he is indulged, he often falls into fainting fits. It is also called *fames canina*, canine appetite. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BULITHUS

Pages 870-871

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> found either in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-bladder, BULK of a SHIP, the whole content in the hold for the stowage of goods. BULK-HEADS are partitions made athwart the ship with boards, by which one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is divided from the other; as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cabin, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-room, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-room, and several other divisions. The bulk-head afore is the partition between the forecastle and gratings in the head.

BULL

Pages 871-876

George, bishop of St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, in 1634; and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. The first benefice he enjoyed was that of St George's, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, whence he rose successively to be rector of Suddington in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, prebendary of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a>, and in 1705 bishop of St David's. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> he enjoyed about four years, and died in 1709. During the usurpation of Cromwell, he adhered steadily, though still with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, to the forms of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; and in the reign of James II. preached very strenuously against the errors of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. He wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Nicene <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. 2. Apostolical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. 3. Primitive apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; and other works. BULL. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Wild Bulls. The wild bulls, now so numerous on the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, are said to have sprung from one bull and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> cows, which were carried thither by some of the first conquerors. For the manner of hunting these, see Buccaneers. Bull, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. See Astronomy Index. Bulls Eye, among seamen, a small, obscure, sublime cloud, ruddy in the middle, that sometimes appears to mariners, and is the immediate forerunner of a great storm at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Bull-Fighting, a sport <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> much in vogue among the Spaniards and Portuguese, consisting in a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of a cavalier or torero against a wild bull, either on foot or on horseback, by riding at him with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>. The Spaniards have bull-fights, i.e., feasts attended with shows, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St John, the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, &c. This sport the Spaniards received from the Moors, among whom it was celebrated with great eclat. Some think that the Moors might have received the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and they from the Greeks. Dr Plot is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the Taurinae, among the Thessalians, who first instituted this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and of whom Julius Caesar learned and brought it to Rome, were the origin both of the Spanish and Portuguese bull-fighting, and of the English bull-running. This practice was prohibited by Pope Pius V. under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> incurred ipsa facto. But succeeding popes have granted several mitigations in behalf of the torreadores. From the following account of a bull-feast in the Coliseum at Rome 1332, extracted from Muratori by Mr Gibbon, the reader may form some idea of the pomp, the ceremonies, and the danger which attended these exhibitions. "A general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> invited the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> to exercise their skill and courage in this perilous adventure. The Roman ladies were marshalled in three squadrons, and seated in three balconies, which on this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the third of September, were lined with scarlet cloth. The fair Jacova di Rovere led the matrons from beyond the Tiber, a pure and native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who still represent the features and character of antiquity. The remainder of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was divided between the Colonna and Ursini families: the two factions were proud of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> bands; the charms of Savella Ursini are mentioned with praise; and the Colonna regretted the absence of the youngest of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, who had sprained her ankle in the garden of Nero's tower. The lots of the champions were drawn by an old and respectable citizen; and they descended into the arena or pit, to encounter the wild bulls, on foot as it should seem, with a single spear. Amidst the crowd, our annalist has selected the names, colours, and devices of 20 of the most conspicuous knights. Several of the names are the most illustrious of Rome and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> State; Malatesta, Polenta, della Valle, Cafarello, Savelli, Cappoccio, Conti, Annibaldi, Altieri, Corsi. The colours were adapted to their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and situation. And the devices are expressive of hope or despair, and breathe the spirit of gallantry and arms. "I am alone, like the youngest of the Horatii," the confidence of an intrepid stranger; "I live disconsolate," a weeping widower; "I burn under the ashes," a discreet lover; "I adore Lavinia or Lucretia," the ambiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: "My faith is as pure," the motto of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>: "Who is stronger than myself?" of a lion's hide: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I am drowned in blood, what a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>!" the wish of ferocious courage. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> or prudence of the Ursini restrained them from the field, which was occupied by three of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> rivals, whose <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> denoted the lofty greatness of the Colonna name: "Though sad, I am strong;" "Strong as I am great;" "If I <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> (addressing himself to the spectators) you fall with me:"—intimating (says the writer), that while the other families were the subjects of the Vatican, they alone were the supporters of the Capitol. The combats of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> were dangerous and bloody. Every champion successively encountered a wild bull; and the victory may be ascribed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, since no more than eleven were left on the field, with the loss of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> wounded and 18 killed on the side of their adversaries. Some of the noblest families might mourn; but the pomp of the funerals, in the churches of St John Lateran and St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Maggiore, afforded a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> holiday to the people. Doubtless it was not in such conflicts that the blood of the Romans should have been shed; yet, in blaming their rashness, we are compelled to applaud their gallantry; and the noble volunteers, who display their magnificence and risk their lives under the balconies of the fair, excite a more generous sympathy than the thousands of captives and malefactors who were reluctantly dragged to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of slaughter." A striking relic of barbarity in the Spanish manners of the present day, is the excessive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to bull fights, a spectacle which shocks the delicacy of every other people in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Many Spaniards consider this practice as the sure means of preserving that energy by which they are characterized, and of habituating them to violent emotions, which are terrible only to timid minds. But it seems difficult to comprehend what relation there is between bravery and a spectacle where the assistants now run no danger; where the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> prove by the few accidents which befall them, that theirs has nothing in it very interesting; and where the unhappy victims meet only with certain death as the reward of their vigour and courage. Another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> have little or no influence on the disposition of the mind is, that children, old men, and people of all ages, stations, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, assist at them, and yet their being accustomed to such bloody entertainments appears neither to correct their weakness and timidity, nor alter the mildness of their manners. The bull-fights are very expensive; but they bring great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to the undertakers. The worst places cost two or four reals, according as they are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The price of the highest is a dollar. When the price of the horses and bulls, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of the torreadores, have been paid out of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, the rest is generally appropriated to pious foundations; at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> it forms one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> funds of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. It is only during <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> that these combats are exhibited, because the season then permits the spectators to sit in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and because the bulls are then more vigorous. Those which are of the best breed are condemned to this kind of sacrifice; and connoisseurs are so well acquainted with their distinguishing marks, that as soon as a bull appears upon the arena, arena, they can mention the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he was rear- ed. This arena is a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> surrounded by about a dozen of seats, rising one above another; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>- est of which only is covered. The boxes occupy the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the edifice. In some cities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a> for example, which have no place particularly set apart for these combats, the principal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is converted in- to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. The balconies of the houses are widen- ed, so as to project over the streets which end there; and it is really a very interesting sight to see the diffe- rent classes of people assembled round this square, wait- ing for the signal when the entertainment is to com- mence, and exhibiting every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> sign of impa- tience and joy. The spectacle commences by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> around the square, in which appear, both on horseback and on foot, the combatants who are to attack the fierce animal; after which two al- guazils, dressed in perukes and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> robes, advance with great gravity on horseback; who go and ask from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the entertainment an order for it to commence. A signal is immediately given; and the animal, which was before shut up in a kind of hovel with a door opening into the square, soon makes his appearance. The officers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, who have nothing to do with the bull, prudently hasten to re- tire, and their flight is a prelude to the cruel <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>- sure which the spectators are about to enjoy. The bull, however, is received with loud shouts, and almost stun- ned by the noisy expressions of their joy. He has to contest first against the picadores, combatants on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>- back, who, dressed according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Spanish manner, and as it were fixed to their saddles, wait for him, each being armed with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> lance. This ex- ercise, which requires strength, courage, and dexterity, is not considered as disgraceful. Formerly the greatest lords did not disdain to practise it; even at present some of the hidalgos solicit for the honour of fight- ing the bull on horseback, and they are then previous- ly presented to the people, under the auspices of a pa- tron, who is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> one of the principal personages at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The picadores, whoever they may be, open the scene. It often happens that the bull, without being provoked, darts upon them, and everybody entertains a favour- able opinion of his courage. If, notwithstanding the sharp-pointed weapon which defends his attack, he re- turns immediately to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, their shouts are re- doabled, as their joy is converted into enthusiasm; but if the bull, struck with terror, appears pacific, and avoids his persecutors, by walking round the square in a timid manner, he is hooted at and hissed by the whole spectators, and all those near whom he passes load him with blows and reproaches. He seems then to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy, who has some great crime to expiate; or a victim, in the sacrifice of which all the people are interested. If nothing can awaken his courage, he is judged unworthy of being tormented by men; the cry of perros, perros, brings forth new enemies against him, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> dogs are let loose upon him, which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> him by the neck and ears in a furious manner. The animal then finds the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of those wea- pons with which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has furnished him; he tosses the dogs into the air, who fall <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stunned, and sometimes mangled; they however recover, renew the combat, and generally finish by overcoming their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a>- versary, who thus perishes ignobly. If, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he presents himself with a good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, he runs a longer and nobler, but a much more painful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the tragedy belongs to the comba- tants on horseback; this is the most animated and bloody of all the scenes, and often the most disgusting. The irritated animal braves the pointed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> which makes deep wounds in his neck, attacks with fury the innocent horse who carries his enemy, rips up his sides, and overturns him together with his rider. The lat- ter, then dismounted and disarmed, would be exposed to imminent danger, did not combatants on foot, called chulos, come to divert the bull's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and to pro- voke him, by shaking before him different pieces of cloth of various colours. It is, however, at their own risk that they thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the dismounted horseman; for the bull sometimes pursues them, and they have then need for all their agility. They often escape from him by letting fall in his way the piece of stuff which was their only arms, and against which the deceived animal expends all his fury. Sometimes he does not accept this substitute, and the combatant has no other resource but to throw himself speedily over a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, six feet high, which incloses the interior part of the arena. In some places this barrier is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and the interme- diate space forms a kind of circular gallery, behind which the pursued torreadore is in safety. But when the barrier is single, the bull attempts to jump over it, and often succeeds.
