The reader may easily imagine in what consternation the nearest of the spectators then are; their haste to get out of the way, and to crowd to the upper benches, becomes often more fatal to them than even the fury of the bull, who, stumbling at every step, on account of the narrowness of the place and the inequality of the ground, thinks rather of his own safety than of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, and besides soon falls under the blows which are given him from all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Except in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, which are very rare, he im- mediately returns. His adversary recovered, has had <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to get up; he immediately remounts his horse, provided the latter is not killed or rendered unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and the attack commences; but he is often obliged to change his horse several times. Expressions cannot then be found to celebrate these acts of prov- ess, which for several days become the favourite topic of conversation. The horses, very affecting models of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, courage, and docility, may be seen treading under their feet their own bloody entrails, which drop from their sides half torn open, and yet obeying, for some time after, the hand which conducts them to new tortures. Spectators of delicacy are then filled with disgust, which converts their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> into pain. A new act is however preparing, which reconciles them to the entertainment. As soon as it is concluded that the bull has been sufficiently tormented by the comba- tants on horseback, they retire and leave him to be irritated by those on foot. The latter, who are called banderilleros, go before the animal; and the moment he darts upon them they plunge into his neck, two by two, a kind of darts called banderillas, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of which are hooked, and which are ornamented with small streamers made of coloured <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. The fury of the bull is now redoubled; he roars, tosses his head, and the vain efforts which he makes serve only to in- crease crease the pain of his wounds: this last scene calls forth all the agility of his adversaries. The spectators at first tremble for them, when they behold them braving so near the horns of this formidable animal; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, well exercised, aim their blows so skilfully, and they avoid the danger so nimbly, that after having seen them a few times, one neither pities nor admires them, and their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and dexterity seem only to be a small episode of the tragedy, which concludes in the following manner: When the vigour of the bull appears to be almost exhausted; when his blood issuing from twenty wounds, streams along his neck and moistens his robust sides; and when the people, tired of one object, demand another victim; the president of the entertainment gives the signal of death, which is announced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of trumpets. The matador then advances, and all the rest quit the arena; with one hand he holds a long dagger, and with the other a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, which he waves backwards and forwards before his adversary. They both stop and gaze at one another: and while the agility of the matador deceives the impetuosity of the bull, the pleasure of the spectators, which was for some time suspended, is again awakened into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Sometimes the bull remains motionless, throws up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his feet, and appears as if meditating revenge. The bull in this condition, and the matador who calculates his motions and divines his projects, form a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> which an able <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> might not disdain to delineate. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> in silence beholds this dumb scene. The matador at length gives the mortal blow; and if the animal immediately falls, a thousand voices proclaim with loud shouts the triumph of the conqueror; but if the blow is not decisive, if the bull survives and seeks still to brave the fatal steel, murmurs succeed to applause, and the matador, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> was about to be raised to the skies, is considered only as an unskilled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>. He endeavours to be soon revenged, and to disarm his judges of their severity. His zeal sometimes degenerates into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> fury, and his partisans tremble for the consequences of his imprudence. He at length directs his blows better. The animal vomits up blood; he staggers and falls, while his conqueror is intoxicated with the applauses of the people. Three mules, ornamented with bells and streamers, come to terminate the tragedy. A rope is tied around the bull's horns, which have betrayed his valour, and the animal, which but a little before was furious, and proud, is dragged ignominiously from the arena which he has honoured, and leaves only the traces of his blood and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his exploits, which are soon effaced on the appearance of his successors. On each of the days set apart for these entertainments, six are thus sacrificed in the morning, and twelve in the afternoon, at least in Madrid. The three last are given exclusively to the matador, who, without the assistance of the picadores, exerts his ingenuity to vary the pleasure of the spectators. Sometimes he causes them to be combated by some intrepid stranger, who attacks them mounted on the back of another bull, and sometimes he matches them with a bear; this last method is generally destined for the pleasure of the populace. The points of the bull's horns are concealed by something wrapped round them, which breaks their force. The animal, which in this state is called Em- bolado, has power neither to pierce nor to tear his antagonist. The amateurs then descend in great numbers to torment him, each after his own manner, and often expiate this cruel pleasure by violent contusions; but the bull always falls at length under the stroke of the matador. The few spectators who are not infected with the general madness of this sport, regret that those wretched animals do not, at least, purchase their lives at the expense of so many torments and so many efforts of courage; they would willingly assist them to escape from their persecutors. In the minds of such spectators, disgust succeeds compassion, and satiety succeeds disgust. Such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of uniform scenes makes that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> become languid, which this spectacle, on its commencement, seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. But to connoisseurs, who have thoroughly studied all the stratagems of the bull, the resources of his address and fury, and the different methods of irritating, tormenting, and deceiving him, none of these scenes resembles another, and they pity those frivolous observers who cannot remark all their varieties. The Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> are very sensible of the moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> inconveniences arising from this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of frenzy. They have long since perceived, that among a people whom they wish to encourage to labour, it is the cause of much disorder and dissipation; and that it hurts <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, by destroying a great number of robust animals, which might be usefully employed: but they are obliged to manage with caution a taste which it might be dangerous to attempt to abolish precipitately. They are, however, far from encouraging it. The court itself formerly reckoned bull-fights among the number of its festivals, which were given at certain periods. The Plaza-Mayor was the theatre of them, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family honoured them with their presence. His guards presided there in good order. His halberdiers formed the interior circle of the scene: and their long weapons, held out in a defensive posture, were the only barrier which they opposed against the dangerous caprices of the bull. These entertainments, which by way of excellence, were called Fiestas Reales, are become very rare. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> III., who endeavoured to polish the nation, and to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their attention to useful objects, was very desirous of destroying a taste in which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> nothing but inconveniences; but he was too wise to employ violent means for that purpose. He, however, confined the number of bull-fights to those, the profits of which were applied to the support of some charitable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, with an intention of substituting for these other funds afterwards. Bull-fights, by these means being rendered less frequent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, perhaps, gradually lose their attractions, until more favourable circumstances permit the entire abolition of them. Bull-Running, denotes a feudal custom obtaining in the honour of Tutbury in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>; where, anciently, on the day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of our Lady, a bull is turned loose by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> to the minstrels; who, if they can catch him before he passes the river Dove, are to have him for their own, or, in lieu thereof, to receive each 40 pence; in consideration of which custom they pay 20 pence yearly to the said lord. Bull and Boar. By the custom of some places, the parson is obliged to keep a bull and boar for the use of his parishioners, in consideration of his having <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> of calves and pigs, &c. Bull-Frog. See Rana, Herpetology Index. Bull-Head, or Miller's Thumb. See Cottus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Bull, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, a written <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> dispatched, by order of the pope, from the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; and sealed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, being written on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, by which it is partly distinguished from a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>; see the article Brief.—It is a kind of apostolical rescript, or edict; and is chiefly in use in matters of justice or grace. If the former be the intention of the bull, the lead is hung by a hempen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>; if the latter, by a silken thread. It is this pendent lead, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, which is, properly speaking, the bull, and which is impressed on one side with the heads of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, and on the other with the name of the pope and the year of his pontificate. The bull is written in an old, round, Gothic letter, and is divided into five parts, the narrative of the fact, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, the clause, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, and the salutation, in which the pope styles himself servus servorum, i.e. the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of servants. These instruments, besides the lead hanging to them, have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, with some texts of scripture, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> motto, about it. Bulls are granted for the consecration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, the promotion to benefices, and the celebration of jubilees, &c. Bull in Cena Domini, a particular bull read every year, on the day of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUNDY_THURSDAY">Maundy Thursday</a>, in the pope's presence, containing excommunications and anathemas against heretics, and all who disturb or oppose the jurisdiction of the holy see. After the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the bull, the pope throws a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torch in the public place, to denote the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Bull, an edict, or imperial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, made by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Charles IV. reputed to be the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the German empire. It is called golden, because it has a golden seal, in the form of a pope's bull, tied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cords of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>: upon one side is the emperor represented sitting on his throne, and on the other the capitol of Rome. It is also called Caroline, on Charles IV.'s account. Till the publication of the golden bull, the form and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of an emperor were dubious and undetermined, and the number of the electors not fixed. This solemn edict regulated the functions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and pre-eminences of the electors. The original, which is in Latin, on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, is preserved at Francfort: this ordonnance, containing 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> or chapters, was approved of by all the princes of the empire, and remains still in force. Silver Bulls were not in so frequent use; though we do not want instances of them. Leaden Bulls were sent by the emperors of Constantinople to despots, patriarchs, and princes; and the like were also used by the grandees of the Imperial court, as well as by the kings of France, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, &c. and by bishops, patriarchs, and popes. It is to be observed, that the leaden bulls of these last had, on one side, the name of the pope or bishop <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. Polydore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes Pope Stephen III. the first who used leaden bulls, about the year 772. But others find instances of them as early as Silvester, Leo I. and Gregory the great. The latter popes, besides their own names, strike the figures of St Peter and St Paul on their bulls, a practice first introduced by Pope Paschal II. But why, in these bulls, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of St Paul is on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and that of St Peter on the left side, is a question, which has occasioned many conjectures and disputes. Waxen Bulls are said to have been first brought into England by the Normans. They were in frequent use among the Greek emperors, who thus sealed letters to their wives, mothers, and sons. Of these there were two sorts, one red, and the other green. Bulla, or Differ, in <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>; a genus belonging to the order of vernes testacea. It is an animal of the snail kind: the shell consists of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, convoluted, and without any pricks; the aperture is narrowish, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, longitudinal, and entire at the base; the columella is smooth and oblique. There are 23 species; four of them found in the British seas; the rest chiefly natives of the Asiatic and Atlantic oceans. See Conchology Index. Bullæ, in antiquity, a kind of ornaments much in use among the ancient Romans. Mr Whittaker* <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> is of opinion that they were originally formed of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> among all ranks of people; and it is certain that they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> so to the last among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>. He also imagines, that at first the bulla was intended as an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMULET">amulet</a> rather than an ornament; as a proof of which he tells us that the bullæ were frequently impressed with the figure of the sexual parts. It is universally asserted by the critics, that the bullæ were made hollow for the reception of an amulet; but this Mr Whittaker contradicts from the figure of a golden one lately found at Manchester, which had no aperture whereby an amulet could have been introduced.—Pliny refers the original of the bulla to the elder Tarquin, who gave one with the pretexta to his son, because at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14 he had with his own hand killed an enemy; and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of him it was afterwards assumed by other patricians. Others affirm that the bulla was given by that king to the sons of all the patricians who had borne civil offices. Lastly, others allege, that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> first introduced the bulla, and gave it to Tullus Hostilius, the first child born of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of the Sabines.—As to the form of the bulla, Mr Whittaker informs us that they were originally made in the shape of hearts; but they did not always retain the form of a heart, any more than they were always made of leather. As the wealth of the state and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of individuals increased, the young patrician distinguished himself by a bulla of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, while the common people wore the amulet of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The figure of the heart then became so generally round, some even having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of an heart upon them, that there are not many of the original form to be found in the cabinets of the curious. The form is naturally varied from a complete circle to that of a segment; and this was the shape of the above-mentioned bulla found at Manchester. When the youth arrived at 15 years of age, they hung up their bullæ about the necks of their gods <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARES">lares</a>. We are further informed, that the bullæ were not only hung about the necks of young men, but of horses also. We may add, that bullæ were sometimes allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; whence the phrase statua bullæ. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULLE">BULLE</a> was also the denomination given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other metallic ornaments made after the same form; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> bulle seems to include all gold and silver ornaments of a roundish form, whether worn on the habits of men, the trappings of horses, or the like. Such were those decorations used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> on their doors and belts. The bulle of doors were a kind of large-headed nails fastened on the doors of the rich, and kept bright with great care. The doors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were sometimes adorned with golden bulle. Mr Bandelot takes the bulle worn by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> on their belts to be something more than <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> ornaments. They seem to have been considered as preservations from dangers and diseases, and even means of acquiring glory, and other advantages. The like may perhaps be extended to the bulle on doors, which were probably placed there as a security to them from being broken or violated.

BULLE ALSO

Pages 876-876

e also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> hung up in the public courts, to distinguish which days were fasti, and which nefasti; answering in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>.

BULLET

Pages 876-876

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leaden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, wherewith fire arms are loaded. Bullets are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in iron <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, consisting of two concave hemispheres, with a handle whereby to hold them; and between them is a hole, called the gate, at which to pour in the melted metal. The chaps or hemispheres of bullet-moulds are first punched, being blood-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, with a round-ended <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a>, of the shape and nearly of the size of the intended bullets. To cleanse the insides they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a bullet bore, which consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> shank, having a globe at one end, wherewith to bore the inside of a mould clean, and of the intended size.

BULLEYN

Pages 876-876

WILLIAM, a learned physician and botanist, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the reign of Henry VIII. and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> being his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he travelled through various parts of England, Scotland, and Germany, chiefly with an intention to improve his knowledge in that science. In the reign of Edward VI. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, Mr Bulleyn appears, from his remarks on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to have resided at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, or in that neighbourhood, and also to have spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Bloxhall in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>; but he afterwards removed into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and settled at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, where he practised physic with considerable reputation and success. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> at this time was Sir Thomas Hilton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, baron of Hilton, who was governor of Tinmouth castle in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> and Mary. In 1560, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and soon after his arrival, was accused by William Hilton of Bidick of having murdered his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Sir Thomas, our author's friend and patron. He was arraigned before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and honourably acquitted. This Hilton afterwards hired some villains to assassinate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>; but this attempt proving ineffectual, he had him arrested on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for debt, and he remained for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time in prison. During this confinement, Dr Bulleyn composed several of those works which raised his reputation as a medical writer. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1576, and was buried in St Giles's Cripplegate, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> with his brother the divine, who died 13 years before, and in which John Fox the martyrologist was interred 11 years after. Dr Bulleyn appears from his writings to have been well acquainted with the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek, Roman, and Arabian physicians. According to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> practice, his books, were they generally known, would be of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but as he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius and fertile imagination, they are by no means barren of entertainment. He wrote, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, 1559, 8vo. 2. A regimen against the Pleurisy, 8vo, London, 1562. 3. Bulleyn's Bulwark of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> against all Sickness, Soresness, and Wounds that dooe daily assault Mankind, London, printed by John <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, 1562, folio. This includes, The Government of Health. 4. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> both pleasant and pietifull, wherein is a goodlie regimen against the fever pestilence, with a consolation and comfort against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, London, 1564, 8vo; 1569, 8vo; very scarce. There is a wooden print of the author prefixed to the first edition of his Government of Health; also a small one engraved by Stukeley in 1722.

BULLIALDUS

Pages 876-876

ISMAEL, an eminent astronomer, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAON">Laon</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France in 1605. He travelled in his youth for the sake of improvement; and afterwards published several works, among which are, 1. De natura lucis. 2. Philolaus. 3. Astronomia philolaica, opus novum, in quo motus planetarum per novam et veram hypothesen demonstrantur. 4. Astronomicae philolaicae fundamenta clariss explicate et asserta adversus Zethi Wardi impugnationem. He also wrote a piece <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two upon <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. In 1661, he paid Hevelius a visit at Dantzig, for the sake of seeing his optical and astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>. Afterwards he became a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and died there in 1694.

BULLINGER

Pages 876-876

HENRY, born at Bremgarten in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in 1504, was an eminent Zeuingian minister, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> supporter of the reformation, and employed in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> negotiations. He composed many books, one against <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> in particular. He died in 1575.

BULLION

Pages 876-877

uncoined <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are called so, either when smelted from the native ore, and not perfectly refined; or when they are perfectly refined, but melted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in bars or ingots, or in any unwrought body, of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness. When gold and silver are in their purity, they are so soft and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, that they cannot well be brought into any fashion for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, without being first reduced and hardened with an alloy for some other baser metal. To prevent these abuses which some might be tempted to commit in the making of such alloys, the legislators of civilized countries have ordained, that there shall be no more than a certain proportion of a baser metal to a particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pure gold or silver, in order to make them of the fineness of what is called the standard gold or silver of such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. According to the laws of England, all sorts of wrought plate in general ought to be made to the legal standard; and the price of our standard gold and silver is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rule whereby to set a value on their bullion, whether the same be ingots, bars, dust, or foreign specie: whence it is easy to conceive that the value of bullion cannot be exactly known, without being first assayed, that the exact quantity of pure metal therein contained may be determined, and consequently whether it be above or below the standard. Silver and gold, whether coined or uncoined (though used for a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of other things), are no less a commodity than wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, or cloth; and may, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, be exported as much to the national advantage as any other commodity.

BULLOCK

Pages 877-877

the same with an ox, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gelded bull. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, Mamalia <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BULTER

Pages 877-877

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote the refuse of meat after dressing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the cloth wherein it is dressed, otherwise called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-cloth.

BUMICILLI

Pages 877-877

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Mahometans in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and Barbary, who pretend to fight with devils, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> appear in a fright and covered with wounds and bruises. About the full <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> they counterfeit a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> in the presence of all the people, which lasts for two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three hours, and is performed with assagais or javelins, till they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> quite spent.

BUNDLE

Pages 877-877

a collection of things wrapped up together. Of baste-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, harness-plates, and glovers knives, ten make a bundle; of Hamburgh yarn, 20 skeans; of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>-rods, three feet the band.

BUNEL

Pages 877-877
PETER, a native of Thoulouse, was one of the most elegant writers of the Latin tongue in the 16th century, but was still more conspicuous for the regularity of his manners. He did not seek either for riches or lucrative employments; but, contented with the bare necessaries of life, applied himself wholly to the improvement of his mind. He died at Turin in 1547, aged 47; and has left behind him some Latin epistles, which are written with the utmost purity. The magistrates of Thoulouse have a bust of him in marble, placed in their town-house. The most correct edition of his Letters is that of Henry Stephens in 1581.

BUNGAY

Pages 877-877

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, situated on the river Waveney, about 32 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 35. N. Lat. 52. 35.

BUNIAS

Pages 877-877

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the 39th <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, Siliqueae, belonging to the tetrodynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, for which there is no English name. The silicula is deciduous, four-sided, muricated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shagreened with unequal pointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. There are eight <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; all of them annual plants, but none of them possessed of any remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>.

BUNIUM

Pages 877-877

Pig-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>-nut. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BUNT of a Sail, the middle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, formed designedly into a bag or cavity, that the sail may gather more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. It is used mostly in topsails, because the courses are generally cut <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, or with but small allowance for bunt or compass. The bunt holds much leeward wind; that is, it hangs much to leeward. Bunt-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a>, are small lines made fast to the bottom of the sails, in the middle part of the bolt-rope, to a cringle, and are so reeved through a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, seized to the yard. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to trice up the bunt of the sail, for the better furling it up. BUNTING. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBERIZA">Emberiza</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

BUNTINGFORD

Pages 877-877

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, with a market on Mondays, and two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 29th, and November 30th, for pedlars wares. It is a good thoroughfare town, distant 31 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Easting-W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 6. N. Lat. 51. 55.

BUNTZEL

Pages 877-877
or BUNTZLAU, a town of Silesia, in the duchy of Jauer. The greatest part of the houses are built with stone, and there were formerly rich mines in the neighbourhood. It is in the common road to Leipsic; and the trade is in earthen ware, of which great quantities are made. E. Long. 15. 50. N. Lat. 51. 12.

BUNYAN

Pages 877-877

JOHN, author of the Pilgrim's Progress, was born at Elstow, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, in 1628. He was the son of a tinker; and, in the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reprobate, and a soldier in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>: but being at length deeply struck with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his guilt, he laid aside his profligate courses, became remarkable for his sobriety, and applied himself to obtain some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of learning. About the year 1655, he was admitted a member of a Baptist <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at Bedford, and was soon after chosen their preacher: but, in 1665, being taken up, and tried for presuming to preach, he was cruelly sentenced to perpetual banishment; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> committed to jail, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> obliged him to learn to make <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-tagged thread-laces for his support: to add to his distress, he had a wife and several children, among whom was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> who was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. In this unjust and cruel confinement he was detained twelve years and a half, and during that time wrote many of his tracts; but he was at length discharged by the humane interposition of Dr Barlow. When <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> was published, he was chosen pastor of a congregation at Bedford. He at length died of a fever at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the 31st of August 1688, aged 60. He also wrote an allegory, called The Holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>. His Pilgrim's Progress has been translated into most European languages; and his works have been collected together, and printed in two volumes folio.

BUOY

Pages 877-878

in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> cask, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, fastened by a rope to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the anchor is situated, that the ship may not come too near it, to entangle her cable about the stock or the flukes of it. Buoys are of various kinds; as, Con-Buoys: these are in the form of a cone; and of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> are all the buoys which are floated over dangerous banks and shallows, as a warning to passing ships, that they may avoid them. They are extremely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> that they may be seen at a distance; and are fastened by strong chains to the anchors which are sunk for this purpose at such places. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">Nun</a>-Buoys are shaped like the middle frustum of two cones, abutting upon one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> base, being casks which are large in the middle, and tapering nearly to a point at each end. Wooden-Buoys are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, sometimes in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, and sometimes in that of a nun-buoy; they are furnished with one or two holes, in which to fix a short piece of rope, whose two ends, being spliced together, make a sort of circle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, called the strop. Cable-Buoys, are common casks employed to buoy up the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> in different places from rocky ground. In the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, every ship is moored with at least three cables, and has three or four of these buoys on each cable for this purpose. **Slings of the Buoy**, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> which are fastened about it, and by which it is hung: they are curiously spliced around it, something resembling the braces of a drum. **To stream the Buoy**, is to let it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the ship's side into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; which is always done before they let go the anchor, that it may not be retarded by the buoy-rope as it sinks to the bottom. **Buoy-Rope**, the rope which fastens the buoy to the anchor: it should be little more than equal in length to the depth of the water where the anchor lies, as it is intended to float near, or immediately above, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of it, that the pilot may at all times know the situation thereof. See Plate XXXIII. Fig. 1. No. 3., where b is the anchor, c the buoy-rope, and d the buoy floating on the surface of the water. The buoy-rope is often extremely useful otherwise, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the anchor when the cable is broke. It should always, therefore, be of sufficient strength for this purpose, or else the anchor may be lost through negligence. **Buoy of the Nore**, is a buoy placed at the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> mariners how to avoid a dangerous sand.

BUOYANT

Pages 878-878

something which, by its aptness to float, bears up other more ponderous and weighty things. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUOY">Buoy</a>.

BUPALUS

Pages 878-878

a celebrated sculptor, and native of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Chios, was son, grandson, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandson of sculptors. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, named Athenis, of the same profession. They flourished in the 6th Olympiad: and were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Hipponax, a poet of an ugly and despicable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Our sculptors diverted themselves in representing him under a ridiculous form. But Hipponax wrote so sharp a satire against them, that they hanged themselves, as some say. Pliny, however, does not allow this; but says, on the contrary, that, after Hipponax had taken his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, they made several fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in several places; particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Chios, which was placed very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and appeared with a frowning countenance to those that came in, and with a pleasant one to those that went out. There were several statues at Rome made by them; and they worked only in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Paros. Pausanias mentions Bupales as a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> as well as sculptor; but says nothing of Athenis. **BUPHAGA.** See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BURGH-BOTE

Pages 880-881

E signifies contribution towards the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> repairing of castles, or walls, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of a borough or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. By a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Athelstan, the castles and walls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> were to be repaired, and burgh-bote levied every year within a fortnight after rogation days. No person whatever was exempt from this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; the king himself could not exempt a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> from burgh-bote; yet, in after times, exemptions appear to have been frequently granted; insomuch, that, according to Cowell, the word burgh-bote came to be chiefly used to denote not the service, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> or exemption from it. BURGH-BRECHE, or brech, a fine imposed on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of a town, or burgh, for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of peace among them. BURGH-MAILS, were yearly payments to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Scotland, introduced by Malcolm III. and resembling the FEE-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">FARM</a> rents of burgs in England. See MAIL. BURGH-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, an officer in the tin <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, who directs and lays out the meers for the workmen, &c., otherwise denominated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>-master. BURGERMASTER. See BURGOMASTER. BURGHMOTTE, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of a borough. By the laws of King Edgar, the burghmote was to be held thrice in the year; by those of Henry I. 12 times. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">BURGLARY</a>, or NOCTURNAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">HOUSE</a>-BREAKING, (burgi latrocinium), which by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English law was called hameseken, a word also used in the law of Scotland, but in a somewhat different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, has always been looked upon as a very heinous offence: not only because of the abundant terror it carries with it, but also as it is a forcible invasion and disturbance of that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of habitation which every individual might acquire even in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; an invasion which, in such a state, would be sure to be punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, unless the assailant were stronger. But, in civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, the laws come into the assistance of the weaker party: and besides that they leave him this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> right of killing the aggressor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he can, they also protect and avenge him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the assailant is too powerful. And the law has so particular and tender a regard to the immunity of a man's house, that it styles it his castle, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never suffer it to be violated with impunity; agreeing herein with the sentiments of ancient Rome. For this reason no outward doors can in general be broken open to execute any civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, though in criminal causes the public safety supersedes the private*. Hence also in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> arises the animadversion of the law upon eaves-droppers, nuisancers, and incendiaries: and to this principle it must be assigned, that a man may assemble people together lawfully (at least if they do not exceed 11), without danger of raising a riot, rout, or unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, in order to protect his house; which he is not permitted to do in any other case. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a burglar, as given us by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, is "he that by night breaketh and entereth in a mansion house, with intent to commit a felony." In this definition there are four things to be considered; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the manner, and the intent. 1. The time must be by night, and not by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for in the daytime there is no burglary; i.e., if there be daylight or crepusculum enough, begun or left, to discern a man's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> within. But this does not extend to moonlight; for then many midnight burglaries would go unpunished: and besides the malignity of the offence does not consist so much in its being done in the dark, as at the dead of night; when all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, except beasts of prey, are at rest; when <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> has disarmed the owner, and rendered his castle defenceless. 2. As to the place. It must be, according to Sir Edward's Coke's definition, in a mansion-house: for no distant barn, warehouse, or the like, are under the same privileges, nor looked upon as a man's castle of defence; nor is a breaking open of houses wherein no man resides, and which for the time being are not mansion-houses, attended with the same circumstances of midnight terror. A house, however, wherein a man sometimes resides, and which the owner hath left only for a short season, animo revertendi, is the object of burglary, though no one be in it at the time of the fact committed. And if the barn, stable, or warehouse, be parcel of the mansion-house, though not under the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> or contiguous, a burglary may be committed therein; for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> house protects and privileges all its branches and appurtenances, if within the curtilage or homestead. A chamber in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, or an inn of court, where each inhabitant hath a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, is, to all other purposes as well as this, the mansion-house of the owner. So also is a room or lodging in any private house the mansion for the time being of the lodger; if the owner doth not himself dwell in the house, or if he and the lodger enter by different outward doors. But if the owner himself lies in the house, and hath but one outward door at which he and his lodgers enter, such lodgers seem only to be inmates, and all their apartments to be parcel of the one dwelling house of the owner. 3. As to the manner of committing burglary: there must be both a breaking and an entry to complete it. But they need not be both done at once; for if a hole be broken one night, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a> enter the next night through the same, they are burglars. There must be an actual breaking; as at least, by breaking or taking out the glass of, or otherwise opening, a window; picking a lock, or opening it with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>; nay, by lifting up the latch of a door, or unloosing any other fastening which the owner has provided. But if a person leaves his doors or windows open, it is his own folly and negligence; and if a man enters therein, it is no burglary; yet, if he afterwards unlocks an inner or chamber door, it is so. But to come <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a chimney is held a burglarious entry: for that is as much closed as the nature of things will permit. So also, to knock at a door, and, upon opening it, to rush in with a felonious intent; or under pretence of taking lodgings to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon the landlord and rob him; or to procure a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> admittance in order to search for traitors, and then to bind the constable and rob the house; all these entries have been adjudged burglary. Burglary, though there was no actual breaking: for the law will not suffer itself to be trifled with by such evasions, especially under the cloak of legal process. As for the entry, any the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of it, with any part of the body, or with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> held in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is sufficient: as, to step over the threshold, to put a hand or hook in at a window to draw out goods, or a pistol to demand one's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, are all of them burglarious entries. The entry may be before the breaking, as well as after; for by statute 12 <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, c. 7, if a person enters into the dwelling-house of another, without breaking in, either by day or by night, with an intent to commit felony, or, being in such house, shall commit any felony; and shall in the night <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out of the same; this is declared to be burglary. 4. As to the intent; it is clear that such breaking and entry must be with a felonious intent, otherwise it is only a trespass. And it is the same, whether such intention be actually carried into execution, or only demonstrated by some attempt or overt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> is to judge. Burglary is a felony at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, but within the benefit of clergy. Burglary in any house belonging to the plate-glass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with intent to steal the stock or utensils, is by statute 13 Geo. III. c. 3, declared to be single felony, and punished with transportation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years.

BURGOMASTER

Pages 881-881

Burghermaster, Bourgermester, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Burgemeester, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and Germany. The power and jurisdiction of the burgomaster are not the same in all places, every town having its particular customs and regulations; at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> there are four chosen by the voices of all those people in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> who have either been burgomasters or echevins. They dispose of all under offices that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, keep the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, and enjoy a salary but of 500 guilders; all feasts, public entertainments, &c., being defrayed out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. The word is formed from the two Flemish words, bourger, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a>, or citizen; and mester, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. Some express it in Latin by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, others by senator.—Mr Brenau observes, that burghermaster in Holland, answers to what is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> in England, attorney at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPEIGNE">Compeigne</a>, capitoul at Thoulouse, consul in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, &c.

BURGOO

Pages 881-881
or Burgout, a sea-faring dish, made of whole oatmeal, or groats, boiled in water till they burst; then mixed with butter. It is a cheap and strengthening diet. Burgoo, otherwise called loboloby, is held by Cockburn very proper to correct that thickness of humours and costiveness to which the other diet of sailors much disposes them. Yet the burgoo victualling is the least liked of all their provisions, because of the scanty allowance of butter to it. The same author thinks it might be worth the consideration of those to whom the care of the seamen is committed, to contrive to render this food more agreeable to them.

BURGOS

Pages 881-881

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Old Castile, with an archbishop's see, erected in 1574. It is surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months in the year, and the other three excessively hot. It is seated on the declivity of a hill, on the top of which there is a strong castle, and the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town is watered by the river Alancon. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> avenue to the city is by a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over this river, which leads to a beautiful gate, adorned with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of several kings of Spain. The town is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous; but the houses are ill built, and the streets are narrow and dirty, except some few, especially that which leads to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. There are several squares adorned with fountains and statues. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the middle of the city is surrounded with fine houses, with piazzas to each. The cathedral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a masterpiece of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and one of the finest in all Spain. The church of the Augustines is remarkable for its beautiful and rich chapel of the holy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a>. There are several fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and nunneries; one of which last contains 150 nuns, who must all be of noble <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. They have likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, very richly endowed; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they speak the best Castilian, that is, the purest Spanish, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 7. N. Lat. 42° 20'.

BURGUNDIONES

Pages 881-881

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of the Vandili or Wandili. Claverius places them about the Warta, a river of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; though the conjectures on the seat of these people are doubtful; and no wonder, because the Roman expeditions terminated at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>. They afterwards removed to the Cisalbin Germany, and at length to Celtic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and gave name to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>.

BURGUNDY

Pages 881-881

a late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of France, which now forms the three departments, of Cote d'Or, Saone and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YONNE">Yonne</a>. It contains, besides the government of Burgundy, La Bresse, La Bugey, and the district of Gex; having Champagne on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Lyonnais on the south, Franche Compte on the east, and Nivernais and Bourbonnois on the west. Its length from north to south is about 45 leagues, and its breadth from east to west about 30. It is very fertile in corn, wine, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>; being watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, the Dehune, which falls into the Saone, the Brebine or Bourbine, the Armançon, the Ouche, and the Tille. There are some noted mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in it, with subterraneous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and plenty of ochre. For a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it had dukes of its own, subordinate to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France; but at last, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. upon the failure of the heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, seized upon it, and annexed it to his crown. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places are Dijon, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUXERRE">Auxerre</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUTUN">Autun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> l'Ancy, &c.

BURIAL

Pages 881-882

the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of a deceased person. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of burial are looked upon in all countries, and at all times, as a debt so sacred, that such as neglected to discharge it were thought accursed: hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called them justa, and the Greeks ἱεραὶ, ἱεραῖαι, &c., words implying the inviolable obligation which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has laid upon the living to take care of the obsequies of the dead. Nor are we to wonder that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and Romans were extremely solicitous about the interment of their deceased friends, since they were strongly persuaded that their souls could not be admitted into the Elysian fields till their bodies were committed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it happened that they never obtained the rites of burial, they were excluded from the happy mansions for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 100 years. For this reason it was considered as a duty duty incumbent upon all travellers who should meet with a dead body in their way, to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> dust <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mould upon it three times; and of these three handfuls one at least was cast upon the head. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> likewise considered it as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> misfortune if they were not laid in the sepulchres of their fathers; for which reason, such as died in foreign countries had usually their ashes brought home, and interred with those of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. But notwithstanding their great care in the burials of the dead, there were some persons whom they thought unworthy of that last office, and to whom therefore they refused it: such were, 1. Public or private enemies. 2. Such as betrayed or conspired against their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. 3. Tyrants, who were always looked upon as enemies to their country. 4. Villains guilty of sacrilege. 5. Such as died in debt, whose bodies belonged to their creditors. And, 6. Some particular offenders, who suffered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Of those who were allowed the rites of burial, some were distinguished by particular circumstances of disgrace attending their interment: thus persons killed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> were buried apart by themselves, being thought odious to the gods; those who wasted their patrimony forfeited the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of being buried in the sepulchres of their fathers; and those who were guilty of self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> were privately deposited in the ground, without the accustomed solemnities. Among the Jews, the privilege of burial was denied only to self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>, who were thrown out to rot upon the ground. In the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, though good men always desired the privilege of interment, yet they were not, like the heathens, so concerned for their bodies, as to think it any detriment to them, if either the barbarity of an enemy, or some other accident, deprived them of this privilege. The primitive Christian church denied the more solemn rites of burial only to unbaptized persons, self-murderers, and excommunicated persons who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> obstinate and impenitent, in a manifest contempt of the church's censures. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of burial among the Jews was never particularly determined. We find they had graves in the town and country, upon the highways, in gardens, and upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Among the Greeks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were made repositories for the dead in the primitive ages; yet the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in latter ages, with them, as well as with the Romans and other heathen nations, was to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead without their cities, and chiefly by the highways. Among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, burying in cities was not allowed for the first 300 years, nor in churches for many ages after, the dead bodies being first deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, and porches and porticoes of the church; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> burying-places were forbidden till the 12th century. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of burial, with all the ceremonies accompanying it, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">Funeral Rites</a>.

BURICK

Pages 882-882

a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It was taken by the French in 1672, who demolished the fortifications. It is agreeably seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, over against Wesel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 8. N. Lat. 51. 38.

BURIDAN

Pages 882-882

JOHN, a native of Bethune, in Artois, was one of the most celebrated philosophers of the 14th century. He taught in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; and wrote commentaries on logic, morality, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. Aventinus relates, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Ockam; and that, being expelled Paris by the power of the Realists, which was superior to that of the Nominalists, he went into Germany, where he founded the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. From him came the proverb of the ass of Buridan, so famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Buridan supposed a hungry ass fixed at an exactly equal distance between two bushels of oats: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an ass, as much pressed by thirst as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, between a bushel of oats and a pail of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, each of them acting equally on his senses. Having made this supposition, he desired to know what the ass would do? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he was answered that he would remain immovable, then he concluded he would die of hunger between two bushels of oats, or of both hunger and thirst, with corn and water within his reach. This appeared absurd, and brought the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> on his side; but if it was replied, that the ass would not be so stupid as to die of hunger or thirst in such a situation, Then (said he), the ass has free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, or is it possible that of two equal weights one should outweigh the other? These two consequences appeared equally absurd; and thus Buridan, by this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOPHISM">sophism</a>, perplexed the philosophers, and his ass became famous in the schools.
