No style nor stigma. ORDER I. MONANDRIA. 1034. ZANNICHELLIA, or Three-headed Pond-weed. One <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; viz. palustris. 1035. CERATOCARPUS. One species; viz. arenarius, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. 1426. ARTOCARPU, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>-fruit. Two species; viz. incisa, integrifolia.—It has a cylindric amentum or catkin, which thickens gradually, and is covered with flowers; the male and female in a different amentum. In the male, the calyx is two-valved, and the corolla is wanting. In the female, there is no calyx; nor corolla; the stylus is one, and the drupa is many-celled. Though this tree had been mentioned by many voyagers, particularly by Dampier, by Rumphius, and by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson, yet very little notice seems to have been taken of it till the return of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis from the South seas, and since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by others who have touched at Otaheite and some countries in the East Indies. Captain Dampier relates, that in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUAM">Guam</a>, one of the Ladrones <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, "there is a certain fruit called the bread-fruit, growing on a tree as big as our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> apple-trees, with dark leaves. The fruit is round, and grows on the boughs like apples, of the bigness of a good <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-loaf; when ripe, it turns <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, soft, and sweet; but the natives take it green, and bake it in an oven till the rind is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; this they scrape off, and eat the inside, which is soft and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, like the inside of new baked bread, having neither seed nor <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is kept above 24 hours it is harsh. As this fruit is in season eight months in the year, the natives feed upon no other sort of bread during that time. They told us that all the Ladrones islands had plenty of it. I never heard of it in any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>." Rumphius, after describing the tree, observes, that "the fruit is shaped like a heart, and increases to the size of a child's head. Its surface or rind is thick, green, and covered everywhere with warts of a quadrangular or hexagonal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, like cut diamonds, but without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. The more flat and smooth these warts are, the fewer seeds are contained in the fruit, and the greater is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pith, and that of a more glutinous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The internal part of the rind, or peel, consists of a fleshy substance, full of twisted fibres, which have the appearance of fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; these adhere to, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> form it. The fleshy part of this fruit becomes softer towards the middle, where there is a small cavity formed without any nuts or seeds, except in one species, which has but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and this sort is not good, unless it is baked or prepared some other way; but if the outward rind be taken off, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> dried and afterwards boiled with meat as we do cabbage, it has then the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of artichoke bottoms. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOYNA">Amboyna</a> dress it in the liquor of cocoa nuts; but they prefer it roasted on coals till the outward part or peel is burnt. They afterwards cut it into pieces, and eat it with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the cocoa-nut. Some people make fritters of it, or fry it in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and others, as the Sumatrans, dry the internal soft part, and keep it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> instead of bread with other food. It affords a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nourishment, and is very satisfying, therefore proper for hardworking people: and being of a gentle astringent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, is good for persons of a laxative <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body. It is more nourishing boiled in our manner with fat meat than roasted on coals. The milky juice which distils from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, boiled with the cocoa-nut oil, makes a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-lime. This tree is to be found on the eastern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and in the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is called soccus and soccum copos. It grows likewise about the town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, and in Ballega and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, and is known there by the name of soccum." In Anson's voyage we are informed, "that the rima, or bread-fruit tree, is common in all the Ladrones islands and some of the Philippines. It is somewhat larger than our apple tree, and bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> dark-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> with five indentures on each side. The fruit hangs on the boughs like apples; and is of the size of a penny loaf, with a thick tough rind, which when full ripe turns yellow. The natives gather it before it is quite ripe, and bake it till the crust is pretty black; when they rasp it, and there remains a pretty loaf, with a tender yellow crust, and the crumb of it is soft and sweet as a new baked roll; it is without any seeds or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. This fruit the inhabitants enjoy for about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months; during which they never eat any other kind of bread: but they are obliged to bake it every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for when it grows a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a>, it becomes harsh and husky, somewhat like the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a> bread made in the west of England. There is, however, a remedy for this; which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the loaf into slices when it is new, and drying it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, by which it is changed into the pleasantest rusk that can be eaten." Captain Cook, in his voyage, observes, that this fruit not only serves as a substitute for bread among the inhabitants of Otaheite and the neighbouring islands, but also, variously dressed, composes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of their food. It grows on a tree that is about the size of a middling oak; its leaves are frequently a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, of an oblong shape, deeply sinuated like those of the fig-tree, which they resemble in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and consistence, and in the exuding of a milky juice upon being broken. The fruit is about the size and shape of a new-born child's head; and the surface is reticulated, not much unlike a truffle; it is covered with a thin skin, and has a core about as big as the handle of a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. The eatable part lies between the skin and the core; it is as white as snow, and somewhat of the consistence of new bread; it must be roasted before it is eaten, being first divided into three or four parts; its taste is insipid, with a slight sweetness, somewhat resembling that of the crumb of wheaten bread mixed with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> artichoke. This fruit is also cooked in a kind of oven, which renders it soft, and something like a boiled potato; not quite so farinaceous as a good one, but more so than those of the middling sort. Of the bread-fruit they also make three dishes, by putting either <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or the milk of the cocoa nut to it, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> it to a paste with a stone pestle, and afterwards mixing it with ripe plantains, bananas, or the sour paste which they call mahie. The mahie, which is likewise made to serve as a succedaneum for ripe bread-fruit before the season comes on, is thus made: The fruit of the bread-tree is gathered thered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> before it is perfectly ripe; and being laid in heaps, is closely covered with leaves: in this state it undergoes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and becomes disagreeably sweet; the core is then taken out entire, which is done by gently pulling out the stalk, and the rest of the fruit is thrown into a hole which is dug for that purpose, generally in the houses, and neatly lined in the bottom and sides with grass: the whole is then covered with leaves and heavy stones laid upon them; in this state it undergoes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fermentation, and becomes sour, after which it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> suffer no change for many months. It is taken out of the hole as it is wanted for use; and being made into balls, it is wrapped up in leaves and baked; after it is dressed, it will keep five or six weeks. It is eaten both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hot; and the natives seldom make a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> without it, though to Europeans the taste is as disagreeable as that of a pickled olive generally is the first time it is eaten. The fruit itself is in season eight months in the year, and the mahie supplies the inhabitants during the other four. To procure this principal article of their food (the bread fruit), costs these happy people no trouble or labour except climbing up a tree: the tree which produces it does not indeed grow spontaneously; but if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> ten of them in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> time, which he may do in about an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he will as completely fulfil his duty to his own and future generations, as the native of our less temperate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> can do by ploughing in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of winter, and reaping in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, as often as these seasons return; even if, after he has procured bread for his present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, he should convert a surplus into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and lay it up for his children. We have said that there are two species of artocarpus, viz. the incisa, with gashed leaves; and the integrifolia, with entire leaves. There is also said to be another distinction, into that which bears fruit with stones or seeds, and that in which the fruit has none. The parts of fructification of that tree which bears the fruit without stones are defective. The ammentum, or catkin, which contains the male parts, never expands. The styli, or female parts of the fruit, are likewise deficient. From which it follows, that there can be no stones or seeds, and therefore that this tree can be propagated only by suckers or layers; although it is abundantly evident, that it must have originally proceeded from the seed-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> bread-fruit tree. Instances of this kind we sometimes find in European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; such as the barberry, and the Corinthian grape from Zant, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called currants, which can therefore be increased only by layers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>. Dr Solander was assured by the oldest inhabitants of Otaheite and the adjoining islands, that they well remembered there was formerly plenty of the seed-bearing bread-fruit; but they had been neglected upon account of the preference given to the bread-fruit without seeds, which they propagate by suckers. The British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> sent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Bligh in the Bounty in 1787 to Otaheite to procure and transport to our West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> colonies this valuable plant. The project was at that time unsuccessful, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> of the ship's crew, who seized the vessel, and carried her back to Otaheite. The object, however, was accomplished at a future <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and the bread-fruit is now reared in Jamaica and the other West India islands. Plants of this genus have also been brought to His Majesty's gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>. The taste of the fruit is said to be a sort of medium between the tate of common wheaten bread, and the taste of a boiled potato. Those who prefer potatoes to ordinary bread also prefer the bread-fruit to it. Cynomorium. One species; viz. coccineum. Jamaica. Nipa. One species; viz. fruticance. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Chara. Four species; viz. * flexilis, * hispida, * torrentosa, * vulgaris. Elaterium, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>-gourd. Two species; viz. carthaginiense, trifoliatum. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. Phyllachne. One species; viz. philinosa. Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>. Casuarina. Two species; viz. equisetifolias, nodiflora. E. Indies, New S. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. Ægoptricon. One species; viz. betulinum. Surinam, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAYENNE">Cayenne</a>. Order II. DIANDRIA. Anguria. Three species; viz. trilobata, pedata, trifoliata. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Lemma, or Duck-meat. Five species; viz. * gibba, * <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, * polyrhiza, * trisulca, arbiza. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Order III. TRIANDRIA. Typha, Cat-s-tail, Reed-mace. Two species; viz. * angustifolia, * latifolia. Sparganium, or Burr-reed. Four species; viz. * erectum, * natans, * ramosum, * simplex. Zea, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> Wheat. One species; viz. mays. America. Coix, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>'s-tears. One species; viz. lacryma. E. Indies. Trifticum. Stamens 5. (2) Cal. 5-leaved. Cor. 5-petaled. Styles 4. Caps. 3-celled. **S. leaves strap-shaped, upper leaves oblique; catkins monandra downy; one stamen.—Rose willow, or purple willow. Withering. Called by Linnaeus S. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PURPUREA">purpurea</a>. Baskets, eradles, and all sorts of twig-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> are made of its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, slender, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> shoots.** - **S. leaves oblong, spear-shaped; flowers with three triandra. stamens, sometimes two. Smooth willow.—The bark, in doses of one or two drams, cures agues.** - **S. leaves <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped, acute; flowers with five sta-pentandra mens. Sweet willow, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>-leaved willow. Called by Linnaeus S. hermaphroditica. The wood crackles greatly in the fire. The dried leaves afford a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> dye. Used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> to make the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sort of baskets.** - **S. leaves egg-spear-shaped, acute, smooth above, ser-vitellina;** <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> like gristle. **Yellow willow.**—The wood is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and very tough. The shoots are used by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>-makers. * S. leaves egg-spear-shaped; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>-stalks toothed with glands. **Crack willow.**—A quick grower, and bears cropping. Thrives in any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> moist. The bark in doses of one or two drams cures agues. * S. leaves strap-spear-shaped, acute. **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> willow.**—The twigs much sought after by basket-makers. * S. leaves spear-strap-shaped, very long, acute, silky underneath; branches rod-like. **Oxier.**—Much used for making hoops, and the larger baskets. Is planted to prevent the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> from being washed away by torrents. * S. leaves spear-shaped, tapering to a point, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, downy on both sides; the lowermost serratures glandular. **White willow.** Grows quick, and bears lopping. The bark collected in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> when full of sap, and dried by a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, is extremely valuable, as a substitute for Peruvian bark, in the cure of intermittent fevers. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Horses, cows, sheep, and goats, eat the leaves and young shoots. If a shady walk with willows is wanted, male sets only ought to be planted, otherwise they will speedily multiply so as to form a thicket instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. **ORDER III. TRIANDRIA.** 1100. **Empetrum**, or Berry-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> Heath. Two species; viz. * nigrum, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBUM">album</a>. * E. with stems trailing.—The berries boiled with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> afford a dark purple dye. Eaten in quantities they occasion headach. 1101. **Osyris**, or Poets-cassia. Two species; viz. alba, japonica. South Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. 1431. **Maba.** One species; viz. elliptica. Tongataboo, Namoka. 1331. **Restis.** <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> species; viz. paniculatus, verticillaris, dichotomus, vimineus, triflorus, simplex, elegia, cernuus, teretorum. C. of G. Hope. 1102. **Excoecaria**, or Aloe wood. One species; viz. agallocha. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOYNA">Amboyna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. 1280. **Caturus.** Two species; viz. spiciflorus, ramiflorus. East and West Indies. **ORDER IV. TETRANDRIA.** 1103. **Trophis.** One species; viz. americana. Jamaica. 1104. **Batis.** One species; viz. maritima. Jamaica. 1105. **Viscum**, or Mistletoe. Nine species; viz. * album, rubrum, purpureum, opuntioides, capense, verticillatum, pauciflorum, terrestrre, rotundiflorum. Europe, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, West Indies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. * V. leaves spear-shaped, blunt; stem forked; spikes axillary. **White mistletoe.**—A singular parasitical evergreen plant. The barren plant opposite to the fertile one. The root insinuates itself into the substance of the tree on which it grows. Blossom greenish white. Berries whitish. Birdlime may be made from the berries or the bark. Birds having swallowed the berries, void them unchanged upon trees, where they take root. No art has hitherto been able to make them take root in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Sheep eat it greedily; and in the southern English counties, where chiefly it grows, it is often torn from the trees to feed them. It is said to preserve them from the rot. If the berries, when fully ripe, be rubbed on the smooth bark of almost any tree, they will adhere closely, and produce plants the following winter. 1432. **Montinia.** One species; viz. acris. C. of G. Hope. 1106. **Hippophae**, or Sea-buckthorn. Two species; viz. * rhamnoides, canadensis. * H. leaves spear-shaped.—Cows refuse it. Horses, rhomgoats, and sheep eat it. The berries are very acid, with rather an austere vinous flavour. The fishermen of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bothnia prepare a rob from them, which imparts a grateful flavour to fresh fish. In sunny and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> situations it is planted for hedges. 1107. **Myrica**, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">Candle</a>-berry Myrtle, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">Gale</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> species; viz. * gale, cerifera, athiopica, querifolia, cordifolia, trifoliata. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, Cape, North America. * M. leaves spear-shaped, somewhat serrated; stem gale, shrub-like. **Sweet willow, Dutch myrtle, gale, goule.** Dyed in autumn, it dyes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> yellow. It is used to tan calfskins. The Welch ladies bunch it under their beds to keep off fleas and moths, and give it as a vermifuge in powder and infusion, applying it also externally to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. Its essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> rises in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The catkins boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> throw up a waxy scum fit to make candles. From the M. cerifera the myrtle candles are prepared. **ORDER V. PENTANDRIA.** 1108. **Pistacia**, or Pistacia-nut. Five species; viz. trifolia, narbonensis, vera, terebinthus, lentiscus. South Europe, Barbary, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The P. vera, with leaves unequal winged, leaflets nearly egg-shaped, bent back, produces a moderately large nut, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> greenish kernel, with a reddish skin. The tree grows spontaneously in Persia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and the Archipelago; and has been found able to produce fruit in England. Pistachio nuts have a pleasant, sweet,unctuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, resembling almonds, and are esteemed by some in certain weaknesses, and in emaciated habits. The P. lentiscus with leaves abruptly winged, and spear-shaped leaflets, in like manner bears our winters. The wood is brought to us in thick knotty pieces, with an ash-coloured bark and white within, of a rough somewhat pungent taste, and a grateful but faint smell. A decoction of it, under the pompous appellation of aurum potabile, potable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, is recommended by the Germans in catarrhs, nausea, and weakness of stomach. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHIO">Chio</a>, this tree affords mastic, which is a resinous substance brought from thence in small yellowish transparent grains or tears, of a pleasant smell, especially when heated. It is recommended in old coughs, dysenteries and all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of laxity. Zanthoxylum. Two species; viz. clava-herculis, trifoliatum. Astronium. One species; viz. graveolens. South America. Canarium. One species; viz. commune. India. Antidesma, or Chinese Laurel. One species; alexiteria. E. Indies, China, Japan. Iresine. One species; viz. celosia. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, Jamaica. Spinacia, or Spinage. Two species; viz. oleracea, fera. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. Acnida, or Virginian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a>. One species, viz. cannabina. Virginia. Cannabis, or Hemp. One species; viz. sativa. India. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Humulus, or Hop. One species; viz. * lupulus. Europe.—Cultivated in England to preserve malt liquors. The young shoots are eaten in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> instead of asparagus. Strong cloth is in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> made from the stalks, which are soaked in water all winter, and in the spring dressed like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. A decoction of the roots, or from 20 to 30 grains of the extract, is said to be sudorific. Zanonia. One species; viz. indica. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> of Malabar. Fevillea. Two species; viz. trilobata, cordifolia. W. Indies. Order VI. Hexandria. Tamus, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Bryony. Two species; viz. * communis, cretica. South Europe, Cape. Smilax, or Rough Bindweed. 14 species; viz. aspera, excelsa, zealiana, sarsaparilla, china, rotundifolia, laurifolia, tannoides, caduca, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">nox</a>, herbacea, tetragona, lanceolata, pseudochina. South Europe, East Indies, North America. Rajania. Five species; viz. hastata, cordata, quinquefolia, quinata, hexaphylla. Japan, North America, West Indies. Dioscorea, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Yam. 12 species; viz. pentaphylla, triphylla, trifida, aculeata, alata, bulbifera, sativa, villosa, oppositifolia, septemloba, quinquelobata, japonica. East and West Indies, North America. Order VII. Octandria. Populus, or Poplar-tree. Five species; viz. * alba, * nigra, * tremula, balsamifera, heterophylla. South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Italy, Archipelago, North America. * P. leaves nearly triangular, toothed, and regular; cottony underneath. White poplar.—It loves low situations, and flourishes best in clay. It grows quick and bears cropping, but is unfavourable to pasturage. The wood is soft, white, and stringy, and makes good wainscoting, being little subject to swell or shrink. Floors, laths, packing boxes, and turners <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, are made of it. Horses, sheep, and goats eat it. Cows are not fond of it. * P. leaves circular, toothed, and angular; smooth on tremula, both sides. Aspen, aspen tree, trembling poplar.—This tree grows in all soils, but worst in clay. It impoverishes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, destroys the grass; and the numerous shoots of the roots spread so near the surface of the earth, that they permit nothing else to grow; but rise in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, whether they are wanted or not. It is easily transplanted. The wood is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, white, smooth, woolly, soft, durable in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The bark is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of beavers. The bark of the young trees is made into torches. * P. leaves trowel-shaped, tapering to a point, serrated, nigra. smooth on both sides. Black poplar.—It loves a moist black soil, grows rapidly, and bears cropping. The bark being light like cork, supports the nets of fishermen. Cattle eat it. Rhodiola, or Rose-root. One species; viz. * rosea.—The root, particularly when dried, has the fragrance of a rose; but cultivated in a garden it loses most of its sweetness. Margaritaria. One species; viz. nobilis. Surinam. Order VIII. Enneandra. Mercurialis, or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. Three species; viz. * annua, * perennis, tomentosa, perennis. Europe. * M. stem undivided, leaves rough. Dogs mercury.—It is noxious to sheep, and deleterious to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. In drying, it turns blue. Steeped in water it affords a fine deep blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; which, however, is destructible both by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. Hydrocharis, or Frog-bit. One species; viz. * morsus ranae. Order IX. Decandra. Carica, or Papaw tree. Two species; viz. papaya, posoposa. E. and W. Indies. Kiggelaria. One species; viz. africana. C. of G. Hope. Schinus, or Indian Mastick tree. Two species; viz. mollis, areira. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>. Coriaria, or Myrtle-leaved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMACH">Sumach</a>. Two species; viz. myrtifolia, ruscifolia. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, S. France, Peru. Order X. Dodeandra. Euclea. One species; viz. racemosa. C. of G. Hope. Datisca, or Base Hemp. Two species; viz. cannabina, hirta. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, N. America. Menispermum, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>-seed. Species; viz. canadense, virginicum, japonicum, carolinum. carolinum, cocalus, crispum, acutum, orbiculatum, hirsutum, myostoides, trilobum. N. America, Japan. ORDER XI. POLYANDRIA. 1133. CLIFFORTIA. 18 species; viz. odorata, ilicifolia, ruscifolia, ferruginea, graminosa, polygoniflora, filiflora, crenata, pulchella, trifoliata, sarmentosa, strobilifera, obcordata, ternata, juniperina, falcata, teretifolia, ericefolia. C. of G. Hope. 1432. HEDYCARIA. One species; viz. dentata. N. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. ORDER XII. MONADELPHIA. 1134. JUNIPERUS, or Juniper-tree. 11 species; viz. * communis, thurifera, barbadensis, bermudiana, chinensis, sabina, virginiana, oxycedrus, phoenicea, lycina. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERMUDAS">Bermudas</a>, America. * J. leaves three together, expanding, sharp pointed, longer than the berry.—It grows in all soils and situations, and to a corresponding variety of sizes. It is easily transplanted, and bears cropping. Grass will not grow beneath it, but the *ovena pratensis* destroys it. The wood is hard and durable. The bark may be made into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>. The berries are two years in ripening.—When bruised they afford a pleasant diuretic liquor, but it is not easy to prevent its growing sour. It is esteemed a good antiscorbutic. Ardent spirits, impregnated with the essential oil of those berries, is termed gin, though it is said that some distillers know how to produce the same effect, by means of the spirit of turpentine. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">Gum</a> sandarach, more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called pounce, is the product of this tree. Horses, sheep, and goats eat it. From the *J. lycina*, a gum resin called *olibanum* is produced. From the *J. sabina*, is extracted an essential oil, which is accounted a most powerful emmenagogue. It is a warm, irritating, aperient medicine. 1135. TAXUS, or Yew-tree. Four species; viz. *baccata, nucifera, macrophylla, verticillata*. Eur. Cape, Jap. N. America. T. leaves solitary, strap-shaped, prickle-pointed, near baccate together; receptacle of the male flowers somewhat globose.—It grows best on a moist loamy soil, and languishes in bogs and dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It bears transplanting, even when old; and, as an evergreen hedge, is a valuable screen to delicate plants. The wood is used for bows, axletrees, spoons, cups, cogs for mill-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> gates for fish ponds, which hardly ever decay. The berries are sweet, viscid, and harmless. The fresh leaves are fatal to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> species. 1136. EPHEDRA, or Shrubby <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>-tail. Two species; viz. distachya, monostachya. Siberia, France, Spain. 1138. CISSAMPELOS. Five species; viz. pareira, caapeba, smilacina, fruticosa, capensis. Cape, America. 1836. NAPEA. Two species; viz. levis, scabra. Virginia. 1137. ADELIA. Three species; viz. bernardia, ricinella, acidota. Jamaica. ORDER XIII. SYNGENESIA. 1139. RUSCUS, or Knee-bolly, or Butchers-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>. Five species; viz. *aculeatus, hypophyllam, hypoglossum, androgynus, racemosus*. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, Fr. Italy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>. ORDER XIV. GYNANDRIA. 1140. CLUTIA. Nine species; viz. alaternoides, polygonoides, pulchella, hirta, tomentosa, retusa, cluteria, stipularis, acuminata. In the class Diocia are 55 Genera, including 219 Species, of which 38 are found in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

CLASSIS XXIII

POLYGAMIA (o). ORDO I. MONOECIA. 1141. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">MUSA</a>. (3) Cal. nullus. Cor. 2-petala. Stam. 6, 1 fert. Pist. 1. Baccia infera. (3) Cal. nullus. Cor. 2-petala. Stam. 6, 5 perfect. Pist. 1. Baccia nulla. M. (3) No cal. Cor. 2-petaled. Stam. 6, 1 fertile. Pist. 1. Berry inferior. (3) No cal. Cor. 2-petaled. Stam. 6, 5 perfect. Pist. 1. No berry. (o) The character of this class consists of the following circumstances: that every plant belonging to it produces, 1st, Hermaphrodite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, that is, flowers having both stamens and pistils in the same flower; and, 2dly, In addition to the hermaphrodite flowers, the same plant produces also other flowers, not hermaphrodite, but either <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, that is, which have stamens, one or more, without pistils, or the reverse. The hermaphrodite maphrodite flowers of this class are usually imperfect in one of their parts (either stamens or pistils), which renders an additional male or female flower necessary. Sometimes there are two hermaphrodite flowers on the same plant of different powers; and this circumstance constitutes the polygamy, or is understood to bring the plant under the present class. As in the two former classes, the male and female flowers are here distinguished by prefixing to them the figures (1) and (2). The hermaphrodite flowers are here marked (3). 1332. HERMAS. (1) Cal. 3-parted. No cor. Stamens 3. (1) and (2) both within the same common receptacle, with distinct partial fructifications. ORDER ORDER I. MONOECIA. 1141. Musa, or Plantain-tree. Three <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; viz. paradissaica, sapientum, troglobydarum. E. and W. Indies. 1144. Veratrum, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Hellebore. Three species; viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBUM">album</a>, nigrum, luteum. Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, N. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.—The V. album grows spontaneously on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and Germany. The root is nauseous and acrid. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> wounded, when fresh, it emits an acid juice, which is said to prove dangerous when mixed with the blood by an wound. The powder of the dry root applied to an issue, occasions violent purging. Sniffed up the nose, it is a strong, but not always a safe sternutatory. It is also a violent emetic. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used it in desperate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> practice rejects it, though it is said to have been given with success to the amount of a scruple in cases of mania. 1333. Spinifex. One species; viz. quartzosus. E. Indies. 1145. Andropogon, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">Beard</a>-grass. 25 species; viz. caricosum, contortum, crinitum, divaricatum, grallus, nutans, ciliatum, serratum, cotuliferum, cymbarium, squarrosum, prostratum, alopecuroides, distachyum, schenanthus, virginicum, bicornue, hirtum, insulare, barbatum, nardus, muticum, ischeum, fasciculatum, polydactylon. S. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, E. and W. Indies, America. The A. nardus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> nard or spikenard, as it comes from the East Indies, is a matted congeries of fibres issuing from one head, and probably forming the root of the plant. Spikenard has a warm, pungent, bitterish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and a strong not very agreeable smell. It is stomachic and carminative; and said to be alexipharmac, diuretic, and emmenagogue; but it is at present little employed. 1146. Holcus, or Indian Millet. 14 species; viz. *avenaceus, *lanatus, *mollis, spicatus, bicolor, sorghum, halpeensis, saccharatus, laxus, striatus, serratos, odoratus, latifolius, pertusus. N. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, N. America. * H. husks two-flowered, woolly; hermaphrodite floret awnless; male floret with a bent awn, inclosed in the calyx.—This grass flourishes well on any moist <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and grows very generally, except on the most dry and barren ones. It should be sown chiefly with a view to pasturage by sheep. It makes a soft spongy hay unfit for horses. 1147. Apluda. Four species; viz. mutica, aristata, zeugites, digitata. E. and W. Indies, N. America. 1148. Ischænum. Two species; viz. muticum, aristatum. India, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, Carolina. 1149. Cenchrus, or Hedgehog-grass. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> species; viz. racemosus, lappaceus, muricatus, capitatus, echinatus, tribuloides, ciliaris, granularis, frutescens. S. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, W. Indies. 1150. Äegilops, or Hard-grass. Four species; viz. ovata, caudata, trunicalis, squarrosa. S. Europe, Carolina. 1334. Manisuris. One species; viz. myurus. E. and W. Indies, N. America. 1151. Valantia, or Crosswort. Eight species; viz. *aparine, *cruciate, muralis, hispida, cucullaria, articulata, glabra, hypocarpa. Austria, S. Europe, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>, Jamaica. 1152. Parietaria, or Pellitory. Eight species; viz. *officinalis, indica, judaica, lucitanica, urticafolia, cretica, zeylanica, microphylla. S. Europe, Canaries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>. 1153. Atriplex, or Orache, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Purslane-tree. 12 species; viz. *hastata, *lacinata, *littoralis, *patula, *pedunculata, *portulacoides, halymus, glauca, rosea, sibirica, tatarica, hortensis. Europe, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, America. 1283. Terminalia, or Benzoin. Two species; viz. catappa, benzoin. E. Indies.—From the last of these species a resin of the same name is supposed to be extracted, though others represent it as the product of another plant called styrax benzoe. Benzoin is used in perfumes, and as a cosmetic. 160. Brabeium, or African Almond. One species; viz. stellulifolium. 1154. Clusia, or Balsam-tree. Four species; viz. rosea, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, flava, venosa. America, Jamaica. 1142. Ophioxylum. One species; viz. serpentinum. E. Indies. 1155. Acer, Maple-tree. 17 species; viz. *campestre, *pseudoplanatus, semipervirens, tataricum, rubrum, saccharinum, dissectum, japonicum, palmatum, septemlobum, pictum, platanoides, pennsylvanicum, monspessulanum, creticum, trifidum, negundo. Europe, N. America, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. *A. leaves 5-lobed, blunt, unequally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>; flowers pseudo-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> pendent bunches. Sycamore tree, sy-planatus. Camo maple.—It flourishes best in open places and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> ground, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive in a richer soil. It grows quick, is easily transplanted, bears cropping, and the grass flourishes under its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. It is said to grow well near the sea, and that a plantation of these trees, at 50 feet asunder, with three sea sallow thorns between every two of them, will make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> sufficient to defend the herbage of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the sea spray. Gent. Mag. 1757, p. 252. The wood is soft and very white, and is used by the turners. By <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORING">boring</a> a hole into the body of the tree, when the sap rises in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, a sweetish watery liquor is obtained, which is used in making wine, and, if impassivated, affords a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. From the A. saccharinum large quantities of sugar are annually thus made in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America. See United States, and Sugar. 1143. Celtis, or Lote, Nettle-tree. Three species; viz. australis, occidentalis, orientalis. S. Europe, Virginia, W. Indies. 1157. Gowania, or Chew-stick. One species; viz. domingensis. West Indies. 1132. Hermas. Five species; viz. depauperata, gigantea, capitata, quinquedentata, ciliata. C. of G. Hope. 1158. Mimosa, or Sensitive Plant. 53 species; viz. simplicifolia, inga, sagifolia, nodosa, natans, bigemina, unguis-cati, tergemina, latifolia, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PURPUREA">purpurea</a>, reticulata, viva, circinalis, cinerea, cauta, sensitiva, pudica, entada, scandens, plena, virgata, punctata, pernambucana, arborea, lebbeck, odoratissima, speciosa, vaga, latisliliqua, polystachya, muricata, peregrina, glauca, cinerea, cornigera, catechu, horrida, cherna, latronum, tortuosa, sarnesiana, nilotica, pigra, asperata, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENEGAL">senegal</a>, cesia, pinnata, intisia, semispinosa, quadrivalvis, tenuifolia, ceratonia, tamarindifolia. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, E. and W. Indies, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. —The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of this genus possess the singular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of shrinking or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> in their leaves, when touched, which has obtained for them the English appellation of sensitive plants. From the species M. catechu a vegetable extract is obtained, which has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> improperly received the appellation of terra japonica or Japan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. This extract is outwardly of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, internally of a dark <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, with a slight <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. It is capable of being reduced to the state of a powder; and is a mild but powerful astringent. It is particularly useful in alvine fluxes; and where these require astringents, no one is so beneficial. It is likewise employed in uterine profusion, and in laxity and debility of the viscera in general. It is often suffered to dissolve leisurely in the mouth, as a topical astringent, for laxities and exulcerations of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, for aphthous ulcers in the mouth, and similar affections: and it is in some other cases applied externally under the form of solution, and as an ointment. Catechu dissolves in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with the exception of its impurities, which amount to an eighth part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Rectified spirit dissolves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-eighths of the pure <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> into a red liquor, leaving, undissolved, an insipid mucilaginous substance. The best form of administering it is that of simple infusion in warm water, with the addition of some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> or cassia. From the M. nilotica <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic exudes, the uses of which are well known to be extremely numerous. The inspissated juice of the unripe fruit of this tree is termed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a>, and is used as a mild astringent medicine. ORDER II. DIOECIA. 1159. Gleditsia, or Three-horned Acacia. Two species; viz. triacanthos, inermis. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, N. America. 1160. Fraxinus, or Ash-tree. Three species; viz. * excelsior, ornus, americana. S. Europe, N. America. excelsior. * F. leaflets serrated; flowers without petals.—It flourishes best in groves, but grows in a rich soil, though in the open field. It bears transplanting and lopping. Horses, cows, sheep, and goats, eat it; but it is said to spoil the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of cows. It will give a good, though not a beautiful green, to cloths that have been dyed blue. The wood is nearly as good when young as when old. It is hard and tough, and much used to make the tools employed in husbandry. The bark is used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> calf-skin. An infusion of the leaves, from half an ounce to an ounce, is a very good purge; and a decoction of two drams of the bark, or of six drams of the leaves, has been used to cure agues. 1161. Diospyros, or Indian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">Date</a>-plum. Five species; viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTUS">lotus</a>, virginiana, kaki, hirsute, ebenum. Italy, Barbary, Ceylon, N. America, Japan. 1163. Nyssa, or Tupelo-tree. One species; viz. aquatica. N. America. 1164. Anthofermum, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">Amber</a>-tree. Three species; viz. athiopicum, ciliare, herbaceum. C. of G. Hope. 1336. Stilbe. Three species; viz. pinasta, ericoides, cernua. C. of G. Hope. 1165. Arctopus. One species; viz. echinatus. C. of G. Hope. 1162. Pisonia, or Fingrida. Two species; viz. aculeata, inermis. W. Indies. 1166. Panax, or Ginseng. Five species; viz. quinquefolium, trifolium, spinosa, arborea, fruticosum. China, North America, West Indies.—The root of the P. quinquefolium is the ginseng of the Chinese, of which they have an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, regarding it as an universal restorative in all decays from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, intemperance, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. It is also found in North America, and frequently exported from thence to China. It has a very sweet taste, accompanied with a slight bitterness and warmth. 1335. Chrysitrix. One species; viz. capensis. C. of G. Hope. ORDER III. TRIOECIA. 1168. Ceratonia, or Crab-tree, St John's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>. One species; viz. siliqua. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>. 1168. Ficus, or Fig-tree. 15 species; viz. carica, sycamorus, religiosa, benjamina, benghalensis, indica, racemosa, pertusa, pumila, toxicaria, maculata, trigona, hispida, heterophylla, microcarpa. S. Europe, India, China, America.—The dried fruit of the F. carica, or ordinary fig-tree, is sometimes used in medicine as a soft emollient sweet substance. It is much esteemed by some as a suppurative; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is applied as warm as it can well be endured. In the class Polygamia are 34 Genera, including 222 Species, of which 15 are found in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

CLASSIS XXIV

Pages 303-308

CRYPTOGAMIA. ORDO I. FERNS. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. Fructificationes spicatae. * E Spike scattered. Fructifications target-shaped, valved at the base. C. (1) Catkin tiled. Pollen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dust covering the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. (2) Sheath <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-shaped. Drupe with a woody kernel. Z. (1) A cone with scales covered beneath with pollen. (2) A cone with scales in each border. Drupe solitary. O. A 2-rowed spike. Fructifications 5-valved. O. A jointed spike. Fructifications cut round. O. Spike branchy. Fructifications 2-valved. Sect. II. Fructificationes frondosae, in the under sur- <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. A. A spot occupying the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISC">disc</a>. P. Distinct spots on the disc. (o) This class contains a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vegetables whose stamens and pistils are too minute to admit of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> which prevails through the preceding classes. The structure too of these vegetables differs con- siderably from that of other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The Filices or Ferns constitute the first order. Their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are generally disposed in spots or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on the under surface of the leaves, but sometimes in spikes. In the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> flowers the anthers are found sitting or sup- ported on a very short filament, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped or globular, scattered on the under surface of the leaves. The male flowers unite so as to form a spike or bunch, or form lines or dots underneath the leaves, either on the surface at the edge, or at the point. In some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> they entirely cover the under surface. None of the flowers have any corolla, or even a calyx, excepting perhaps a scale formed from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, opening, containing globules. The seeds are very minute and globular. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order, called Musci or Mosses, have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> parts of fructification inclosed in a veil, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a>- heres to the top of the ripe capsules, and covers it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">Capsule</a> opening transversely. Stem leafy. Leaves mem- branaceous, reticulated; after being dead, reviving when soaked in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. In general the stamens and pistils are on separate flowers on the same or distinct plants. The third order, or Algae, includes a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of plants which scarcely admit of a distinction of root, stem, and leaf; much less can the parts of their flowers be described. Their substance is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-like or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-like, mem- branaceous or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>, jelly-like or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>-like, or resembling calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The female fructifications are either found in saucers or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>, as in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LICHENS">lichens</a>; in hollow bladder, as in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUCUS">fucus</a>; or dispersed through the sub- stance of the plant, as in ulva. The aquatic genera, which grow on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, are called, in ordinary lan- guage, sea-weeds, or sea-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and, by incineration, produce soda or mineral alkali. The lichens are of much importance in the economy of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They grow on the barest rocks, and their remains form a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on which better vegetables afterwards flourish. Some of them afford valuable colours. The order of Fungi, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">Mushrooms</a>, consists of plants mostly of a cork-like texture, and short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, bear- ing their seeds either in gills or tubes, or attached to fibres or to a spongy substance. As little is known of their fructification, the generic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are taken from their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form. 1176. *Hemionitis.* Lineae disci decussantes. 1178. *Asplenium.* Lineae disci subparalleliae, variæ. 1175. *Blechnum.* Lineae disci costæ utrinque adjacentes. 1177. *Lonchitis.* Lineae marginis ad sinus. 1174. *Pteris.* Lineae marginis ad peripheriam. 1180. *Adiantum.* Maculae apicem margini reflexo obtecutum. 1181. *Trichomanes.* Fr. solitariae, margini ipsi insertæ. **Sect. Male fern, male polypody.—The Siberians boil it in their ale, and are fond of the flavour it imparts. The powder of the root is a remedy for expelling the tape-worm. A liquid lubricating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> is given to the patient; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> costive, a common glyster. Accordingly, the Scandinavians line the inside of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> with it to defend them against fire. 1188. BUxbaUMIA. Amer. Jam. 1199. BLASIA. One species; British. 1200. RICCA, Marsh Liverwort. Five species; British. Jamaica. 1202. LICHEN, or Liverwort. 218 species; all British. Also Cape, India, America. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Dundonald obtained a patent, dated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 31, 1802, for the discovery of a substitute for the foreign <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, to be obtained from the plants of this genus. The specification of his lordship's patent is in these terms: "My <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> consists in procuring a substitute or substitutes for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENEGAL">senegal</a>, or other gums, from the class of plants called in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> lichens; from the plants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, previous to being steeped in water, or after being steeped; likewise from the bark or rind of the willow or lime tree. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for obtaining the gum may be varied according to circumstances, and is done by washing the materials in water, digestion, and boilings, and with or without the aid of fixed or volatile alkaline salts or their solutions. "It does not appear, from such trials as I have hitherto made, that there is any very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the produce of gum from the lichen collected from different trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>: all of them answer equally well for yielding a gum fit for calico-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. The lichen is most abundant on the trees which grow in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> stiff clay soil, and particularly if situated at some considerable height above sea level. It should be pulled in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, otherwise it is apt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> in the pulling; besides, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, requiring to be dried before it can with safety be laid up in the storehouse, where, if put in dry, it may be kept for years. Should a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it not be found in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, it may be had in almost unlimited abundance in Sweden, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and in the northern parts of America, where it grows to the length of from a foot to 18 inches, depressing the branches of the trees by its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. There is, however, every reason to believe that a sufficient quantity is to be had in this country. According to information received from botanists, it takes three or four years in coming to maturity or its full size; so that a crop from the same tree may be had every fourth year. The lichen does not consist entirely of a gummy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; there is the outer skin or cuticle, below that a green resinous matter. The remainder of the plant consists of partly gum, partly somewhat analogous to animal substances, and a small proportion of fibrous matter, which cannot be dissolved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of alkaline salts. "The first process in preparing gum from the lichen, is to free it of the outer skin of the plant and the resinous matter. This is done by scalding the lichen two or three times with boiling water, allowing it to remain so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the water as by absorbing it to swell; in doing this the skin cracks, and comes off along with, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the resinous matter; or it may be freed from them by gently boiling the lichen for about 15 or 20 minutes, then washing it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water." water, laying it afterwards on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or brick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, where it should lie for 10 or 12 hours, perhaps more. The reason for this is, that the exposure for that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, greatly facilitates the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of the gum. "The scalded lichen is then to be put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> boiler, with a due proportion of water, say three Scots pints, or two wine gallons, to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of lichen, and boiled during 10 or 12 hours, adding about a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an ounce of soda or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> ashes for every pound of lichen; or instead of these salts, about two ounces of volatile alkali. The boiling should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> until the liquor acquires a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of gummy consistence. It is then to be taken out of the boiler, allowed to drain or drip through a wire or haircloth searce. The residuum to be put into a haircloth bag or bags, and to be squeezed in a press similar to that which is used by the melters or rinders of tallow. "The first boiling does not extract the whole of the gum. The lichen should be boiled a second, or even a third time, repeating the process as above described, diminishing at each process the quantity of water and the quantity of alkali, which a little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon point out: when three boilings are employed, the gummy extract of the last boiling should be kept for the first boiling of a fresh batch of lichen; the extract proceeding from the first and second boilings should be mixed together, and evaporated to the consistence necessary for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> or press printing. The evaporating vessels should be of tin or thin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, placed over a range of stoves, and moderately heated by fire, or the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of water. It has been neglected to state, that before evaporating the gummy extract to the consistence necessary, it should be kept 10 or 12 hours, so as to allow the sediment or dregs to subside. The clean liquor may either be drawn off by a syphon, or the dregs may be drawn off by a cock at the bottom of the wooden vessel; the bottom of which should be made sloping, higher at the back than the fore part, in order that the dregs may run more completely off. The proportion of gummy matter remaining in the dregs may be got off by mixing them with a due proportion of boiling water, allowing the liquor to clear, and proceeding as above directed, employing this weak solution for boiling the next batch of lichen. When volatile alkali is used, the boiler should be of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, as volatile alkali acts on copper. Hemp, flax, and the bark of the willow and lime trees, or sea weed, are to be heated in a similar manner, to extract the gum or mucilage contained in them. Likewise it is intended that this patent shall include every tree, plant, or vegetable of whatever kind, from whence a mucilage or gum is to be obtained by the action of volatile or fixed alkaline salts, or their solutions, when used in the processes of maceration, digestion, or boiling these vegetable matters; being a method of obtaining a mucilage or gum never before practised and adopted by any other person." The above invention was for some time practised to a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> by the calico-printers in the west of Scotland, where it was found to answer for almost all colours. We have heard, however, that the use of it has been discontinued; whether from the price of gum senegal, for which it was employed as a substitute, having fallen, or that it has otherwise failed of its effect, we have not been informed. * L. tubercles <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, crust clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>.—Grows only calcareous on limestone rocks. When dried, powdered, and steeped in urine, it is used to dye scarlet by the Welsh and the inhabitants of the Orkneys. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is said to be very fine. * L. saucers white, mealy, with yellowish white, thick, parellus, blunt borders; crust <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> white.—Grows on rocks, walls, trunks of trees, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITMUS">Litmus</a> is prepared from this species. For this purpose it is collected from the rocks in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in casks. * L. saucers yellow, with a white border; crust whitish, tartareus.—Grows on rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> it is gathered for the dyers. It gives a purple colour. * L. saucers dull purple; leaves hoary, smooth, blunt, omphalomy-cleft, sprinkled with rising dots. Cork, corker, lodges, or arcell.—It dyes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, or a dull but durable crimson or purple, paler but more lasting than that of orchal. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> it is prepared by steeping in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> urine, adding a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> to it, and making it up into balls with lime. Wool dyed with it, and then dipped in the blue vat, becomes of a beautiful purple. With rotten oak it makes a dark brown. It has been used as a styptic. * L. tubercles brown; plant hoary, hollow, much rangiferi-branched; terminating branches turned downwards.—nus. The Laplanders could not exist without this plant, which feeds, and even fattens, their rein-deer. * L. plant lemon-coloured, upright, much branched; vulpinus, branches nearly of a length, angular; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> unequal.—In Norway they mix this plant with powdered glass, and strew it upon dead carcases to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> wolves. * L. saucers brown, white on the outside, on pedicles; prunastrus. Foliage nearly white, quite white and cottony underneath; pitted rather than upright.—It imbibes and retains odours in a remarkable degree, and is therefore the basis of many perfumed powders. * L. saucers <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> brown, mostly on the edges of the fo-pulmonaria-riage; leaves green, jagged, blunt, smooth; pitted, rius, downy underneath. Lungwort, hazel-rag, or hazel-crottes.—It is recommended for consumptive cases. Woollen cloth, boiled in it, is said to become of a durable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> it is used to dye stockings of a durable brown. * L. saucers red brown; foliage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green, wrinkled, cooperatus, waved at the edge, creeping.—In Ireland and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, it is used to dye wool of an orange colour. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERGE">Serge</a>, dyed with it, becomes of a lemon colour; but, if previously infused and boiled in urine, of a russet brown. * L. saucers black, flattish; foliage gray brown, consist-pustulata, ing of a single leaf, circular, slightly lobed, sprinkled with a black brain-like powder; pitted underneath.—A beautiful red colour may be prepared from it (Linnaeus). It may be converted into an exceedingly black paint. 1208. Byssus. 12 species; British. 1204. Tremella, or Star-jelly. 19 species; British. 1206. Ulva, or Laver. 14 species; British. 1205. HISTORY OF BOTANY

Pages 309-344

HAVING thus stated the botanical arrangement contrived by Linnæus, which proceeds upon the supposition of the existence of a sexual system in the vegetable world; we proceed to take notice of some other important circumstances connected with this branch of science, more particularly its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> orders, as opposed to the above <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> classification of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Writers upon <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. The origin of this science, like that of most others, cannot be found out from the most ancient histories; but it is very probable, that some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of botanical knowledge has existed in every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the world. The first botanical writings of which we have any account are those of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who we are informed by Scripture wrote a treatise upon this subject; which, however, is absolutely lost, not being quoted by any ancient author, nor the least fragment of it remaining. Among the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and other ancient philosophers, wrote treatises on plants; but their works are also lost; and from the quotations that yet remain in the works of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, Dioscorides, and Pliny, we learn, that those first botanical writings could convey but very little information. The historical era of botany, therefore, commences with Theophrastus the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. He was born at Eresium, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>; and flourished in the third century before the Christian era, being about 100 years <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is entitled The History of Plants, and treats of their origin, origin, propagation, anatomy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>; of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and of vegetation. It consisted originally of ten books; but of which only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> are now extant. In these, vegetables are distributed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> classes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> primary divisions; which have for their object, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of plant; their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of growth; their size, as trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, as pot herbs, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCULENT">esculent</a> grains; and their lactescence, or the liquor, of whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, that flows from plants when cut. In his work, above 500 different plants are described. The next botanist of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> was Dioscorides, a Grecian by birth, but under the Roman empire, being near 300 years posterior to Theophrastus. He describes about 600 plants; and these he has arranged, from their uses in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy, into four classes, which are thus designed: aromatics; alimentary vegetables, or such as serve for food; medicinal, and vinous plants. Almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Dioscorides flourished Antonius <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a>, Cato, Varro, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, and Columella; the first, author of a treatise still extant on the plant betony; the four others celebrated for their useful tracts on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and rural economy. Pliny the Elder, in his voluminous work entitled The History of the World, hath a botanical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is contained in 15 books. In these, besides the plants of Theophrastus and Dioscorides, he has given descriptions of several new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, extracted probably from works which would otherwise have been totally lost. Pliny uses scarce any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of arrangement, except the ancient, but very incorrect, distinction into trees, shrubs, and herbs. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, however, extends not only to botanical distinctions, but to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, agriculture, and whatever is connected either more nearly or remotely with the science of plants. He gives descriptions of above 1000 different species; but from the want of a proper systematic arrangement, it is often difficult, and perhaps impossible, to determine what plants he or other ancient botanists do really describe. This want of precision in properly arranging their plants was the reason why the botany of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was always very limited, and after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Pliny declined so rapidly. On the destruction of the Western empire by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> and other barbarous nations, it is not to be thought that botany could survive any more than the other sciences. It was not till near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the eighth century, that the ancient botany began again to appear in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. Serapion, well known in medicine, stands first in the Arabian catalogue of botanists; to him succeeded Razis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, Averrhoes Actuarius, &c. An author known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> Apuleius, or Apoliensis, of whose Herbarium very old manuscript copies are preserved in some curious <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, is supposed to have lived near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The works of most of these botanists, however, were only translations and compilations from the Greek writers; so that, for want of a proper systematic arrangement, the science sunk a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time into total oblivion. For near 400 years after Abengueft, an Arabian physician who flourished in the end of the 12th century, scarce any attempts were made in the botanical way. Some obscure writers indeed appeared in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; as Arnoldus de Ville Nova; Platearius; Matheus Sylvaticus; and Bartholomew Glanvil, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Bartholomeus Anglus, a Franciscan monk, descended of the family of the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, who lived in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward III. and wrote a book of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a>, entitled De proprietatibus rerum, which was translated into English by John de Trevisa in 1398: but though all these wrote of plants, they were so totally destitute of method, that their works remain one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>, from whence it is impossible to extract any thing intelligible. On the revival of letters in the beginning of the 16th century, the botany of the ancients was restored a second time. The Greek writings were translated into Latin the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Europe. Gaza, a Greek refugee at Rome, made elegant translations of Aristotle and Theophrastus, who afterwards were commented upon by Scaliger and Stapel. Dioscorides was also translated and commented on. His best commentators are Hermolaus Barbarus, Fuchscius, Ruellius Cordus, Gesner, and Matthiolus.
